Although this review comes with a "Thumbs Up" be aware that this isn't a wholehearted recommendation. This is more for people that played through Dark Souls 2 and are wondering if it is worth the money. Obviously if you are a newcomer then this is the best place to start considering it comes with all the DLC and a few minor improvements. Unless you are a newcomer to the franchise itself in which case you should definitely start with the first Dark Souls.
Scholar of the First Sin was announced immediately after the final expansion was released and I like many others was pretty irritated about. I purchased it recently on PC due to the sale although I also have the PS4 version as well. Having ignored it for nearly six months I feel I can look at this a little more objectively.
Whether this update is worth purchasing really depends on how much you enjoyed the vanilla version. Enemy placements have been tweaked, NPC summon signs and invasions are much more prominent and a few creative elements have been added in certain places (some of which are admittedly pretty interesting). There is also a ring in the game that allows you to control Soul Memory to a certain degree, although this is a band aid solution and doesn't really fix the core problem. Lighting seems to be improved and makes torches less optional in a couple of places but if you are looking for E3 levels of fidelity then you should probably keep moving. Lastly, a character very important to the lore makes multiple appearances. Speaking of lore, item descriptions have also been given the once over.
All in all, the game feels very familiar but also quite different. All the above mentioned tweaks and alterations to progression paths (you'll be using more Fragrant Branches of Yore than usual) make this update feel akin to a Director's Cut or Extended Edition bluray with all the added extras from the previous iterations. If you loved the regular game and don't mind starting from scratch (saves don't carry over) then it could be worth it. However the vanilla game has been updated via patch to include most of the features that aren't related to performance so it really does depend on how much you want the extra player count, slightly better lighting and enemy placement re-shuffle. If you weren't much of a fan to begin with then nothing here is going to change that.
So, should you buy it?
Newcomers... Definitely.
Longtime Players... Yes, if you want to spice things up a little. But Not essential.
Casual Players... Don't bother, you probably won't appreciate or care about any of the changes.

Gone Home is less of a game and more of an experience set exclusively in a big house using first person perspective. Not like Myst or Shadowgate, but like a first person shooter where you can walk around like Dear Esther or Half Life 2 without the guns. If you like to explore, read notes, listen to audio journals and be immersed in a fiction you might enjoy it. The basic premise is that you're in an empty house and you need to discover why. There's no real emphasis on why, you just explore. The house has a history to it and so do the characters you'll hear about. You'll never see the characters outside of a photo here and there. Heck you never even see yourself outside of a passport. There might be 3+ bathrooms in this house but there are no mirrors.
The story is set in 1995 and while I'm not into story, the developers did a good job of presenting it as immerse as they could. You'll hear 90s punk music, find Super Nintendo cartridges and see plenty VHS movie names. It hinges heavily on 90s nostalgia and lesbians. Most of what you will find goes through a history of a teenager's love interest with another young woman. There are side stories such as the house's history and the previous owner's death.
The house is pretty open from the start, you are able to explore freely with very little limitations. You'll find secret paths, compartments, visit several rooms, turn on dozens of lights, read notes, listen to well voiced audio journals and examine things, but never really do anything with them. You can open doors, throw objects and put them back. Again, your job is to discover what happened. Unravel the story. The only real challenge is to find half hidden notes under couches, keys and combinations to locks and safes. There is no way to lose, you will get through Gone Home if you keep going.
There is no run button, just walk, look, crouch and zoom in. Again, its an exploration experience. In the menu you have a map of visited rooms, a list of journal entries, and a small inventory that you don't really need. You just collect keys. Its not like you need to see the keys, because the game recognizes that you have them when you look at a door.
Gone Home is over in under 2 hours and that was with me exploring and reading everything. It is an easy sit through and play, but for $20 there is no way I can recommend it. Even for $10. It is interactive fiction, with zero replay value.

I feel bad giving this game a "Not Recommended". Maybe this isn't the game for me. I can appreciate the attention to detail and the atmospheric conditions, and what the game is trying to represent and convey, but the experience was disappointing to me - I felt no real connection with the story, it came across a little 'rich kids problems' given the setting of the house, this seems trivial but when you are being immersed into an environment, you can't help but notice the pure scale of the house and how it relates to how the main character of the journal lives and feels.
I was disappointed there was no real character development of Katie at all really - a few scraps here and there, but never beyond surface level, and even for Sam I just couldn't make that progression in creating an emotional bond with this character (and trust me, it is by no means that I am ignorant to the situation she is in, as I have parallels in my own life I can draw from). Why was there such a build up to an occult/horror undertone and then to drop it completely? The initial feeling of tenseness soon dropped to 'is it over yet?'It didn't help that the game feels poorly optimised, and it was rare that the game played entirely smoothly.
There are many interactive story titles breaking the mould in terms of storytelling and immersion - I just felt this didn't quite hit the mark. I would have been shocked to buy this for €20 though - there are books with far more depth in storytelling for half that price, and that's the only thing I can compare this to - an interactive book that has good intentions, and flickers of somthing great, but fails to really capture my heart and mind.

-=June 18th, 1916=-
It was a day like any other day: Frenchmen waving baguettes in the air while shouting "Viva La France!" and throwing their berets in the air, Britons sitting around a fire with their teapots steaming and their monocles getting fogged up while one sits off to the side opening canned crumpet with his teeth, and Canadians playing a game of hockey on the frozen Flemish soil while chugging maple syrup. Truly, there was not a more normal day here on the western front. I crouch in my dugout with my buddy Hanz; we have a picture of glorious Kaiser Wilhelm captioned, "Gott Mit Uns!" hanging on the wall. I stroke his majestic waxed moustache for good luck. The whistle blows. Stuffing the picture in my jacket, I leap over the top with Hanz following right behind me.
There is a boom. I am showered in a torrent of blood as Hanz is blown apart by a mortar round directly to the sternum. Lying on the ground with most of his ribs and vital organs nowhere to be seen, Hanz shouts, "Nice mortar!". In the distance, I hear a Brit shout back, "Thanks mate!". RIP Hanz. Nevertheless, I charge on right at the baguette twirling Poilu, who, glass of wine in one hand, white flag in the other, cry "Mon Dieu!" as I jump into the trench and begin skewering them for Der Kaiser. All surrender. None survive. The incest-ridden Tommies are coming now. One shouts, "Oii! It be 6'bong ya git! That's tea time, you damn hun!" and he fires his Lee Enfield at me. Not being of superior German quality like my Ruhr made Gewehr, the bullet invariably bounces off my Pickelhaulbe and kills the Canadian's goaly. I then take a shot and blow all of the crooked teeth out of the Brit's mouth. The Canadians are mad that their goaly's dead though, so they run at me hockey sticks drawn, shouting, "Eh! You hoser! You ruined our game, eh!" Sadly, most, drunk on maple syrup, trip on the slippery ice and crack their skulls. Those that make it to me begin to beat me with their hockey sticks. I feel numb. Then, all is white. All is quite. Der Kaiser reaches his hand out to  me and I take it. I have no fear for Der Kaiser is with me now. Der Kaiser sees all. Der Kaiser hears all. Der Kaiser is all. Heil Der Kaiser!
-=November 11th, 1918=-

Germany's forces prevail as the French all surrender and the British swim back home to watch soccer, using their teeth to carve boats out of trees. The Canadians summarily abandoned their posts and beat each other to death after a controversial hockey game. German boots beat on the streets of Paris! Heil Der Kaiser!

TLDR: It's more of the same. If you can get SotFS for a fair price and enjoyed DkS2, you'll enjoy it all the same. I actually want to give a negative review since it's so similar to DkS2 and slightly more annoying, but it's still a great game.
Vanilla Dark Souls 2 is probably one of the better games made in the past 5 years or so. Despite being better than the majority of third person games, DkS2 is not as good as Dark Souls, in my opinion.
Some of the issues I had with (patched) vanilla DkS2:
- Movement felt slightly floaty.
- Popping multiple souls was introduced, but offering Covenant items was still indivdual.
- Combat in general:
-- Running past every enemy and rushing to the boss and dying on the way once or twice could be faster and safer than fighting through the enemies.
-- Enemy tracking being insanely accurate, especially with overhead slams.
-- Animations relating to combat were annoyihg in the way that the attack from enemies generally finishes before the animation does, leading to unnecessary situations where you get hit. The spider people in Tseldora Cavern are especially guilty of this.
-- DkS2 introduced more multiple foe encounters, which in Dark Souls (1), would be managable, but the changes to combat that DkS2 had caused player animations to be longer lasting and stationary. In boss fights (with only 1 enemy), this can lead to a calculating, reactionary and patient style of combat. However, in many mob pve situations it is extremely easy to be overwhelmed in melee-only gameplay.
-- Using a shield to defend might be considered, but you will get locked into the blocking animation for a full second after being hit, leading to drawn-out fights especially against mobs, having to assess if you even have enough stamina to attack and roll or risk being hit.
For lack of time, those are the more pressing criticisms that I have.
As far as I can tell, in Scholar Souls, the tracking issues has been lessened to the point where I wouldn't consider it a problem anymore. Animations are still late compared to the actual hit, but enemies do seem to need to follow the rules now: the Tseldora spider people are actually possible to walk up to and hit safely (or so I notice).
The downside is that Scholar increases the enemy count in many areas. Some of the biggest annoyances in combat are dealing with the hordes that appear, as well as ambushes that you *actually* have no way of noticing.
Scholar is strange in that it fixed some important problems, such as the 60fps durability issue, while making other problems, such as being overwhelmed by enemies, worse.
Overall, it's better *and* worse than vanilla DkS2. If you liked DkS2, you'll enjoy Scholar.

Great and Terrible, Best Game Ever and All Other Games, and of course, Gitting Gud and Being a Filthy Casul. Then from the dark, the Gamers came, and found the Majesty of Souls within the games. Demon’s, The First of the Great Games, Dark Souls and its Son’s of Bro, Bloodborne, The Lord of Playstation and its faithful fans. And Dark Souls 2, so easily forgotten.
With the strength of Miyazaki, they challenged the other Games. Bloodborne’s mighty atmosphere peeled apart their weak aesthetics. Dark Souls weaved great lorestorms. Demon’s Souls unleashed a miasma of level design and the feels. And Lords of the Fallen betrayed other games, and the lesser Games were no more.
Thus began the Age of From. But soon the online will fade and only PvE will remain. Even now there are only a few on Demon’s Souls servers, and man sees not light, but only endless nights of New Game +. And amongst the Souls players are seen, carriers of the accursed Zweihander.
Yes, indeed. The Legend Never Dies. And in this land, the online players are corralled and destroyed in PVP, where they rage quit, to await the end of their game session... This is your fate.

This game is probably the best representation of WWI in a videogame in existance at the moment. Great maps, great trench layout, awesome authentic weaponry, and a great development team make this game a winner. This game also has free content updates with new squads, weapons, and maps being added every few months.
The squad gameplay is awesome! Squads are split into 4 classes each with its own weapons and different playsyles like some have grenades, machine guns, and even can add a scope to their rifle and play as a sharpshooter (there is also standard weapons that you can use if you get attached to a specific weapon). You can rank squads and get different abilities and passive perks as you play with friends (as well as late war uniforms for your soldier). Each squad gets its own special call in abilites that the officer of each squad can use. Canadians and Stormtroopers can call in 4 different types of poison gas depending on squad level ranging from Chlorine gas all the way up to Mustard gas. Landser, Poilus, and Tommies get artillery strikes that become more powerful the higher the rank your squad is. Lastly the Alpenjager and Chasseurs are able to call in recon planes that reveal enemies underneath the planes path and at higher levels can become a precision bomb strike as well as a recon run.
Trench warfare is where the game excels. It forces people to think tactically and not the run and gun mentality so many first person shooters force upon people these days (You can try but more times then not you're going to get killed). You will be crawling or sprinting across no mans land A LOT. Stopping in no mans land usually means instant death, unless hiding in one of the many ditches or craters strewn about. You will have to dodge bullets from enemy machine gunners and snipers, while at the same time praying the sharpshooters on your team can take out the enemy MG or sniper. Battles in the trenches are fantastic, with trench clearing and holding the trench from counterattack being the best part. Some squads like the Canadians and Stormtroopers are specialized in trench assault with some roles coming with melee weapons, tons of grenades, in the case for the Canadians a revolver with a bayonet attached, and for the Stormtroopers the MP18i SMG is available. Another effective tool for clearing out trenches is the bayonet and pistols become deadly in tenches between some with high stopping power and others with a faster fire rate. And don't forget about poison gas. When gas hits it becomes don your gasmask quickly or die. Gas will limit visibility in the trench and will result in close quarters and oftentimes hand to hand combat.
I personally rate this game 10/10. For a small developing team to produce such a high quality game and to be able to produce new content for free every few months and to bring out performance patches every couple of weeks is aweome! This game is all about patience, precision, and to make the first shot count. Those who like Red Orchestra  will love this game. You will die, and when first starting out you will die a lot till you get used to the pace and tactics. Those who like Call of Duty and Battlefield, while the gameplay tries to deter a run and gun playstye, the game makes up with a killer action packed, bullets flying everwhere, explosions all over the place WWI experience that you will never forget.
I highly recommend this game, its worth every penny!

First of all, I want to say that I love the Souls series. I've played both Dark Souls and Dark Souls 2 for several hundred hours each. If I had the money I would buy Demon's Souls and Bloodborne too. I already gave the original Dark Souls 2 a positive review:
However, I'm somewhat disappointed by the Scholar of Sin version of Dark Souls 2. The main reason is due to the ramped up difficulty. It's not too hard for me (keep your "git gud" comments to yourself), but it's harder than it needs to be.
No, I'm not going to complain about the "cash grab" that some people are moaning about. At least not directly. This is a business after all and the more profitable Dark Souls is, the more similar games we can expect in the future. For example, I was surprised to learn that Namco Bandai (publisher of Dark Souls) is also the publisher behind Lords of the Fallen.
One small thing I want to mention before getting to the main part of my review is that I had trouble getting x360ce working with my controller even though I didn't have any problems using it with Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls.
Aside from the graphics improvement, the item and enemy placements have changed in this new version. By doing this, they were able to make the game even harder. Why would they do this? The answer is simple. They wanted to offer something new to people who had already played through Dark Souls 2. There were many news stories about this increase in difficulty that served to generate hype for the new version (although many people would have still bought the new version even if nothing changed except the graphics).
I've heard from many people who were pleased by this increase in difficulty. However, this comes at the cost of discouraging new people to the series. Dark Souls and other Souls games are already unfriendly to newcomers as it is. While I would prefer the game to be easier, I am more concerned that this is going to turn off people who try this game out as their first souls game. For those new to the series I would recommend playing the first Dark Souls which I believe is a better game overall.
Aside from turning off new players to the series, the increased difficulty attracts elitist fanboys that try to impose their ideals on others. This isn't as much as an issue, but it still can get annoying. One streamer I know had to switch to sub only mode during his blind playthrough of Dark Souls due to that chaos caused by random people causing trouble in chat.
I have every intention of playing through this new version of Dark Souls 2 as well as the DLCs which I haven't played (and have heard they are the hardest content of any Souls game). The DLCs thankfully are unchanged although I suppose some people who have already played the DLCs will be disappointed that nothing has changed.
I'm quite surprised at how many people say Dark Souls 2 is easier than the first game. About a month or two ago I went back to Dark souls 1 and finished a playthrough with a character that didn't use magic or a shield (both of which I was very dependent on when I first started playing the games). I beat most of the bosses in the second half of the game (including the first 2 DLC bosses) on my first try and I only summoned an NPC for two of those fights. So while the first game was quite challenging, the difficulty was more fair for the player compared to Dark Souls 2. I'm not a fan of the platforming challenges in Dark Souls 1, but overall I think the difficulty was handled better.

First off, this game isn't for everyone. It has no action or puzzles and in a sense is basically a walking simulator. For those of you who do not like interactive story games, DO NOT buy this game! For those of you who do, continue reading below. I will also warn whomever is reading this that this review will be quite lengthy, but will hopefully help you decide whether or not this game is for you.
I do not play many indie games, so when I saw this game for sale on Steam I thought I would give it a try. You play as a girl named Katie who comes home from a year long trip in Europe to find her house empty. The basis of the game is to "explore" the house and to find out what happened to your family. I say explore rather sarcastically, because even though you have to hunt for clues around the house, the game is very linear and you are forced to follow a set path. The game itself is also VERY short. I took my time to explore the house and I still clocked in at only about 2 hours at the end of the game. You can look it up online but you can literally beat this game in less than one minute if you know what to look for. So for a $20 price tag, this game is akin to highway robbery and even at a discounted price it is tough to justify.
Now the story itself I mildly enjoyed. First off, the "main" story revolves around your sister Sam, who turns out to be a lesbian very early on in the story. I personally don't mind the LGBT themes in movies and games, as long as they are not shoehorned in (which usually indicates some sort of agenda versus good storytelling). This game kinda toed the line in that regard, as I actually started to laugh as they made the not so subtle reveal. There are also other storylines that are put in the game for some reason but are not fully fleshed out, leaving the player to wonder why they were ever in the game in the first place. The most prominent example are the whole "exercism" and "psycho house" themes. Now while I realize the developers have said that there is no violence or horror in this game and it is just about exploration, it seems counter-intuitive to create a dark and forboding environment if they were not going to fully utilize it. I really did like how a lot of the story was told by the clues left around the house like letters and notes, and piecing the story together for yourself. I'll also mention that while some of the nostalgia themes from the 1990's were appreciated (I personally enjoyed the numerous X-Files references), the fact that this game is set in that time period really has no effect on the story whatsoever.
To sum it all up, I liked this game. However, the underdeveloped story and characters and the extremely short playtime are too big of faults to overlook. Add in the fact that there is no replayablility to this game and the $20 price tag and you have a recipe for disaster. I am glad I did not pay full price for this game and I can guarantee you this review would be drastically different if I had. If you see this game on sale for a dollar or two, I'd say give it a try, but at the end of the day you really aren't missing anything by passing it up.

First of all, I want to say that I love the Souls series. I've played both Dark Souls and Dark Souls 2 for several hundred hours each. If I had the money I would buy Demon's Souls and Bloodborne too. I already gave the original Dark Souls 2 a positive review:
However, I'm somewhat disappointed by the Scholar of Sin version of Dark Souls 2. The main reason is due to the ramped up difficulty. It's not too hard for me (keep your "git gud" comments to yourself), but it's harder than it needs to be.
No, I'm not going to complain about the "cash grab" that some people are moaning about. At least not directly. This is a business after all and the more profitable Dark Souls is, the more similar games we can expect in the future. For example, I was surprised to learn that Namco Bandai (publisher of Dark Souls) is also the publisher behind Lords of the Fallen.
One small thing I want to mention before getting to the main part of my review is that I had trouble getting x360ce working with my controller even though I didn't have any problems using it with Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls.
Aside from the graphics improvement, the item and enemy placements have changed in this new version. By doing this, they were able to make the game even harder. Why would they do this? The answer is simple. They wanted to offer something new to people who had already played through Dark Souls 2. There were many news stories about this increase in difficulty that served to generate hype for the new version (although many people would have still bought the new version even if nothing changed except the graphics).
I've heard from many people who were pleased by this increase in difficulty. However, this comes at the cost of discouraging new people to the series. Dark Souls and other Souls games are already unfriendly to newcomers as it is. While I would prefer the game to be easier, I am more concerned that this is going to turn off people who try this game out as their first souls game. For those new to the series I would recommend playing the first Dark Souls which I believe is a better game overall.
Aside from turning off new players to the series, the increased difficulty attracts elitist fanboys that try to impose their ideals on others. This isn't as much as an issue, but it still can get annoying. One streamer I know had to switch to sub only mode during his blind playthrough of Dark Souls due to that chaos caused by random people causing trouble in chat.
I have every intention of playing through this new version of Dark Souls 2 as well as the DLCs which I haven't played (and have heard they are the hardest content of any Souls game). The DLCs thankfully are unchanged although I suppose some people who have already played the DLCs will be disappointed that nothing has changed.
I'm quite surprised at how many people say Dark Souls 2 is easier than the first game. About a month or two ago I went back to Dark souls 1 and finished a playthrough with a character that didn't use magic or a shield (both of which I was very dependent on when I first started playing the games). I beat most of the bosses in the second half of the game (including the first 2 DLC bosses) on my first try and I only summoned an NPC for two of those fights. So while the first game was quite challenging, the difficulty was more fair for the player compared to Dark Souls 2. I'm not a fan of the platforming challenges in Dark Souls 1, but overall I think the difficulty was handled better.

Five Nights at Chuck E. Cheese's 2 is the third installment of series. It starts off with Schmidt MIke's best friend Garfield who time travels into the future of 1986 trying to stop Mike Schmidt from killing the animatronics. However, the predator, Garfield, soon becomes the prey of Mike Snitch for he has hacked into the animatronics and force them against Garfield. Garfield then has to sit in the room to keep the animatronics at bay with a flashlight and Chica's mask. In the new installment, the added plenty, like the flashlight and mask above. Along with more, these being a few: no doors, a forcefield to keep them at bay, new animatronics, like Sparky the Dog, the revealed the killer, Mikes Chmidt, and the helping companion Balloon Boy. In addition, Cawthon Scott changed the map and added to it, now the animatronics have to catch the player, Garfield, through vents which, for some strange reason, possibly to help Garfield breathe for the future has a lot of lung cancer patients, are big enough for animatronics to crawl through and have cameras in them because crime has shot up in the future. Going with the new animatronics, the owners of Fredbear's Family Diner have remodeled Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck (into Daffy the Chicken), Winnie the Pooh, Tigger, and Chuck E. Cheese. Much like last game, Christopher Robin drops helpful hints throughout the game, and he figured out a way to give you unlimited power so your friends, the animatronics, won't get trapped in the dark, for they are afraid of the dark. Tigger tries his best to play with you, but you have to quickscope the forcefield so you're Darude Sandstorm Fan Player doesn't go off when Tigger pounces on you. The new mini-games are great too. The mini-games have you social linking the animatronics, in which carry onto the game that allows the animatronics to do various things, such as, but not limited to: saving you, replacing your flashlight batteries, increasing paycheck, and more. Overall this game is great, but the main turn-off is the fact that this game supports animatronic abuse for Old Bugs Bunny's face was ripped off and Schmike Idt forces the animatronics to go against their will, making them slaves. Only people who love slavery, abuse, and hatred for animatronics would buy this game and love it.

In short, it contains all DLC for DS2, new enemy placements, and a over all better game. Definitely harder than the first in areas, but in others, it is a bit more forgiving. Slightl graphical and audio upgrades also improve the look and feel of the game. It really feels like the definitive way the game was meant to be played. Very much recommeded, whether you are new to the Souls series or not.

First of all, I want to say that I love the Souls series. I've played both Dark Souls and Dark Souls 2 for several hundred hours each. If I had the money I would buy Demon's Souls and Bloodborne too. I already gave the original Dark Souls 2 a positive review:
However, I'm somewhat disappointed by the Scholar of Sin version of Dark Souls 2. The main reason is due to the ramped up difficulty. It's not too hard for me (keep your "git gud" comments to yourself), but it's harder than it needs to be.
No, I'm not going to complain about the "cash grab" that some people are moaning about. At least not directly. This is a business after all and the more profitable Dark Souls is, the more similar games we can expect in the future. For example, I was surprised to learn that Namco Bandai (publisher of Dark Souls) is also the publisher behind Lords of the Fallen.
One small thing I want to mention before getting to the main part of my review is that I had trouble getting x360ce working with my controller even though I didn't have any problems using it with Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls.
Aside from the graphics improvement, the item and enemy placements have changed in this new version. By doing this, they were able to make the game even harder. Why would they do this? The answer is simple. They wanted to offer something new to people who had already played through Dark Souls 2. There were many news stories about this increase in difficulty that served to generate hype for the new version (although many people would have still bought the new version even if nothing changed except the graphics).
I've heard from many people who were pleased by this increase in difficulty. However, this comes at the cost of discouraging new people to the series. Dark Souls and other Souls games are already unfriendly to newcomers as it is. While I would prefer the game to be easier, I am more concerned that this is going to turn off people who try this game out as their first souls game. For those new to the series I would recommend playing the first Dark Souls which I believe is a better game overall.
Aside from turning off new players to the series, the increased difficulty attracts elitist fanboys that try to impose their ideals on others. This isn't as much as an issue, but it still can get annoying. One streamer I know had to switch to sub only mode during his blind playthrough of Dark Souls due to that chaos caused by random people causing trouble in chat.
I have every intention of playing through this new version of Dark Souls 2 as well as the DLCs which I haven't played (and have heard they are the hardest content of any Souls game). The DLCs thankfully are unchanged although I suppose some people who have already played the DLCs will be disappointed that nothing has changed.
I'm quite surprised at how many people say Dark Souls 2 is easier than the first game. About a month or two ago I went back to Dark souls 1 and finished a playthrough with a character that didn't use magic or a shield (both of which I was very dependent on when I first started playing the games). I beat most of the bosses in the second half of the game (including the first 2 DLC bosses) on my first try and I only summoned an NPC for two of those fights. So while the first game was quite challenging, the difficulty was more fair for the player compared to Dark Souls 2. I'm not a fan of the platforming challenges in Dark Souls 1, but overall I think the difficulty was handled better.

Comparisons between Gone Home and Dear Esther are not improper; both are exploration storytelling games without any killing, looting, or what many would consider "traditional" gaming.  But both are powerful in their way, excellent at creating and maintaining an atmospheric setting which is beautiful to behold and interact with.  There is a bit more puzzle-solving to be had in Gone Home whereas with Dear Esther the story gradually unfolds organically as you move through the landscape.  Both are short, but I didn't feel cheated.  If you prefer action-packed games where the story is explicitly spelled out for you, this is not for you.  On the other hand, if you enjoy leisurely exploring well-designed environments with lovingly-rendered details and many secrets for you to discover, this game will probably be right up your alley.  I thoroughly enjoyed my time with it and expect to replay it at least once to see what secrets I might have missed.  I will note that I purchased this on sale and I probably wouldn't pay full price for it as it is so short, so bear that in mind and perhaps pick it up during one of the frequent sales if it intrigues you.

GTA on steroids, I got this on sale for $3 and is probably the best $3 I have spent, however, the normal price of $15 is still worth it if you don't want to wait for a sale.
Though the title might be for the storyline, it might be better suited as Just BEcause. You can and do anything and blow anything up for the heck of it. Best of all there's no waiting to get your hands on awesome hardware like helicopters or rocket launchers (plenty of enemies and places with them). Highly recommend if you want a cheap (in price, not quality) game to entertain you for many hours.
Probably the most overpowered weapon/ability is your grappling hook, which you start with and always have. Enemy on a mounted turret? Just grapple him and pull him off. Attack helicopter on your butt? Grapple it and punch the pilot out and take it over. No vehicle to get around? Just grapple onto a tree, mountain side, tall building, etc. and from there grapple onto another tree/cliff side/building/etc. If you get high enough (via grappling) you can jump and open a parachute (which is always available) while falling and grapple the ground (or other object) to move yourself in that direction.  Then there's attaching two objects (including enemies) together, such as attaching a soldier to a passing car, or a helicopter to a military truck/tank... physics will do the rest for you. Its main limitation is its range, but its not painfully short.
Also there's a Multiplayer Mod that as of this writing is in early but playable stages and I believe is free. Ex: you can attach a tank to a helicopter and have a friend fly while you're in the tank shooting the cannon. It is also loads of fun and should only continue to get better with updates.

Units dressed in bright blue (Again with the stupid French) Wear the damn uniforms ingame and always get blasted first because they stick out so bad.
This is not a game for people who want to run around solo feeling overpowered, this is for people who can appreciate cowering in a crater hoping artillery doesnt get called in, afraid to stick your head out because it WILL get blown off.
They are adding more weapons, american squads (The game works off squads, you play as a member of a real life squad and this defines your gear) And gore to make it the most in your face horrifying war experience to date, flamethrowers crisp your comrades as you try desperately to shoot the man weilding the horrible weapon through smoke, fire, and your own fogged gas mask.
This Is Verdun.

This is an example of how video games can be masterful storytelling mediums. The game puts you into the shoes of Katie Greenbriar, having just returned from a year long trip from Europe. You arrive home in the dead of night, in the middle of a rainstorm. From there, you go through and explore the house, piecing together what has transpired in your absence.
I got this game during a sale, but it's well worth the base price as well. It's a beautifully story driven game with immersive music and (for anyone who was alive in the 90's) a sense of nostalgia as well, yet even if you weren't, it doesn't rely on nostalgia to bring the reader back in time. I cannot reccomened this game enough, 10/10.

It really surprises me that there's still tons of people that play this game, but it also confuses me at the same time because how old is this game? 10 years old or something like that. There are only two reasons why I bought this game and I'm going to be perfectly clear on that, 1) I got it for Gmod textures just like everybody else that's buying this game now and 2) I bought it out of curiosity to see what the game was like back when it was in its glory days. After playing it for about a few weeks I can easily say I didn't have the fun I expected, mainly because I can't. If you're new to this game franchise don't expect it to be anything like Call of duty or Battlefield, you will get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked pretty fast if you play thinking that.
Now I wouldn't go off and say that this is the most tactical first person shooter ever, it's really not, but it requires a lot of teamwork, a lot of patience and good aiming, mostly headshots, so if you can't hit anyone in the head you're not going to get anywhere. I really like how this game encourages teamwork and that if you can't do that you're going to get steamrolled unless you're a complete badass, I also like how there was a long list of weapons that you could use to customize and suit your needs. I also really like playing on those servers that allow up to 40 people on them that make for some really good 20 versus 20 matches, those can be very chaotic but at the same time that's what makes it extremely fun to play.
Unfortunately I'm already running out of good things to say about this game and I really hate the fact that I have to say that. Overall the biggest problems with this game is its community, it feels wrong to really dislike a game because of the people that play it but in counterstrike sources case that's the truth.  Just like you would expect the community is full of nothing but haters, spammers, trolls, screaming 11-year-olds and people who think they're on top of the world just because they can kill you with a sniper rifle and while there are some good people, the bad mostly outweighs it. It's not only that but most of the servers you will go on will have people that are only willing to play one map which is usually dust or office and to make it even worse some of these people have the most inappropriate sprays I have ever seen. To add the icing on the cake there are some people that of been playing counterstrike source for years and are completely relentless against new players. We all know who I'm talking about, the people that can take you down in an instant as soon as you round the corner or the people that know every perfect peeking spot that you never thought to look at, I can't tell you how frustrating it is to walk 20 feet away from spawn only to get headshot across the map by a desert eagle when everyone in existence would agree that it was an impossible shot to make, yet these "veterans" are able to do it on a regular basis. It's even more of an insult when you light them up with the entire magazine of your gun and they can take it like a champ and still kill you by shooting you once, by the way this all happens normally in casual servers.
If you're out there looking for a new first person shooter to get behind it's hard for me to recommend counterstrike source unless you're extremely confident, a unnaturally perfect shot or can deal with some of the weird/annoying people that play this game or you need it for Gmod textures. Besides this is an old game, like a 12 year old game, I think there are a lot of other multiplayer shooters out there that are new and way more worth our time. Don't give me hate, I'm just one person with one opinion.

If you heard that Gone Home is severely overpriced and overrated and you're still thinking about buying a copy, whoever told you that is right and deserves a gold star. ('You Tried')
Gone Home is a game that you will finish in roughly two hours, even if you backtrack and look at absolutely everything as I did, listen to everything, and pay close attention to every detail. For the time that you play it, if you enjoy a good storyline, you will enjoy Gone Home.
However.
Gone Home is not worth $20. Luckily, I bought it when it was on sale for $5.
It is a 'love story' that ends too quickly and is not ended well. However, the experience building up to the ending is worthwhile and if you have a heart, you'll likely become at least a little bit attached to the main character. (No, not the character you're playing of course! Rather, her teenaged sister who is having one too many problems.)
The ending was not what I expected and to be honest, I believe my expectation would have suited the game more! (If you played it, I think we all expected the same thing in the attic.)
To sum it up, Gone Home is a short fairly enjoyable experience but along with that, it is also overpriced and in my honest opinion, not immersive enough to play through a second time unless you missed the *SPOILER* sex note *SPOILER* like I did the first go around.

Interesting and innovative in many ways, but not better than the average shooters out there.
Goods:
- Variety of 'weapons' and tactics of gameplay, completely different according to which 'class' of 'soldier' you choose to play every time you respone. Lots of 'classes' to select from.
- Acceptable to nice graphics (for my taste), allowing playing on not 'top edge' computers. Do not expect Battlefield 3 graphics. Check the in-game videos on the web.
- Very interesting consept mixing human and dino combat. Funny moments during my gameplay experience.
- The developers have made a good effort to build a profesional and high quality feeling on loading screens, 'skins' design and overall feeling of the game.
Bads:
- Small 'battle maps'. Good becouse it is easy to learn them and memorise paths, camping corners, dangerouse places etc, but to me the maps feels like the size of the small maps of CallOfDuty2. COD2 had also bigger maps thougth and the gameplay in thesmall ones was OK. The maps here are less than 1/6 of the Battlefield-2 maps for example. Restricting tactigal-strategy combat.
- Shooting line was feeling a bit strange for me. With everything other than sniper rifle, I had enemies zoomed in my ironsights, but the bullets were shooting around the crosshair, regardless that I was motionless. Looks to me that there is an 'arrea of recoil' like counter strike etc games, but wihtout the expanding-shrinking crossair interface. In general, phisics of bulleting looked to me as below average. A rare theme for an FPS and great attention to historical accuracy do very little to make up for a good fun game.
The maps are always the same leading people memorising them and knowing the best camping spots from wich to utterly dominate the matches, I know it's world war 1 but camping doesn't really make for an appealing core gameplay mechanic and that's what this game is 80% all about. The other team camps while the other team tries to get lucky and dislodge the camping side before it's switched around.
The maps while visually appealing suffer from same problem as Red Orchestra 2 blocky and completely static, artillery barrages don't mold the terrain or damage the structures and decals littered on the map, there aren't even penetration values present so a centimeter thick plate of sheet metal will protect you from anything.
The character models are stiff and clunky bouncing awkwardly around over uneven terrain and the hitboxes are seemingly utterly random, spamming a pistol from the hip to the general direction of an enemy is just as effective as taking time to aim a rifle trough ironsights and holding you breath, both seem to have 50/50 chance of accomplishing something.
Ammo and grenades cannot be restocked, though considering the frequency at which you'll die, that rarely poses a problem. Although basing your inevitable death as a core gameplay mechanic isn't awfully appealing either.
While it's refreshing someone has taken up the effort to make a dedicated game based around World War one I feel like a PvP first person shooter might had not been the right genre to approch the subject with.
You don't really get the sense of scale with Verdun that you're part of a larger battle, maybe mixing steadily spawning A.I bots to bolster the player numbers might do the trick but overall Verdun is still very crude and clunky as an FPS game in itself, while visually impressive the game feels more like a mod for Battlefield 1942 that came out in 2002.

I absolutely hate this game.
And I say that with some amount of awe. Gone home does a horrifyingly good job of exploiting every little fear you ever had while you were home alone, but were always too cool to admit to; as a matter of fact, it absolutely preys upon it. You hear your own footsteps, the doors creak open when you move through the rooms, and naturally, there's a thunderstorm raging outside. It's the type of game that reminds you why you bolted upstairs the second you turned off the lights (and maybe still do).
Coming home from studying abroad only to discover that your family has disappeared (rather cryptically) doesn't exactly lift the mood right off the bat. After which time, you stumble across a series of notes, most of which are bits and pieces of your younger sister's life as she made her way through her teens while you were at school. Most tell a story, build her character, and construct a narrative around a very lovable girl, only to have the occasional "Please don't tell mom and dad about the attic." thrown in for good ominous measure.
Have I finished the game? No. But it scares the ♥♥♥♥ out of me. Realistic horror is what I find really gets to me, and this game thrives on it. And yet the gameplay is a strange and jaunty ebb and flow of emotional backstory with dark, shadowy undertones. I find I can't play it for long, but I still keep coming back to play it more.
In short, I hate playing this game. It makes me anxious, antsy, and jumpy.

I really WANT to love this game, but in its current state, the only way to play it as it is intended to be played is on Night 2.  What I mean by this is that you are supposed to keep track of where your enemies are at all times by checking each room through the cameras while frequently winding the music box and protecting yourself with the mask... in theory. In practice, however, it inevitably breaks down into this formula:
Night 1: You get attacked once, maybe twice by only 1 enemy (Bonnie 2.0, who moves very slowly and very predictably), not counting the Marionette. Cakewalk.
Night 2: Optimized difficulty. You have to balance the music box, your immediate surroundings, and your distant surroundings to fend off all the anamatronics. Foxy and the Marionette will murder the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you if you neglect the music box or the hallway lights.
Nights 3-6: There is so much♥♥♥♥♥♥going on, you're basically only checking and responding to the immediate areas around the office while sparing the 5 seconds you have between encounters to wind the music box. If you spend ANY time searching for the anamatronics outside of the vents or the front hallway, you are wasting your time and WILL die, considering that there are now 11 of the ♥♥♥♥ers out for your flesh instead of the first game's 5 - and that at ANY given time ONE of them WILL be poking their head into your office if they're not already right in front of you.
For the latter 2/3rds of the game, all it is (in it's current state, as of this review,) is just spamming lights, lights, lights, mask, music box, mask, lights, and lights and lights. Do it fast enough, you win. Stagger your pace, Freddy ♥♥♥♥s your face.
...still, the game is such a novelty, I can't NOT recommend it.

This game is purely for PVP. I didn't even go through the DLC because after finishing the main story, I was so emotionally drained from all the damage they'd done to the Souls as a title. Nothing stays consistent with the first game. Dark Souls already had plot holes, but Dark Souls 2 often contradicts its predecessor or just refuses to mention it. Item descriptions will often have almost no lore or importance comparatively. To give you an idea, I will provide an example below:
"Black♥♥♥♥♥♥♥of Hackzorer"
A♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that is black in color and
coated in DNA from somebody.
This black♥♥♥♥♥♥♥once belonged to a
bitter steam user named Hackzorer.
That's about all the lore you'll get from an item. Some boss weapons will have better item descriptions, but I envy you if you have the patience to do a completion playthrough.
Multiplayer is pretty fun. Parrying is way harder than in the first and third installments, but the weapon variety makes fighting other players more interesting. I'm a bit angry about them adding Adaptability as a stat, but other than that it doesn't change the meta too much. You still see warrior-sorcerers and havels, along with naked dudes carrying the largest weapons. Shields don't seem very effective compared to the other two Dark Souls games, with the stamina that gets drained per block pretty high compared to the other games. Instead of kicking, this game added shield break which allows a critical hit on the defender, so shields just put you in position to be riposted.
I beat the game twice. Once was alone as an Armstrong FMA cosplay where I only wore gloves and pants while using double caestus. The other time was Coop as a cleric where I only used starter gear with healing miracles to keep my friend's health up while we beat the game and explored all the main story content.
I wish I hadn't bought this game, because DS3 makes references to it and every time I am reminded of this game I get a headache. That said, I got my money's worth out of it despite my grievances.

Apaixonado por Terror?
Gosta de Adrenalina em seu coração?
Pois bem, em Julho de 2014, o criador Scott Cawthon produziu um brilhante jogo com uma jogabilidade e mecanica unica e inovador para o genero Terror Point & Click, surgiu o jogo Five Nights at Freddy's.
Com a popularidade do jogo, Scott Cawthon decidiu anunciar seu novo projeto em outubro, o tão esperado pelos fãs Five Nights at Freddy's 2, Scott tinha planejado lançar somente em 2015, mas orgulhoso em testar seu jogo e ao saber que não tinha nenhum bug, ele decidiu lançar no dia 11 de Novembro de 2014.
Five Nights at Freddy's 2, uma experiencia de terror inovador que mistura muitos medos em um jogo, tão assustador quanto o primeiro jogo.
No primeiro jogo, o seu unico objetivo era sobreviver 5 noites(da 00:00 até 06:00) seu unico equipamento é dois interruptores que pode ligar e desligar a luz e abrir e fechar a porta dos dois lados, e um tablet que permite que voce possa vigiar 4 Animatronics atravez de cameras, onde voce deve manter alerta, pois os 4 Animatronics vão até a sua oficina e te matar, e tomar muito cuidado, pois tem limite de energia que são gastos nas luzes, nas portas e no tablet.
Extra:Ao passar das 5 noites, voce libera a noite 6, tão dificil quando as outras noites, e se voce passar da noite 6, voce libera Noite 7(ou Custom Night), permitindo que possa modificar a Inteligencia Artificial dos Animatronics de 0 até 20
Ja em Five Nights at Freddy's 2, o criador quis manter a mesma mecanica do primeiro jogo, porem muito mais inovador, removendo a mecanica da energia que foi substituido por Lanterna(Onde voce pode iluminar os lugares clicando CTRL)e portas tambem foram removidas, substituidas por 2 dutos de ventilação nos lados(Cada um possui um botão para iluminar) e uma entrada na frente. Mas, fique alerta, pois não são apenas 4 Animatronics tentando ir até a  sua oficina, são agora 10 perigos, 4 novos Animatronics, 4 velhos Animatronics do primeiro jogo, 1 Marionette(Voce deve manter a musica sempre tocando, se esquecer da musica e ela desligar, Game Over) e um Balloon boy que se ele entrar na sua sala, sua Lanterna estara indisponivel até dar Game Over. O jogo mantem tambem os mesmos Extras da noite 6 e 7 do primeiro jogo.
Recomendado para todo mundo que curte jogos de Terror.

What can I say about Gone Home that hasn't been said already?
Gone Home is rightfully lauded as a step in the right direction for video games as an art form. It comes at a moment in time where games are slowly gaining artistic legitimacy in the mainstream. Beyond the Call of Duty's and Assassin's Creed's of the gaming world, exist small and powerful games like Gone Home.
Gone Home tells a compelling story and builds real, living, breathing characters better than most games, heck, better than most novels. It strings you along at first, knowing your expectations better than you yourself know, feeding you atmosphere and shadow, and does so until the very end. And based on that knowledge, it takes the player's expectations and guides them past the cliches and norms of video gaming and invites the player to witness something truly remarkable, uncommon and unrelentingly human. And in so doing, it creates a worthwhile experience.
Gone Home is what a video game should strive to be. To create a transcendent and immersive experience. The thunder, the rain, the voice acting, the attention to detail, the excellent writing, the music selection, the creaks and moans of the ancient, spooky house settling. All of it combines and creates a tense, yet, mature and emotionally rich story.
Gone Home is a love letter to what every video gamer holds deepest in his or her heart: exploration. What secrets lie in the dark corners of the basement? Between the walls, in the attic adorned with red lights and locked tightly and ominously with a hidden key?
Gone Home is not only an unforgettable game, it's an unforgettable experience.
I cannot recommend it enough.

Whether it can be considered a game or not, is something I'm not even going to mention. Interesting as the argument may be, I simply don't care much about what is ultimately merely a discussion on terminology.
What this game does (if you let it), it does well; very well, actually. And what it does is immersing you in the life of this family, your (as in, the protagonist Kaitlin's) little sister's in particular. It makes you curious, it makes you wonder, it makes you doubt and/or fear at times (either it's intentional, or I've read too many Holmes stories and tend to jump too easily to sinister conclusions) and most importantly, it makes you care. Now, of course I can't make generic statements, so you should interpret the above in sense that it made ME, specifically, do all those things; but I think it would have the same effect on most people who were willing enough to devote to Gone Home the few hours it requires to tell its story.
So, to sum up. If you're looking for monsters, quests, loot, or just any form of traditional gameplay, you're better off looking elsewhere - this has, after all, been termed a 'walking simulator' by some. And indeed, walking, reading/listening and occasionally picking up stuff is all you actively do here.
But if you're looking for a well-narrated story told through a medium which (due to its interactivity) heightens the immersion much more than a movie or television series could do (I'm not sure how it would compare to a book, but maybe they're too different for an actually valid comparison), then you're in the right place.

This game is great. This game will not jump scare you, it doesn't have any deep mysteries, there is absolutely nothing paranormal in it; it is the most normal, boring, ordinary look at the mediocre life of a rather typical and lackluster American family in the middle of the 90s. There is no big moral lesson, your sanity is never challenged, there is no punchline. It's just taking a trip back in time and taking a look at very personal, definitive moment in the history of a family that has no relevance to anybody but them. It throws a lot of people off because it is unconventional, but if you think the developers failed to be "artsy" you may be getting it wrong. Maybe we're not used to plain honest unpretentious storytelling games.
Somebody said that you shouldn't play this game if you aren't a 90s kid and I think she's onto something. A 90s kid is around 40 years old right now. Old enough to realize how this stupid little moments have tremendous impacts on our lives and how well captured they are in this game, even though when you're a teen they seem unimportant. Now as a 90s kid the nostalgia was strong with this one and I think they achieved a real time travel effect.
This is a beautiful time travel game about nothing, the length is right. You should play it but maybe not for $19.99.

Let me get a couple of things out of the way. There is already plenty of writing concerning this game spanning from its unprecedented merits to the accusations that Gone Home is not a game at all. The latter is a ridiculously pedantic. Gone Home is a game in the tradition of the Point-and-Click Adventure, a discovery-driven genre supporting basic controls for exploration, except that it is in 3D. Before The Sims rocked the world of (casual) PC gaming, Myst was the industry’s top-selling game—a Point-and-Click game. In other words, the critics out there who denounce Gone Home as anything but a game need to conduct some rudimentary research before polluting the internet with their nonsense.
Indubitably, Gone Home is a brilliantly-written experience.
....
However, Once I became aware of Gone Home’s modus operandai–The Fullbright Company’s attempt at evoking an empathetic response to this charade of a “coming of age” story that is actually a “coming out” story–I became increasingly disinterested this element of the game, half-listening to the recordings as I rummaged for clues concerning Terry, Jan, and Katie. I don’t believe that The Fullbright Company was trying to “push an agenda” so much as they (in reference to the four members of the company with one of them one of them of them being LGBT) were simply (re)creating a typical experience of a, arguably two, LGBT girl(s) living in the 90’s. As is the case for most adolescents, companionship becomes an obsession that consumes daily life in totality, so one should expect that the narrative be reflective of this. If that was the objective (and it was, according to designer Steve Gaynor) then the game succeeds in its mission. However, when executed as deliberately as is realized in Gone Home, the subject matter becomes a clobbering rather than tender message. Sam and Lonnie are lesbians. I get it. I even accept it. But I don’t have to  condone it.

This is a fantastic first person exploration game.  If walking around in house, inspecting objects, and piecing together a story is not something you enjoy, don't buy it.  It'll still be here for the rest of us.  One of my weird things I like in certain games are "clutter" ie objects that make a world feel "lived in".  Not many games get it right for me.  Gone Home does a brilliant job of creating an authentic feeling home that a family lives in with the various little touches.  Example: peeling stickers on the main character's desk, messy rooms, etc.  Gone Home does an outstanding job with creating a rich atmosphere that I personally can relate to.  The game is kind of eerie, reminding me of when I was a kid being home alone kind of eerie.
Growing up in the 90's, Gone Home struck a very peculiar chord with me, but might not do so for others.  This game is often criticized for not being very "gamey", but I personally didn't really care or see why they (Fullbright) would need to make it like that,  Gone Home is more of an experience rather than a game, and it's an experience I think is worth someone's time.

I want to start out first and foremost by saying that this is a fantastic game, with a few flaws. The game is very short and in terms of more bang for your buck you are looking at the wrong game. I personally paid 3 bucks for it on the summer sale and that is a great price. It is a game that can easily be beaten in around 2 hours on your first playthrough and there is little to no replay value here. There is also not much to be said about the gameplay aspect of the game. You basically walk around the house. There is no combat, and no enimies. But despite those reasons this is a fantastic game. This game does a great job of creating an amazing atmosphere. The atmosphere rivals that of games like Bioshock, the metro series, and The Last of Us. I found myself getting chills throughout the entire game. The story of the game revolves around the playable character trying to find out what happened to her family upon her return home and it focuses mainly on her younger sister. I felt very attached to the characters at the end of the game despite only knowing them for 2 hours.
Overall this is an amazing game that, if you consider yourself a gamer, you should play. But at the right price.

The story is about a someone who comes home to an empty house, and then explores the house. You then hear a story about the Player characters' sister and her struggles in understanding her feelings about one of her closest friends. The main problem I see, is the game is a walking simulator with the audio diary of a teenage girl attached to it, and really there isn't enough in that to keep me enthralled.
(Don't get me wrong, It isn't that I dislike walking simulators, because I think that "The Stanley Parable" is potentially one of my favorite games of all time) But...
Personally I didn't really enjoy it. I felt more emotion in playing a comicbook zombie game (The Walking Dead) than I did while playing this. Even though there are many things that I can relate to in the games subject matter including some things about the main story plot, but I rarely felt a shred of emotion whilst playing it.
Some might just write this off and say I'm dead inside or whatever. But I know that isn't entirely true because there were times that  I wanted the story to be more about her problems with her adjusting to a new environment and school (meaning a bunch of problems with making friends and bullying) and that TO ME would have made for a much better story and probably would have invoked more of an emotional response from me than the actual game ever did.
I would recommend buying it just on the off chance that you would like it much more than I did. But other than that chance that the game would hit your feeling much harder than it did mine, I would not recommend it.

The story is about a someone who comes home to an empty house, and then explores the house. You then hear a story about the Player characters' sister and her struggles in understanding her feelings about one of her closest friends. The main problem I see, is the game is a walking simulator with the audio diary of a teenage girl attached to it, and really there isn't enough in that to keep me enthralled.
(Don't get me wrong, It isn't that I dislike walking simulators, because I think that "The Stanley Parable" is potentially one of my favorite games of all time) But...
Personally I didn't really enjoy it. I felt more emotion in playing a comicbook zombie game (The Walking Dead) than I did while playing this. Even though there are many things that I can relate to in the games subject matter including some things about the main story plot, but I rarely felt a shred of emotion whilst playing it.
Some might just write this off and say I'm dead inside or whatever. But I know that isn't entirely true because there were times that  I wanted the story to be more about her problems with her adjusting to a new environment and school (meaning a bunch of problems with making friends and bullying) and that TO ME would have made for a much better story and probably would have invoked more of an emotional response from me than the actual game ever did.
I would recommend buying it just on the off chance that you would like it much more than I did. But other than that chance that the game would hit your feeling much harder than it did mine, I would not recommend it.

Gone Home is an exploration based game where you play as a daughter who has returned home from her trip to Europe. Upon entering your family home, you find the entire house deserted. There are no immediate clues as to what happened here. Where is your family?
The GOOD:
+ The atmosphere is spot on. The lighting, the sound effects, and the enviornment are built to convey a strong sense of mystery and a fair amount of tension/suspense.
+ The voice acting is fantastic.
+ I'm not going to comment on how good/bad the story is because that is relative to each individual player. Some people will enjoy this story while others will not. Play it for yourself to decide. Overall though, I feel like the story is well written (I'm not referring to the subject matter/plot, I'm just saying the story has good pacing and in general feels like it was written by a professional writer).
The BAD:
+ Gone Home is very short. On a first playthrough, you will most likely finish the game in under two hours.
+ The actual story matter may not interest all players. Again, the story is well written, but I don't think the subject matter is for everyone.
+ I think there could have been more story given to the mother and father. They are just as much a mystery as Sam and yet you get very little infmoration on them. I wanted to know what happened to the entire family, not just 1/3 of it.
+ I feel like the asking price of 19.99 is a bit far fetched for a game that takes under two hours to finish. 9.99 seems fair.
Overall, Gone Home is a nice piece of story telling. While a bit on the short side, the actual game is executed quite well. The atmosphere and the voice acting were the two main selling points for me. Gone Home takes about two hours to finish.

A fun and more importantly, fresh FPS set in WW1. I'm Sort of getting tired of WW2 games and I yearn for more varied offerings.
This game is fun but also fustrating since after all it's trench warfare. Charging into open flat fields or crater filled fields provide little cover or concealment and what time your running for you life either towards, or away from the enemy; you are going to be in a very personal relationship with the ground, and crawling around in the dirt or grass praying you don't get shot, and you will be shot from many angles and varying distances as the maps are huge.
I really like Verdun, however, enemies blend in a little too much in the distance as pop in of graphic background textures is a thing, and the fog of war/ draw distance, which may be realistic and intentional, makes everything fuzzy and washed out.
I had a scoped sniper rifle and a guy with a revolver out shot me from 500 meters away and often times I'll have my rifle pointed directly at an enemy machine gunner and know for a fact he's there and he just seems invisible to me. Also hit detection seems off to me, as many times I'll be ducking behind cover and strafing but still get shot and die even though it looked like I made it in the crater or I dropped the guy in front of me and I should be okay. I play Insurgency and Red Orchestra 2 so I can handle fast and furious gun play in close quarters but it seems like mutual deaths or random victors in close combat pistol shooting matches are common to me.
I hate to say it, but I kind of prefer the ironsights and bolt action rifles of Red Orchestra 2, as I seem to get less eye strain shooting in that game versus Verdun. Maybe it's just my eyes, but I had to turn down the contrast to make the game darker to see enemies in the many sun bleached environments.
Melee combat is difficult if you don't have a bayonet which gives you a little reach. Swiping with a butt of a rifle stock or if using a knife, shovel or trench club, you practically have to be standing in the same pixel your enemy is and keep moving forward and rubbing into them like your at a night club.
Despite what I've said which might seem negative, I still love this game and it's gratifying when you win, but also when you lose as WW1 was very much a titterboard match, as the few miles you won in todays battle, will be lost tomorrow, or even in the same day.

I went into this game with no expectations and no prior knowledge. It drops you in an empty house with a storm outside, building a nice spooky atmosphere. A cheesy teen romance is not praise-worthy and it's not material to be the focal point of a game.
I love "interactive stories" more than most people and finding all the little pieces grabbed me at first, but the plot was predictable, uninteresting, and very run-of-the-mill. Hints of the mother cheating and the father's struggles with writing are only briefly mentioned before the focus returns to the stupid romance. The weak plot is unacceptable in a game that focuses so heavily on story (walking and clicking are the only gameplay mechanics - you can't even jump).
TL;DR: This game is well executed, but not good. Weak points include the plot and the unsatisfying, underwhelming ending.

Gone home is a really engaging game that is driven by an immersive narrative told through various notes and object around the house. I've always enjoyed games that try to tell stories and this is no exception.  Remember those time when you've uncovered a new piece of lore through an object or journal entry in an RPG? This game kinda does that and does it really well to tell a story about the ongoings of the Greenbriar family from the point of view of Kaitlin Greenbriar who has just returned from a period overseas.
One importat thing to consider before buying this game is that "traditional" gameplay is almost non existent. The game's interactions are to pick up and examine object as well as read notes and letters and examine pictures. Some objects trigger voice overs. Its kinda like a slightly interactive book almost. I personally really like that the story was told this way but i know a few others out the may not. (You've been warned!)
Pros:
+ interesting story, kept me in suspense to find out what happens in the end
+ great voice acting really pulls you into the narrative (great writing for the "dialogues" too)
+ really nice soundtrack that really enhances the mood of the story (go get it!)
+ developer commentary reveals many cool easter eggs and insightful stuff that went into the making of the game (Played it a second time for this feature, so worth it.)
+ Environment/setting. everything form the old vhs tapes to room decorations tells you more about the family members.
Cons:
+ short game. Some people might not like the short length but I didn't mine the game's length of roughly 2 hours , i   thought it fit the story to tell it in that short a time. Imho any longer might have been too draggy for such a game.
+ i think the asking price of this game is  a little steep but I really recommend to get this game at the next steam sale (...i did).
+ replayability. I would liken this to a good book you would pick up once after a long while to read. Other than that i don't imagine playing this game many times over consecutively.

Stories can be told in many forms, and Gone Home is a novel take on the telling of a simple but poignant story. The environment, which is based entirely within a single, large mansion, is made to be extremely immersive, with TVs, casette players, and the ambience of a summer storm providing a consistent amount of background sound. The experience is pretty interesting, and it's quite cool to be exploring a 90s era mansion with the ability to pick up and examine the huge variety of objects scattered throughout the house. The pacing of the story itself is done so by your own interactions, allowing for a story-driven exploration game that takes hours to complete or a fast paced run through this seemingly deserted mansion. This isn't a game that everyone can get into, and it is definitely a stretch to purchase it at full price. However, if you ever feel the need for a few hours of relaxation with a somewhat compelling story, and happen to find Gone Home on sale, it is definitely worth your time and money.

Sure, the graphics remind me of Call of Duty 1, but I pretty much stopped noticing/caring before too long because this game is great. This is one of the only multiplayer games I've played that always feels challenging but also allows everyone to get at least a kill or two before too long. It's a lot like Red Orchestra except not constantly dominated by snipers and players with fully auto weapons. Playing as an NCO (squad leader) is also a lot less complicated in this game than most, without feeling too dumbed down- basically you get to run around with a semi-auto pistol (often a serious advantage) and rain mortar or mustard gas death down upon the opposition. What more could one ask for? The playing field feels much more level than in most games because pretty much everyone's toting an iron sighted bolt action rifle, sneaking around winding trenches or sprinting across the crater-pocked no man's land. I highly recommend this game to anyone interested in WW1 (like, seriously, how many games are set in WW1?) or anyone just looking for a relatively mature and friendly group of players. It's also nice because you can tell the developers have put a lot of work into the details, like period music in the main menu (how many WW1 era song do YOU know?) and well thought out maps based on historical research of actual WW1 battlefields. Plus, the game is a work in progress, with updates (weapons, improved graphics, gore etc.) coming out soon. So, it'll only get better, and it's already well worth the $20. Join us in the trenches!

* You don't own Dark Souls 2 but think you want to play it.

* You have Dark Souls 2 and the DLCs already, and aren't interested in the PVP/COOP aspects too much.
* You have Dark Souls 2, but don't enjoy it too much because you feel it can't quite fill the boots of Dark Souls 1. This version of Dark Souls 2 will not fix your issues. It will make Dark Souls 2 even more, well, Dark Souls 2.

Home alone is not for everyone.  This is no fighting, no action, no villains to defeat, and no princess to save.  This is just a slice of life story about a girl returning home to figure out what happened to her family while she was away. The visuals are beautiful, and if you grew up in the 90s the references will bring a smile to your face.
The game is short, but I disagree with the consensus that this is a bad thing.  To get the most out of this game, you need to take your time digging around the house. Can't find where to go next, put the computer down and come back later: if you are rushing you will be missing the point of the game. You can tell a lot about people by the items they keep, and it is those little details that builds on the main plot. There are loose threads left over that could be tied up, but if the plot was extended much farther this could make the game over stay its welcome.  For the story it was telling, the play time is reasonable.
Take caution when reading up on this game, the spoilers kill the experience. I agree that $19.99 is a lot for such a short game, so I recommend waiting until it is on discount.   There is no replay value in this game, other than going back over to see if you missed anything the first time around. My rating is a 4/5, it may not be perfect but worth checking out at least once.
