Verdun is that type of game that keeps you on for hours and hours, however, there as many features as it has, there are also flaws to match it up.
First of all, the game requires serious optimization. I'm not talking FPS-wise. There are things such as micro lag and stuttering. The animations are not smooth, it feels as if everyone's model is animated in a maximum of 15 frames, mostly because the movement is very rough. There are also things such as hitboxes to take into account, which are very poorly constructed.
Second of all, the game requires more work on the weapons and general combat system. The weapons have close to no sway, the artillery is represented by falling pieces of metal that MIGHT fall on top of someone's head and give you a hit mark, or if you're really lucky, it might even explode and give you a kill. They need to buff them up. The weapons, and I'm referring to automatic and semi-automatic weapons, excluding the bolt-action rifles, need some work. You can spam them over and over without a problem, although, they have little damage and poor accuracy, which may suit the lack of recoil and sway.
To end it all off, the game requires some work, not worth buying right not, at least not at full price. However, the game is awfully fun, especially with friends. The squad leveling is interesting, the systems are nice, the models are nice, the textures are very nice, it's all nice, except for the mentioned major flaws.
EDIT (25/03/2016): After the Horror of War expansion they just added, this game is awesome. Worth every single euro. The stuttering has been fixed, weapons are awesome, the performance is awesome. It's great.

Warface is a free-to-play FPS PvP\PvE game. I will cover several criterias to help you decide if this title is worth your time. If you would like just a quick summary of the review, go to the bottom.
This being a free to play FPS title, I'm going to get the elephant out of the room, that being the cash shop.
When you first enter the cash shop, you'll be put on the Top Items list, which lists the most purchased items, and most likely you'll see a gun.
I can hear you thinking, and I thought the same. I compared the paid weapons to the basics, and found there was not only a very small boost in certain stats (example, gun has more reserve ammo, literally 1 point more of accuracy and 30 more RPM, which is rate of fire, simply put.) and that they are also only event guns, i.e. halloween based weapons.
While the weapon does do more damage to NPCs in the PvE modes, it has no real effect on PvP.
On top of this, pretty much everything in the cash shop is dirt cheap, same thing for the in-game currency shop, everything is very cheap. Half of the weapons are timed and can be quite expensive to keep buying, however, Warface has quite an interesting remedy for this.
On the lobby screens, you can select 1 of 3 types of gear to unlock, weapons, armor, and accessories. Once you unlock a weapon, it's permanant.  And you get a free one after unlocking. Now, these weapons require repairs after a game, and some people complained about this being expensive.
This was not my case, as a single game of Free For All, my gun cost around 20 - 50 dollars to repair, not very much considering you win around 150 - 300 dollars a match, even more so if you have VIP, which I'll cover next.
VIP status comes in two forms, Basic and Mega. Mega granting a whopping 180% EXP boost per match, along with 130% faster arsenal unlocking and 165% more money per match. This sounds really expensive to buy, right?
Well, kind of. A single day of Mega is roughly 2 US dollars, 50 cents. A week being just around 8 dollars. However, if you can't afford this, basic still offers generous boosts such as 100% more EXP,  50% faster arsenal unlocks and 75% more money earned, this comes to a grand total of about 3 US dollars a months time.
Granted, these prices are 33% and 25% off respectively, it's still not as expensive as some games make it.
Okay, so we covered VIP and the shop, so how does this play? Will you
to buy anything from the shop?
Well, the answer to those questions are Very good, and probably.
I hate to compare games, however to give you a rough idea how this game feels, it
similar to the Call of Duty franchise in way of movement and gun play, however the gunplay is a bit different, considering you can change out accessories on your gun in the middle of the game.
Don't like your gun being loud? Slap a suppressor on it mid match and wreck in silence!
Another thing this game does is rewards good accuracy and personal skill as opposed to wallet skill. You can top frag no problem with just the starter rifle, shotgun, smg or sniper, if you're good with it. Headshots are almost always a 1 hit kill, unless you're far away. On top of this you gain extra points for a headshot kill, which points being the modifier that determines top player, you'll want headshots, and a lot of them!
On to another familiar, yet great feature of the movement system as well as combat system, sliding. When sprinting you can fall to the ground and slide rather quickly accross the floor, getting kills while sliding merit a lot of points, getting a headshot kill while sliding is even more points, so get good with sliding if you want to be top dog!
With how the movement and guns feel, experience from most shooters will apply here. I played a lot of Call of Duty and even more Unreal Tournament, and my first game I quickly adapted to the feel of Warface, allowing me to do very well in my first few games.
I will mention that this isn't the best optimized game, and with how fast paced this game is, you'll want a minimum of 40 FPS.
High latency is an issue in PvP however. As there are players from across the globe, a lot of players have abysmal ping, usually 65% or more per match will be single red bars. This cna be extremely frustrating.
Camping is very problematic in Team Death Match and other modes, Snipers are pain, and there are 1 hit kill sniper rifles, a few actually.
Community is extremely toxic, full of russians, BRs and children.
After being forced out of the rookie channel at level 13, expect to be put up against very high levels, including level 77s.
Is this game worth it? Yes! This game is very addictive and you should absolutely give it a try!
With how the cash shop has been done, this game is very far from Pay2Win, which makes Warface a breath of fresh air. The combat is satisfying, fast paced, and highly rewards a player's skill and aim as opposed to your wallet capacity.
There's something for everyone in Warface, If you're a PvP lover, this game is a great addition to your library. If you prefer PvE, the modes offered in Warface are supurb and tons of fun.
Download this game and get your Warface on!

Would I recommend this game? Yes, and no. Depends on the person I'm talking to, really. So here's what I think:
You should get Dark Souls II: SotFS edition if:
* You don't own Dark Souls 2 but think you want to play it.
* You own Dark Souls 2, but none of the DLCs.
* You are a huge Souls/DkS 2 fan and want to get every last game and version.
* You play Dark Souls 2 mainly for the PVP/coop.
* You're interested in trying the Souls games for the first time, but not quite sure what to pick. You're not willing to spend 5 minutes looking for, and installing a 3rd party patch to make a poor PC-port(Dark Souls 1) tolerable.
You shouldn't get Dark Souls II: SotFS edition if:
* You have Dark Souls 2 and the DLCs already, and aren't interested in the PVP/COOP aspects too much.
* You have Dark Souls 2, but don't enjoy it too much because you feel it can't quite fill the boots of Dark Souls 1. This version of Dark Souls 2 will not fix your issues. It will make Dark Souls 2 even more, well, Dark Souls 2.
* You are new and interested in the Souls games, but not quite sure what to pick. Looking for, and installing a 3rd party patch to make the poor Dark Souls 1 pc-port enjoyable is not a big deal for you.
I own the original Dark Souls 2 + all the DLCs, and have played through them multiple times. I personally think the changes to the graphics and gameplay of vanilla Dark Souls 2 were absolutely not worth the 15€ price I had to pay. To be completely honest and blunt, it pretty much feels like a small scale "enhanced edition" overhaul mod. Skyrim modders have done far more impressive things to that game.
On one hand it is cool that they changed the enemy and item placements to make a playthrough partly a new and refreshing experience, but on the other hand it's often just the regular enemies of the area multiplied by 2 or 3 to make things more challenging. Unfortunately, many times this also makes progressing through the area much more of a tedious grind. The updated graphics are nice, and the game is very pretty to look at. Still, it's not a huge improvement, and I have been much more impressed by the ENB graphical modifications to vanilla Dark Souls 2.

I'm undecided about the recommendation, because it's too binary to express my feelings for this game. IN SHORT: unless it's at least 70% off sale, don't bother getting this game. If it's on sale, you may consider it.
Many of the negative reviews and comments that I read about this game are from people who obviously didn't do their homework before they bought this game. It's not a spooky survival game, it's not a puzzle adventure game. Stop saying "zero replayability" if you don't know the genre. No game in this genre is fun to replay, when you already know the story.
This is an exploration game in the style of Scratches. Not saying it's like Scratches, but the gameplay is similar: you walk around picking up clues to find out a story. I know many players hated the story and I know why, but perhaps it's a sound warning: if you have an issue against the LGBT community, stay away from this game.
What I liked about this game:
* The 1995 visuals, posters, mixed tapes, VHS videos, etc.
* Voice acting wasn't bad.
What I didn't like about this game:
* There were too few puzzles and actual secrets to be found, which is one reason some players found it boring.
* The story starts off interesting. The first clues that Sam has a crush on another girl spiked my interest and curiosity. But then the plot becomes cheesy and predictable along the way. As much as I applaud including homosexuality in a positive light in a game (and I do applaud that very much), the story itself was kind of weak. In an exploration game, a predictable story kills off the joy of discovering clues.
At original price, it's monstrously overpriced for the length of the game, even if you take your sweet time to look at every single thing in every single corner of the house. If you're interested, I would recommend getting it on sale, and a GOOD one, as I said before, at least 70% off.

2013's Game of the Year.  Game of the Everything.  Just... goddamnit.
Gone Home strips the world down to one house on one particular night and elevates the mundane into something special.  It's not a game where you save the world.  It's a snapshot of the life of the people who live in the house (and of the 90s in general), from the taped episodes of X-Files to the mixtapes and 'zines you'll find in the house.  The journey is the destination in this game.  Every piece of paper, note, card, and other little bits of miscellanea are lovingly crafted at high resolutions so you can turn them over and get a sense of the other people who held them.
It's a slow game, meant to be savored and thought about.  There's no action to speak of.  That's what the game is.  If that sounds bad to you, don't buy it.  If it intrigues you, it is worth every penny.  The story is one of the best game stories I've ever experienced.  It's one of those things that, when it was over, just made me stop and think about it for a good half hour.
It's not a game for everyone.  But it's the perfect game for me.  I love Gone Home so much.

Gone Home gives you an interestingly casual premise. You're a young woman returning from home to find that none of your family members are there. Although this sounds like the intro to a horror movie, it's not. Nothing jumps at you, nothing scares you, and nothing makes you travel a certain path. Instead, you're given the liberty of searching around the house for clues as to what had happened. I won't spoil anything here, but the story is pretty interesting and sweet in a way. It's a very real game, and I'm afriad i can't say much else about that. But I will say that I finished this game in one sitting, and the satisfaction of slowly coming to realize what had happened made me feel like a true detective. However, this game was far too short for my expectations, and I honestly think it wasn't worth the money, having absolutly no replayability. There wasn't any action at all, but it's still something interesting to go through whether with friends or by yourself. (My experience involved me playing with two of my relatives watching. They found it just as fun to watch as to play.)

There are two varying experiences that can be found in this game:
There are those that play multiplayer, which is dominated by players with horrible ping, and there are those that play co-op so that they do not have to worry about the horrible ping.
The gameplay when most or of the players on both teams have a good ping is absolutely amazing; you'll feel immersed in the fast-paced feel of the battle and you'll feel like you weren't cheesed when you get killed.
If most players have horrible ping (and that amount of poor ping players unfortunately increases with your rank), you'll find yourself getting one-shotted by SMGs from people that instantly hit the floor and slide without a bit of animation to them.
Snipers get the worst end of the deal, usually getting some of your quick-reflex shots being punished because you have a good ping; some shots don't even register on enemies with a high ping.
If they could filter players by ping or maybe even kick players from matches with high ping, this game would be golden.

Dark Souls 2 captures the essence of story telling in the best way, in that it doesn't tell the story per-say. You have to piece it together in order to get a real sense of what's going on. This is the real reason I play RPGs. I play RPGs for the story aspect and to find out exactly how 10 the world is on a scale of 1 to buggered.
The thing that really gets me is that many, many moons ago I played the original game which was created by those awful, disgusting, beautiful Japanese people at "From Software" called Demons Souls (bit of a mouthful, like gargling sweaty marbles) and I absolutely loved every gosh darn sword to the face, dragon breath, respawning at the bonfire, constantly crying seconds of it. Dark Souls II however has pretty much perfected the game model, after the first Dark Souls game and it's pretty easy to see why. When you first start out in the game (playing on maximum graphics of course, I'm not a complete monster) it appears you're in some kind of forest. With the quality of visuals available, it's easy to see why it's received critical acclaim for it's graphics alone.
The gameplay is robust and pretty difficult to break. Let's be honest, the main thing people come to the reviews for is glitches so I'll share one with you. One day, wandering through Heide's Tower of Flame searching for poor, laggard knights to slay for their armor, I came across a phantom who invaded my world called "TImmeh". I'll always remember you Timmeh as I blasted you off the edge of the cliff with nothing but my great club.
It's one of these moments where you realise that the stalwart hero of the land named "T1tty B1tty" can slay the mother of all demons in nothing but his pants with a wooden plank and that's the beauty of Dark Souls 2.
I would definitely recommend this game to friends. It's a game that requires a level of patience and also a level of psychotic concentration. I would advise playing it whilst everyone you live with is not home, otherwise you may shout at your granny for coming over to see you because you're in the middle of fighting that "big f*cking b*stard in that sh*tty c*nt tower"

A lot of people get up in arms about whether or not this thing is a "game" or "interactive fiction" or a "walking simulator". The point is: There are plenty of games with equal or less mechanics and objectives than Gone Home. Gome Home is a game that thives on "environmental storytelling", which means using the surroundings of the player to give the player narrative information without with dialogue or a cutscene. The developers of the game last worked on DLC to Bioshock 2 (a series known for this stuff), so it's no suprise that they use the same tricks. Notes left around, rooms in various states to give clues to what happened in the past, and voice over narration while you play. The problem is that even if the way the story is presented is okay, the story it's telling has to be good, especially when there are no engaging mechanics or interesting gameplay scenarios. The game is basically a teenage romance novel in interactive form. You run around a house alone uncovering a dysfunctional family's deepest secrets through notes laid out in the open in convienient chronologic order. The primary story (and only narrated one) is of a troubled lonely teenage girl who finds friendship and love through a super special awesome young woman and has to deal with a her dissaproving christian parents. While the subplots with the parents were kind of interesting, I just feel the story is kind of trite and mediocre. It just plays out like a teenage wishfufillment novel. There's nothing wrong with a grounded, realistic story,  but it's so predictable and leaves plenty of headscratching plot holes at the end. And the way the house is set up in such an absurd fashion with the notes and the arbitrary key hunt doesn't aid in the believability. The only other appeal to this game if you aren't into shoddy gay love stories would I guess be nostalgia factor, considering the house is plastered in gratuitous 90's iconography.

Gone Home is a game that I have a feeling a lot of people won't enjoy, which is unfortunate. While I am a gamer who will appreciate a game regardless of it's preference for gameplay or story, I know that other people in the community are not as lenient as I, and will probably judge Gone Home for it's lack actual challenge or how it's barely even a game at all and more an interactive story, where the players explore an empty, unfamiliar house looking for any clue as to where your family has gone.
And while these criticisms are indeed understandable, I personally cannot agree with them. As an experience, a story and as an overall game, Gone Home is simply wonderful. Right from the beginning it had me truly entranced and curious and not once did my interest or sense of immersion falter. While certainly the story is nothing new or interesting, it drags you in slowly and has a very nice pacing to it. As each and every one of Sam's Journal entries ended, I eagerly awaited the next and I was never ever dissappointed.
Even the little hints and tidbits you find that aren't part of the main story are interesting. The game always pushes you along with new, exciting things to find or read or listen to so you never ever feel bored.
This is of course, assuming you are interested in games for their story rather than gameplay.
The atmosphere as well is perfect; as you step further into the eerie, vacant house, each and every noise seeks to give you a sense of unease; turning the house upside down to find your answers creates a very tangible sense of curiosity which I could never ever shake; your heart will then warm as you read or listen to a letter or journal entry.
While it may be a tad overpriced at £14.99, especially for the three hours of gameplay that it offers you, but I would personally say that it is worth the entry price and if you can pick it up on sale then even better!

This is half game, half art.  With this being said, I purchased this game in a sale...first things first, this is NOT worth the full price.  However, I do have to recommend this for a variety of reasons...
This is very much an indie game to me.  There are those "games" that are created to tell a story.  Not every game is about a heroic tale across the world.  Sometimes, they can convey a simple message.
This message can either be understood by girls in their late teens or adults past their mid 20's.  I was whole heartedly impressed.
However, I was expecting a different, darker ending...it would have been just as poetic...but it would have changed the message dramatically.
Regardless, the graphics are done very well for what it is.  There was a lot of attention to detail, and I ran into zero issues with bugs.  I could definitely do without the punk rock music though...I enjoyed the music from the "narrated" messages far more.
The game was short.  I feel like I completed 100% in 2.5 hours, as you can see with my play time.  There was ONE point where I was stuck for a short period of time, but other than that I feel as if the game played very fluidly.
I wouldn't recommend this game for a lot of people.  However, for those that appreciate games as art, pick this title up to show your support for unconventional game designers.  There is definitely something to be taken from this one.
Graphics- 8/10
Sound-7/10 (Those cassettes were awful...otherwise it would have been a 9)
Story-9/10
Replayability-2/10 (Not much new, but it's still a great story to hear again)
Controls-10/10
Overall-8/10

Verdun is an absolutely marvelous game, a World War I FPS released at a perfect time, opportune to honor the 100th anniversary of The Great War itself. I have never seen such an endeavor to bring the gaming world the experiences of trench warfare so powerfully. Other games simply do not immerse you in the First World War as this one does. I think if a soldier of the war were to see the game he'd agree it is spot on with most of the aspects of the battles. Verdun, though it still has some kinks to it and room to be improved upon, is already a fantastic game, one of my very top favorites. I delight to wonder what it has in store for us in the many exciting updates to come!
If you enjoy history, are a military buff, war-lover, or simply want a new and different FPS to play, Verdun will satsify you, I believe. It takes war seriously, and one has to adjust to the strategies, tactics, and methods of World War I. As I said before, it is still a new game, and is not without its bugs and errors, but in time, Verdun will shape out to be one of best games portraying war to come out in years, and hopefully years to come. Verdun deserves a lot.

Inside the confines of the fort we defend our newly gained territory. The end of a tunnel on the left side of the map is covered by german machine gunners and riflemen. I call in another mortar strike at the end of the tunnel. Four more dead are added to my tally. I pull the pin on my mills bomb and throw, doing the same with another. Soon enough six more germans lie dead at my hands. Feeling the rush of success I charge forward with my revolver, blaring my whistle in signal for my squad to come and support. Well, this is my second review for a game on here.  My first one for The Elder Scrolls: Skyrim wasn't all that hot, so It's time to start acting my age and be more specific.  I'll still sound pretty rusty, but hopefully as time goes by I'll be more thorough with my reviews and be more specific about my experiences and and opinions.  Sorry, but bear with me on this one.
Over all, even with a decent premise and a unique take in story telling, I wasn't too impressed.
Audio/Visuals - Takes place in a first person view through an enire house that tells a story about a family.  Given the fact that the team was not the bloated size of most AAA game publishers, the atmosphere on here is actually pretty good.  Shadows casted when you turn on lights, examining objects when you pick them up (and seeing the 5.99 sticker on the holiday duck?  Priceless folks!), the thunderstorm echoing through the halls and room as you unravel the mystery of what has been going on with your family since your year round trip across Europe adds up to a great atmosphere of wonder and curiosity.  The minimal system requirements means that you can experience this short adventure without the fear of having to call the fire department.  Just make sure to get a good pair of headphones and turn the lights off.
Gameplay - The meat and bones of any game.  If your looking to grab a full infantry kit, tack on an ACOG on that spify SCAR-H and go blow up some 'dem brown folks because F.R.E.E.D.O.M.........
......no, not here.  The game has an interesting take on exploration, going from room to room, interacting with drawers, turning on light switches, reading documents and journals, picking up seemingly mundane objects and discovering clues, and piecing together the whereabouts of your family (and specifically, the whereabouts of your sister).  Think along the lines of Dear Esther.
Story - You'll see a lot of opinions claiming that the game only got it's positive exposure due to it's take on a current civil rights movement right now.  Sadly, Im beginning to agree with them.  It's difficult for me to share it without spoiling the entire story, and I'd think it's better for you to go along with the narrative then read about it here.  But all I can say is that it overall plays out in the end like a run of the mill MTV movie special.  It's the same old story that has been better told through better channels.
Overall, I was just dissapointed with this game.  I knew better then to go in expecting the likes of Fallout or Morrowind.  And I was taken in by the amount of exploration and mystery that surrounded the happenings of the family.  But while the game is proof that videogames can definitely be a great meduim for art (hell, in this day of age wackjobs consider aborted fetuses a form of art), unfortinately it loses it's luster as it goes on, turing into a tale that just jumps on the bandwagon of pop culture.

Co-op and PVP covenants are the strong point of this game in comparison to the last, and make it a game worth revisiting after completion. There are some memorable boss battles and encounters that stand out in a playthrough. There are also some interesting new ideas not present in previous titles.
The setbacks that I personally found bothersome included the deadzone in player movement, the almost nonexistent stamina bar, and the parry system. The Scholar of the First Sin Edition simply adds DLC and a frustrating amount of PvE ganking. The design seems to be adding enemies in numbers rather than improving upon level flow. These were all strengths of the old games so I found it confusing when I suddenly noticed these mechanics and their flaws.
Again, DSII is a great title and is well worth picking up and experiencing. Just don't expect the greatness of DeS or DSI.

Any other review will be able to tell you this is a great cooperative (and competetive) FPS that succeeds in feeling like a WWI Trench Simulator while also being loads of fun. Instead of beating the dead horse, I'll cut to the chase.
I had two HUGE concerns for Verdun upon buying, and chances are, you will too.
-IS VERDUN DYING? ARE THERE NOT ENOUGH PLAYERS?-
-IS IT RIDDLED WITH PERFORMANCE ISSUES?-
When I bought this game, there were 300 players online. I knew I was making a risky investment, because for all I knew, 299 of those players were not in my area, didn't speak english, or were very hardcore players making the experience of a newbie frustrating.
All these turned out to be false. Don't fret at the lower player numbers! Seriously, even outside of peak hours I never had a problem finding a game, so DON'T let the lack of thousands of players stop you from buying this game.
As for the performance issues, I found that many reviewers cautioned others from purchasing Verdun after a patch in November. Apparently, the game could barely run at all for a while. Once again, this proved to be fixed by now (Jan 19). I have a perfectly midrange PC, and I have never even had a semblence of connection issues.
A must buy for those who aren't into the FPS experiences on Steam atm; Verdun is simultaneously a breath of fresh air while also being even more squad focused than Battlefield games (my favorite AAA FPS franchise).
My favorite FPS experience in a long time.

This game was so great that I bought  a JAZZ mug from the TopatoCo online store. Honestly, I absolutely love the game strictly from a nostalgia standpoint. Apparently the developers at Fullbright used a 1994 or 1995 Sears magazine as referrence. The story is pretty awesome and it's amazing what they pulled off in terms of character development simply from having you snoop around a house.
I did however have no connection to the mid-20's woman I was playing as (Katie?), instead I imagined that it was myself snooping through their house. You don't really learn much about Katie other than she's returned from a trip in Europe and that she has a sister and family that's missing.
The story was pretty basic and uninspiring. The protagonist's backstory does not matter and you really don't find out anything about the supposed female character you're supposed to be playing. I found this to be quite annoying, and honestly forgot who or what I was playing. I felt like a snoopy ghost. The strangest thing about this game is that the entire time I played it, I wanted to know more about the origins of the house, my uncle, my mother's affair, and my father's struggles as a writer much more than where the hell my lesbian sister went off to.
In conclusion, Gone Home leans heavily on nostalgia and has heavy sentimental value and pulled at all of those dusty 90's heartstrings. Though I don't recommend it at its current price of $20+, you should maybe give it a spin when it drops to $5. Finally, the soundtrack is actually pretty nice, but I suggest you avoid playing any cassette tapes you may find lying arounf in the game.

Just so you know, minor yet "necessary" spoilers ahead.
I tried to avoid hearing about any of the finer details of this game as much as possible since there was apparently some kind of "twist" to the story and it was supposedly better to go into it on your own terms rather than really knowing anything about it. All I did know was that it took place entirely within a single, large house that you explore at your own leisure, there was no combat of any form or enemies to speak of, and it was NOT a horror game. Here's the problem though, it goes so hard out of its way to present itself otherwise that even knowing all of the above I still couldn't help but get sucked into the atmosphere and brace myself for something supernatural and otherworldly (presumably part of this upcoming twist?) for pretty much the entirety of my time with it. You'll see what I mean...
Right from the very start, before you even begin the game, Gone Home's opening gambit is a title screen showing a creepy looking house slathered in chilling tones of dark purples and indigos set under a night sky and situated somewhere seemingly in the middle of the dark woods, the only sign of relief being a single lit window upstairs and an invitingly open front door teasing your curiosity. This is essentially the standard set-up to any number of relatively generic horror movies where you already know what the characters in it seem so impossibly oblivious to, that everything is going to go rapidly downhill from here. Once you actually start the game it only further reinforces those initial impressions and continues to hammer them deeper into your consciousness as it plays with your perceptions and expectations.
It opens with you standing inside a large, dimly lit porch, the doors ahead and behind locked shut, a heavy barrage of rain pours down the windows and obscures the view outside which shows only darkness and a handful of trees immediately in front of the house, and from the very start right up until the end of the 3-5 hour experience wind howls and thunder cracks as it fully flavours the unsettling ambience. Once inside the main building lights flicker and floorboards creak behind locked doors, then notes littered around the various rooms and corridors speak of a ghostly presence within the walls of the house and the sordid past of its previous, troubled occupants and the bad reputation it has among the small town's inhabitants. Even after finishing the game and going back to revisit some of the rooms and passages, despite knowing there's no threat of harm, I still can't help but feel uneasy as I slowly walk through the unfamiliar dwelling, so well crafted is the tense somewhat oppressive atmosphere. In fact, I can't help but be reminded of Amnesia: The Dark Descent as it plays like a version of that without its more perilous, menacing aspects, and even interactive objects are highlighted with a faint blue glow. It really does well and truly feel like the setting for a horror game through and through. And that's exactly the problem I have with the game, it's not a horror story, it's a love story.
You play as Kaitlin Greenbriar who returns home in the early hours of the morning after travelling across Europe for the past year and finds the house completely devoid of life. Her sister, Samantha, has left a note on the door saying she had to leave and doesn't want anyone to try finding her, setting you up to search for clues as to the whereabouts of Sam and the rest of the family. Answers come in the form of scraps of paper, notes, journal entries and various environmental clues scattered throughout the house which you gradually piece together to learn the full story. What's revealed is the tale of young love being discovered and blossoming over the course of the past year as well as the adversity it faces in that time. It's a fairly sweet, touching little story that may encourage or inspire some people to persevere in their own life, and if it really does end up helping anyone who identifies with the issues it deals with then that's great. But the problem is, when the game pulls this sleight of hand on the player and tries so hard to present one reality before then unveiling another, these two main elements of haunted house gameplay and "love's young dream" storytelling feel hugely at odds against each other. Maybe had I known this before starting I would have been able to enjoy it a lot more, but instead I felt let down by neither elements reaching the potential that they could have were they to be the sole focus of a game in their own right.
So I think your enjoyment here will depend largely upon how well-equipped you are with the knowledge of what to expect in your time with the game. There's no creatures to jump out at you, no ghosts or aliens at the heart of it all, no bodies in the basement or suicidal girl dangling in the attic, no shocks or twist endings of being dead and stuck in limbo, just a quaint love story, great voice acting, and lots of loving nods to '90s Western pop culture. Go into it knowing this and chances are you'll enjoy it, otherwise you risk walking away feeling a tad cheated by the content hidden behind the presentation.
Despite my gripes with it, I'm still going to give this a "thumbs up" since Steam doesn't allow anything between a positive or negative, though mainly because, while I wouldn't necessarily be in any hurry to push someone towards this, I certainly wouldn't ever try to talk anyone out of it either, although the arguably high price point really doesn't do it any favours. So instead of a thumbs up or down, imagine an open hand pivoting from side to side in a feeble "meh" gesture and that'll probably best sum up my overall recommendation for this game.

People say all the time about games "not for everyone". I kind of tend to ignore that now (really? Not everyone on the planet is going to enjoy this?! No way!) because it seems like something that should be fairly obvious. HOWEVER, if one game does actually deserve the dreaded "not for everyone" tag, it's this one.
Gone Home is not a "typical" game by any stretch of the imagination. The actual gameplay revolves around simply exploring a house. This involves picking up items and examining them, listening to mixtapes (the fact that the game takes place in the pre-iPod glory days of the 1990s is key), and reading notes. It's up to you to piece the story together as you go, and really the only driving forces compelling you to go on are your own curiosity and the degree to which you become invested in the story. To say anything about that story is to do this game a great disservice, you really should go in unspoiled. Suffice it to say (to use my least favorite phrase) it won't appeal to everyone, but I personally found it hard not to get invested in it, which is a testament to the game's quality.
To me, whether or not you enjoy Gone Home largely comes down to where you stand on the "games as art" question. If you believe that games can skew into the art territory, you owe it to yourself to play this game. If you don't, and tend to view games as more mindless/reflexive/action oriented pastime (not judging; I think games can be both and there's no need to "choose sides"), you should probably skip this. Honestly, if you're here reading this review you should probably know enough about Gone Home and your own tastes to know whether or not you should give this game a go.
Overall, I found this game to be an amazing experience, one that pushes the medium of gaming further into the "art" territory. It has a lot to say, and says it in a very simplistic but effective way that's certainly atypical for the medium. My only knock is that it's quite short, and $20 is a fairly steep ask for the amount of time that you will likely spend with it. Still, if gamers as a whole want to see gaming as a medium taken more seriously as a legitimate art form, perhaps that isn't such a high price to pay after all.

A domestic mystery game with a fairly-obvious but lovely and well-written story. Over its short length, it managed to induce several human emotions in my corporeal mind-body. The game is not intended to be a horror game, per se, but it *is* undeniably eerie walking around in a large, empty house with electrical problems. Descending into the dark, unfinished basement of this home, for instance, induced the same nonsensical nervousness that I feel when entering any dark, unfinished basement in the IRLs. It's quite an immersive game, packed to the brim with period nostalgia, and an excellent soundtrack featuring a couple of early, contemporary riot grrrl bands. I find that, since finishing it, the game has been kind of rolling around in my head like a good book or movie. Clearly, the devs put a lot of love & work into this game, and I really enjoyed what they created here, but I can't help but feel that the off-sale asking price is a little steep -- if you're down with lonely, actionless exploration (and I don't see how that could fail to appeal), do yourself a favor & pick this up next time it goes on sale.

I'll say this straight up - this is a game that was made for the critics, not the gamers. It's the gaming equivalent of one of those oddball 'powerful studies of human emotion' that always end up in the Critic's top 10 lists that no-one ever has ever heard of.
I'm not going to add or subtract points based on the game's genre - this game is upfront and honest about what it is and if that's not your cup of tea, you likely would be aware of this before you hit the buy button.
I guess my biggest problem is that it's, oddly, all style and no substance. The atmosphere it evokes is first class - the audio is fantastic, the voice acting is excellent, and the soundtrack is great. The devs obviously went to great lengths to create an image of a 1990s house, with dozens of nostalgic references for us old farts who were growing up back then. And on top of this, it creates a genuine unease in the player from the get go. Straight away you read a note on the door that is downright ominous, and the answerphone has messages from a sobbing unknown girl desperate to speak to your sister. The place is empty... apparently, the thunderstorm outside and creaking floorboards start to play tricks with your awareness. Was that just a shadow or is someone else in the house? What the hell is going on?
If it had stuck like this then it would have been great, but at the risk of spoiling it, the storyline goes nowhere (my initial guess as to what might have happened turned out to be 90% accurate, and that was after 10 mins), and as time goes on your initial belief that there is more to this story then meets the eye is is proven false and you're left with a, frankly, mundane tale that raises questions about what the point behind the game was.
Therein lies the problem. A lack of combat and a lack of puzzles are quite acceptable in this genre, what isn't is a lack of interesting story.
It's a hard game to review. On some level I can see why it got such a reception amongst the critics - as I say, it's atmosphere is fantastic. Unfortunately, the storyline just isn't up the atmosphere it generates, and the fact that it's totally 100% linear mean it has little replayability. £15 for this game is far too much - I bought it for about £5 back in a sale and err on the side of 'yes' as to whether it's worth that.
If you see it going cheap, then by all means, get this. While it lasts, it's great - it's just not a game to play if you're hoping for an interesting story to go with it's interesting premise.

I bought this during the summer sale, and I absolutely love it and have played through it multiple times* because I like the story and how it is presented. There are several intertwined storylines to discover, some of which you will likely encounter in a semi-linear way, some of which you will have to sort of piece together as you find bits of clues in the wrong order, and some of which you may actually miss the first time playing through. It also does a good job of making the house creepy and the sheer amount of objects to interact with makes it feel more authentic. It's very detailed, too. For instance, there are no devices missing cords that should have them. No "battery operated lamps" if you will, and a lot of details in the objects, beyond the more narrative stuff, to expand your sense of who the characters are.  I also like that this is cross platform.  I dislike Windows and prefer to use Linux wherever possible.  Seeing games that are supported for my OS is cool.  I know that some people are complaining about the length of this game (about 2 hrs average playthrough) but frankly, that's the price of interesting indie games.  You're talking about small teams that simply don't have a lot of resources.  Want 40 hour games padded with artificial difficulty that could have taken half as long if only the good parts were kept?  Buy something conventional from a well-known publisher.  If you want to have interesting new experiences that an established publisher would find too risky, buy something like this and try not to worry so much about the length.  I highly recommend this game.
*though not quiiiite as many times as my hours on record suggest. I think I left it running one time

Gone Home is a novel little voyeur's paradise. It takes you to a very grounded setting and lets you peer in to the lives of average people and their trials. Ultimately, though, the gameplay measures are too thin for even its meagre two-hour runtime, and the story cannot carry the weight of its absence.
Dubbed a "walking simulator", the game is a minimalist take on the interactive story genre. You don't really make any decisions in the game, nor is there much gameplay to go around. You can't fail or screw anything up -- you go forward and look at things and that's it, and there are not a great deal of secrets to miss. The main draw of the game is the exploration and detail in the (limited) play area. Every item you pick up tells you something about the world you've found yourself in, from the price sticker on a little duck key hider to the posters on the wall. And for a while, it works. The little details come together quite organically, with little notes calling attention to details you may or may not have caught in each room and telling you something about the character of the people involved.
But after the first half of the game, everything starts to seem really threadbare. You've long since gathered the plotline and found the pieces that mattered. You know the outcome, and the details start feeling sparse and repetitive. Where I found myself peering at photos and flipping them in circles before placing them respectfully back on the table at the beginning, I began to lose patience with it and started leaving every light in the house on as I tore through. Some of the details would harken back to things you'd long since discovered, but the timeline started feeling inconsistent as a result. The structure of the story felt increasingly contrived, with the game failing to convince the player that its main conceit -- moving through time as you moved through the house -- held any narrative value at all. The contrivances and predictability culminated in an ending that was especially unsatisfying (perhaps worse, because it didn't seem to consider the implications of what had occurred).
Despite its short playtime, the game can't hold up for the duration, and that's pretty disappointing. In a way, it was an interesting experiment, and perhaps worth seeing if you're interested in the gaming medium and the evolution of narrative in games. But as a player looking for an entertaining weekend game or a poignant story, you will not find it here.

I would not describe gone home as a horror game and even a mystery game is pushing it. Although there is initial tension it quickly dissipates. This did prove fruitful as I found things out about the minor plotlines that I would have otherwise missed. After about 15 minutes I was considering the possibility of it being more like Myst and prepared myself for some nice complicated puzzles. Unfortunately there were no puzzles!

If you would like a good story-telling experience then Gone Home is probably for you but consider that £15 is a lot of money to pay for what you are getting.

So first off this is the first review I have ever written on steam. Secondly I feel compelled to write this because I did play Five Nights at Freddys 1, and when I found out they were coming out with a sequel a short time after I lost my sh**. Now I made it to the 5th night on the 1st one, but right when the clock was about to strike 6am and that cheap labor paycheck smell filling my nose and tantalizing my tastebuds,  I got double teamed Freddy of course being the victor. With that my last impression of the game I dove into number 2 excited and of course....scared. First off their seems to be more story and different perspectives apart from being inside the office the entire time (though that is where the game takes place), which I like a lot. Sh** get's real fast, you need to be more on your toes in this one... I had Foxy kill me in the middle of the callers speech while I was starring at "Kid's cove". The animatronics both old and new I feel fit the theme, the old ones being completely horrifying and the new ones appearing "super kid friendly". The atmosphere is done well in the sequel, but I do have some complaints if not a critique. Number one, the flash light is awesome and the fact that the building lights are unlimited is a plus, BUT there are times where I can't access the flashlight at all ,I push the button I hear a noise but the light does not illuminate the hallway. This can happen several times and in the heat of the moment it does not help (probably intentional, but now I come to my second point). When you do light up an enemy that is deterred by light (the old models, IE FOXY) I'll start flashing him a billion times (as much as one can with battery power) and I have no way of telling if it is effective...and me not knowing if he's going to ♥♥♥♥ off or not so I perodically strobe  him from time to time till he does disappear. I would of preferred maybe an animation of sorts, and him scampering off in the darkness would of been way more terrifying, then him standing there and having you strobe him to death... He literally just stands there and takes it is what I'm saying, Also I was also super hyped for the marionette, but when I saw him he looks almost a bit too happy...and a little plain. Perhaps the simplicity is scary but I expected him to look a bit more intimidating......if it was real life and he jumped at me I would beat him to death. All in all it has been an enjoyable experience, currently on night three. I just wish their were more animations of movement on camera, or in the hallway reacting to the light. The first one had Foxxy running at you, and in my opinion that was one of the scarier moments in the game. Mostly because they are usually still....and you don't expect them to be sprinting at you full spped.

A very fun, fast paced WWI trench warfare first person shooter.  The game has a unique progression system; where not only you progress through levels gaining the ability to access different weapon setups, but you also gain squad levels through playing with other players.  The more you play with the same players the higher your squad rank will progress.  These squad levels are not reset after leaving the game, but each set of players you have played with squad rank is saved and when you team up with them again your squad levels resume where you left off.  All 4 members of the squad are counted in the formula.  The action is fast-paced and brutal.  The enviroment is beautiful and the graphics are very good set at either low or a high.
If you are a fan of first person shooters or WWI or historical warfare games, this game is for you.

Terrorists and Counter-terrorists, fighting for a bomb or for a group of hostages, on small maps, using Source engine. That's all it took to make CSS a classic among FPS.
Indeed, despite its simple-looking gameplay, CSS is a very tactical game. Maps are small but very well-thought, usually balanced, and offering many possibilies regarding strategies of defense/attack. The CS series has also a trademark that makes it either exhilarating or annoying, depending on which side of the barrel you are : when you die, you lose all your equipments (paid with your hard-earned virtual money), and you don't respawn until the end of the round. This allow for quick-paced rounds, and memorable stressful situations for the player.
Moreover, the game was conceived to be reinforced by its community. To this date, there are thousands of unofficial maps, using custom game mods (surf, deathmatch, zombie, racing...), whit many great ones among them.
All of this makes CSS a great game, with huge gameplay possiblities, a fun experience event for newcomers in the world of videogames.

Without any competition, Verdun is the best and only WWI shooter on the market.
But it has legs and will probably stand up to whatever may come in the future.
Remember that wall of a difficulty curve in Red Orchestra (a comparably realistic shooter experience)?
That doesn't happen here.
Sure, you have it tough in the beginning, but after you get to grips with a few of the maps and realise that you need to keep your noggin down, you end up pulling your weight pretty fast.
It's got a good amount of maps, a varied series of tactics to be employed in conquering trenches, some working better than others depending upon the map, and you have every chance of killing a level 100 vet even as a level 1 grunt.
Le good:
The attention to detail is amazing.
Squadding up with friends is a blast and a half, it really gets you into the moment.
There's variety in weapons/roles/squads.
The weapons feel satisfying.
Graphic representations of every projectile that flies around lets you see mortar shots incoming, muzzle flashes, bullet trajectories.
Le bad:
Takes a while to get used to targetting, especially in close combat.
Mesh issues still pop up once in a while, prompting you to get stuck in texture.
A few bugs still arise and cause you to teleport 50 metres across the map with little to no warning.
All in all, the bad things about this game are mostly technical issues, which are slowly but surely being taken care of by the devs who are pouring their heart into this.
If you want a realistic, historical, atmospheric, tense shooter that tackles The Great War, this one's for you.
And if people give you flak about it feeling contrived because you get executed for deserting, they probably know ♥♥♥♥ all about WWI - don't mind 'em, send 'em back to school and get 'em to brush up on their history.
This is the best and most realistic depiction of a war in a game, shooter or otherwise.
P.S. alright, alright, there's no friendly fire. Sorry. Deal with it, eh?

Good luck to the developers. I'll check back in a few months and see if it gets any better.

This game is absolutely spectacular (although I'd suggest checking your computer's capabilities before running it... It overheats mine every time I play). After completing the campaign, I realized exactly what makes this game so great: it's a parody and a stereotype thrown together. It takes everything good about action games (the fast-paced combat, the multiple combat styles, the open-world experience, and of course the cool vehicles) and puts it together with a plot making fun of every lame action stereotype (ethnic/nationality stereotypes, a crazed villain who thinks himself invincible, the frivolous use of high-powered weaponry, absurd combat situations, and even prototype technology that makes no sense). The game's campaign can be laugh-out-loud hilarious at times, with your character Rico playing the perfect combination of straight man amongst all of these walking examples of humorous racism and classic badass. And I promise you, the replay value of the game is nigh infinite. Even though I did all of the side missions before completing the campaign, and had worked my way through a fair amount of the hidden bonus assignments, I was still only 33% done with the game upon completion of the campaign- almost a month and a half after I bought it. And those were just the big strides in the campaign and side missions. If you're looking for a long-replayable, action-packed, funny, and all-around enjoyable game, I absolutely recommend Just Cause 2. And no, you don't have to play the first one. Actually, don't play the first one.

I'm a huge fan of open world games, from the original GTA way back in the 90's right up to it's latest incarnation GTAIV. I've also enjoyed Shenmue, Dragon Quest, Bully, Fallout, Farcry, Spiderman, Burnout, Arkham City..... any genre, any platform- it's easily my favourite type of gameworld. But the mechanics make a game and Just Cause 2 has the most fun mechanics I've ever played with. The possibilities are only limited to your imagination....... and skill.
......
Wanna steal a fighterjet? Cool, Rico can do that. Wanna fly that plane toward a bridge, jump on top and surf the jet under the bridge? Fine, Rico can do that. Wanna jump from a building flying through death defying gaps and before hitting the ground, release your parachute and walk away unharmed? Rico can do that one too. Really, once you get the hang of the controls the game comes to life in a way I've experienced in no other.
......
That would be my recommendation over if it wasn't for one final thing. Just Cause 2 Multiplayer. It's exactly what it sounds like and so much more. This is a mod that allows over 2000 players to join a single server, playing together on the same map. Nobody should allow themselves to ignore the fact that this really is a landmark in gaming. Never has a game of action orientated 3rd person shooting/jumping/driving been played on this scale. The closest would be something like GTAIV multiplayer on PC with up to 32 players. 2000+ Players is a whole new league above and beyond what I ever thought possible. You should try it >

Well, this game is a difficult one to rate, especially since all the hype was generated about the game made it seem so extremely prosperous and grand. Looking on it hard though made the game give me mixed feelings about it.
First off, I've played through FNAF1 already through night 6, and have gotten past night 4 on FNAF2 at the point I'm writing this review, and I've watched many playthroughs by many individuals and have been trying to get a solid view on the game.
FNAF1 was great because no-one saw anything like it before, and was a great and scary surprise to play and watch. The closest thing that it was compared to was Night Trap on Sega CD, which was more of a lighthearted goofy game, than one intended to give you nightmares. FNAF1 also incorporated animatronics that were haunted, bringing a new element to the horror genre that wasn't touched on too much. The game also included the idea of not being able to move about at all, where you couldn't try to run and hide from impending doom. You only had a limited power supply and two doors and a set of cameras to be able to try and ensure your safety. Because of these factors, FNAF1 gained great popularity and hype.
Now FNAF2 comes out, and it (more or less) is the same game as before, with a few more additional animatronics and changes in mechanics (power is now the marionette box and flashlight, freddy mask is the equivalent of the doors). Since most people who came to play FNAF2 had already played FNAF1, mostly everyone expected the same level of fear and fright in the game, without much confusion.
FNAF2 turned more into the 20/20/20/20 mode from FNAF1, and walked farther away from the initial fear factor the first game gave us (though this is in my opinion, yours may not be the same as mine). With the incorporation of the music box and the need to flash the flashlight, the game became more of a camera-mask-swapping-fest than a slower more fear induced game like the first game was.
Now, I'm not going to bash FNAF2 for going this route, as it still is a challenging game to play, but it was brought about to be a "horror" game, meaning a truly frightening atmosphere, and gameplay that would occasionally cause you to be thrown off on occasion and be put into an alarmed state, pulling you into the game to understand it, and then scaring you to death.
FNAF2 doesn't have as much of the scare factor, or paranormal activity that the first game had, making it a game of just shielding yourself in time, where you essentially "parry" off attacks from the various animatronics using the mask, while trying to keep the music box wound up.
The idea of parrying off attacks may sound similar to FNAF1, but FNAF1 brought the idea that you aren't able to keep up your defenses forever, that you will have to leave yourself vulnerable to attack on occasion, or else you will ultimately exhaust your ability to stay defended, making each person who played anxious if they were going to make it or not.
FNAF2 sorta had this, but it became more frustrating as the mask could almost be worn indefinitely, and the flashlight usually would not run out of power. The most error prone thing that would happen is having to deal with the music box being wound up, where then that leads you having to step away from the possibly scary atmosphere to wind it up and ensure it doesn't run out. FNAF1 didn't really have you having to that, but you did have to check on foxy on occasion (which you still do in FNAF2 but with a flashlight and audio cues).
Then on top of the music box, the Freddy mask usage with the older animatronics is very difficult, not impossible, but difficult, leading the player to feeling more frustrated than scared in many situations when they are attacked/killed by them.
Like I said, It's a hard game, and is a challenge, but it walked a bit too far from it's roots to keep that same "feeling" the first game gave you.
The main thing that the game does offer that was a major part of the previous game was the story, where this one leaves more little bits to find to understand what exactly is going on in the little universe of FNAF, but without giving you too much, keeping you pondering and interested. But with more kinda explained, it also kinda removes that curiosity that drove many people to enjoy FNAF1 in the first place, and kinda takes away from the old experience as well (in my opinion).
There also some other factors that made FNAF2 better/worse than the previous game, but I'll list them here in pro/con form.
PROS:
1. New animatronics to deal with, leading to new patterns and strategies to develop
2. Challenging, good for those who wish to try and really beat the game
3. Expansions on the original FNAF story.
4. More of Scott's great artwork for the animatronics
5. Satisfying to beat (for both challenge and story factors)
CONS:
1. No options menu (not major, but would've been nice)
2. Stuck in 4:3 ratio (would've been nice if it rendered widescreen properly)
3. Freddy mask very difficult to use with older animatronics (might not be true if it gets patched/nerfed, but is at this time)
4. Atmosphere just not as "scary" as the first game was.
5. Little to no paranormal activity (no hallucinations, or sudden changes in how the characters interacted with the cameras)
6. Game mechanics take away from the horror (it's more of a game of luck and snappy actions than one of resource conservation and fear)
7. Less hidden of a story (the details of the story are more obvious in FNAF2, instead of being more mysterious like in FNAF1)
OTHER THOUGHTS:
I think the game could've turned out much better if the game hadn't received as much hype as it did, and was given time to tailor it to perfect specifications. As much as I enjoyed scott's work and his effort, and his early release surprise, the game just lacked that perfect frightening polish that could've made the game really shine, as the framework is certainly there, but it just isn't tailored for the fear factor.
If there could be patches/DLC/Mods/etc that could remedy that factor, then this game may still have the potential to be great. Til then, the game is a challenging one to play, but won't give you that nightmarish experience the first one brought.
I'd recommend you trying out the demo first to see if this review holds up for you, and if you find the game is still enjoyable to play, then go ahead and buy it. If you are looking for that original experience you got with the first FNAF game, you might not enjoy this game as much.
If you haven't played FNAF1 yet, I do recommend playing it and then coming over to try this game out.

Updated Version of Dark Souls 2, including all DLCs, slightly better graphics and some Gameplay changes.
As always this review is just my own opinion and what I think about this game. If you notice any mistakes I made (apart from grammar mistakes) feel free to report them in the comments.
While you play through Dark Soul 2, you will notice that there is not much of a Story, except for the Player waking up in a strange field and fighting his way through hordes of monsters and undead. That is because you will have to talk to the people, look at your surroundings and read item descriptions to get pieces, with which you can unravel the past of Lordran, Drangleic and the Curse of the Undead. Once you get yourself to read and listen carefully, you will notice that the Story is mysterious, complex and very interesting.
You die. A lot. But you probably know that already. Apart from that, the combat system is the essence of this game and boy is it good. Wether you play with a Greatsword, a Lance or a Staff, fast and intense fights that also require some tactics are guaranteed and bosses that will sometimes leave you sleepless, because you just have to try for the 20th time to kill that f*cker, are common. The level system (collecting souls from enemies to level up), bonfires that serve as checkpoints and the strange inhabitants of Lordran fit good in the world of Dark Souls 2.
While the graphics really are not too good, it sure looks beautiful wandering around in old ruins, along steep cliffs and jump into deep holes. The lights and shadows also look stunning most of the time, but some sharper textures would not do any harm. The overall performance is good and not laggy at all, but 60 FPS is the max. you can get.
The game uses the right background music in the right environments and the sounds while fighting are realistic and epic too. It also has some creepy soundtracks that really fit the dark nature of the game.
As said before, this game includes Dark Souls 2 and its three DLCs (Crown of the Ivory/Iron/Sunken King). There are a lot of areas to explore and you probably have to retry some parts because you die. Depending on how fast and skilled you are, the game offers about 50-80 hours of challenges and dying. There is also a NG+ (and NG++, NG+++,... for that matter) which offers stronger enemies (and even some new ones), some new items and bosses have some unseen special moves.
People can enter your session randomly at certain places and challenge you, but you can also invade other players yourself, help them defeat bosses or duel against each other. Matchmaking is determined by the total number of collected souls, so fights won´t be too unfair, but sometimes being invaded is just annoying. If you enjoy the Multipayer, it can easily add 30 more hours to your overall playtime.
Dark Souls 2:  Scholar of the First Sin is a dark and mysterious RPG for people who like RPGs, dark fantasy worlds and games that are a bit harder than the rest. Even if you don´t like these things you should give this game a try, but just if you don´t mind dying over and over again.

Gone Home...It's a difficult game to describe, or even categorize, but if I had to put a label on it, I suppose Interactive Story would do?
The game sets you off as Katie Greenbriar who returns from a year long trip out of the Country back to her family's home. Right from the very beginning, it's obvious that something is amiss, it's shortly after midnight and there's nobody home.
As you explore the home (or rather, mansion), you'll start uncovering things about Sam (Katie's sister and the central figure of the plot), their Parents and even the mansion itself until ultimately, everything falls into place, revealing some (but not all, some is left up to the imagination imo) of the important plot points.
When you get right down to it, this is a very simple game and the gameplay mechanics involve a set of very simple actions: Walking, Crouching, Picking up objects (to view, read, move, etc) and the main objective is to explore the mansion, while occasionally finding entries from Sam's Journal which further the plot and sometimes keys that open up sections of the mansion so you can continue exploring.
Graphically speaking, the game looks pretty nice, especially the lighting and shadows. At first glance, it might give the impression that it's a Horror game, but it's not...far from it, slightly creepy at some points, yes...but it's not a horror game. That said, my computer had trouble running it at max settings on 1920 x 1080, which forced me to drop Anti Aliasing, not a game breaking issue, but worth taking note of, as the game may not perform very well on older hardware.
As for the Sound/Music, nothing particularly worth noting, there's a theme going on about Metal and/or Rock music, but it's not my cup of tea, so I usually skipped that music as often as I could. The sound effects are generally well done though and while I repeat, it's not a horror game, sometimes the constant rain and thunder outside as well as the flicking lights or creaking floorboards kinda tense up the atmosphere which I found rather good.
So...bottomline. is it worth buying? If you like a story-driven game, yes...most definitely. I particularly found the story moving and IMO, was worth experiencing. However, if you feel like there must be more then plot along to drive a game, I suggest moving along, as you probably won't enjoy this game, I'm aware that all this game really has to offer is a very well written and thought out plot that you can blow through in 2 - 3 hours and not much more and while that's fine by me, because I enjoyed said plot, I know it won't be everyone's cup of tea.

I’m a concept guy, so what attracted me to Gone Home was its concept: you are given a large house and its many belongings to interact with, and from this you piece together the story of the people that live there. What’s great about this is it’s most definitely a game and not just an interactive novel; you can essentially approach the house and thus the story in any order you wish, and go back to previous sections if need be. How they were able to craft a story with recurring subplots, metaphors, foreshadowing, symbols, humor, and character moments through some scraps of paper littered through the house is not only innovative, but a marvel.
Other games have told stories through notes but none have done so with such singularity as this (why is it we have to turn to indies for singularity now?). It feels like if the opening house segment in The Last of Us was turned into a whole game.
But besides singularity, Gone Home has another major difference from major AAA games: setting. While other note-strewn games take place in worlds where society has crumbled, Gone Home is much more familiar: Oregon, 1995. What’s special is how it layers this setting; 1995 is fresh and exciting at first, and it throws some tasteful nostalgia at you, but as you dig deeper you see why the setting is the way it is. This is a story that could only be told in the 90s, both in its subject matter and how it’s told (no cell phones or internet). But more than anything the 90s make this relatable to the most amount of people, which is oh so important. You will see either yourself or people you know in these characters, and at times your blood will boil with anger and you will cheer with joy for the characters. You just don’t see this level of relatability in most AAA games, it’s very emotional. I must also make a special note of voice actress Sarah Grayson who plays Sam, and brings to life a character you never actually meet.
The objects you interact with are very well “written”, maybe a bit contrived at times but they really tell a story by themselves and in the context of the larger narrative. The look and quality of them is great; in many ways this game has the singularity and focus of an indie game and the production values and detail of a AAA release. This is all wrapped in technology that remembers the location of everything you touch in the house, it really makes it feel real.
It’s pretty cool to track tendencies as you go through this virtual house; I would turn out the lights, put everything back neatly in its place, put a tape in and immediately take it back out, turn off the fan when I really wanted to turn off the real life fan, etc.
It’s also cool how inclusive and user-friendly this experience is. Not only is this apparent in the story and the game options, but the game also avoids proprietary puzzles, gives you a map for convenience’s sake, stores all the diaries in your menus, etc. It comes together to make it a really light and accessible experience.
Speaking of, avoiding proprietary mechanics imo is a big plus; not only does it make the game more focused but it also lets you create the experience for yourself. So instead of say, creating a timeline of events or something in your inventory, it really leaves it up to you to piece together what happened, using the established rules of the game. This also extends to achievements; the game is missing them, which is probably a good thing as it means it really is up to the player when they’ve gotten enough out of their experience, and not some arbitrary achievements.
I love how well this game fits together, again it really layers and explains itself. Take the house itself; the family recently moved which explains why your character is unfamiliar with it, and begins the idea of Sam being new to the school. It’s also nicknamed the “psycho house”, which develops a lot of intrigue and mystery for the player. This idea is then used as the method to bring Sam and Lonnie together to the house, as well as giving them continuous reasons to come back to the house and write notes with the haunted subplot. It gives the game a bit of atmosphere. And then as it goes it explains who the person was that lived there, and why there are convenient secret passages and even goes to explain why a certain character is the way they are. It’s just really intricate. Other examples include the darkroom, and the family portrait at the beginning of the game. I also should mention the protagonist is done really well, for the game being first-person she has a lot of personality, but at the same time they cleverly packed up all her possessions while she was away and never unpacked them, not only creating more mystery but also allowing you to imprint yourself on the character more.
So yeah the game isn’t scary and doesn’t have any “gameplay” to it, but all the same this is definitely a game through and through, and at the very least a very tightly constructed, emotional story. I like this game a lot.

Gone Home takes the epistolary narrative techniques that underpinned Fallout and BioShock so convincingly, and packages them into a powerful and refreshing combat-free experience.
I'm aware a lot of people who paid full price for this game felt ripped off for various reasons - that it was too short or that the story wasn't compelling enough. I picked up Gone Home in the Summer Sale, and I think it was worth it for the price (a few dollars) for two reasons - the novelty of no combat, and the 1990s walk down memory lane.
I don't know if I'd call this a "game" so much as an interactive story, but I found it satisfying nonetheless. Part of this was, surprisingly, the lack of combat: I never would have thought a game without action could sustain my attention through to completion. At first I was sure something bad would happen because the atmosphere in the abandoned house was just so creepy! When it finally sunk in that nothing was going to leap out of the shadows and tear me to pieces, I felt more relaxed and free to enjoy exploring without having to look over my shoulder. The no-fighting aspect was a nice change, and Gone Home has proven it's possible to craft a thought-provoking narrative without what many may have considered an essential element.
The thing that impressed me most is the accuracy with which the developers have constructed the house as a microcosm of 1990s awesomeness. The text can be read against a backdrop of '90s third-wave feminism, which is in keeping with the game's riot-grrl themes, although I don't want to give too much away. The bedrooms are replete with punk posters, VHS tapes and NO INTERNET - there's even a typewriter in the office, and a darkroom because there was this stuff called film that went in things called cameras back then. Call me a '90s tragic, but I spent ages flipping the cassette tape cases open and closed, just as a way of soaking up the nostalgia.
This game is perfect for people who enjoy obsessively examining everything and who love to piece together the narrative on their own terms. It's also a nice break from killing things - because we should all take a break from killing things now and again, right?
