Ok, here are your options. You can buy this package and get three multiplayer games. Or you can buy the retail version of Half Life 2 and get Counter Strike:Source, Half Life 2 Deathmatch, and the story version of HL2. Basically, with this package versus HL2 retail, you will be trading the story version of HL2 for the multiplayer game Day of Defeat and whatever price difference there is.
Now with that out of the way, I'd assume you are looking at this page because you are interested in Counter Strike: Source. Good choice. There is a reason CS:S is the number one online game in the world. The game is amazing......it's that simple.
The game is set up around the premise of Terrorists vs. Counter-Terrorists. When you first join a server you choose which side you want to be on, the main difference being the weapons you will have access to. During the game each team has a different goal. One some levels the Terrorists have to plant a bomb while the Counter-Terrorists try to stop them. On other levels the Counter-Terrorists try to rescue some hostages while the Terrorists try to stop them. During each round you get 1 life. That's it! This means if you die you have to sit around and wait until the round is over. It's not a big deal though, the levels are generally small and well designed, and rounds don't usually last very long. Some of the positives of this system are that it discourages "Rambo" type play where people will just run around with guns blazing, of course some people still do that, but most people are more concerned about being careful with their life.
The graphics in this game are amazing! All the particle, smoke and water effects are extremely well done. There is a reason the Source graphics engine is so popular and it shows in this game. If you don't have an up-to-date computer you may have to sacrifice some visuals for performance, but the Source engine scales quite well, so as long as you aren't years behind you should be able to find settings that work.
A heads up to any parents up there, there is a good amount of blood in this game and obviously it is centered around shooting other people, so you may want to keep that in mind if you are purchasing for a kid.
Now we move on to the actual gameplay. I already touched on the one life per round aspect of this game, but as a new player you should be prepared to die...... a lot! You will die over and over and you will never kill anyone. That is a fact, and if you are going to buy this game it would serve you well to just accept that right now. Having played First Person Shooters in the past will help a bit, but you will still be nothing but a bullet absorber when you first start out. The learning curve on this game is a bit steep, and there are many people out there who have been playing this game for years. They have the aiming system down to a science and know every level like the back of their hand. There is also a little weapon called the AWP, which is a sniper rifle you will get to know very well. Mainly by the amount of times you are killed by it. This is a one shot one kill weapon and there are some players out there who simply don't miss with it. Suffice to say it can be quit frustrating when you are constantly killed from 200 yards while you barely get a chance to even see who shot you.
The point of all this is that it will require a bit of patience to learn this game and get to a skill level where you can be competitive. There is a neat little option where you can start your own server and fill it with "bots", which are computer controlled characters, and use this as practice. You can even set the difficulty level of the bots. While no AI can compete with human intelligence this is a good way to get better at the game and learn the levels if you are getting frustrated on real servers.
Overall, it's a great game that is being updated constantly with new levels and features. If you can get past the learning curve you will be rewarded with a satisfying online shooter that you will be playing for years to come. If you are easily frustrated and do not want to put in the time it takes to get good at this game you may want to pass on this and try something else.

From my experience, Verdun is a very polarizing game in terms of who likes it. I have many friends who play games just like it, but can't get into it (probably because they are bad at it), and then I have friends who play it just as much as I do. I must admit, in the beginning it may seem like you are playing a less than favorable game, as you will endure many deaths after getting shot from who knows where. Once you get a feel for the game, you will be able to not only survive, but distinguish targets from the same distance they hit you and finally get your revenge. The game is balanced enough where they can balance out the usual long range tempo with sudden and unpredictable outbursts of close range combat which is where most people find their favorite aspects of the game. The classes are very balanced and are available to all players (no stupid grinding to rank up is required in order to use flame throwers or mortars). Plus, there is a class which gives you only a shovel and a crapton of grenades, so that's fun too. I would definetly reccomend the game, but only if you are reasonably sure you could enjoy something that is actually challenging.

Updated Version of Dark Souls 2, including all DLCs, slightly better graphics and some Gameplay changes.
As always this review is just my own opinion and what I think about this game. If you notice any mistakes I made (apart from grammar mistakes) feel free to report them in the comments.
While you play through Dark Soul 2, you will notice that there is not much of a Story, except for the Player waking up in a strange field and fighting his way through hordes of monsters and undead. That is because you will have to talk to the people, look at your surroundings and read item descriptions to get pieces, with which you can unravel the past of Lordran, Drangleic and the Curse of the Undead. Once you get yourself to read and listen carefully, you will notice that the Story is mysterious, complex and very interesting.
You die. A lot. But you probably know that already. Apart from that, the combat system is the essence of this game and boy is it good. Wether you play with a Greatsword, a Lance or a Staff, fast and intense fights that also require some tactics are guaranteed and bosses that will sometimes leave you sleepless, because you just have to try for the 20th time to kill that f*cker, are common. The level system (collecting souls from enemies to level up), bonfires that serve as checkpoints and the strange inhabitants of Lordran fit good in the world of Dark Souls 2.
While the graphics really are not too good, it sure looks beautiful wandering around in old ruins, along steep cliffs and jump into deep holes. The lights and shadows also look stunning most of the time, but some sharper textures would not do any harm. The overall performance is good and not laggy at all, but 60 FPS is the max. you can get.
The game uses the right background music in the right environments and the sounds while fighting are realistic and epic too. It also has some creepy soundtracks that really fit the dark nature of the game.
As said before, this game includes Dark Souls 2 and its three DLCs (Crown of the Ivory/Iron/Sunken King). There are a lot of areas to explore and you probably have to retry some parts because you die. Depending on how fast and skilled you are, the game offers about 50-80 hours of challenges and dying. There is also a NG+ (and NG++, NG+++,... for that matter) which offers stronger enemies (and even some new ones), some new items and bosses have some unseen special moves.
People can enter your session randomly at certain places and challenge you, but you can also invade other players yourself, help them defeat bosses or duel against each other. Matchmaking is determined by the total number of collected souls, so fights won´t be too unfair, but sometimes being invaded is just annoying. If you enjoy the Multipayer, it can easily add 30 more hours to your overall playtime.
Dark Souls 2:  Scholar of the First Sin is a dark and mysterious RPG for people who like RPGs, dark fantasy worlds and games that are a bit harder than the rest. Even if you don´t like these things you should give this game a try, but just if you don´t mind dying over and over again.

**SPOILER FREE REVIEW (Unless you don't want it to be :D)**
So, where to begin with Gone Home? In a nutshell, Gone Home is another entry in the "visual novel" genre of games comprised by other titles like Dear Esther, The Writer, and so on and so forth. Despite the greatness of other such games, Gone Home is terrible and not worth an ounce of your time. So here's why:
Without spoiling anything, the basis of Gone Home's plot is that you are Katie Greenbriar; a girl just returning from a semester abroad in Europe only to find her home in Oregon, which her family recently moved into, "mysteriously" empty. Subsequently, it is your job to snoop around the house like Sherlock Homes and uncover clues as to what is happening. Then (still no spoilers) the backstory behind why the house is "abandoned" has to do with your sister Sam who is in 11th grade and experiencing her first love interest. I will not delve any further into the story just in case I can't persuade you to not buy this abhorrent piece of trash, but all I can tell you is that within 45 minutes of playing the game (about half way through in my case, and yes i did pick up every item and explore every room) you will know EXACTLY how the game will end. I kid you not; Gone Home's "surprise ending" is about as remarkable as watching an episode of Dora the Explorer (that is to say not much at all). Now, moving on, let me adress why this game is so critically aclaimed. As you can see on metacritic, Gone Home has an absurdly high (imo) average critic rating of 86, while the user rating is 5.4. The reasoning behind this is because Gone Home is one of those games that might as well say in the description (and pardon my french) "DEAR GAME CRITICS, if you do not hail me as one of the greatest games of all time and the most moving game you've every played, you will be pigeon-holed by the rest of the game-critics community and seen as an unsophisticated, uneducated, arrogant f**ktard." Let me elaborate further: Since Gone Home is protrayed by the Fullbright Company as a "moving", "artistic", and "expressive" story, game critics want to also seem "sophisticated" and "artistic" in that same respect by waxing lyrical about Gone Home and "how personally it spoke to them". Moreover, Gone Home has many (forced and annoying) references to the '90's in it and seeing as  A LOT of game reviewers today were born in the late '80's and early '90's they eat that stuff up. To finish off this section, let's examine why Gone Home is in no way whatsoever "artistic", "moving", or "sophisticated". The story is probably the most pathetic and lame thing I have ever witnesses in any medium. The writing is down right melodramatic (which is about the only thing that matches up with the '90's :-/) and fake; as if they had a 14 year old girl at The Gap pick up the nearest pencil she could find, take a napkin from the foodcourt, and write out the first love story that came to her head. There is nothing unique whatsoever about Sam's lovestory and it fully embraces every "budding relationship" cliche known to man. Moreover, despite some people who don't recommend this game saying the voice acting is exceptional, I beg to differ. The voices sound flat and fail to convey little emotion. In short, every journal, story, and note you read that has to do with Sam's love story (pretty much all of them) adds up to a pile of bad writing not even fit for a live action Nickelodeon show.
Gone home's gamplay is flat out bad; there's no other word for it, it's just bad. Before I start ranting again, here is THE ONLY thing I will commend Gone Home for, and that is how it manages to make the house feel lived in; it's a very large house, but there's just enough furniture, books, belongings, etc. to make the house feel real and the decorating is quite realistic which probably helped cloud-headed pretentious reviewers feel more "immersed" in the game. Now, back to the bad aspects which, you guessed it, is literally everything else! The ONLY interaction you will ever have in Gone Home is picking up miscellaneous objects which sometimes  trigger Sam's "journal entries/notes for Katie", opening doors, and entering lock combonations. Believe me you, I've played many adventure games in my time so I'm very used to this type of gameplay; hell, my favorite game of all time is The Walking Dead The Game (which I played on my PS Vita so please do not respond "You don't have The Walking Dead a**hole :-/"). However, Gone Home is, simply put, boring when you are not progressing the story (that is if you even like the story which, obviously, I do not); all you do is pick up poorly textured objects, and fumble around with '90's memorabailia; rotating them around like a whirlgig (Katie would make a great chemist due to her exceptional rotating skills which you'll be doing every god-damn 10 seconds only to find that you will never find any hidden messages, images, or compartments on these objects in the entire game). In fact, taking out the ability to pick up and examine objects in Gone Home would vastly improve it seeing as the inclusion of it in the first place is a failed attempt at adding "some" interaction/gameplay to keep the player interested, but in actuallity, this ability makes the game even more drawn out than my grandpa's undies since almost every player, including myself, will take the time to pick up EVERY....FREAKIN'...OBJECT. Moreover, this would streamline the story and allow the game to do what it truly intends: rip off it's players with a truly terrible story. Other games, like Dear Esther, already realized that literally no interaction whatsoever is better than some so that the player can realize what the true nature of the game is and not be confused by being able to pick up more objects than there are milk containers in Half Life 2.
Go ahead and look at Gone Home's store page and look for it's price. You will find it is 20 U.S. dollars, thus leading you to believe it must have a significant amount of content. I mean, by that logic, Gone Home should offer as much content as games like CS GO, FTL, Spelunky, The Walking Dead, Rust, Skyrim, Dark Souls 1 and other games that are at very similar price points on steam. Moreover, for literally under a dollar, you could buy a humle bundle with amazing games like Bioshock and Xcom: UFO Defense from the 2k Humble Bundle or Thief Gold and Hitman from the Square Enix Humble Bundle that's on sale at this point in time. Well, jokes on you if you thought anything even close to that was true, because what if I told you that you can beat Gone Home in less than a minute when you know what to do? What's more, what if I told you I've actually read forum posts/stories of people accidently finding the hidden room that holds the key which you need to finish the game within minutes of their first play through, then proceeding to finish the game when they think they're merely doing what they're supposed to, only to find out they already beat the piece of trash? Well, whether you believe these things or not, they (much like Robert Ripley's stories) are horrifyingly true. Gone Home isn't worth $20, or $3, or even $1 since that same amount of money would be better spent on ANYTHING else, hell go buy a chicken burger at McDonald's!
In conclusion, Gone Home is a bad game, made by bad writers, for pretentious people, and you should NEVER buy it. Also, for those brave enough, here's the spoiler of THE WHOLE GAME (yes, it's that short),

I just want to add my two cents here. I loved this game. I can see why other people didn't, though, but I'd like to try to defend it.
Gone Home is narrative intensive, and it explores new ways to tell a story that are only possible through videogames. There are no guns or enemies, but there are plenty of puzzles. Here's the thing, though, while you do have to collect hints and piece them together, the game won't make a satisfying "ding" when you've found one, or give you points when you've reached a conclusion. It won't even ever tell you if the conclusion you've reached is the correct one. For most of the storylines, it won't even tell you what the puzzle was to begin with. It's up to the player to search thoroughly, find out that there is a mystery to be solved, then figure it out on their own, in their own head.
A lot of people call this pretentious BS, but this is weird and I'm guessing it's exclusive to gamers, because other narrative mediums have been doing this kind of thing for quite some time. I don't believe anybody would call out a book for not telling you what to do with it, or not giving you an achievement for understanding it correctly.
If you can't take a game with no game overs and no hand holding whatsoever, then you will hate this. If you're excited about games that experiment with new narrative techniques, then give this a go.
And yes, you can finish it in under 2 minutes, but consider that your "bad ending", if you must.

The tide of World War II is about to change. Dinosaurs have been resurrected by the Axis to be the formidable foe against the Allies. I bought this game years ago and went in thinking it was a single player first person shooter. You vs dinosaurs! Maybe I should read descriptions. Dino D-Day is a multiplayer online first person shooter set in the 1940s. There are 9 maps to choose from and a server list to find a game. You can even play offline or alone with bots and its every bit as fun.
The teams each have their own characters. I hesitate to say classes, because everyone feels unique. Sure both teams have a medic, but they're both different. Each of the 16 characters are different and relegated to humans and dinosaurs. The Axis has six dinosaur characters and three humans. The Allies have six humans and one dinosaur named Trigger. The dinosaurs have longer stamina to run around the map, so they don't run head on into gunfire from humans. Humans are weaker, but to balance it, they're smaller. The bigger the dinosaur, the more health it has. Changing between characters is easy like Team Fortress 2.
The dinosaurs all play differently and it doesn't take that long to understand how they work. Maybe 10 minutes to be effective and efficient killers. Trigger, on the Allies side plays in 3rd per-dinosaur. He can jump and use a machine gun that needs to cool down. On the Axis, there's a Stygimoloch that plays similar with a cool down machine gun. Desmatosuchus is a slow tank that takes a lot of damage, fires very slowly and murders quickly. To balance him, he's a slow mover and so wide he can't fit through normal doorways. There is a raptor that is fast, plays in first per-dinosaur, melee kills quick, can leap, a high jump and pounce with the alt fire button in the air. A bigger dilophosaurus in 3rd person that can quickly run and head ram things to death. Not just that, it can pick up one of the goats found in most maps and heave them at the Allies. Compsognathus is the smallest third person dinosaur. Because of this, you're under the sight line of most humans. Your lack of health is gained in stealth. Plus, you can simply explode at will. Its beautiful. The final dinosaur is the Microraptor that plays in first dinosaur. It has wings and while it can't fly it can flap to keep it in the air to spit acid that blinds enemies. Not just that, but it can cling to walls and ceilings. Cling, but not wall run or anything like that.
It is the gameplay diversity and the uniqueness of all characters that really set this game apart. The humans all have their own weapons that not only feel good to use, but effective too. Most of the weapons except the shotguns have iron sights with their alt fire button.
On the Allies, you have Hardgrave, with a gun, a pistol, a grenade and his bare fists to box with dinosaurs. Spencer has his primary weapon, a pistol, his fists and a sticky bomb. Lob it out, stick it to an enemy and watch as they bring it home. Piat is the heaviest human, he uses a shotgun, a rocket launcher that only holds one rocket at a time to balance it out and smoke grenade. No fists, no melee, just big damage. Vike is a sniper, with a pistol and a rabbit. Why a rabbit? Its bait. If a carnivorous (or omnivorous) dinosaur finds the rabbit, they eat, disabling them, which gives Vike time to user her sniper rifle for one dead dino. Camille is the medic of the Allies, but in Dino D-Day the medic packs are different. She throws out the pack and when her team is near the pack, they regenerate health. So she can help her team with a machine gun, luger and fists if need be. Frank is the last member of the allies, he has a machine gun, a one shot shotgun, grenades, his fists and his devilishly good looks. Over on the Axis side, you have Streicher with a gun, machine gun, stick grenade and knife. Allies use fists, sissies like the Axis use knives. Hissman is the sniper who has a luger, stick grenade and knife. He can also summon a pterodactyl to dive bomb and explode. Wolfgang is the medic of the Axis with a machine gun, luger, knife and medi-pack.
Dino D-Day has undergone a major graphics change and the artwork looks fantastic. It has an art style true to the 1940s propaganda. Ole time radio broadcasts on the main menu go a long way for making an immersive experience. The game has come a long way in three years. There are more maps and better graphics, even after all this time. The game also has taken out references to Hitler and swastikas. There are now black crosses in white circles on red banners. So it still feels like Nazi swastikas, but its not. That's still okay. It doesn't hinder the fun.
In case you haven't heard, the game uses the Source engine. So there are a lot of comparisons between this game and other Source games like Counter-Strike: Global Offense and Day of Defeat. It plays as easily as those games with a lot of freedom to tailor the controls to what you want them to be. A lot of the maps feel like they could be in CS:GO. They feel like deserts and small villas, all while having elements of dinosaurs in them.
The Axis is the red team with blue health and the Allies are the blue team with red health. It is a bit confusing in the game. I say red and blue, because of the color of their logos. There are no actual team colors. Characters have their own non team specific attire, which can make it confusing on the battle field. How does a new player know what team that player is on? If they're on your team, they have a logo floating above their head. Anything else should get shot and killed. The problem is seeing things. A lot of times the players blend in. The night maps make it difficult to see other players, which is good for a stealth advantage. Shorter dinosaurs can hide in grass.
Each of the maps has three or four modes: Deathmatch, King of the Hill, Control Points and a few maps have objectives. The objectives in those maps are pretty simple. The allies will pick up a bomb in their spawn room and set the bomb at a specific target. The bombs take a few moments to arm, then throw and then they explode after ten seconds or so. It doesn't feel like a game changer. Speaking of the spawn room, you can find unlimited health and ammo. Outside of the base, its tougher to find health. Enemies drop ammunition. Even if you're a raptor that doesn't need ammunition, by picking it up, you're denying the enemy from having it.
Some maps are designed for T-rex deathmatches. These maps have the deadly giant under Axis control. A player from the Axis is randomly selected to be the tyranical beast. As T-rex you move slowly through the streets in a third person view, using a dual machine gun that needs to cool down. The T-rex can also belt out a roar that knocks the human Allies off their feet. Not your allies, I mean 'the Allies.' Once they're off their feet, you can slowly march over to them and eat them for extra health. You'll be lucky to eat someone, it doesn't happen that often. Playing as the T-rex is a lot of fun and even playing against it is a lot of fun. Sure the rex is only on the Axis team, but its balanced to the point where its so giant that all you need to do is run to a smaller area where it can't get you. Then its forced to waste time walking around buildings through giant openings to find where the action went to.
In all, it might sound like a gimmick, but there is fun here. Not just the premise. The game feels balanced. There are a few ways to play to have your own fun. There are now dinosaurs on both teams so people don't flood to the Axis side saying, 'dinoz yay the new kittenz of the game world!' The developers have updated and upgraded the graphics. The Source engine is a great engine to play a first person shooter. The community is still playing the game. Give it a try again if its not your first time. It has been on sale for $1.

Dark Souls II is a wonderful game and even though it has a few shortcomings it is a legitimately enjoyable experience all the way through with enough replayability to definitely get your money's worth.
First off, if you're new to the souls series this is the perfect place to start off. People who are hardcore fans of the series might groan and say that Dark Souls (1) is the best game in the series and is where everyone should start off, but honestly it is not the most beginner friendly game and you will probably get frustrated and quit. If you hear the huge circlejerk about how the souls series is the hardest game series ever, a majority of that probably comes from people who are new to the series who started with Demon's Souls and Dark Souls 1, which are much more confusing and hard games for somebody who hasn't played one before. Dark Souls 2 has a more casual start, and [in my personal opinion] more refined gameplay. If you're new though and on a budget, you might want to get the original game first as the scholar of the first sin won't offer you anything as a new player other than the DLC areas- while cool and arguably the best areas in the game, not neccessary for the overall experience.
Dark Souls II is highly controversial for coming after the amazing Dark Souls, which is claimed by many to be one of the best games ever made. Some people go as far to say that dark souls II is one of the
games ever made, listing off a barrage of reasons for 2 hours about how flawed it is in comparison to the original. It kind of makes me feel sad that it gets this rep though, because it's what got me into the souls series after getting angry and giving up on the original dark souls without getting even past Undead Burg (yes I know). Is Dark Souls II a perfect game? No. It is however, a great game with it's own strengths compared to the original Dark Souls.
In Dark Souls II you are an undead chosen one who once again has to go light a bunch of bonfires and ultimately save the world from falling into darkness. While the plot gets a bit more complicated than that, it's ultimately a straight line through a bunch of weird areas straight up until the end. The story is not really the high point of the souls games to begin with though- the extremely deep lore is what the games are more known for. Does it hold up in Dark Souls II? No, not really. To be honest, Dark Souls II is the weakest of the series when it comes to lore. While there is still a huge chunk of readable text in the form of item descriptions you can read up on, none of it seems to be as interesting or unique as the original game. I don't want to be a spoilsport but it feels like an executive gathered a bunch of writers into a room and went "Ok this world is old and people forget things easily" and told them that was it and shooed them out. HOWEVER, despite all this, Scholar of the First Sin adds a bunch of additional lore (along with the DLC) and it is all fantastic in comparison to the base game. It tries to patch together Dark Souls II's spotty storytelling and adds an additional ending that the player can follow. The DLC's lore is also almost on par with Dark Souls 1's in terms of quality.
The gameplay is where Dark Souls II really shines. There is a vast variety of builds and tons of weapons and armour to choose from, and because of this you could potentially play hundreds of online matches with no two being the same (unfortunately because of meta and popular youtubers this isn't the case). The gameplay itself is crisper and overall more refined than the original game, having minor differences like rolling changes and power stancing adding up to a much more fun combat experience than the first game. The level design is another mild negative though- while the level design is still fantastic compared to other RPG games not of the souls series, it seems kind of lazy and less inventive than it's predecessors. The branching paths Dark Souls II has never really interconnect like the first game, and there's no real super inventive shortcuts to make travel easy, instead relying on the quick travel to bonfire mechanic (a mechanic that I am very glad is in the game, but it promotes lazy level design). The bosses also aren't as unique as the previous games, and end up mostly being guys in giant suits of armour with bigger and bigger swords as the game goes on. But overall, the core gameplay makes it fun enough to ignore these few negatives, and there are cool levels and bosses in the game regardless.
If you're new to the series, start here. Dark Souls II has worse storytelling/worldbuilding/lore than the rest of the series, but has much better gameplay and build variety. It's also easier despite claiming to be harder. The DLC is worth getting Scholar of the First Sin for, being some of the best content in the game both lorewise and gameplaywise.

This is not a game about horror. This is a two-hour journey about feelings.
It has been made clear that this is not a product for everyone, but for me it was quite the experience.
Through the scattered pieces of paper, I got to know the characters and their personality without even meeting them. I couldn't help to sympathize and identify myself with them and their situations. And that, in my opinion, denotes an awesome job in writing which I even found somewhat innovative.
Sadly, the ending felt short of my expectations, probably due to the straight-forward main story.
Sound is where this title shines. Nice suiting music coupled with superb voice-acting bring the main protagonist to life in a very believable and emotive way.
Graphics are nice, boosting a good work in textures but -unfortunately- they don't always seem to blend properly. Occasionally proportions looked off to me, specially at default FOV.
The 90's theme the game is set is very well done, so expect some nostalgia.
Gameplay wise, there are some annoyances which forced me to disable some options in favour of immersion.
Its weakest point, as already stated by many, is its price tag.
We have seen similar products with much more duration and replay value for much less.
With almost no replayability, $20 is simply too much.
In-game developer commentary has been added, but due to quality issues I wasn't too kin on listening to all of them.
Despite its flaws, this is the kind of experience that will have you speaking and thinking for a couple of days.
Best played during a rainy night, and at the same time as a friend so you can then share views.
I strongly recommend this title, but at a discounted sale price.

I'd say this game is just a Call of Duty clone with dinosaurs, but it is actually quite different. Instead, it plays a lot like Team Fortress 2 (most likely because it runs off of what looks like the Source engine). The game doesn't fling you into a chincey "First person shooter...but with DINOSAURS!!!!11!!11!" mentality because the game is actually well balanced, with even the Tyrannosaurus Rex being well balanced. It features plenty of playable reptilian friends along with those of the homosapian nature, and neither class is overpowered. A definite buy (especially at it's 90% off sale at .99 cents)!
PROS:
Play as different dinosaurs that aren't gimmicky
Well balanced game overall
Pretty good map design
Audio is clean
Doesn't feel repititious like CoD or Battlefield because of the Dinosaur mechanic and their strengths and weaknesses
Definitely asking a good price for the game
CONS (with opinions):
Game engine could've been better, something that doesn't feel too Valve-y, could've utilized higher detail engines (Unreal would've been perfect in my opinion).
Even with the selection of Dinosaurs, more would've definitely been better.
The wait to respawn mechanic gets old. Fast.
Switching class in spawn kills you (and restarts the respawn timer).
Other than that, the game is pretty good.
IS IT WORTH YOUR TIME AND $$$ - YES
WILL IT SATISFY YOUR DINO FPS HUNGER - YES
IS THE GAME REALLY FUN AND FRESH FEELING - YES
WILL THE GAME MAKE YOU RAGE - PROBABLY AT TIMES

Five Nights at Freddy's 2 squanders a few attempts at being a truly remarkable sequel to a surprise hit, and instead gives us a lot more of the same, with some shortcuts tossed in for good measure.
It's still a fun game, don't get me wrong, but by drastically expanding the roster of characters, this game becomes a titanic jump-scare-a-thon and it winds up desensitizing you to the experience beyond half way in.
In Five Nights at Freddy's 1 we had 4 animatronics (Plus one easter egg one) that actually ran through some pretty unique animations when they killed the player. Foxy even runs down a hallway , revealing that the animatronics CAN actually move.
In Five Nights at Freddy's 2 we have a roster of 11 animatronics, and all the jump scares are simple motion tweens or have such minimal animation that there isn't even enough time to really get scared by what you're seeing.
I think i've had a more fun time exploring the lore of the game and coming up with theories about the plot than I have had playing the game. And while that isn't exactly a bad thing, it does leave me wondering ... what warranted the jump in price? What about this game is so much better than the first to warrant the extra money?
There are no options to adjust your resolution, no graphical options in the least. You still have 7 nights, with the 7th being the custom night, and you have a chance to play some minigames in this one when you die. Simple 30 second atari style games.
Still, it provides a fun experience to the majority of people. So I will have to reccommend it, I can't just say its a bad game. Flawed? Yes. Rehash? Maybe. Money Grab? Debateable. Fun? Yeah, yeah it is.

Sometimes you play a game for action. A chance to kill and slaughter a thousand faceless enemies in order to complete your heroic goal. And sometimes you will play a game to kill time, maybe solve a puzzle, toss some candy together on facebook or a thousand other distractions.
Gone Home is not either of those games. It doesn't have enemies, I guess it sort of has puzzles, but it isn't about that. it isn't about finding clues, or anything like that.
Gone Home is a story. A story that, while it is set 10 years ago, it still rings home with many people and families today. Gone Home is humanity in a simple exploration.
If you want a game with action and adventure, and a princess to save in a distant castle, or a game with complicated and engaging puzzles that will take you hours to unravel, this is not the game for you.
If you want a game with endless content and hundreds, if not thousands of hours of replay value, this is not the game for you.
if however, you want a game with a good short story to it and a bit of exploration, both of the play area, and the way familys work....
This game just might be for you.

You know how the slogan of Dwarf Fortress is "Losing is fun"? This game's motto should be "Dying is fun".
This is a very historically accurate WW1 FPS. This is a very authentic WW1 FPS. And one thing that it captures particularly well, from what I can tell, is that you mean nothing. You're not even a cog in a machine, you're a particle in a duststorm. You will die a lot, for stupid and unlucky reasons. And you will kill, not due to your skill, or superior tactics, or experience, but mostly because the poor sucker at the other end of the barrel just happened to be in one of those unlucky situations in which you have died countless times yourself.
If you want to know how WW1 killed the romanticism of war, play it. If you like historically accurate games, play it. If you like the idea of dying a lot in a multiplayer shooter, play it. Otherwise don't, because although the game doesn't suck as much as being in the trenches of WW1, it still strives to.

Five nights at freddys 2 is a huge improvement from the original.
First of all, ALL of the animatronics are scarier then before, And have many new tricks for old and new players. Night 1 can be a bit overwelming for some, but, when yout ake a step back you realize that the game gives you LOTS of time on Night 1 and 2 to be able to stop the animatronics, though that anxiety feeling still sets in. I also love how the power has been partially removed, allowing players to search the cameras, use them to stop the animatronics, while still having a system where they need to watch their actions.
New Players will like this game because it is a genuine horror expirence, Night 1 will allow you to explore, but not feel safe as it did with the last game, The difficulty level as well is slow to rise, giving new players time to devolope strategies for each animatronic, Only then to throw in a new one to keep the player on edge.
Old Players will love this game because it has many old and new part of the old games, The story is expanded upon and leaves much speculation, The story is also much more fleshed out then the last game. New animatronics will feel similar to the old ones, but still have tricks up their sleeve that can freak out the player, and keep them on edge. What has happened? It is the 1990's, an era when cellphones still aren't popular and the internet is barely a thing. You come home to your family's house after a year abroad and find... no one. Everyone is gone. Your mother, your father, and your younger sister have all disappeared. What is going on?
Gone Home is not an action title. If you are looking to fire guns at zombies or run from ravenous dogs, you will be sorely disappointed. And though you are exploring a vast house, it is not a puzzler, a la 7th Guest. The best way to describe it is as an 'interactive narrative.' The game has a story to tell and emotions it wishes to convey. It doesn't do this by scaring you, though you will still be frightened of what you may or may not find in this huge, abandoned house.
The game is first and foremost a storytelling device, and therefore is not necessarily meant to be played twice (though it certainly could be) and replay value is low. That being said, it is worth it for that one playthrough, like a book that you know will never leave your shelf once your finish it, even though the memory of it lasts, nestled in the impression it has left upon you.
Perhaps you will laugh. Perhaps you will cry. I did both. As I wiped away the tears I had to stop and remind myself that it was a videogame that had done this to me.

Graphics are functional but dated, the squad system is good but not intuitive. The thing that will frustrate you the most (apart from the ever prevelant bugs) is the very thing that is pivital to the game - running over no mans land and dying again and again in order to get a glimpse of the enemies trench.
Although released at the end of April 2015, it still feels a little unfinished with bugs and poor optimisation. The devs were active but I would say seem less active after release (which is understandable). The test will be if they can continue to polish and add content to the game and take it forward incrementally to take it from an ok game to a really great game. Whether they have the time and effort do so will remain to be seen.
In it's current state however, it's worth picking up on sale if you are a fan of FPS, if only to experience something a little different.

I'd recommend Verdun on a sale day. While it's a great concept for an FPS, presented reasonably well, in practice it has some issues. The interface is somewhat clunky and fairly poorly explained in-game, and the game is really only worth playing for extended periods of time if you've got a squad of friends to play with you. There's a lot of interesting tactical possibilities presented by the squads, but again their progression system and abilities aren't very well-explained.
While it certainly captures the ambiance of WW1, the gameplay doesn't quite fit- massive cratered moonscapes are fun to fight over, but the team sizes are so minute that you often feel as if you're fighting over an abandonned field and not a massive frontline. The prevalence of artillery and limited weaponry, especially when it comes to automatics, is interesting, but the much-touted poison gas feature is an inconvenience at the worst of times. You'll almost never see anyone die to gas, or even treat it as a threat.
I did a lot of dying in a filth-encrusted trench in northern France, which was what I expected, but the experience still needs polish.

I loved loved loved Gone Home! Knowing absolutely nothing about the game, I started it late at night, alone in my living room, and was immediately drawn into what I assumed would be a typical horror plot simply because I was playing a lone girl exploring a dark old mansion. But the storyline kept surprising me with subtle twists and moments of quiet normalcy and I found myself more excited to uncover the next clue than afraid to open the next door. Although I wasn't ready for it to be over after maybe three hours of play, by the end I felt satisfied with the story I'd been told and the role I'd played to hear it.
The pacing and delivery are definitely not for everyone. Although the story moves at about the speed you choose to move it, Gone Home won't satisfy any cravings for action-packed or twitchy gameplay, and if your preferred level of character development and plot is "tell me why I'm here and what to do so I can go do it," you might be frustrated by the style. But if you have a few hours to delve into a richly detailed, interactive story experience, it's definitely worth it.

was my first Dark Souls II experience. I played the first game and loved it, despite its bad PC optimization and unstable online. Therefore, this re-release was an excellent opportunity to finally try the sequel.
Compared to the first part, in the sequel the developers tried to make better what had already been good, improving things which had flaws and adding new content. Did they succeed? Partially.
improved and balanced the RPG-elements, added lots of new weapons, items, sorceries, added new lore elements which connect to DS I and expand the universe, improved online features, controls, interface, etc. The main story is alright, and I think it's more comprehensible than in DS I, so you don't need to watch lore videos on YouTube after you beat the game to understand what just happened.
The combat is intense and fun. Enemies’ AI has been improved; it’s now harder to predict and memorize their attacks. In DS II you often are outnumbered, which is alright, but sometimes it gets annoying. Also enemy placements in some areas may be a major pain in the neck (I speak to you, Heide's Tower of Flame!).
Besides, there are other more serious flaws. Level-design is often disappointing. While some locations look good, others are mediocre at best, with textures repeating over and over, with empty places lacking details, and with horrible backgrounds. Ironically, level design in DLCs is great and is better than most locations from the core game (especially
and
DLCs). Enemies and especially bosses design is often not so good too. Many bosses resemble bosses from DS I too much. Presence of some enemies in several locations makes no sense.
Some items were changed in a strange way, compared to DS I. For some reason
made armor almost useless. Even heaviest upgraded armor sets offer little noticeable protection. The game almost forces you to play as a dexterity build character or a mage.
On the bright side, Dark Souls II has amazing optimization, unlike its predecessor. It runs smoothly with 60 FPS on highest settings, hardly ever dropping below, say, 57 FPS. Everything in the game moves very smoothly and animations are great and realistic. The game uses DX11, so you can't play it, if your GPU doesn't support it.
To sum up, Dark Souls II had a lot of potential and could have been an
sequel. However, even though it has some problems, it’s still a nice game. If you loved Dark Souls I, try the sequel. If you haven’t played Dark Souls at all, start with DS I and move to DS II Scholar of the First Sin, as there’s no point in buying original DS II now when we have Scholar.

Gone Home is often, rightfully, compared to Dear Esther. But where Dear Esther tells a complex story that requires some effort to decipher, Gone Home tells a story about a teenager who doesn't get along with her parents. Much of the gameplay in Gone Home is enjoyable exploration of a weird old house, and finding a lot of the interactable objects is satisfying enough. What isn't satisfying to me is both the length of the game and the story.
While Dear Esther can be completed in half an hour, Gone Home takes somewhat longer, upwards of two or three hours if you aren't following a guide. That said, Gone Home feels, when you're finished, like you didn't really experience much. Like you didn't get your money's worth. This is partially due to the actual time it takes to complete the game, and partially due to the story itself. I won't spoil anything, but it's essentially a story about a teenage girl who does teenage girl things. While there's nothing wrong with that at all, it's not the kind of thing I'm playing a video game to experience.
I recommend this game if you can get it for under 66% off (That's about $6.66 American). At full price it just won't feel satisfying. Even the frequent sale price of $10 left me disappointed with the amount of content.

Gone Home has some problems.  The story is extremely straightforward and falls into the same category of “heartwarming” dreck as a bad Lifetime movie.  The mechanics that Gone Home uses to deliver its story are an interesting version of the Valve-styled method of ambient story-telling and there is a lot of detail put into making sure that the player understands the different motivations of the main characters through items the player finds in the game.  Unfortunately, there is no expansion on a lot of the details that would give weight to a story like this.  I was already fully invested with the main characters by the halfway point, but I don’t feel there was enough motivation given to some of the important peripheral characters in the story.  And the ending!  Oh god, the ending…
I played this game in an evening sitting.  When I had finished the game, I went to sleep content with how the story ended.  Once I woke up the next morning, I immediately realized how awful the main characters had been and what they had done.  I couldn’t shake this feeling that by sympathizing with what made the characters’ struggle unique and touching, the storywriters had snuck a bomb on me with the ending.  My sympathy for the main characters was shattered.  Is this bad?  Is it bad that I immediately see what should be a simple love story and then immediately proceed to rip it apart?  Am I expecting too much from what should be a simple and effective plot?  I’m still not sure two weeks after finishing the game.
Ultimately, I do recommend Gone Home in spite of my problems with the execution of its story.  It is a unique experience and games like this don’t come along often enough.

It's still not Dark Souls 1, but there's a lot of things they've fixed. (+)
1) You get access to the other two blacksmiths much faster. Ornifex, with the Shadow Woods route opening up earlier, and Bastille's whatshisname, with the Dull Ember located in a less fuky position.
2) Less explodymummies! This includes Grave of Saints, Lost Bastille and Dragon Aerie (there's actually more there, but the whole area becomes skippable).
3) More summons to really break boss AI.
4) The thing that looked like a shortcut in No-Man's Wharf, is now actually a shortcut.
Then there's things that they just changed for no real reason. (-)
1) The area where the non-boss Pursuer appears first time has hollows scattered around (and other places too with many extra fodder enemies for no good reason).
2) There's a firebreath spamming dragon before Ornstein, with the actual Ornstein fight still being pis easy.
3) More of those non-lock-on-able invisible enemies that are almost impossible to hit with certain weapons (spears etc).
4) They lessened the damage you do with Lightning Spears, AND you only have a third of their uses. While still giving the option to buy them an unlimited amount. So for high Faith and Attunement characters, they're still very much spammable, but crippled under 50 Faith characters.
And then there's things they still haven't changed
1) Enemies with weird turntable-y attack tracking (all of them), or attacks connecting before the attack (Gutter dogs), or animation not correspoding what they're actually doing (hollow soldiers attacking with the shield WHILE also guarding with it somehow).
2) Heavy weapons not tracking. They had it right for the DLC weapons, why is Greatsword still messed up?
3) Shrine of Amana.
4) Not enough materials.
Overall it's a better game, not by much, but I recommend it over the original.

I never got around to play the original Just Cause. Mainly because my computer has always had issues with it, and Just Cause 2 pretty much improves the first game in all levels. Just Cause 2 is a third-person action game, and when I say action game I mean crazy jumping-from-airplanes-and-blowing-up-cities - sort of an action game. Rico, the protagonist, is like James Bond on steroids. You can pretty much do whatever you want, in a world at least twenty times (!) bigger than San Andreas, and five times bigger than World of Warcraft.
Pick your vehicle; helicopter, airplane, sports car, moped, tuk tuk etc. and pick a random location; beach, jungle, city, highway, mountain etc. to ram, stunt, blow up, crash, projectile etc. with it. Or just hook yourself to someones boat and enjoy the eyecandies of this tropical paradise. Or hook the same guy's boat into an airplane, and see him take off. Or hook the airplane to a skyscraper and see it torpedo into a ball of flames. Your choice.
The grappling hook, amongst other things, is what lift this game up from the pleasant, boring and realistic open-world games. You can use this Godly thing to pretty much survive any situation. Are you falling from insane height? No problem, just hook towards the ground and survive - Or just precipitate your parachute, that works too. It lacks actually physics though, you can't use your hook to decapitate moped drivers for example, a feature that I would want for Just Cause 3!
Sure the game is far from being realistic and serious, but with great looks, insanely huge map and more vehicles and weapons than you can count - who cares if it's unrealistic? You can stand on a plane while towing another one mid-air, for God's sake! I completely recommend this title if you are even remotely intersted in action, open-world and/or just plain time-consuming roaming and freedom. There is currently a third-party mod in the works, adding Multiplayer. It adds a whole new meaning to the already balls-chaotic world, and makes it go beyond the edge.

After buying a proper gaming pc and discarding my old poptart of a laptop i've changed my view on this game's new HD upgrade. Here's a short summary:
The Souls Franchise is by far one of the best game franchises out there, but I felt, after my first run through Vanilla Dark Souls 2, that the sequel to the infamously brutal Dark Souls 1 was lacking in the difficulty that the original had set in stone. Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin addresses that.... but in a way that let me down a little.
Let me explain something: If people say your game is too easy compared to the original, you should probably go back and study what made the original so harrowingly difficult, yet enjoyable. The difficulty curve in Scholar of the First Sin is so artificial it hurts. Simply adding more enemies to make the playerbase happy is not an adequate way to satisfy their needs and wants for a more naturally difficult experience.
That being said, Dark Souls 2 was a good game in the way that it adds obscure flavor to the mix, for better or for worse, regardless of how easy it was.
The verdict here is that Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin is good, but some players, including myself, will notice how the dev team lazily threw together a harder obstacle course to make us happy.

This review has been modified from the original, which can be found
The Fullbright team went above and beyond making the house and its occupants come alive even though no one is at home. It’s like the house takes on the personality of each of its inhabitants, weaving an immersive, intricate story that is also interactive. I almost felt bad rummaging through belongings because the developers do such a great job of conveying the intimacy of a person’s living space. Like a real home, everyone has their own private living space. The library, office, and bar belong to the father while the mom has her greenhouse and kitchen. Oscar, the deceased uncle, still haunts the basement with his possessions, while Sam inhabits the upper rooms. Surprisingly, while the parents stay within their respective areas, Sam overtakes the whole house, laying claim to rooms that aren’t even hers.  This in of itself speaks volumes about Sam.
There are an array of items that delve into each family member’s personalities, relationships, and struggles while adding layers of complexity to their decisions and coping mechanisms, particularly for the dad and Sam.
As far as game mechanics go, Gone Home is not a puzzle exploration game. It is still a game, nonetheless. It’s a simple point-and-click  interaction with the surrounding environment in order to better understand the people in the house and where they have gone. I don’t believe Fullbright’s intention for the game was for people to focus on solving a puzzle. It’s designed to be an artistic, interactive platform for exploring young love and the human condition of one family, and in that, they excelled. This requires patience and a personal investment on the part of the gamer with Kate’s family.
Understandably, this type of game is not for everyone. If you go into it perceiving it to be a horror/puzzle themed game (or have certain disdain for love stories) then it will fall short of your expectations. If you’re a person who doesn’t have the patience to thoroughly search a house for clues, and desire more of an action-packed rush, then this game is probably not for you. Likewise, if you are a person that needs resolution at the end of your games, then you may want to skip on buying this one because you’ll be left disappointed.
Personally, I think the game is incredible. I was floored by all the rich detail and love that the Fullbright team poured into it. While the mechanics of Gone Home are not meant to be difficult or complex, the game itself challenges you to identify and empathize with the family – perhaps even relate to them.
The only significant drawback to the game is that it is insanely short. It took me two hours to complete it, and once the story concludes, there isn’t any replay value to it. It is still worth playing through once, however, because it is an amazing rendering of a family trying to find its identity. If the price of the game versus the amount of total playing hours concerns you, wait for it to go on sale in order to justify the cost.

Gone Home is an exploration game to find out the history of yourself, your sister and your parents. That's the core of the game, it is more like an interactive story at your own pace, it does not have any decision making points or anything, just a regular linear storyline.
The sound design is awesome, it's the best thing in the game. You will feel very immersive in the game, the ambience, the TV's, radios, the doors, light switches, everything in the house has a great sound. Also, the voice acting is so great that when you start to know more the person in those dialogs you will try to find everyone to keep listening to it and know all about it.
The visual design isn't that great but the interaction in your house is pretty nice, you can grab, read and open almost anything you see and all the 90's references are very good too.
The gameplay was the negative point of the game for me. I miss an option to run or walk a little bit faster in the house because it is so big and in some moments I felt worried to find out what was really going on and the character looks so distant and so indifferent about what was presented to me that I felt disconnected. I wanted to find out that was happened, I was feeling the story, immersed in it, but I couldn't react that way. I was an robot without feeling. And that was very frustrating.
So, if you want a good interactive story with a great voice acting and sound (even when your character doesn't seems to react at all) you should try this title. If it's not the case and you want some control in the story or making decisions, this is not a game for you.

I liked this game but there are a few caveats.
You pick up items and look at them. You will be reading a lot of notes and things. Listen to music and some logs. That is it.
This game is about the characters who inhabit a regular world in the year 1995 and their story arcs. Nothing more, Nothing less.
Since the game's subject matter is about being in highschool in the mid '90s, I found the story very relateable and authentic to the experience. I can see younger or older people not relating as well and end up disconnected from the subject matter.
Normal price is about $20 which is pretty rough for 2 hours of gameplay. Wait for a sale.
However, I did replay it 3 times, finding new things each time. First run, then with commentary, then with a non-gamer friend. It works well as a gateway game due to relateable subject matter and easy gameplay.
I like how it took its horror trappings and eventually upends them with a nice real world touch. It uses your normal expectations of creepy gaming against itself. The dark rooms, running for the light switch, etc...
Would I want every game to be exploration with no combat, no puzzles, no managament? No, but this is a nice break from the norm.
One review of bioshock infinite said "it would be a lot better without the tacked on, dull, combat", well, I guess Gone Home finally answers that.

I went into this game not knowing anything about it but Steam's description.  I was expecting your run of the mill horror/suspense game.  That wasn't what I got.  Not even close.
Horror games where you're locked in a creepy abandoned house during a storm are a dime a dozen.  I can look around any corner and find one. However, the experience I got playing Gone Home is something I've honestly never seen in a video game before.  It's very nontraditional gameplay.  You don't spend the game searching for matches or shooting at ghosts or bad guys.  It's not action-packed.  It's entirely emotion-driven, but it's eminently well-crafted.
I went in expecting a few hours of flinching horror, and instead I got a short but deeply human story with evocative, honest writing and beautiful, heartfelt narration.  It wasn't what I was expecting, but it was very worth the time spent playing it.

As many of you have probably figured from the game's extremely mixed reception, Gone Home is basically a story-driven exploration game in an ambient sense; where most of the story comes from the objects and notes in the environment, occasionally followed by narrated sequences of the diary-entries of a teenage girl called Samantha (Sam).
Mechanically, the game is slightly poorly optimised, but as it's barely vital in a game like this, I'll let it slide.
Trying to search for every little piece of writing around the house (which you are confined in, unfolding the series of events in Sam's life) is somewhat tedious, really, but not overwhelmingly so. I spent around four hours in the game, because i scoured everywhere quite methodically. Realistically, the game is around two to three hours long, so it might be wise to wait for a sale with the price being as high as it is.
Now for the writing, voice-acting and atmosphere.
The narration is excellent- in fact even some of the best I've heard. Along with the writing. It portrays a pretty cheesy story structure, but is presented in such a genuine fashion- you can really see there was heart put into this project. The little notes, pictures and slips of paper really show well what's going on in the house, though the parts about Sam's parents aren't nearly as thrilling, mainly focusing on work. But they all add nicely to the atmosphere, which, unfortunately can be a little strained due to the player scouring every little nook and cranny. I'd suggest looking up some stuff you missed after completing the game, as certain bits of dialogue are very, and I mean, VERY cryptic to get.
Personally, I think the emotion carried through the narration, the amazingly well done ambient soundtrack that played along them and the general setting of the game all make for an experience I'm glad I didn't miss. Even if the product was a little short and pricey. Money well spent on a sale.
(Also the 90s vibe you get off this is very enjoyable!)

I'm all about the either challenging or relaxing coop experience, ranging from the tactically-focused "insane" difficulty or the laid-back (but will still sometimes defeat you) "normal" difficulty.
You can unlock some weapons for free using the vendor system. As far as weapons that aren't in the vendor list go, you don't earn currency fast enough to buy much permanently, maybe 1-2 within your first 3 weeks of playing. Repairing your gear is another thing that holds this game back, because the repair cost should be less. As it is, you will often refrain from using the best gear you unlock very often because it also costs the most to repair. If you are wearing a full set of high-tier armor and using a high-tier weapon (which aren't always the "BEST" weapons mind you) your repair cost can be more than what you earn from completing a level!
But all things considered I love the experience of this game! Would FAMAS again.

This game really had me on edge until I googled and found out it wasn't, as I feared it might be, a horror game. This might make some people unhappy, but not me. I'm no great lover of jump scares. I don't know if this game will appeal to most, but it's a quiet, difficult story about a teen struggling to find her identity in the mid 90s and the older sister who comes home to find her family has changed dramatically while she was abroad. TL;DR: A flawed, but decent title that is a risky buy due to population issues, but if you are lucky to get into a match, it is quite an interesting experience
--
Dino D-Day is a rather old title that, unlike TF2, wasn't so lucky at getting wildly popular. As hard as it tries, it struggles to keep a healthy population, it being considered lucky to even find a server with 15 people playing on it, and even moreso if you have an elite player who played for years on your team.. Otherwise it wasn't gonna be a lot of fun.
Maybe the reason it died out was due to balancing issues, some weapons and classes being far more useful than others and, in skilled hands, can cause half the server to ragequit. Hardgrave, a class that uses an M1-Grand, could be considered the most powerful Allied class in the game because of how strangely powerful his main weapon is and the fact that he can charge up a meter that allows him to go rambo with his fist for a short time. Vets of the game tend to use this guy a lot, and it isn't hard to see why.
And that is just the Allies, the Axis have some issues with balancing as well, such as a sniper who seems to be able to call down air strikes more often compared to the Allies, or how their dinos tend to suddenly become amazingly more powerful in smaller scale battles just to name two. Of course, player experience is also a factor, so don't expect a noob to  dominate the whole server because he chose Hardgrave. A guy with 1000 hours, however...
Maybe the reason the game died down so hard was because people were no longer amused by the idea of nazi dinos anymore... At first, you would hear about people constantly trying to get on the Axis side just so they could run about as a T-rex or raptor and nom faces off while getting a laugh at how silly it was. But maybe now the gimmic lost its luster, considering how few fans remain, let alone how many people leave just weeks after a sale boosts it up by 100 people. Not like the dinos are that great anyways, considering their steep learning curves and lack of proper training simulation to help people better understand how their critters work. And even with experience, larger scale battles are probably better fought with German infantry and gun-mounted dinos, since melee combat would be rather risky with all the gunfire.. Smaller scale battles, on the other hand, make it consideribly easy for melee dinos, unless your target is a master marksmen.
Now, I know you probably are confused by the big wall of text that makes the game out to be bad, but... Despite its many flaws, I still had fun in this game. Sure, balancing issues are annoying, and the small population means you are going to be forced to fight against elite players who will hand you your butt over and over again till you give up and leave, let alone the fact that after an hour or less of play, a server with 20 people will soon be reduced to 8 (which is dreadfully dull). But, if you ARE able to get into a good game, it can be fairly enjoyable. I had my fair share of good times with the game, and got my money's worth out of it at least. The dinos, while not perfect, do add an interesting new twist to gameplay and forces you to rethink how you play an FPS game, where more often than not, sometimes you have to drop your gun and punch a raptor in the face to death.
Although the game is a fairly decent change of pace compared to more bland FPS games out there, I still feel I should warn you that if you DO get this, pray that there is still a population left.. As I said before, it is still struggling with the population, and the game just isn't as fun 4V4 compared to 8V8 or higher.

Reviewing is boring so here is a recipe for pancakes,
Ingredients:
4tbsp plain flour (about 100g)
1 large free range egg
½ pint semi-skimmed milk + water (about 300ml - ¾ milk ¼ water)
Pinch of salt
Butter for frying
How to make pancakes:
Sieve the flour and salt into a large bowl and make a well in the mixture.
Break in the egg and stir to make a breadcrumby mix.
In a jug add 1/3 of a pint of milk and top up with water to make 1/2 a pint (200ml milk, 100ml water) - this makes a lovely light batter.
Add the milk and the water mix bit by bit, beating constantly to avoid lumps.
Tip:*If you have a food processor just throw all the ingredients in and zap until smooth!
Pop a large frying pan over a medium heat.
Add a large knob of butter (roughly 50g) and melt.
Pour the excess butter into a small bowl and reserve it for later.
Using a ladle pour a spoonful of the pancake batter into the hot pan and swirl to get a full covering - cook for about 1 min each side (it's ready when it's easy to flip over).
Serve immediately with sugar and lemon or other exciting toppings.

To be honest, I was a bit worried when I saw how quickly this game's release date was pushed up (early 2015 was the first tentative date). But after some quality play time, I can safely say that Five Nights at Freddy's 2 is a solid sequel that doesn't feel rushed in the slightest.
First, let's get the obvious out of the way. FN@F 2 follows the same tried and true formula as its predecessor: You are working the night shift at a family-friendly pizzeria that is home to a group of bright and cheery animatronic characters... all of which come alive after midnight and try to kill you. Holed up in your office with nothing but camera feeds, a flashlight, and a mask modeled after the pizzeria's mascot, your goal is to survive through all six hours of your shift for five nights, with each night much harder than the last.
Compared to the original Five Nights at Freddy's, the sequel has an insane difficulty curve. Twice the number of hostile animatronics means three times the stress of micromanaging your cameras and lights to keep tabs on everything. There are no doors to protect you this time. Instead, when an animatronic gets close, you must don the Freddy Fazbear mask given to you to trick them into thinking you're one of them, where they will ignore you and eventually leave the room. However, you cannot use your flashlight or check the cameras while the mask is on. And sometimes, if you are REALLY unlucky, the animatronics will attack you anyway.
But without a doubt the hardest feature in this game is a music box in one of the rooms which must be remotely wound up and kept running at all times. If the music box stops playing at any time, your death is all but guaranteed at the hands of a demented marionette. And the further you are in the game, the faster the music box winds down. It's a unique replacement for the original's limited power supply, but needlessly frustrating. A single second taken to wind up the music box is all that's needed for an animatronic to jump you, and more often than not a few animatronics will camp right outside the office, forcing you to don the Freddy mask and sit there helplessly as the music box completely winds down. If the AI ever felt unfair in the first game, then it blatantly and mercilessly cheats in this one.
In spite of this, as a whole the game is scary fun, and in some ways even more terrifying than the original. A few mysteries from the plot of the original game are cleared up, giving you a better understanding of series' dark and horrific lore. If you enjoy games that ramp on the tension, then scare you right out of your seat when you least expect it, this game, and by extension the original Five Nights at Freddy's, is right up your alley.

I've been dragged by a very powerful narrative, the one developed in Gone Home. Not only is it about that narrative, it's also about how it intertwined with the gameplay. The feeling of being myself the one that is unfolding the story that is wrapped in that house is very intense. I experienced a lot of things, I've been making up different stories as I was examining the house and the traces left behind. I thought something terrible happened to Sam, to the family; have their parents got divorced? have her father killed her mother? I also believed that Sam and Lonnie committed suicide! (it seems to be a recurrent thought on other players).
Why do I get to think all those things? Even though there is sometimes a voice-over that narrates some of the events that happened during Katie's (yourself) leave, most of the time you are picking up pieces of the story by the traces left behind by the family, textual and non. That's the magic of the game. The story is probably quite linear, but I don't know what would have happened if I had not scrutinised every part of the house in the proper order. And that's the incredible thing about this game and video games in general: if I have the freedom of choosing my own pace, what to see and what not (in this case that's absolutely true), why did I follow a way of playing that allowed me to create a meaningful experience? Could I have had a meaningful experience playing in a very different way? Now it's impossible to know! Well, according to this entry posted by Gaynor on The Fullbright Company website, that could have been possible. But as I already know the story as it was intended to be experienced, I suppose it doesn't matter anyway.
It's incredibly well played, though. For instance, one of the first things you do is to listen to two recorded messages in the answering machine (besides the one you left). The second is specially disturbing. You won't know what all that was about until the very last moment of the game. Or when you just see a colourful skull (made in Mexico) but it's not until you advance in the game that you know where it come from (a trip of Lonnie to Mexico). It's that kind of idea of leaving pieces of the story scattered all around the house, without explicitly linking them together, which makes this game so unique. Nevertheless, I have to stress again that the mechanics, the playability, the game experience, the interactivity are essential to the game. It's not just a narrative-driven game. Not at all. It's an exploration game, that's the best description, as proposed by its developers. Essential to the experience is the idea of exploration, touching, seeing, flipping and reading things. There is no narrative without playability. It wouldn't make sense.

In relation to the story, the pieces of "what happened" are just that, pieces, traces, nothing too much explicit. You have to fill the gaps and... well, not only do you just reconstruct the last year's events when you were abroad, but you also get deep into the history of the family, things that happened before you were born, while you can intuit psychological aspects of your relatives and their relationships. And that's the key, you are left with a lot of space to speculate and never is stated in a very explicit way (uncle Oscar issues, the relationship between your grandfather and your father, your father's career, your mother's affairs and career, your neighbour Daniel, your sister's complex process of self-awareness, etcetera.).
And all of this is achieved through a list of agents and mediators: Sam's voice-over triggered after some exploration events; your own descriptions of things before you actually touch them (sometimes is funny like, "barf", "Oh no..", or even refusing to continue to read a letter); the different inscriptions (official communications, personal messages, handwritten, letters, drawings, etcetera.), the objects in the house that can be grabbed and examined; the music; the map; the doors, drawers, and secret doors; the house; the combinations; the keys; the pictures and the paintings.

While not as remarkable as Dark Souls, Dark Souls 2 is still a good timesink!
This game seems slightly easier than the previous one and the world isn't as memorable. The main reason for this is that you get access to fast travel right from the start. A lot of the areas are more linear and since you can freely warp between safe zones you'll ignore most of the areas once you've travelled through them once. They lack the reasonable connectivity of the previous game too. That's not to say that there aren't any nice looking areas in this game, it's just you end up spending less time travelling through them and the immersion takes a hit. I enjoyed planning for long trips in DS1 and as a result I probably know Undead Burg better than my actual neighbourhood! (If you hated the constant back and forth in DS1, then this isn't a complaint for you!)
Combat- and techwise this game is an improvement from Dark Souls, everything seems to flow and work better and there's probably even more options for building and gearing your character. Multiplayer is active as hell (even on higher levels I kept getting invaded all the time, human or hollow) and connectivity issues seem non-existent, even with the region lock off. Some in-game systems have been changed for the better and some complications have been streamlined, like now you can swap freely between covenants without penalties, or helping others in co-op heals away your "cursed" healthbar and makes you human again. You'll probably still need to consult a wiki to figure some things out or find out how many secrets you've missed.
There's a story that probably makes sense only when you connect all the dots, but then again it was similar in Dark Souls how you probably started making lore connections only after completing the game at least once. These are not games to play only for the story. DS1 and DS2 are connected only via references so it's not like you'd miss out on the plot starting with this one.
Not having played Demon's Souls I can't compare to that, but while I found a lot of the designs in DS1 groundbreaking and really innovative, DS2 has more recycling going on. Most of the equipment and enemy types and even bosses seem to be brought back and instead of creative monster design about 90% of the things you fight in DS2 are humanoid armoured enemies. Less imaginative. Then again, maybe it's just that I played DS1 first?
The three expansions packed into this edition were good, they weren't over in an hour and they felt a lot more challenging than most of the stuff in the base game, the Fume Knight encounter especially. Not having played DS2 without this Scholar of the First Sin edition I couldn't really say what all the other changes/additions were, but there's more stuff now making this the best deal for newcomers. The pricing sucks if you were an early adopter but that's how it always goes with GOTY editions.
While Dark Souls 2 is eventually more forgettable than the previous one, I still enjoyed my time through it, it is a great game. Dark Souls (1) even with some jankiness is still the most important game of this decade in my opinion, so you should complete that one first (and maybe learn something about yourself in the process). Once that's done and you still hunger for more, then Dark Souls 2 is a fine game to continue with, even if it isn't as groundbreaking. Just make sure you have lots of time, it's not a short experience.
Come to think of it, Dark Souls 1/2 are kind of the original MMO experience for me, like it was 10 years ago. There's huge worlds to explore and weird monsters to encounter, you get to figure out your gear and once in a while when you're immersed some other player appears to backstab you, so you're constantly on your toes. And no subscription fees or micropayments!
