Reviewing is boring so here is a recipe for pancakes,
Ingredients:
4tbsp plain flour (about 100g)
1 large free range egg
½ pint semi-skimmed milk + water (about 300ml - ¾ milk ¼ water)
Pinch of salt
Butter for frying
How to make pancakes:
Sieve the flour and salt into a large bowl and make a well in the mixture.
Break in the egg and stir to make a breadcrumby mix.
In a jug add 1/3 of a pint of milk and top up with water to make 1/2 a pint (200ml milk, 100ml water) - this makes a lovely light batter.
Add the milk and the water mix bit by bit, beating constantly to avoid lumps.
Tip:*If you have a food processor just throw all the ingredients in and zap until smooth!
Pop a large frying pan over a medium heat.
Add a large knob of butter (roughly 50g) and melt.
Pour the excess butter into a small bowl and reserve it for later.
Using a ladle pour a spoonful of the pancake batter into the hot pan and swirl to get a full covering - cook for about 1 min each side (it's ready when it's easy to flip over).
Serve immediately with sugar and lemon or other exciting toppings.

As a huge fan of the series, I say that Dark Souls 2 is a good game. Despite being easier than its predecessors (Demon`s Souls (PS exclusive) and Dark Souls) it is still a very challenging game. The PvP is better than Dark Souls.
In my opinion:
Pros:
+ combat system + the first time you play dark souls or its predecessors it is noticible that combat is not underated as it is for exemple in Skyrim (which is a very good game too). Facing multiple enemies is an overwelming task, normally resulting in death. This is not a hack and slash game like Diablo, where you face 5 to 20 enemies and you hit 3 spells and obliterate them. Back to one of my favorite games...when you play skyrim you don`t feel the weapon impact on the enemy, it just slices through as if there isn`t an obstacle. + game difficulty + this game is hard ... not very hard and not even close to impossible where computer usually cheats to kill you. Therefore, you can have lots of fun trying to crawl your way through the game.

This is an amazing game. This, for me, is actualy a refreshing game. The atmosphere, the surroundings, the weapons and even it's high amount of realism (wich I love in games), everything makes you feel like you're in world war one. And let's be honost, there are not many games that actualy use the world war one setting. Most of it is futuristic, present time oriented and almost none of it is based on actual history. In one word, I would discribe this game as beautifull.
In order to kill a man, you have to fire a well placed shot. It is incredibly easy to miss your target, but when you hit him, he is down and he's not getting up. So this is quite realistic. Not like most first person shooters where you have to empty a  30 round clip in the general area in order to kill him or her. However, missing you're target can be quite frustrating, because most of the time, that person is not going to mis you.
So, YOU can be killed just as easily and that is where my biggest frustration of the game comes to play. It is incredibly easy, to spawn, run toward the enemy because you have to engage them in order to get a foothold in their trenches and get killed in les then 3 seconds. Enemys can be everywhere. And thats when the waiting period of 11 second and some time even 15 seconds or more starts. If this happens once, no problem. If this happens several of times in a row, well, then it gets really frustrating. It really makes you hold back.
In a way, it makes the game more realistic. It invokes fear of dieing in the game, because everybody hates waiting for relatively long periods of time. And thus, you play more carefull and you hold back more in order to stay alive longer. Longer than you have to wait to respawn and have more time and more chances to actualy try and kill a man. However, if to many people on your team are holding back, this can cost your team the round.
For me personaly, if it happens to often that I have to wait longer to spawn than I have actualy played after I spawned. than, the fun is gone fairly quick. That is why I can't play the game for longer than an hour. So the only thing I would like to have changed if I had a saying in this game, is that the waiting time to respawn would be cut down by half, to about 6 or 7 seconds. Even then, the game will not be remotely near anything of the Call of Duty franchise, wich I loath so dearly. And with that I mean certain aspects of Call of Duty like fast paced gameplay or lack of realism
Nevertheless, I would recomend this game to everybody, because it is fun when your not dieing constantly.

Verdun – What, who, how? (a review by Muffs(ie))
-----------------------------------------------------
Verdun is a first person world war 1 trench warfare game by  M2H and Blackmill Games.
As the title says, the game is based on ‘The Battle of Verdun’ which began in February 1916 and lasted about 10 months. Around 700 000 soldiers died, were wounded or went missing during that battle.
But enough history, let’s get right into the game itself.
You’ll most likely play the ‘Frontlines game-mode’ where two teams have to cross no man’s land in an attempt to reach the opponents’ trench, get a foothold and finally take the trench. So this game is mainly based around momentum, if your team is on the offensive side, you can charge into the battlefield towards the enemies that are trying to defend their trench line.
You’ll need to really work together as a team to cross the no mans’ land and get in the other trench. More information about teams and squads comes later in this review.
This game mode can become a bit tedious, where you’re waiting in your trench for the enemy to come, but the enemy doesn’t come at all. You’ll sit there for a good 5-ish minutes before eventually getting killed by a mortar.
Most of the games I’ve played were very even and ended in a tie game, which isn’t as rewarding as winning a match.
Other than the ‘Frontlines’ game mode, there are two more game modes. These are:
* Rifles-only team deathmatch
* Normal deathmatch
But the most amount of players are playing the ‘Frontlines’ game mode. And those other two are just a bit ignored.
There are 2 main sides which fight against each other and these are the ‘Entente Powers’ and the ‘Central Powers’. Both sides have 4 different squads with 4 players in those squads, every squad has its own role such as recon or attack.
Depending on the squad type, the squad leader or NCO can call in specials commands such as artillery support, gas assaults or an airplane recon.
It’s important that every player in the squad and in the team communicates with each other to let them know what’s happening. I’ve found that if your team is just shooting around and doing what they want to do, you’ll probably lose your trench in no time.
On to the maps! Most maps are huge, but that’s needed in a trench-warfare based game. You need to have that bit of freedom to outflank the enemy trench.
That being said, I think the maps look decent enough for a first person shooter. Many trenches, stacks of logs, barbed wire, metal sheets, craters, mud, water… are thrown on the battlefield to give it that authentic feel that you’re really in the battle. And I think that  M2H & Blackmill Games have done a great job with the maps and the variety in them, hats off to those 2 there!
There is a huge amount of guns to choose from and to unlock after you level up in your squad.
- Most of the guns are bolt-action rifles and are pretty fun to use. Especially when you can kill that soldier that’s sprinting trough no mans’ land with a headshot.
- Sniper rifles are a nice add-on to help defend your trench from attacking soldiers or to take out mounted machine gunners when your team is attacking, but they can be a pain in the *** when you’re trying to cross no mans’ land.
- Heavy machine guns have to be mounted on the ground before you can use them accurately. They are really overpowered if you don’t have a good sniper or grenadier to take them out before you push. Otherwise your push will just be ripped to shreds when you set foot in the trench.
- Pistols are mostly used by the NCO and can be quite useful when taking the enemies’ trench.
- Sub-machine guns are a bit overpowered to be quite honest. They tear trough the soldiers like a hot knife through a piece of butter.
In conclusion: Verdun is one of the best (if not THE best) world war one first person shooter out there at the moment. It makes you feel as if you’re fighting in the trenches yourself with water in your boots, your gun jamming, grenades exploding left and right, being stuck in barbed wire.. It all adds onto that authentic feel the game gives you and that is what Verdun is all about!

Better than most games but worse than the rest of the series.
Play them first (Dark Souls and Demon Souls - Bloodborne is also fantastic).
To elaborate, Dark Souls 2 has a huge flaw in my opinion and that is its dodgy dodging system:
- The amount of invincibilty frames within a roll are dependant on a stat which can cause situations where it feels like you have been damaged unfairly: this is completely against the general trend of the series being harsh but fair which is a trend that I and many others value highly as it enhances satisfaction when you do something right and decreases frustration when you fail because you know you weren't treated unfairly.
- The speed and distance of your rolls are determined by your encumberence which is common trait between most of the games in the series, excluding Bloodborne, and is a good thing in my opinion as it encourages careful planning when constructing builds and increases realism by making it difficult for a guy in stone armour to flip all over the place while making it relatively easy for a guy in cloth to move with much agility. The problem with this in Dark Souls 2 is that pretty much the same animation is used for the different levels of encumberence when rolling, excluding far extremes such as when a player is wearing so much armour that their character can barely run; while this may not seem like such a big deal, it can cause invisible problems for new players: when I first played this game on the Xbox 360 I had no idea that I had a vastly inferior roll at 60 or 70% compared to 10% because, unlike it's predecessors, the rolls look almost the same. This is likely because it would have taken alot of time to animate the many different rolls( like 10 or something around that mark) compared to the few types of rolls in Dark Souls( I think there's 3) and so they chose to use the same animation and merely tinker with the technicalities of each roll under a certain threshold( 80% I believe). Anyway, this caused my ignorant past self to fail to see that the reason I was finding it so hard to dodge things was because I could only roll a couple feetd due to my equipment weight and I think that it could have been handled in a better way.
- The hit boxes are just atrocious with swords that have hitboxes five times as thick as their blade and twice as long. This is all I need to say. It makes the game feel unfair and frustrating. (Edit. I have played some more PvP and it's an even bigger issue there. This may be a problem with latency but, judging by the words of other players and the hitboxes of NPCs, I doubt it is entirely down to that.)
The placement of enemies in this game runs counter to the merits of its combat system which can also lead to frustrating situations when you are surrounded and limited by a system designed for one on one combat. Not much to say about this again as it will suffice to say that it feels like this game was designed by a completely different team to the other games of the series(Actually, I beleive it was which would explain a lot) and therefore lacks the same feel careful placement; this could be seen as a good thing for variety's sake but in this case I think more of the same would have done just fine.
The designs of the enemies and bosses in this game are also rather bland as the game repeatedly presents you with "Big guy in armour with huge weapon" and "Huge guy in armour with big weapon" which contrasts greatly with the creativity of the enemies in the other games such as the wisps in Dark Souls(they're not what you would think), the amygdalas in bloodborne and cool bosses like Sif - a huge bloody wolf wielding a sword in his mouth protecting the grave of his master. This left me sighing every time I encounter another uninspired enemy wherever I went in Dark Souls 2.
Another problem, which may be down to the internet of myself and the people I have played with, is latency in PvP. I have found this to be another facet of the menagerie of things that cause frustration in the PvP of Dark Souls 2; I'm not saying that this is not a problem with most games, but lag combined with awful hitboxes and dodgy dodging has managed to♥♥♥♥♥♥me off to no end when playing in PvP. I will say that it is extremely satisfying when PvP goes well.
I find that this is a common theme in Dark Souls 2: when it gets it right, it REALLY gets it right; it is just unfortunate that this a rarity.
An example of when the game gets it right is weapon variety. Just like the other games in the series, excluding Bloodborne again, the replayability of this game is vastly expanded by the large amount of options when equiping your character which can breed a great many play styles(Bloodborne is excused because the weapons in that game are more versatile than those found in DeS, DaS and DaS2).
The game is also pretty pretty! Unfortunately, the DirectX upgrade for Scholar of the First Sin has split the communtiy as From Software decided to host separate servers for DX9 and DX11(I may be wrong on the version numbers) which means that players of different versions cannot interact within the game. This means that there are less people to play with on both servers and only serves to shrink the in-game community.
This game is very meh, for the most part, and left me with a sour taste in my mouth every time I stopped playing. I have tried four different builds (Str, Dex, Int and Pyro) and have yet to find anything as satisfying as any one build in Dark Souls. I will say that you should probably play this game out of principle but be warned that it pales in comparison to Dark Souls. It will probably have a few ups and many downs but this is probably worth enduring so that you can fully enjoy Dark Souls 3 when it comes out; Miyazaki, the director of Dark Souls, is working on Dark Souls 3, whereas he did not work on Dark Souls 2 which should hopefully mean that it will be of a much higher standard than Dark Souls 2. We can only wait and see.
Further edit: I never get frustrated at Dark Souls 1 - The game feels like it treats me fairly - but whenever I turn this game off it's because I feel like it has cheated me. I hate that I hate this game and I'm so god damn glad that DS3 looks good.

A shameful display, in my little opinion.

I don't like Dark Souls 2. Here's why. (I'm comparing it to Dark Souls 1, by the way.)
TL:DR: The makers of Dark Souls 2 didn't quite understand why Dark Souls 1's difficulty made it good. They just made it hard for the sake of it being hard.
PROS
-Better graphics
-(Kind of) Bigger world to explore
-You can now go human anywhere at any time
-Backstabbing is a bit better
-Beards & tattoos
-Enemy AI is better
-You can now teleport between bonfires right away
CONS
-Every time you die, you lose ~5% of your max health, which you have to go human to get back
-Whenever you block an enemy's attack with a shield, they are not staggered, meaning you have to wait until they are completely done attacking for you to have a small attack window
-Enemy AI is better
-The enemy's weapons all have huge hitboxes, making rolling much harder to do
-Instead of starting out with 5 Estus Flasks, you start out with zero until a certain part of the game, where you get one. Each time you upgrade the Estus Flask, you don't make them more powerful, you just get one more to use
-Instead of healing instantly as soon as the healing animation starts, you heal ~75% of your health over a course of a few seconds after the healing animation finishes, meaning you have a few seconds of standing there doing nothing, during which enemies can hit you and cancel the healing process
-The more common healing items are variants of Lifegems, the most common of which are not regained at bonfires, but can be bought from a limited supply from a few merchants, or found on enemy bodies or around the world. These Lifegems heal ~75% of your health over a course of what feels like 10 seconds
-You have to teleport back to the second bonfire in the game whenever you want to level up, which the game never directly tells you
Awesome.

As a huge fan of the series, I say that Dark Souls 2 is a good game. Despite being easier than its predecessors (Demon`s Souls (PS exclusive) and Dark Souls) it is still a very challenging game. The PvP is better than Dark Souls.
In my opinion:
Pros:
+ combat system + the first time you play dark souls or its predecessors it is noticible that combat is not underated as it is for exemple in Skyrim (which is a very good game too). Facing multiple enemies is an overwelming task, normally resulting in death. This is not a hack and slash game like Diablo, where you face 5 to 20 enemies and you hit 3 spells and obliterate them. Back to one of my favorite games...when you play skyrim you don`t feel the weapon impact on the enemy, it just slices through as if there isn`t an obstacle. But the Poise system and the game physics itself make you feel like you are in a true combat.
+ game difficulty + this game is hard ... not very hard and not even close to impossible where computer usually cheats to kill you. Therefore, you can have lots of fun trying to crawl your way through the game.
+ character versatility + you can create any kind of character ... a full plate warrior hold a great sword... a cleric casting heals and lightning bolts ... a naked guy casting spells... a rogue with light armor and backstabing... a caster with heavy armor ... ANYTHING ... people tend to use greatswords as you will see in multiplayer ... i think Freud explains
+ panoply of items + lots of cool items and spells ... good looking gear
Cons:
- PAUSE - this game DOES NOT pause. So you should expect some problems in real life when you just CAN`T let the joystick go. Thou i think this is fun, i died a couple of times because of this.
- the world -  i don`t know how to explain this. The cenario is fantastic and the atmosphere is CREEPY. But ... i don`t know something is missing... so i say ... imagine SKYRIM but with this game`s physics and an ominous atmhosphere.
- the NPCs - this is not my opinion ...but people always complain to me about this feature. They say the NPCs are miles high on LSD because dialog makes no sense. Some say that japanese dialog are novele-vague, just like their animes, don`t make sense. BUT... i think this is what the game proposes ... everyone you meet in the game is DEAD and LOOSING their minds... including you!
As a fan: play this game, but before, play Demon Soul`s

The game has two boring support classes and two average offence classes.
Support:
Medic has a really short range shotgun that is practically useless, a medikit he can heal people with and a defib.
Engineer has claymores, an SMG which is only good at short range and an armor repair kit.
Offence:
Assault has an assault rifle which is good at short and mid range, ammo packs he can give people (including himself).
Sniper has a sniper rifle which is good at mid and long range.
There's various PvP game modes, Co-Op and survival Co-Op.
PvP:
You'll get spawncamped/wrecked by players with the best gear and a lot of experience.
Co-Op:
It's boring and repetive. You get ranked by how fast you did everything.
Survival Co-Op:
The only thing that is even remotely fun. It takes several hours to beat and is insanely hard without a really good team and good equipment. You need tokens to play it. The game gives three tokens every day that you can save for another day.
The store has two ways you can buy things. You can buy stuff with real money or in-game cash. It takes forever to grind for the money you need for equipment, which you recieve at the end of a Co-Op mission/PvP match.
There's also Crown equipment, which is the best stuff in the game. You get Crowns by getting a lot of killscore in Co-Op missions and doing said missions under ten minutes. This is impossible without a team with good gear. The Crown equipment lasts a single day and takes a ridiculous amount of Crowns to actually get it.
The maximum amount of Crowns you get varies on difficulty.
Easy: None.
Normal: Around 20 or 30 Crowns
Hard: 56 Crowns
Insane: No idea, but I'd guess it's somewhere around 100 or 160 Crowns.
The amount of Crowns needed to buy a single piece Crown equipment is around thousands and you can get Crowns from a misson ONCE PER DAY. You can beat your earlier score to get more Crowns, but once you've reached the max per misson, you won't get any more crowns.
Don't play this game. It's boring and sucks fun out of you.

This is  relatively short game, different to anything you have ever experienced before. You start of as Katie, a 20 year old just returning home from a year in europe. However you return home to an empty house. This is set in 1995, before you could just call someone on their mobile phone to find out where they are, so you explore the house.
The controls are very simple, You use the arrow keys to move forward, back, left and right, and then you can use shift to pick things up. That it. Simple. The game is very simple to, you move around the house to try and find out where you family members are - your sister sam, and your mother and father.
The game primarely revolves around the sister - sam, however depending on how long you want to spend on the game yourself, you can find out information about the character's mother, father and even great uncle, whoms house they are currently living in.
While it feels like a horror game, with something going to jump scare you any minute, that doesn't happen, rather you keep on exploring until all the pieces of the puzzel click. And that's it. The game's over. It doesn't feel sudden. In fact, you can feel it building up to the end from the very get go, but it was an unsatisfying ending. Without going into too much detail, and spoiling it, I will say that it left a bad taste in my mouth. But I feel as if that was the point of the game, that's how it was meant to end.
Regardless of how I felt about the ending, I can honestly say I enjoyed this game. I finished it within an hour and a half, so it isn't a long game, but when you finally figure everything out, when everything clicks about where all the family members are, that is the satifying part. And because of this, I would definitely recomend it to all my friends, expeically if you enjoy indie, art and story based games.

So to preface this, I played Dark Souls and initially hated it. A friend at work persuaded me for months to pick it back up and give it a shot. He also gave me some advice. I eventually relented and picked it up again and fell in love with the game. I should also note, that this was on the xbox. After completing Dark Souls in offline mode I was really looking forward to DS2 and for the PC so I could get more of the online feel of the game. I was pretty excited, purchased SotFS edition and let it download overnight.
I've also never written a review before.
When I started playing I noticed things felt different. I won't lie and say it made me feel good. That little voice in the back of my mind was telling me, "you've seen this before, a good game comes out and then a sequel comes in trying to change the original formula and making it look pretty, to cash in without offering any originality." yeah. I stuffed that feeling down. Probably denial on the fact that I threw 50 ducks away and didn't want to face the truth. I pressed on with the game for a while. You'll notice I don't have that many hours into the game, but I put a lot into DS on my xbox.
Then I started noticing the little things. The hit detection was awful. I noticed combat was feeling pretty gimmicky. Before it was a little freeform, now there seems to be rules and gimmicks. For instance, if the enemy misses but you have n't rolled or blocked you are going to get hit. It appears that you must do either to avoid taking damage even if you have skillfully moved away without doing either. This was big in Dark Souls, because that helped you conserve your stamina. A lot of boss fights I would strip down to my shadow set so I could do hit and runs on bosses to avoid their AoE attack. Circle strafing against enemies is pointless, because they merely pivot without actually doing any footwork.
At first, I wrote this off. I thought to myself, "new game right, so you will have to develop new tactics." And then I noticed the level design. This made combat even more gimmicky. In dark souls, sure there were choke points and places where you had to fight that generally gave you no advantage (like blighttown or Tomb of giants) but it was a matter of finding the right moveset to use in the situation. In DS2, there are traps and ambushes that all feel exactly the same. Couple that with the lousy combat and the game appears to be more of a gimmick with updated graphics and essentially the same plot sequence of Dark Souls. It lacks a lot of originality while changing the basics of what made the prior game great.
It should be noted, that the director of the first game was not much involved with this sequel. So the idea that it feels like someone took something good and ruined it, might be pretty accurate.
At the end of the day I felt mislead. Like so many things in life, you pay good money for something only to find out you paid for a name, not something of quality. That is how I feel about this sequel. I'll probably wait until my next paycheck and buy Dark Souls: PtD edition. I highly recommend the first Dark Souls, but not this one. This is one that you can easily skip. After all, you wouldn't be missing anything that wasn't better done in Dark Souls with the same plot.
[edit] 3/13/16
I've put a lot of time into the game since the last review. Honestly, I stand by the review I already wrote, but I would like to add a few points and note that I picked this game back up to prepare for DS3.
The game still feels incredibly gimmicky, after a while all the boss fights feel the same with the exception of the fume knight. The only boss that was incredibly difficult (globally has a 93% failure rate) that didn't feel like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. I had a hell of a time beating him, but enjoyed it. Sinh was tricky at first but soon I figured him out as well. Anyway, moving on...
The targeting in this game is all sorts of a cluster ♥♥♥♥. If you're in a room full of enemies and you point yourself at the closest one in front of you, 9/10 you're not going to target it. You'll end up targeting something else and most of the time in my case it is something that isn't anywhere near me. One example: Had an enemy in an enclosed platform above me and one directly in front of me. The target locked onto the guy on the platform I couldn't even see. The other issue is when in caves or hallways. You can literally see the enemy in front of you but if he is even slightly close to a corner in a doorway or something you can't target him. All of this might sound lame, if you're a tanky knight with an oversized weapon then it might not matter. You don't have to be as precise. But lets say you're a high dex rapier then precision is incredibly important. You have no swings horizontal or vertical.
Another issue is PVP. The DS2 netcode is pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥ That being said, there are definitely ways to cope with it, but it does change the feel  of the game. There are helpful videos that explain it pretty well, essentially you are not where you think you are, but where you were a half second ago. This explains why you would be getting hit when successfully dodging a player or why your hits won't land when you see your weapon hit them. There definitely is a learning curve, but I feel as though this should have been handled better and made pvp more fluid. I have done some pvp, sometimes I'm very successful sometimes not. No worries, but I definitely feel like the latency should have been dealt with.
Finally, the collision and physics in the game aren't that great. You really do get hit by things you shouldn't have. I honestly hate Havok, I think it is a garbage engine. Every game with Havok feels this way. There were times I couldn't step over a 6 inch curb or step. I would get stuck and naturally hit. I have noticed that in PVE spells have a tendency to hit you after they pass by as well. Now some of this might be solved by playing in offline mode. Which requires you to run steam in offline mode as there is no option to do so in the game menu. I've noticed have have taken hits while being behind the enemy and never touched.
I stopped at the final boss and started the DLCs and have completed two and am in the middle of the third (Ivory Crown). Went and killed a bunch of side bosses and looked for notable loot. After a while it all starts to feel tired, everything feels the same, every boss fight is the same. The problem is that when the difficulty of the game is as such, all these issues and bugs make it less fun and really shouldn't be there given the difficulty. The first game is definitely better, the third might be better than this one (hope so). There are definitely still good qualities about the game. There are still bosses that are interesting. There are still interesting areas like the iron keep and shulva. I just want the game to be more polished and playable.

Not sure what to think of this title. Is it a game or an interactive story? This alone changes the basic nature of how to approach this title. So I'll just split the baby and touch on both.
Game -
Gone Home is a terrible game.
The premise of the game is you explore a large house circa 1995 to uncover a story (this will be part of the story section later) by picking up objects, looking at them and exploring the house. There's not much to love here. The pacing is painful since your avatar walks extremely slowly. The object examination is much like the worst parts of LA Noir where you pick up random cigarette butts. Exciting objects you can pick up and learn more about include:
Pencil
Blank notebook
Shot glass
Soda can
Eraser
Video game cartridge (console itself missing, but cords mysteriously left, rendering it useless)
Empty casette tape cases
The house is littered with random trash that you get to "interact" with, for some reason. The rest of the game is set up as a peck-and-hunt title where you seek out keys to inexplicably locked doors. Good thing Kaitlin came home early because Mom and Dad would be angry at Sam not for (spoiler later in the story section below) but for making them take a goofy route of finding a key in a loose wall panel, unlocking the basement, finding a hidden door just to get tot he hallway to open the door to the kitchen. The ice cream would have melted all over the floor by that point if they decided to stop off and get food on the way home.
And...that's it. There's literally nothing else to do. You play a couple of bad 90s era grunge songs, pick stuff up, and practically nothing else. The presence of a SNES in the pre-release videos (absent in the release game) could have offered up a cool little side game where you played mock retro titles, but that was a missed opportunity.
Interactive Story -
The interactive story side doesn't fare much better.
***WARNING - BEYOND THIS POINT THERE BE SPOILERS***
Throughout the title, there are five storylines that are revealed through looking at the objects that aren't random house junk. The first story is a bit of a slap in the face that centers around the Uncle that died and left the house to your avatar's father. There was discussion of occult events, mysterious deaths, an electrical inspector that couldn't find out why the the electricity randomly failed, and various occult easter eggs hidden around the house, from a creepy crucifix in a hidden room to the sister's, Sam, attempts to contact the ghost. The storyline abruptly ended about 20 minutes in and was never concluded, even if it was a simple "yup, found the problem with the wiring, squirrel built a nest over some wires".
The second story is about Dad's career as a writer. It talks about his attempt at being a published author and his first publisher dropping him when the first two books of his revisionist conspiracy theory history failed to sell well. It talked about how he reviewed stereo equipment to make some cash in the mean time, almost out of desperation. It is implied that this drove him to alcoholism. A third book was agreed to be picked up by a conspiracy theorist publishing group, but there is conflicting information with notes from the Mom to the Dad about not giving up. Again, there is no resolution. Did he actually publish the work? Did it succeed under a different, more targeted label? Did he give up reviewing stereo equipment? The story line, again, abruptly ended with no resolution. Did he ever kick his alcoholism?
The third story centers on Mom and a very brief overview of her life. A Canadian expat, she works for the forestry service. After performing well she was promoted to a supervisory position. This just ends here, no further information, just random background noise.
The fourth story centers on the difficulties Mom and Dad are having in their marriage. There is very little information on this presented and all we know is that the reason the parents are gone is that they're at a counciling retreat. As a running theme, the story doesn't go anywhere and there is no resolution.
The fifth and main storyline is about Sam and her life since your main character left for her European tour. She went through changing changing schools, dealing with rumors of living in a haunted house, discovering and developing her writing talents to the point she won a partial scholarship to a university literary program, and finding one friend in Lonnie. Over the course of their friendship, Sam begins to come to realize she is a lesbian and, surprise, so is Lonnie. They grow closer, to the dismay of their parents who think its just a phase. It touches on the pain, confusion and abandonment that growing up to discover your sexual preference is different and not seen as positively by others.
Then it goes off and turns insulting to the entire LGBT community. Lonnie, being the first LGBT individual Sam ever met, are thus required to immediately fall into deep, true and lasting love. It comes off as "you're lesbian too? Wow, we have so much in common, let's run off together and get married." The entire story played out like a classic coming to terms with sexuality and the inexperience of youth, just from a LGBT point of view. Most people end up figuring out that the first "love" is anything but youthful inexperience of raging hormones creating an attraction to a different person. Where Gone Home flies off the rails is that Sam and Lonnie abandon promising futures to run off together to, who knows, a major theme of this story is "give the audience information then leave them hanging" as it, again, abruptly stops with a casette recording about how Sam decided to run off with Lonnie, Sam abandoning her college future and Lonnie skipping out on the Army that was her dream in life (it's not AWOL or deserting since you can back out any time without penalty before completing Basic). The story never even bothered to mention if that hysterical crying on the answering machine was before or after Sam decided to leave. Is Sam currently in trouble as you ignored the cry for help with a sister in real danger as you slowly padded around the house opening empty underwear drawers? Or did Sam not bother listening to Lonnie on the answering machine when she called Sam after her rather shallow, as the game information presents it, revelation?
A much stronger story would likely have either presented WAY more information over a longer time period on the relationship between Sam and Lonnie that left little doubt that this was legitimate and not just a "first time I'm mutually attracted to someone" scenario or, even better, this. At the end, you go up into the attic photo development studio and find Sam curled up and crying over the loss of her first love. Your character then comforts her and promises to support her through this difficult time. A denumont would then discuss how, despite the fact that their parents never did approve, the emtional stability Sam was provided by her sister gave her the strength to take advantage of the scholarship and, as an older and more mature person, found her true soul mate in someone else. Kaitlin's support gave Sam the strength to develop a healthy, mature relationship with another woman that was built on common understanding and strength, no the "you're the only lesbian in town" presentation we got with the Sam-Lonnie relationship.
So, really, even as an interactive story, it's not that good.
I got it on a sale for around $2.50 or so. At the current (as of this posting) $20, it's a complete ripoff. Even at $2.50, it's hard to recommend this title given the poor pacing and story crafting. The lack of an actual game here is also tough to stomach.

There are typically two aspects to a game review. One being that you are essentially making an argument for or against the purchase of the game by anyone who may happen to read your review. I call this the "Is it worth the money?" aspect. The other is the actual quality of the game. The graphics, the story, gameplay, and overall functionality are things you look at to judge "How awesome is this game?"I want to make clear these two distinct aspects for my review since this game is in fact awesome, but not quite worth the current price of $19.99.
The game begins with you (Katie) coming home from a academic year long trip to Europe. When you arrive at the house, it is empty with a note on the door. The game itself is you searching the house for clues as to where you family has gone to. As you progress you are guided along by narrations from your little sister’s journal. Mechanically it’s a simple first person point and click adventure game. However, gameplay mechanics are really a non issue since this more of a interactive story than it is game. There are no puzzles, no enemies, and no combat. You wonder the house in search of clues and slowly unravel the mystery. The story progression feels very organic, and things fall into place despite not have a strict path to follow. A few locked doors are the only gated aspects to the gameplay. Making a 100% pure story only game not feel like its on rails is quite a feat to pull off. How the story unfolds is why this game is great.
Atmosphere plays a huge part in the story as well. I can’t go into detail for fear of ruining the story, but it’s safe to say they keep the tension pretty high throughout the experience. This is achieved without any overtly horrific things coming on the screen. In short, the game is an exquisite example of how attention to detail and great story telling can turn a game into an unforgettable experience.
So you should go buy it right? Well, maybe. Here’s the rub. The game only took me a couple hours to play, and I’m pretty slow. I picked up every damn cup, every stupid highlighter and search them for messages or clues. I left no stone unturned, and enjoyed it. All of that and it still only took me a few a hours. The game could conceivably be completed in a few minutes if you knew precisely where to go and what to look at. It sort of hurts to say this, but this is in no way a $20 game. If you were buying into a series of these stories, or this was perhaps a beta version of a much longer tale, then yes $20 or $30 would be conceivable. Wait for this game to come on sale again, and buy it…immediately. Anything under $10 and you should be all over this title. I’m looking forward to more like this.

Anyone who is still sceptical about getting this game, please read my review. FNAF 2 is probably the best one out of the 2 games. Some of the questions that people have before getting the game is how do you run out of power now? In FNAF 2, the building no longer runs out of power. So you are able to use the cameras and air vent lights as much as you want. But the thing that DOES run out of power is your flashlight. You are able to use your flashlight to check down the hallway in front of you or by using it while in the cameras to light up whichever room you are looking in. The flashlight is the most important part of the game because of the fact that it helps rid of unwanted animatronics coming down the hall and also shows where the characters are in the rooms since most of the rooms are pretty much black. Moving on. This game is very addicting and easily deserves a 10/10. The main hardest thing about the game is how active the animatronics are right off the bat and the fact that you have to keep a music box winded up. On night 1, Toy Bonnie and Toy Chica come out and are very aggresive right from the start which makes the game very hard straight from the beginning. Many times Toy Freddy will also come out on the 1st night making you have to deal with 3 animatronics right from the start. Also, there is a Marionette. This "doll" hides in a present on Cam 11. This is also where there is a music box you have to wind up almost every couple seconds. By winding up the box, it will keep the Marionette from coming out of hiding and killing you. All together, it is a very tough game having to deal with 11 animatronics, yes you heard me 11. The old gang from FNAF 1 is back and ready to kill :). There is also the Marionette and YES THERE IS GOLDEN FREDDY. Sorry if I am not exactly correct on the amount of animatronics but either way there are a lot. There is also Balloon Boy which is another animatronic you will have to find out about yourself :). In conclusion, FNAF 2 is an amazing and very unique game. I recommend it 10/10 and advise you to buy it! Have fun playing guys! I know I did!

-Undocumented change to status of weapons and health points. Now sniper rifles do A LOT more damage and can often 1 body hit kill human players (COD). The game will go unresponsive and take several minutes to load a map and sometimes even the SERVER crashes. So yeah, when you have the luck to find a server with more than 10 people playing, eventually it will crash and people won't bother to find a new one, or spread to different servers making it impossible to find a consistently full server to play.
-Changed the HUD to the top of the screen.... really? i would understand if they added an option for people that prefered it that way, but nope, they just randomly decided to force change that. Sometimes you'll do really bad in games. Sometimes you'll do really good. Sometimes you'll encounter hackers. Although the servers aren't *very* full all the time, you can usually find at least one full match of any gamemode. You'll die alot, even once you get used to the game. I feel like the game pretty accurately depicts war as in WW1. No matter what game mode, it'll generally take one bullet to put down an enemy. If they don't go down when you shoot them the first time, they'll probably bleed out. You pretty much have to use tactics or you will die. Camping is a necessity, but just don't stay in one or two spots without moving the entire game; so no more running into the middle of a gunfight and coming out fine (cough cough, call of duty).
The game has an interesting rank system, you gain XP from getting score in matches, and everytime you rank up you get like 1 or 2 tokens which you can use to buy rifles, sidearms, and attachments.
The game does have a few quirks, like body launches and weird hitboxes/hit detection, but overall a great experience.
In fact I'd venture to say it is one of the best if not the best multiplayer FPS experiences.
The only bad thing I could find about the game is hackers seem to be somewhat easy to encounter, but this could just be because not many people are online at once.
I'll give it an 8/10.
(-1 point for quirkiness, -1 for hacker encounters/insufficient anti-cheat)
Oh and try not to be to quick to judge for hacks, most of the time they will just get the jump on you, the only reason i say the hackers are frequent is because i encountered two in a row on two different servers. Maybe your experiences are different. Feel free to leave feedback and let me know if i missed anything in my review.

I'm going to rewrite my review because I was recently attacked by hardcore dark souls 2 fans for not providing enough details on my review so here it goes. Although I don't hate dark souls 2 and I think it had alot of potential to it. Not saying its a bad game however I enjoy dark souls 2 however, I criticise on the fact that scholar of the first sin could of provided more. I think improvements such as a better pvp system for the blue sentinels and reintroducing the indicement system as well as dropping the sin system. Another fix I believe that could of worked is that the level design could of been easily fixed by connecting shortcut areas back to previously visited areas rather than being a tunnel with a dead end and removing warping early game and leaving it for end game. Removing soul memory in NG+ would of made a whole lot more sense because of people who are in need of coop in hard areas and bosses as well as fast pvp encounters. Also limiting healing items such as lifegems in NG+ would of brought a true natural challenge into dark souls 2 and preventing the misuse of healing items.
TL;DR: Scholar of the first sin could of had alot of potential however it wasn't fully implemented and I am going to agree with the rest of the community of purchasing this game only on steam sales. However I did encounter the same problems I had with dark souls 2 such as hackers, latency issues, and other related pvp connection issues.

A ridicolous, fun and unique WW2 shooter. Unlike many games set in this time period, this one has a lot of humour to it (even i, who thinks WW2 isn't something to joke about, got quite many laughs when playing this).
As for the game, what sets it apart from most WW2 games (easy to guess with the name it has) is that it has dinosaurs. You can be a Compsognathus and sneek up on enemies, bite them to death. Or you can be the mighty Tyrannosaurus Rex and mow them down with your MG-42, or roar them down, incapacitating them and then eat them up. It's unique and hilarious.
Graphics: The graphics are not the best i've seen, but they're passable. It is obvious that it uses the quite dated source engine, but who cares?
Music: The music is quite good, it sounds pretty much what you can expect in a WW2 propaganda movie.
Overall, Dino D-Day is a unique experience that i can recommend to anyone. It's of course not as good as some other Source Multi-Player FPS's, like Team Fortress 2 or Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, but it's nothenless a fun experience. Pick it up if you have the money for it. :)
End of this review.

As a person who enjoyed parts of the first game but found it to be overall lacking in actual horror, I am glad to say Five Nights 2 exceds the original in almost every way. While I still don't think the game is true horror, it is still fun to play and does a good job of creeping you the player out.
READY FOR FREDDY...
To those who played the original game and enjoyed it, you will be glad to know that much of what made the first game so popular is present in its sequel. You will once again find yourself as a security guard working the night shift at the newly re-opened Freddy Fazbears's Pizzaria. Much of the gameplay from the first game has been carried over, but with enough changes to make it feel new and not just a rehash of the original. You have a little tablet thing you use the check cameras and keep track of the animatronics as well as a few lights to check the area around you. The first thing you will notice right off the bat is you have no doors this time around, this time you are sitting in front of a wide open hallway and you must use a flashlight you have to light it up in order to check for enemies. There are also two air ducts on either side of you that you must check, giving three possible ways to get in in total. Another thing to note is that there are now six animatronics.  Double the Freddy, still not ready. The last new addition is a music box that you have to make sure does not run out.
WHO GOES THERE?
As fun as the game is, it does have a few problems. For example, after night one the charge on the music box begins to drop faster and faster which adds to the tension. The problem is, because you have the music box to deal with as well as checking the vents and the hallway in front of you, you might as well keep your camera set on the room with the music box. The rest of the cameras become pretty much useless. And then there is the damn balloon boy, who will enter your room and start laughing without end thus rendering your lights useless and calling the attention of all of the animatronics (mainly Foxy). As of this moment I have no idea how to deal with the balloon boy, but he is super annoying and only serves to frustrate me instead of making the game more scary. The moment he appears in your room you might as well start over, because there is just no way of dealing with him that I am aware of. Not only that, but the game suffers from problems that the first game had as well. Because you're pretty much doing the same thing over and over again, there is a lack of replayability for you can only do the same thing over and over so many times before it gets dull.
DARK DESCENT...
All in all, Five Nights 2 is a fun game that surpasses the original in almost every way and should offer a few good jumps to those that play it. It might not be the best horror game ever, and it doesn't even come close to such masterpieces as Silent Hill 2 or Amnesia, but it does show that the horror genre still has life left in it and I will take it over games like Resident Evil 6 any day.
Peace and cupcakes,

Short version: Do not buy it for more than 3 euros.
Slightly longer version: Great, a WWI fps, bad, it sucks in realism.
Also it is very far from being elitist, on the contrary it is quite dumbed down to the extreme: duck, get up, shoot, duck. and move on the sides randomly to take great advantage of the secret weapon of WWI: ping, and disappearing bullets (so if you get killed first you do not get to kill the guy you shot at... very realistic implementation of a ballistic system: making it clientside...)
EDIT: I found something positive ! At last ! This is the first FPS I see where we can climb on trees. Well, not the first, WWII OL allowed that too, a long time ago. But still, that deserve some recognition.
RE EDIT: They got rid of that only redeeming feature.
long version:
_The devs do not bother to tell you what patches do, you have to figure it out by yourself.
_No more tree climbing.
_only 32 players (16 on each side) allowed per map.
_The ballistic system is simplistic at best (minimal bullet drop from one end of the map to the other, no wind affecting the bullet).
_the barbed wire is lethal instead of making you a living target for hours.
_the maps are somewhat small and arbitrarily cut. And yet such small sectors would have host hundreds of people instead of 16 per side.
_the squad system is flawed (Cannot choose your battlefield, squads of only 4 people with defined roles, and spawning directly on top of your commander no matter where he is, depending on the squadtype. And people, who are often insulting, can hijack your squad in the name of democracy)
_the attack-counterattack cycle makes no sense whatsoever (especially with only 16 people against 16 in the best case scenario, where is 'the attacker has the manpower advantage ?')
_the games are too short (depends on the map size, seems to be up to 40ish minutes).
_ the animations are bad (you can get killed because on the other players screens, your character will be aiming at the sky when you are in fact crawling).
_the close quarter combat is flawed, Pistols often lose to rifles, melee weapons are only usefull when the other guy is out of ammo, panicking or not facing you.
_The machine gun's first shots are as bad the rest, expect a very low accuracy on medium range, making short bursts very useless for accurate fire. Also the MG rounds kills in 2 shots most of the times while the rifle rounds always kill in one shot, same calibre, almost the same initial velocity, two different outcomes?
_The terrain does not looks the same up close or from afar, and objects will often disappear at long ranges, letting you see players you cannot kill due to an obstacle in front of them.
_The sniper rifles seems extremely bugged since their Free Addon.
_The game is supposed to be finished, yet they released a "free addon" which broke it even more than it used to be, and I would like to point out that an ADDON implies OPTIONAL, here it is mandatory.

First off, don't go into Gone Home expecting a puzzle-solving adventure game or a survival-horror frightfest. Gone Home is a game about the downtime that exists in most other games - those sequences where you're calmly just reading notes or opening cabinets to see what surprises lay hidden inside.
In Gone Home, you're essentially a snoop in your own home, rifling through the personal possession of your family members to piece together the story of who these people are and where they've disappeared. It's a short, 1-2 hour experience, but those minutes pack a powerful emotional punch.
If you're wanting action, deep puzzle-solving, or a lengthy adventure, you will be disappointed in this game. But if you've got an open mind and can appreciate how a story can be told through unconventional means, Gone Home is a fascinating piece of work that will put you through a range of emotions.

Not good at reviews so here is a gluten free bagel recipe
Gluten-Free Bagels
Makes 8
4 tbsp. active dry yeast
3 tbsp. sugar, divided
⅔ cup warm (110° F) water
1 cup gluten-free flour blend (recipe below)
1 cup potato starch
½ cup nonfat dry milk powder or Better Than Milk soy powder
2 tsp. salt
2 tsp. xanthan gum
1 tsp. guar gum
2 tbsp. canola oil, divided
1 large egg
1 tsp. cider vinegar
Brown rice flour, for dusting
1 tbsp. baking soda
Poppy seeds, for garnish (optional)
1. Dissolve the yeast and 1 tsp. sugar in the warm water and set aside, letting the yeast foam for about 5 minutes. Grease a 9×13-inch rimmed baking sheet or line with parchment paper.
2. In the bowl of a heavy-duty stand mixer, combine the yeast mixture, 1 tbsp. plus 2 tsp. of the remaining sugar, flour blend, potato starch, dry milk powder, salt, xanthan gum, guar gum, 1 tbsp. oil, egg and vinegar. Beat on low speed (using a regular beater, not the dough hook) just until blended. Increase the speed to medium-low and beat for 2 minutes, scraping down the sides of the bowl with a spatula if necessary. The dough will be stiff.
3. Divide the dough into eight equal portions. Generously dust each portion with rice flour; then shape into a ball. Flatten to a 3-inch circle, dust again with rice flour, and punch a hole in the center. Pull the dough gently away from the hole to form a 3-inch-diameter bagel with a 1-inch hole in the center. Place the shaped bagel on the baking sheet.
4. Place a rack in the lower third of the oven. Place the bagels in the cold oven. Set the temperature to 325 degrees and bake for 10 minutes. Remove the bagels from the oven, but leave them on the stovetop and increase the oven temperature to 350 degrees.
5. Meanwhile, bring 3 inches of water, the remaining 1 tbsp. sugar, the baking soda, and the remaining 1 tbsp. oil to boil in a Dutch oven. Boil the bagels in batches for 30 seconds, drain them on paper towels, and return them to the baking sheet. Sprinkle with the poppy seeds, if using.
6. Return the baking sheet of bagels to the oven. Bake until the bagels are nicely browned, 25-30 minutes. Cool the bagels on the baking sheet on a wire rack for 15 minutes. Transfer the bagels to the wire rack to cool for another 10 minutes. Serve slightly warm.
Gluten-Free Flour Blend
1½ cups sorghum flour or brown rice flour
1½ cups potato starch or cornstarch
1 cup tapioca flour
Whisk together until thoroughly blended and store, tightly covered, in a dark, dry place.

First of all, let's all recall that this is "a story exploration game" (quote from description, and that's completely accurate and should by itself give you a very good idea of what to expect).  It is about exploring the home of a family and gleaning a very realistic and personal understanding of the various members of that family: who they are, what they love, what problems they are facing.  No, there are no monsters to fight in it.  Yes, if you want to finish it as fast as you can, you could probably get to the end in 20 minutes on your first try and get absolutely nothing out of it.  This is not a game about running through as fast as you can.  If you enjoy taking your time and examining rich environments in depth, then you will enjoy this game.  If an emotive, personal, and down-to-earth story sounds appealing to you, than you will probably enjoy this game also.
I finished the game in about an hour and a half.  Yes, it is short, and no, it has no replay value.  Once you've heard the story, found all the hidden crannies, read all the papers, and thrown all the toilet paper on the floor, that's really about it.  However, I am hesitant to say that it doesn't have much CONTENT.  It has a lot of content; each scene is packed with tons of detail, and brings the never-on-screen characters to life to an incredible degree.  The writing and voice acting is all also quite good.
I've been reading a lot of really good, detailed negative reviews of this game, and I want to say that many of those people have really good points!  I agree that the game seems to go out of it's way to include creepy elements that tease you into expecting it to turn horror at any moment, but then that never goes anywhere.  I think this is a symptom of the game's biggest flaw, which is a lack of unity (also maybe a tad bit of misleading advertising).  While it includes lots of rich detail, several elements of the story start to feel incidental by the end, when you start to realize they're not all going to tie together after all.
However, at the end of the day, I think this game was emotive and believable, and it told it's story elegantly and eloquently.  I would recommend it, although I would not say the game is for everyone.  -- 7/10

Was very cynical of this like many with the whole walking simulator thing, but thanks to the summer 2014 sale finally got it. On multiple levels. I mean, i got it. Everything said of Gone Home is true. If you're not from the era that the devs are aiming for, it won't touch you. But if you came of age in the 1990's then you're going to love this. It's purely emotional and nostalgic, and sure it's quite stereotypically Pacific Northwest and what would not be called emo - but back then there was no emo, really. There was shoegazing, there were VHS tapes, and there was Space Above and Beyond on TV - even though the devs got the dates wrong hahaha.
I cried, no shame in admitting that i think. The mechanics of the game work great, the mood is great, but most of all it's a spectacular period piece. From the second i heard the first notes of the title music (which also plays in-game ALL the time, admittedly), i loved Gone Home.
Kinda feel bad for being a doubter, though the criticism stands: this is a 100% committed period piece. If it was set in the 1970's I would not feel as strongly about it, but it takes place in the era when I became the person I am now, and brings back many vivid memories, good and bad. It's also the polar opposite of stuff like Dark Souls, which I also love. Gone Home is about immersion through relaxation, not challenge. In short, being born between i'd say 1968 and 1980 required ahead, and then quite something!

Gone Home was one of the first games I bought, intrigued by its brief and cryptic description in a Humble Bundle sale. I was pleasantly surprised by the graphics and the scale of the environment - not to mention the eeriness of the environment. Weather sounds, an otherwise silent and seemingly abandoned building... and the developers' bold notion of where to take the story and how it unfolded, including numerous hints about a madman and an obsession with the paranormal. (Hey, it was the 90s. We were all doing it. Even the UK had got the X-Files by then!)
What impressed me the most was the way in which the five characters unfolded, mostly through the detritus of their lives - but also Sam and Lonnie, who got a far more in-depth treatment through letters and journal entries. The idea of a character who's present by their absence isn't a new trope, but to do it in this was was really skilful.
In short, it's not a complex game, or one that requires huge amounts of skill or that will reward you with achievements or days of gameplay. But it is a beautiful piece of writing, evocative, touching... well worth experiencing.

Recommended?  Unfortunately not at this time, no.
I really really wanted to like this game.  And let me say right off the bat -- the graphics are awesome.  The sound is awesome.  The historical detail is enthralling.  Of course, I have no idea what it was like the be in the trenches during World War I but I can imagine that these guys got it right in their portrayal.
Here's the thing about this game.  It is pretty realistic and here's the truth -- a lot of people f*cking died in World War I.  The pace of war weaponry had been so fast that pretty much you could kill at will at a tremendous distance and never even see the dude you were killing.
I'm not a whiner -- I don't mind getting killed 500 times because it is one shot and you're dead.  I'm all for realism.  But like I said A LOT OF PEOPLE F*CKING DIED IN WORLD WAR I.   While playing "Verdun"  it was not uncommon for me to die fifteen, twenty times and have only three or four kills.  And if you watch the leaderboards, the experienced players will often have twice as many deaths as kills.
If you are okay spending most of your game experience waiting to spawn this is for you.
Another issue is one that faces the casual gamer (such as I am) frequently:  the game is unbalanced for the experience players.  You can earn weapon upgrades like a sniper scope for your rifle.  And, unlike Wolfenstein online, your experience doesn't reset at the end of the campaign.  But to earn this in Verdun, you need to be a level 50 (from what I can determine -- one other thing that needs to happen is the developer needs to upgrade their docs).
I'm not the best player in these kind of games and my ping is desparately slow (101 at times) when compared to other players.  After 1.5 hours I'm a level 2, halfway to 3.  This means a ton of hours for me to earn that scope that will allow me to remain alive enough to kill a couple of people.
In addtion to this, it's hard to learn the maps when you're dead and respawning every thirty seconds or so.  And so this adds to the confusion.
Another thing -- deaths are so rapid in this game that I begin to suspect that players are botting.  And so this is something else that the developer needs to police for on its servers.
I have no idea how to solve these problems -- but balance is needed.  I do realize that there are a lot of people out there who are serious gamers who will be intrigued by this game.  But the casual gamer -- you know, those of us who have a life, a family, a career, and soul-crushing student loan debt --  will probably not be able to enjoy this game.
It's a pity, it's a beautiful game.

An interesting concept and story, but not without its issues:
The mechanics of the game are minimal, which itself is not a bad thing. Thomas Was Alone also has very little in the way of complex mechanical interactions, and it was better for it. Gone Home rewards players who explore and try to find out more about the world, but exploring is slow, because walking is slow, and there is no run button, which doesn't make sense to me, even in the context of story: If I came home to find no one there, I'd be running around trying to figure out why.
The story is clearly where the designers focused their effort, and what a story it is. I haven't finished it yet, but so far I like it. It starts fairly slowly, which may put off some people, and you need to be patient for the first 20 minutes or so, but after that the pace really kicks off.

First and foremost, if you're reading this review, it should be known that Gone Home is best approached with as blank as slate as possible. The player's imagination is critical and any prerequisite knowledge/bias towards the game will have an effect on the experience.
So stop reading right now and go play it.
...but if you insist on hearing my opinion or you've already completed your journey through the Greenbriar household, here's a little something:
Let's see. How do I rave about this game without spoiling anything. Even after hearing the glowing reviews and critical appraise about this game, it still caught me completely off-guard. Never did I expect a few hours exploring an empty house to turn into the raw, emotional and utterly breathtaking experience. Telling a story purely through player interaction with the environment can be a tricky thing, but The Fullbright Company accomplishes this task tenfold. There is a beauty in the simplicity of this game that I haven't felt since Journey (which you should also go play if you haven't already), and though it might not work for some, I will aggressively recommend this game to whoever will listen.
Also, I purchased the $30 special edition box set within ten minutes of finishing the game. It's worth it.

Scholar of the first sin is what Dark souls 2 should have been from the beginning.
A difficult game with enemies placed strategically related to lore, rather than randomly scattered.
The revised Soul Memory system, while by no means perfect, is significantly better than the original DKS2 experience for PvP and PvE players alike.
The lore of the game feels more consistent now, with new dialogue and item descriptions subtly improving the overall experience for lore-hunters.
However, there are drawbacks.
SOTFS is even more poorly balanced than DKS2 was originally - sometimes it feels like they have just arbitrarily thrown X amount of enemies in a room without any thought for fairness.
Areas like Shrine of Amana were not reworked to be fairer to the player, instead punishing the player for things outside of their control.
Moreover for original DKS2 owners on PC, upgrading to SOTFS is a very poor deal indeed.
A rare genre in itself, this game could have been better, but also much worse. Overall, whilst a flawed experience and not as good as Dark Souls 1, Dark Souls 2 is definitely worth a try if you like punishing [to the point of often unfair / frustrating] Dark Fantasy RPGs.

As a pure F2P user I can say sure one player who spends his whole paycheck gets a slight advantage, but in every game Iv played so far I have been top of my team (22-10 and 32-6 was the KD last game), and this is after getting out of the noob levels and ending up against people higher level then myself.

Now, with that said, I will explain my pro's and con's with this game.
-Pros
-Basically COD without the killstreaks... and for free!
-Skill wins out every time against a wallet warrior (lets face it, there are no skillfull wallet warriors which is why they have to P2W).
-Co-op is a BLAST along with the "Spec Ops" mission you get to do daily (you earn a token a day, it cost tokens to attempt the missions)
-ONE SHOT SNIPERS! (read down in the cons because there are ways to build against snipers).
-Guns are easy to get with in game money (I got a sniper+assault rifle in the first 2 days I played).
-Cons
-People CAN pay to get ahead quicker, so you may see a low level player fully decked out in gear the rest of us have to earn.
-You can build armor to counter a specific class (some may think of this as a con, but you can build against snipers so they are useless which sucks if you randomly find a whole "anti-sniper" team.
-It takes time to get a full setup of equipment if you want to use all classes (to get full armor/weapon/sidearm it takes about a month for each character).
Overall, if you like COD and hate killstreaks, this game is for you. Havnt lost to a wallet warrior yet, so Ill be interested to see how the game progresses. However, as of now, enjoy paying NOTHING for an awesome game!

Alright, guys. Buckle your seat belts because this is gonna be a long review. Please remember that this consists of my opinion. Its Fun Aswell XD
OVERVIEW
Warface is a first-person shooter that has a Call of Duty-esque vibe to it. While some call it a CoD ripoff, I tend to disagree. Some people like it more than CoD, some don't. Having played both, I personally find Warface more entertaining than the more recent installments of the CoD franchise (i.e. MW3, Ghosts, Advanced Warfare).
CAN I RUN IT?
I have a modern day low-spec PC and I can run Warface comfortably with minimal to no lag. Obviously, it will run different for everyone. If you know your computer specs, you can use this website to find out if you can run it (No download required):
I have found it to be pretty accurate for most games.
SPECIFIC TOPICS
HACKERS
While many reviewers say the game is full of hackers, I disagree. I have played Warface for a reasonable amount of time and have not come across any hackers. The way the game is designed, it is common for a skilled - let me say that again, SKILLED player to obtain 50-60 kills in a single team deathmatch game. While it isn't too common, it isn't a rarity either. Newer players will commonly mistake these skilled players for hackers, but they are clearly not. However, I'm not saying there aren't hackers, because I'm sure there are.
PAY TO WIN
Many reviewers also say this game is pay to win. You can purchase Kredits and boosters that allow you to level up faster and purchase weapons and items that are superior to others. However, I have found that when I play matches I have more difficulty winning against skilled players with typical gear than players with lots of gear that just suck. So, yes, you can buy better stuff, no, it isn't that noticeable in the game.
GAMEMODES
This game has three major categories: Co-op, Versus, and Special Operations (I have not yet unlocked Spec Ops so it will not be covered in this review).
In Co-op, up to five players can play in Regular, Skilled, and Advanced missions to obtain checkpoints and goals in order to get experience and money. (I recommend learning the basics of the game before jumping into Co-op)
Versus is where you will be most often. You will start out being able to play Team Deathmatch, Free for All, and Plant the Bomb (which is basically Casual mode from CS:GO). After achieving rank 9 you will unlock other gamemodes like Capture (Capture the Flag), Storm (Attack and Defend), Domination, and a couple others that I can't remember at the moment. Players below rank 9 are considered "Rookies" and players above rank 9 are considered "Professionals". Rookies can only play with rookies and Professionals with Professionals.
FEATURES
CLANS
This game has clans, where your clan name appears above your username. I don't know too much about clans, but I know there is a way to play clan versus clan.
THE FREAKING SLIDE FEATURE HOLY CRAP
One of the selling points of this game is the slide feature. This is the coolest, most ridiculous feature I have ever seen in an FPS game. It is amazing. While you are sprinting, you can press a button (I don't remember the default key) to slide across the ground. You can ADS (aim down sight), shoot, switch weapons, reload, etc. while sliding. There is nothing more entertaining than sliding by an enemy with a sniper rifle or shotgun and shooting them in the face.
CLASSES
There are 4 classes: Rifleman, Medic, Engineer, and Sniper. Rifleman has an assault rifle or light machine gun, a pistol, a frag grenade, a knife, and ammo boxes to replenish ammo for you or a team mate. Medic has a shotgun, pistol, knife, grenade, health kit (for yourself or a team mate), and a defibrillator. Engineer has a sub machine gun, pistol, knife, grenade, armor patches (to replenish armor for you or a team mate), and a claymore. Sniper has a sniper rifle, pistol, knife, and grenade.
TEAM ASSIST
You and your team mates can help each other get to higher elevations by one team member giving the other a lift. You would be surprised by how many people will actually take 3 seconds out of their day to help you up a wall. I expected it to never happen, like trying to get helped up in TDM in CoD, but surprisingly, a lot of people will help you out.
CUSTOMIZATION
You can customize both your outfit and your username display in Warface. There are different helmets, boots, gloves, and armor that each have different stats and features. For example, a certain type of helmet will allow you to see enemy claymores and mines. You can also customize the way your username appears, with a certain pattern in the background and icons next to your name (these things have to be unlocked by getting achievements).
BUGS/CONS
SERVER LATENCY
Unfortunately, the servers are not very impressive. Some servers are absolutely fine, but sometimes there are servers where it takes a fraction of a second longer to see that you got the kill (this is not my internet, this happens with other people too)
TEAM COLLISION
Team collision is a little wonky in this game. Instead of feeling like you hit a brick wall like in CS:GO, you have more of a push-back feeling like running into a powerful fan. If you're not careful, you can fall of a narrow ledge if you and a team mate try and go at the same time.
THE RANKING UP BUG (Don't worry, it is only aesthetic)
EDIT: THIS HAS BEEN FIXED AS OF October 2015
When you rank up, it will tell you that you rank up to a rank higher than what you are. ALWAYS. It is not too big of a deal though. In the bottom left corner of the regular menu, it will show your correct rank number and name (For example, Rank 9: Private). On the experience progress bar, it will tell you what your next rank will be (For example, NEXT RANK: Private First Class) This is also correct information. However, when you actually rank up, it will tell you that you have become a rank one higher than what you are. So, when you reach Private First Class it will have a message that says You have received the rank Specialist! even though you have not. However, in the menu it will say Rank 10: Private First Class and the progress bar will say NEXT RANK: Specialist. So it's not a big deal, but definitely a noticeable one.
CHOOSE YOUR NAME WISELY
When you register for a Warface account, choose your username wisely. You will only be given the option to create your name once, so be sure its the one you want. If you decide someday that you really want to change your username, you can contact crytek support and they will change your name for you (I know this because I mispelled my name upon registry). They will only allow you to change your name once.
VERDICT
Overall, Warface is an extremely entertaining game for people that like the FPS genre. Although it has some issues (like all games), they ultimately don't affect the game as a whole all that much. I intend to put many more hours into this game. And in the end, DOWNLOAD IT! It's free to play so why not? If you don't like it, no harm done. There's an uninstall button for a reason.
If you liked the review, please let me know by hitting the thumbs up button below. Thanks, guys! Happy gaming!

You won't get anything out of reading reviews for Gone Home. Don't pay $20 or anything close to it, but at least play it so you can form your own opinion. Kinda like how not everyone enjoys certain novels or films, but it's beneficial to experience it and form your own opinion. Gone Home tries to pull at your emotions and therefore will not resonate with everyone (didn't really give me the feels, had some friends feel differently though), and there is no way to know if you're one of those folks until you play it.
That said, here is my "review" -
Gone Home is better described as a "story" or an "experience", rather than a game. You step into the shoes of Katie, a young girl returning home after studying abroad. She is surprised to find the house empty - where are Mom, Dad, and her younger sister Sam?
Looking through her family's belongings - a bottle of hair dye, a letter from her mom's college roommate, a note jotted on the back of a mixtape - Katie unravels what she missed. People and relationships are constantly changing and evolving, families being no exception to this, and Gone Home is relatable and touching in that sense.
Would I recommend Gone Home at the $20 price tag? No. I paid $3 and think that is more of a fair price for what it offers, especially considering exploring everything only takes a little over an hour.

Free of the excessive clutter seen in almost every shooter of the market, Verdun takes the idea of trench warfare and breaks down its fundamental concepts into fantastically accessible gameplay for the player.  In the game's main mode, at any time you are either defending your current trench, or attacking the next one in front. With column like maps with a clear right direction and wrong direction to move you ALWAYS know where to go and what to do in the blasted fields and wastelands of Europe. It is because of this that Verdun naturally causes players to work with their team, even if they don't mean to. You will always have your teammates in the trenches with you, firing at approaching Germans. You will always feel as though you are part of your force.
While the overall game flow is exceptionally straightforward, the weapons and movement are all deftly handled to promote an astonishing level of realism. Armed with a classic bolt action rifle such as the British SMLE, a single round almost always will end in a satisfying crumpling of a hopeful German. With this realistic behavior, death is always a fear as you keep your head down in the trenches, or cry prone in a crater in no mans land and machine gun fire chatters inches above you.
The immersion is completed by the exceptional sound design with immensely satisfying cracks of rifles and the distant (or not so distant) thunder of rolling artillery. Despite its tiny team, Verdun has one of the best soundscapes I've heard.
Surprisingly fantastic, the team has managed to build astonishing artwork of all the military assets used. Most importantly for me however, is the incredible attention paid to the trenches. Puddles of mud are everywhere, clutter from the soldiers living, and the damp dirt engulfing you makes you feel like you in a truly terrible place.
