You probably read other reviews about this game, so this review will be a comparison of this game to Dark Souls 1, and which game you should buy if you had to choose.
Things DKS 1 does better:
- Level Design: Most levels are interconnected with each other, and if you look around each area, you can see where you are going and where you've been. DKS 2 is definitely lacking in this aspect.
- Online System: In DKS 1, people can only cooperate and battle each other if their soul level is withing range. In DKS 2, people connect according to soul memory, which is a number of how many souls you have collected in total. People do not like this because you cannot control soul memory, since collecting souls is natural. There is a ring that prevents you from collecting souls, but that takes up a ring slot, and is not convenient. Overall, the Online System is better in Dark Souls 1.
- PvP: There are problems with Pvp in both games, but Dark souls 1 overall has pvp that is more enjoyable. The meta is more widespead in dark souls 1 compared to dark souls 2, and the combat is much more fast paced and intense. There are hackers in both games, and we just have to deal with them.
Things Dark Souls 2 does better:
- Upgrade Materials and Stones: you get much more of these than you get in dark souls 1. This means that you can have more upgraded weapons per playthrough, and overall a better experience with having more weapons. Also, the upgrade system in this game is much more forgiving and senseful than dks 1.
- Graphics: although this aspect doesn't really matter, dks 2 SotFS edition has better graphics and optimization.
- Durability: Some people may hate this game's durabiliity system, but to me, it makes it more realistic. Weapons will wear out much more quickly than dark souls 1, and if they break, you have to repair it. It makes you plan out your strategy when going through a level, instead of beating the game with just one weapon :p
Although there is much more things to say about these two games, if you're wondering whether to buy this game, you should. You will get tons of hours of gameplay and learn a lot about patience and planning.

Defientely one of the best WW1 shooters on the market. Verdun offers a realistic, gritty take on the inafamous "Battle of Verdun", a final stand for the French that took almost 2 years to resolve. The Trench warfare is fast and gritty, to where 1 shot will almost definitely kill you. Verdun is not a rush-playstyle type of game, every move you make, every step you take, somone's watching you. One misstep, and your life could be taken right from you. Verdun offers over ten factions to play as, in cluding The French, Germans, Ottoman Empire, Belgium, The United States, England and Canada. All of these factions have 2 sub classes placed within them, giving a certain playstyle to that sub class. For example, the US Marine subclass is used for clearing trenches with ease, while the US Doughboy sub-class is used for suppressive fire. The community is acceptable and not filled with 10 year olds trying to be "MLG". Sadly, Verdun isn't perfect. Connection is sometimes goofy and the team balance is sometimes off, causing a crucial game. Overall, Verdun is a solid 9.5/10. It offers a fun, realistic experience that any fan of the time period should enjoy. Once you play one game of Verdun, you will be hooked for a while. Gone Home is not a traditional game and that's what I like most about it. It's a brief experience that tells a very compelling, emotional story through the eyes of a young woman coming back home from a year-long trip abroad. She comes back to a large, deserted house and it is left up to the player to explore the premises and piece together what happened to her family in the time she's been away. The gameplay is incredibly simple, revolving around exploration and close examination of the highly detailed house that she's unfamiliar with (since her family moved in while she's been away). The game evokes a great sense of atmosphere, as it takes place in the early hours of the morning during a particularly nasty thunderstorm. The high point of the experience is the story that unfolds as you find notes and letters that piece together a short history of what's been happening in the lives of Katie's family members, especially her younger sister, Sam. Without spoiling anything, the conclusion was certainly unexpected and moving. Overall, the narrative is unlike just about any other game story that's come before. It comes from a real place, reflecting real heart and commands a nuanced approach to relevant issues that's very rarely seen in games these days. It may not be a "game" in the traditional sense, but it is certainly an experience that everyone should take part in, so that we might start to see what else a game can be and what it can show us.

First and foremost, you must be aware that this game falls under the visual novel/walking simulation genre. Hence, gameplay takes the form of exploration, observation, and reading. The only puzzle-like elements in the game are cracking two locks, so inspecting every nook and cranny for easter eggs is the way to go.
Following the story, you snoop around your empty house for clues as to your family's whereabouts. The game successfully puts the player in Katie's shoes: Having been away for a year and barely moved in to the new house, she's essentially a stranger to her own home. The main story being unraveled is that of Katie's sister, Samantha (Sam), but there are hints of conflict brewing between the parents as well. I appreciate how much detail was put into the home and all the items in it. Nuggets of information about the characters were presented well; letters and notes seemed very believable. (Finding Sam's creative writing about ovaries is a must. It's absolutely hilarious.) You have to remember that it's 1995! Cell phones weren't commonplace, but passing notes and sending letters were. Furthermore, Sam's voice was charming and realistic.
Background music was nice and ambient but not varied, probably an intentional choice for maintaining immersion and a degree of realism. The other sounds that you hear are from playing are phone messages, a record, and some rock and screamo mixed tapes Sam left around.
Next, I did find some fault with the story. I also felt that it was a bit overhyped.
Moreover, something that should have been addressed was the introduction of paranormal elements (ghost hunting, seances, player-purported whispering). The stormy nighttime environment was eerie and contributed to a prolonged sense of dread at some points, but ultimately, nothing scary happens. Maybe the stories of what happened to Katie's family should have been more horrifying to match this element of the game. Otherwise, it doesn't really belong.
Lastly, I don't mind the shortness of the game, but I don't think the content warrants the $20 price tag. I waited until it was around $3 during Steam Summer Sale 2014.
I will still recommend the game because it was okay, and I enjoyed it mildly. While I did not feel impassioned by it, I had a more neutral-positive opinion than negative.

Overview
=======
Five Night's At Freddy's 2 is a truly worthy sequel that without a doubt does justice to its amazing predecessor.
Turning up every single dial on the board with more gameplay mechanics, more animatronics and a vastly increased playing area, it certainly creates even more pressure and desperation for the player than the original game ever did.
Animatronics
==========
All 5 of the old animatronics return, with some additional wear and tear to boot: Freddy, Bonnie, Chica, Foxy and Golden Freddy. They are also joined by some upgraded and shiny new versions of the standard four animatronics- Toy Freddy, Toy Bonnie, Toy Chica and Toy Foxy (affectionately known as 'Mangle' due to the absolute state he is in). As if this fiendish lineup of 9 animatronics was not enough, 2 extra and unique animatronics enter the fray- the Balloon Boy, a seemingly harmless yet incredibly dangerous animatronic which messes with your lights, and the Marionette, an unspeakable terror that is quite simply your doom should it ever escape from the container it is kept in.
Gameplay Mechanics
===============
Freddy likes the dark and now things get even darker. You'll be forced to use the new camera lights in order to see into the darker depths of some of the rooms, but beware the battery meter. You must also keep on turning the jack in the box in order to escape the wrath of the Marionette. Even worse, there are no doors! One must use all of their cunning and alertness to survive the five nights without being completely dismembered by the animatronics. The Freddy Mask can assist with this, as it will fool some of the animatronics into thinking that you are the incredibly psychotic bear himself. Also, beware the new hallunications- will you discover the true story behind this cursed establishment? What is the true role of the Marionette?
Conclusion
========
I give this game a 9/10. It is truly almost perfect.
Pros:
A larger Freddy Fazbear's Pizza to perish in
More animatronics to get destroyed by
The unique graphics which give the game its signature feel return
More gameplay mechanics to offer a new experience
A scary experience
Cons:
Scott seemed to sacrifice a lot of development time (originally aiming for a 2015 release) in order to get this game out as a 'surprise' early release. Though it is indeed cool that we are able to play the game early, one is left wondering, could this game have been so much more if Scott stuck to the original deadline?

Rating this game is difficult. it's not really a game, more so a first person story-telling experience, akin to a short movie you would see on television or in the cinema. The voice narration is amazing, and the story is well written, developed on the setting of a rural country house on a stormy night in the beginning of the 90s.
You play as a girl who has just returned to her family home after travelling across Europe, with no one there. The aim of the game is to find out where everyone has gone. As you journey around the home you can find family details and subtle references to the time period that really suggests it is lived in. Careful attention to detail brings the home to life, really giving it a lived in sense, even if if your journey is a relatively quiet one.
On my system (a relatively poor one) the graphics are relatively poor, the audio is not memorable outside of the narration nor is there much interaction or puzzles. But this"game" is not about any of that. i'd have to compare it to something like Dear Esther or Journey on PS3 where the emotional appeal is the main selling point, not some intricate game-play mechanic.
I would like to make it clear it is not worth picking up for more than a few euro/dollar/pounds (€5 etc max). This is a brief interactive story, not a "true game". So it only could be recommended to someone willing for a short term investment into this emotionally driven tale. Although the experience is short, the payoff is one of the best you can get from a relatively smalll production.

Reviewing Dark Souls 2 is a difficult thing. On one hand it is a fantastic game with a lot of good ideas and marked improvements on the original, though on the other hand it follows a game that gained a cult following due to its artistic vision as much as its technical prowess, and in that regard Dark Souls 2 is a failure.
While normally it is not wise to bog one's views down with the negative at the start of a review, Dark Souls 2 is immediately clear for players of the original in how it has gone wrong. While the setting of Dranglaic is not essentially that different from Lordran from DS1 (generic fantasy world) the tone of the delivery is massively different. Dark Souls is impersonal and in that you are simply an element in that universe that could be there or not and it would make no difference, similar to how S.T.A.L.K.E.R.'s Zone is a place you happen to be appearing in as opposed to being a game about YOU! Dark Souls 2 is personal, it's opening focusing on your character making the journey to Dranglaic and harps on about how you have lost EVERYTHING! Dark Souls gave lore, you were not even being considered in all of that. This mood is furthered by Dark Souls 2's characters treating you as a nuisance, berating you and going to great lengths about how you seek misery and so forth. Dark Souls characters told you what you needed to know, laughed nervously and palmed you off: you are insignificant and their actions speak louder than any overblown script waffling on about darkness and misery ever could.
Why am I waffling on about what would be just story and lore and I'm ignoring the mechanics (as someone who is very mechanically driven these days)? Because the original Dark Souls mood and play was largely formed by said attitudes and ideas. It is clear in the level design, the character and boss placement, item descriptions and where the items are left, basic geography and architectural logic (if you can see it, you can possibly go to it, and it will be where it is supposed to be) that Dark Souls entirety is mechanical, aesthetic or the direct hands on play of it. Some games you can spoil by telling someone the story and telling who kills who while in Dark Souls simply playing the game is the story. Noting where and when you fight someone and the consequences for said actions all flowing with the play.
Dark Souls 2 lacks this mostly. In Dark Souls 2 most of the levels feel half baked and simply ill thought out. The characters lack the weird, uncanny charm of the first game and none of them seem relatable. The tragedy seems largely forced (Vendrik being the exception) and there are no Siffs, Seigmires or Solares. While the writing is not usually enough to hurt a game when it comes to the guts of it, the level design is hampered by some odd changes in mechanics. In the first game you would eventually be able to fast travel via bonfires, but that came at the rough mid-way point. In Dark Souls 2 you can instantly warp between fires from the getgo. This makes the need for shortcuts far less pressing and levels just become bland linier paths from A to B. Sometimes paths diverge and you come to a new point, but even then things seem jankey in how they are executed e.g. the path to the Undead Purgatory is quite a long winding path with lots of hard hitting trash plus a scripted invader, all capped off with a boss that is not entirely clear in how to fight it, meaning numerous attempts to fight it tend to be more gruelling than interesting.
Dark Souls 2 is also huge, as in HUGE huge, possibly just about twice as big as the original game. While this is usually a form of praise here it just feels bloated. While the interconnecting areas of the first game help attach new parts to old areas, Dark Souls 2 just spreads out further and further. The bland map design hardly helps it, but as I progressed I tended to forget the previous section and flat out forget some of the more bland bosses altogether.
Mechanically healing and levelling has also been overhauled in an odd manner. Both seem to reuse mechanical ideas that Demon's Souls used  (though I cant fully comment on that as I have not played said game) where you can stockpile healing items and levelling can only be done at a central hub area and, while that may apparently appease fans of Demon's Souls, in dark souls it cheapens the healing where you have estus flasks AND slow HoT style lifegems. Sure you have to grind or buy the gems, but once you buy about one hundred of the damn things being incidentally hit fighting trash becomes less of an issue. The end result is me being less cautions about how I fight things, taking incidental hits off regular bandits because I really don't feel the need to care as much as I can easily pop a small gem without much fuss. You do have to slowly build up your estus collection, but that has less of a risk / reward feeling than expending humanity at bonfires and running the risk of invasion, only compounding to possibly annoy new players as they lose the non-renewable items learning the ropes.
Levelling is all done via the central bonfire keeper the Emerald Herald, allowing her to allocate your points based on the souls you have collected. This means constantly warping back and forth between the central hub and the various bonfires around the world, busting up the flow. That and the fact that you have to sit through what has become a meme of "Bear... Seek... Seek... Lest" draws out something that could be purely mechanical  into an inconvenient chore. While the Souls series is not truly about convenience, this is possibly unintentional.
Levelling is also somewhat confusing due to the new Soul Memory system, which screws up PvP and coop to a degree, but I'll leave it at that. I've waffled on about things so much now its becoming a pain to try and reiterate what I dislike about the game's systems.
After all that doom and gloom it would be shocking if I had anything nice to say. I do however have a lot to say about how DS2 and how it improves on the original. Two things stand out above all things in the game: The mechanics of fighting and the implementation of multiplayer.
Fighting in Dark Souls 2 is a lot more kinetic than the original. Considering the weighty combat of DS was a major draw for many, this would be an even stronger pull here. Moves feel weighty and as careful as the first game and weapons still run by the logic of "can use this the whole game if you want". The game improves in the context that things feel even more skill based than before. Backstabs and parrying are far harder to pull off here and, as such, there are far fewer cheap moments where you easily bait targets or suddenly find yourself being lagstabbed by some random invader. Movesets feel far more fleshed out and the heavy weapons feel REALLY heavy. Strength builds are viable, magic is viable, agility is viable.  Some moments are harder for some builds here, but the same could be said about the original (my caster against Seath was horrid) but thankfully there is a good degree of flexability for virtually all builds to have an alternative choice in how to play.

Verdun is not like other World War Shooters, because Verdun is actually like a World War. In this case, WWI. That means instead of running around with a silly knife performing ridiculous acrobatic feats and stabbing enemies to death, or wading into battle with an improbably configured, heavily accessorized gun, you'll be crawling across a shattered, shell-pocked wasteland for minutes on end without seeing the enemy, only to get blown up by a lucky mortar shell or find yourself spotted and taken out by a machine gunner. Because that's how WWI was. You'll use the actual weapons fighting men were issued, and their lethality will be accurate— one good hit from a rifle round and you're done. Because that's how WWI was. You'll force a bloody foothold and eventually sweep an enemy trench clean, only to have to defend it from counterattack moments later to hold the few meters you've taken. Because that's how WWI was.
For a relatively little-known shooter, Verdun is impressive— the take-and-hold dynamic of its gameplay is unique and challenging, rewarding lots of different skills and battlefield roles from combat to command. The environments are well designed and evocative, there's period-accurate gear, squads, and dialog. Gameplay is fun and fluid. Teamwork garners great rewards; a single good officer can effectively win a game if the enemy team doesn't have coordination to match and he's got a cooperative squad under him.
In terms of cons: the squad level up dynamic can be a bit inaccessible and those who figure it out tend to have a strong advantage, but it doesn't tip the game too badly. Team coordination sadly lacks, possibly weighed down by the somewhat dated automated dialog system of pressing a series of numbers to autotype important phrases; teamwork might be easier if there were a better way to mark up the map, but any HUD elements or "radar" components would also hurt the organic feel of the game, so it's a bit of being stuck between a rock and a hard place from a dev's perspective, I reckon. I find that the trenches don't end up being used as heavily as one might think; I wonder if this has to do with the way the game is designed or the limitations of scale that online gameplay imposes. The only true complaint I have about Verdun is that I want it to be so much more; if you've ever read Sniping in France you know the crucial roles that intelligence gathering, sapping, and trench raids played in the war, and you also find yourself wishing you could try out the trench mortars and artillery pieces scattered around the map. The scale of the war is also sometimes missing, the charges through the creeping barrage, the whistles blowing men over the top. The developer has bult a wonderful foundation which has the potential to become a market-changing game given the chance.

Hello Everyone, and this is my review for Gone Home.
First off, this game is amazing. I loved every minute of it. Even though I loved the game, there are pros and cons to this title.
PROS:
Not a puzzle game- You can veg out to this game, and not worry about racking your brain with complex puzzle. Plus, there are no monster so you don't have to worry about dying. (Even though that adds content to the game and not everyone sees this as a plus).
Nostalgia!!!!!- This game takes place in the 90s, 1995 to be exact, so many movies that I watched and loved are on VHS such as The Dark Crystal, GhostBusters, and TV series such as the X-Files. Many triggers that will send you wanting to go back to the 90s.
Punk Music- You can find cassettes around the house and listen to the music in the cassette player. It's pretty baller when you can roam around a house and jam out to punk music.
Atmosphere- The house it self was planned out very well. The storm that rolled in gave it that creepy, yet calm environment.
Story- The story was very touching, it engulfed the player of what's going on with the family. The notes, postcards, textbooks, and letters were all done amazingly. Very detailed with objects that were interactivable (sp?). The voice acting was amazing!
Now, unfortunately, the cons:
Lack of content- This game is roughly an hour and a half of game play. It's not terrible, but I wish there was more.
Interactive Objects- There were a lot objects around the house that be touched, moved, and flipped, but there were some things were static and can't be touched such as VHS tapes, Laser Disks and others (Not a serious con, since a developer can't make everything interactive.).
Overall, I think this was a very good game and I would recommend to anyone who wants a game to relax to and be submerged in a gripping story. However, I do not believe the $19.99 is fair (Sorry The FullBright Company) because of the relatively short story. Maybe add a DLC? :)
Thank you for reading this review!

Despite all the negativity from core Souls fans about this game, me being one of them, this game is still amazing. Dark Souls 2 takes a change in direction from Dark Souls 1 and tries a few things out. Rather than complaining about the certain enemies that are incredibly frustrating to kill due to having infinite stamina and poise or the ambiguous lore of Drangleic which at times it seems to make no sense and many other negative things: I'll give some reasons to get this.
The game looks amazing. The lighting effects have been improved on and the armor and weapons in the game react crisply to the light. The environments in this game vary greatly from area to area and, despite some bosses feeling a little lackluster, you do feel like you're exploring Drangleic to the fullest.
Inspired by Demon Souls came the central hub area known as Majula. I much prefer this to Dark Souls 1's more open ended style of having the nearest bonfire as your home. Coming back to Majula to re-stock on supplies, upgrade weapons and level up feels refreshing and calming after spending hours fighting your way through difficult enemies and defeating a boss or two. It's never a problem to go back to Majula as teleportation between bonfires is active right from the beginning. Since the world is so expansive, this design decision makes sense and never feels too easy.
They did a great job with the armor sets and weapons. There are so many different combinations to try out. Sure they might not all be 'viable' from a strict approach to PvE but there is still no end to the fun of trying out every different weapon type. From whips and fist weapons to ultra greatswords and great-bows, there is a weapon there for everyone. All the armor sets looks beautiful in the world, fashion souls is very much alive in Dks2. This is definitely a big plus for someone like me when playing and Open-World Action RPG. I love having this much customisation for my character. Another nice addition is the ease of upgrading weapons - it's not difficult to get your weapon fully upgraded and you aren't restricted to having just 1 or 2 weapons fully upgraded in one playthrough! Also there is dual-wielding.
New to the scumbag spell-casters arsenal is a discipline known as Hexing or Dark Magic. This is similar to things like Dark Bead except it's a whole branch of spellcasting based on dark magic. This broadens the options available to players in a good way - hexes, sorcery, miracles and pyromancy are available to use. Casting spells feels smooth and doesn't feel like you're at a disadvantage plus there are ways to improve casting speed whether it be a ring or by increasing certain stats.
People say Dark Souls 2 was a step backwards and that it was worse than Dark Souls 1. I honestly think in the future it will be considered a necessary evolution of the Souls franchise. The first word that comes to mind when I think of Dark Souls 2 is 'smooth'. The combat mechanics from Dks1 have been polished off - there is a certain fluidity to the game that is bested only by Bloodborne.
If you enjoyed Dark Souls 1 then Dark Souls 2 will be a treat to play. For my first playthrough of Dark Souls 2 back on release date, I was enchanted and played non-stop for almost 2 days. I hope you can appreciate this game for what it is and enjoy it as much as I do!

When I started playing I hadn't really looked into what it was about or any sort of spoilers, but I did know it was an interactive story. I also came to it after playing survival horror games so, as you can imagine, the first crack of thunder kind of freaked the hell out of me. I'm not ashamed to admit I'm a bit of a wuss when it comes to horror games- I expect something to jump out at me from every shadow, I see figures in windows that aren't there... Gone Home is the perfect nightmare for me. Dark rooms, thunder, lightning, door knobs rattling and you're likely to find me hiding under to bed. That said, it was also thrilling. The sheer terror you get from being alone in a giant house in the middle of the night, with no knowledge of what's around you is scarier than any monster anyone could ever dream up. I have to admit, I chickened out and looked up a spoiler about half way through; I couldn't handle the pressure of the unknown! However, even after I discovered that <SPOILER> nothing sinister was going to jump out at me, I was still scared! Which just goes to show how well designed the game was. Those long dark corridors just screamed spooky! All the darkened windows were terrifying, and everytime I spotted one when I turned around, I jumped a little- with those light curtains almost blending in with the wall, the window ends up with this human-esce form! The sheer lack of sound (aside from the thunder) as you creep around the house just adds to the feeling of how alone you are in this creepy old house. Every time I came across a cassette tape I would play it for the entire time I was in that room, and start it again when I left, just to hear something other than creaking when I moved on. As for the music, it was a wonderful nostalgic blast into the ninties!
I do have to say how much I loved the storyline. Trying to figure out what happened to your family through your sisters eyes and discovering what really went on in her life was like someone made this specifically for myself. I hadn't known that one of the main characters was <SPOILER> gay and was pleasantly surprised when I figured it out (before being told such). There are so few games LGBT's can relate to and you usually need to specifically seek them out. I love that this is so well populated. The whole story itself and the way we are drip fed information is expertly done. It was like doing a jigsaw puzzle, and the creators gave us the corner pieces first, the edges and then left us to our own devices to find the rest. The mystery of it all is just the type of thing I love to do.
Every time I walked into a room the first thing I did was turn on the light; when I left the room I closed the door, but I would leave the light on. One of my favorite parts was, after doing this a few times, I found a note to Sam (the sister), from their mother, telling her to turn the lights off, specifically stating that she was "just like your sister." Clever. I feel like the creators knew the player would be leaving lights on (or ALL the lights on).
I do, however, agree that this game is too expensive. It does only go for two hours, which is part of the reason, but mostly because the interest in replay is minimal. Once you know the story you aren't very likely to go back through it again. Maybe after time has passed (like rereading a book) you might have another playthrough. I think the price needs to be halved.
Still, it is a really good game and I would reccommend it to all who like a mystery.

While Dark Souls 2 treads on familiar and beautiful ground in the Souls series, it trips along the way. To start off, Dark Souls 2 can be a bit too unforgiving, even for a Souls game. When the player dies, their maximum health is cut by a small amount, shrinking with every subsequent death after. It punishes the player too much for making mistakes, forcing them to scrounge around for Human Effigies in order to regain their maximum health.
Parries and riposte is more difficult to pull off in 2, giving a longer wind up time to the parry, and not allowing the player to immediately riposte. The whole system is so bad, I tried to avoid it as much as I could for most of my time through the game.
Now despite these faults, Dark Souls 2's gameplay is still farily fun, and still possesses some challenge, albiet not as much as the first, but enough to merit some fun. The game is even more gorgeous and impressive art wise than its predecessor, possessing more nightmarish enemies than ever before, and incredible locales. While the areas are more linear than before, I couldn't help but stop multiple times to appreciate the amazing detail that went into the areas.
Overall, Dark Souls 2 is good. Not great, not amazing, and no where near as good as 1. It's just not as difficult, and possesses wasted mechanics such as the parry and riposte.

This game is a nice FPS. rather addictive and very interesting gameplay.
In terms of graphics, they are acceptable, for such a small game they a suprisingly good, but compared to AAA games, they are sub-par.
That said, the controls and the perfomance is quite acceptable, I have no problems running this game with a solid 60fps.
In terms of the actual game itself, it's a innovative idea and the developpers have handled WWI trench warfare suprisingly well. Machine guns are over-powered and can quite easily, if set up properly, take out half the enemy team. The historical accuracy is very nice. Having to run to the enemy trench across no-man's land, a strip of land between the two trenches filled with barbed wire and pock marked with craters. Usually, youll die to MG fire a long time before you even get to the trench. If, however, you decide to stay in you own trench, nice and cozy, waiting for enemies to walk into your line of fire. then be prepared to get yourself killed by an ememy sniper, waiting for fools to stick their head over the parapet.
As a whole, each squad, and each squad member have a role. the grenadier is good for assault, the MG is very good defensive. the marksmen can pick of targets at a distance and the leader can provide a spawn point and can call in artillery strikes, gas, or even recon planes.
The feel is very nice, when you need to attack, there is a sudden fear that compels you the stay in your trench. You actually fear going out, as you will most likely die. Infact, with this game. you will die. A lot. You will rack up the deathstreak when attempting to attack, but when it's your turn to defend, then sit back and just pick off those fools running out in the open, with almost no cover. that's when you can rack up the kills and make yourself even.
If you got friend that play this game. then be prepared for some serious fun, having squad mates makes this so much more enjoyable.
Overall, this game merits a solid 17/20 and comes highly recommended.

As a gift from a friend, I really wasn't ready for the amount of scares and pressure comin' my way.
The game is nice and seems to play, pretty much the same as the prequel, with a few added features I'll go over right now.
1.Joining the 4 animatronics that everyone is used to, you now have a new set of animatonics that are just as frightening.

The visuals are the same as the first game, but to me it seems to look clearer. The jumpscares are still as scary and somewhat predictable as the first game. And the ambiance is still very unnerveing and tense-keeping.
I can't really talk about the soundtrack since, like the first, the only things you can hear are the screams from the animatronics, the random sounds you hear around the pizzaria, and the music box I spoke of earlier.
To conclude, this game sould not be played by people who still have nightmares from the prequel, or anyone who is very vulnerable to jumpscares. But if you have a death wish, or are, frickin', XxMLG_420_GamerxX, give it a try and see for yourself.

Verdun is a unique game. It's FPS but not like many people have seen before.
I will remind everyone who reads this. Verdun is not like Call of Duty. It is not like Battlefield.
Everyone in a squad must work together. And different squad types must as well. I have logged 16.4 hours on this game so far. I have played in every field in almost every squad if not all of them. From being a sniper, to leading a squad of your own creation, to created a base of fire so your comrades can attack the line. This game has a wide variety of squads. Four for allies and four for central. No squad using the same equipment as another.
As everyone keeps asking on the forums I will just put it here. There is no main campaign and their will be no tanks or horses. The reason being from my perspective is that a campaign would take a massive amount of time to make. Tanks and horses are obsolete because you win by the amount of trenches you hold. And the battlefields, craters and barriers do not favour large equipment pieces.
I like this game a lot because of the point system. You must capture a trench and when you do you get one point of Entente (Allies) or Central (Axis) depending on who you play as. But now you must hold it and the tables turn to the enemy and they must attack it. If you manage to do that you can attack another trench. If you think this is simple, you are wrong. Everyone who plays this game has seen trench lines be fought over with one team capturing it and then another would and this goes on for what seems like an hour but it's only a couple of trenches.
Trench warfare is sweet. One must decide what to carry into the field. Do you have a bayonet? Does this machine gun fire without being mounted? Do you have grenades? Do you have a sidearm? Should you call in artillery or gas? A lot goes through your head when trying to come up with a good plan. However, since this game is not really full of 12 year olds then I would figure the enemy has a good plan too.
Enjoy the game and be a good teamplayer AND KEEP YOUR HEAD DOWN.
Cheers,

Despite all the negativity from core Souls fans about this game, me being one of them, this game is still amazing. Dark Souls 2 takes a change in direction from Dark Souls 1 and tries a few things out. Rather than complaining about the certain enemies that are incredibly frustrating to kill due to having infinite stamina and poise or the ambiguous lore of Drangleic which at times it seems to make no sense and many other negative things: I'll give some reasons to get this.
The game looks amazing. The lighting effects have been improved on and the armor and weapons in the game react crisply to the light. The environments in this game vary greatly from area to area and, despite some bosses feeling a little lackluster, you do feel like you're exploring Drangleic to the fullest.
Inspired by Demon Souls came the central hub area known as Majula. I much prefer this to Dark Souls 1's more open ended style of having the nearest bonfire as your home. Coming back to Majula to re-stock on supplies, upgrade weapons and level up feels refreshing and calming after spending hours fighting your way through difficult enemies and defeating a boss or two. It's never a problem to go back to Majula as teleportation between bonfires is active right from the beginning. Since the world is so expansive, this design decision makes sense and never feels too easy.
They did a great job with the armor sets and weapons. There are so many different combinations to try out. Sure they might not all be 'viable' from a strict approach to PvE but there is still no end to the fun of trying out every different weapon type. From whips and fist weapons to ultra greatswords and great-bows, there is a weapon there for everyone. All the armor sets looks beautiful in the world, fashion souls is very much alive in Dks2. This is definitely a big plus for someone like me when playing and Open-World Action RPG. I love having this much customisation for my character. Another nice addition is the ease of upgrading weapons - it's not difficult to get your weapon fully upgraded and you aren't restricted to having just 1 or 2 weapons fully upgraded in one playthrough! Also there is dual-wielding.
New to the scumbag spell-casters arsenal is a discipline known as Hexing or Dark Magic. This is similar to things like Dark Bead except it's a whole branch of spellcasting based on dark magic. This broadens the options available to players in a good way - hexes, sorcery, miracles and pyromancy are available to use. Casting spells feels smooth and doesn't feel like you're at a disadvantage plus there are ways to improve casting speed whether it be a ring or by increasing certain stats.
People say Dark Souls 2 was a step backwards and that it was worse than Dark Souls 1. I honestly think in the future it will be considered a necessary evolution of the Souls franchise. The first word that comes to mind when I think of Dark Souls 2 is 'smooth'. The combat mechanics from Dks1 have been polished off - there is a certain fluidity to the game that is bested only by Bloodborne.
If you enjoyed Dark Souls 1 then Dark Souls 2 will be a treat to play. For my first playthrough of Dark Souls 2 back on release date, I was enchanted and played non-stop for almost 2 days. I hope you can appreciate this game for what it is and enjoy it as much as I do!

is a short story adventure game involving a single character, named Kaitlin, who has come home (get it?) after a long trip to find her parents and younger sister missing. Kaitlin must piece together whatever pieces of evidence togther to find out what has happened to her family.
The game itself is very well-designed. The house feels very atmospheric, and is kind of fun to explore, picking up all the objects in the environment and examining the little details to piece together whatever story you can find. However, instead of being a dark, brooding, story involving the disappearance of your family, it's mostly just a teenage romance involving two girls, that, while sweet and kind of touching, isn't the "mystery" that I was expecting, and isn't what the game appears to be trying to sell me.
Constant lights flickering on and off, supernatural elements involving the supposed ghost of a dead relative, lights breaking, and the oppressive dread that exists simply from being absolutely alone, appear to be trying to give me the impression that I'm playing some kind of horror game.
Unfortunately for Gone home, I'm not fooled.
That's not to say I didn't like the game, I kind of did, in a way. Hearing the story bits and piecing together the family life of Kaitlin and Sam were touching, and I found a strange sort of catharsis from discovering something important and hearing some narration from Sam.
But other than that, there's really nothing else to say about it. It's so short and so insubstantial that you can beat it in an hour or two, even if you fall asleep at the keyboard or have a stroke mid-game or something. Ironically, it's lengthened by the backtracking, the lack of direction, and the deliberately slow Dear-Esther style walking pace, and it's still incredibly short. And once you're done, there's not really any kind of reason to play it again. And for 20 dollars?! That's criminal! You can get games with subsantially more depth and complexity for free!

Suprisingly, not terrible.  It's pretty much Crysis 1 reskinned and with some extra features and a little bit of monetization.  The controls are pretty dece and responsive.  The graphical options are pretty good (although the lack of an FOV slider annoys me), and it seems to be very well optomized.
Warface is split into three different game modes.  PvP, PvE, and Special Operations.  Now, I haven't spent that much time in PvP, but it's pretty run-of-the-mill as far as a mulitplayer FPS goes.  There's TDM and Deathmatch, a mode called Storm (which is basically rush mode from battlefield on a much smaller scale), CTF, etc, etc.
PvE, is what I have been playing the most.  For a PvE mode in a F2P game, you can actually progress completely independent of the PvP part.  Which, for someone like me who hates PvP for the most part, is great.  The missions are pretty fun, and varied enough that I haven't gotten bored of them, yet.
(DISCLAMER: I only have access to one Special Operation as of this review, which I believe is seasonal.)  So far, Special Operations look like they are more advanced PvE missions.  The one I have been able to play, is a pretty standard horde mode shooter.  It's alright.
Getting items for your character is not as hard as I initally thought.  In matches, you acquire experience points to put towards one of three categories.  Weapons, clothing, and weapon attachments.  Once you unlock one of these, they are permanent, but they do have item HP that decreases with every use.  But they can be easily repaired with a few hundred in game credits, and I average about $4-500 every PvE match.
Overall, it isn't bad.  It's pretty run of the mill and generic, but for what it is, and considering it isn't monetized out the♥♥♥♥♥like some OTHER GAMES *cough*combatarms*cough*.  It's worth a shot

With the release of the (free!) Horrors of War expansion, the developers of Verdun have made a great game even better. Set in WW1, this great shooter delivers on the tension, mindlessness and violence that one imagines when thinking about WW1 battles.
The base mechanics in the game are good - the guns feel good and shoot well, the maps are absolutely excellent and the game modes are well balanced (for the most part) and provide a lot of great battle moments and fun.
In this game, you will die
. Most of the guns kill you in one hit, and players have the opportunity to call in a wide range of support (toxic gas, mortar fire, artillery) to rain fire and death on your position. This game favours careful movement, and one cannot overstate the importance of good map knowledge and cover to stay alive when crossing no-mans-land.
Once you reach the enemy trench, you will have to be even more cautious as you navigate the twists and turns of the enemy trench, with a rifle, grenade or machine gun waiting to end your stint as a successful WW1 soldier at every corner. This creates great, tense and exciting moments, where the thought of having to cross no-mans-land again encourages you to value your life more than you would in faster-paced, arcade shooters.
The new Co-op mode brings an additional game mode for you to enjoy with friends or other people online. As a squad of 4 people, you are up against increasingly numerous waves of enemies rushing across no-mans-land to attack your trench. Although AI soldiers aren't the cleverest enemies you will ever come across (and are far less dangerous than real players), their sheer numbers make the new Co-Op mode a desperate and exciting experience.
The community is relatively small (but you can fix this by buying the game!) but I've never had any trouble finding full servers to enjoy. The community seems to have grown significantly too with the new expansion.
I would wholeheartedly recommend this game. If you have always wanted to play a WW1 shooter, this is as good as it gets. This is also a great game for those of you who prefer tactical, slower-paced FPS games. The (free!) expansion has made a great game into an even better one, adding new guns, new countries (Belgium and the United States) and a new Co-op mode which adds to the already great content this game has. Buy it.

TL;DR - 9/10, Overwatch made in source engine 2 with Dinosaurs and Nazis
Dino D Day is one of those games that you have to play to understand. On the outside, this game looks like a bad Source Engine 2 game with Dinosaurs, but on the inside, it is so much more.
The thought of running around as a Dinosaur alongside Nazis in WWII is as crazy and entertaining as it sounds. There are roughly 9 Dinosaurs to chose from, 8 on the Axis team and 1 on the Allies team, all of which have very unique abilities and playstyles. The smallest Dino, Compy, has you running around the map, scratching at enemies and jumping on their faces, pinning them to the ground and mauling them to death. The most annoying Dino, the Microraptor, is a tiny flying raptor that spits into it's enemies face, blinding them for roughly 7 seconds. And my personal favourite, the Dilo, a medium Dinosaur that picks up live goats and hurls them through enemies, killing them as well as the goat on impact.
The human characters are also very fun to play and well thought out. Initially when playing, the game may seem painfully unbalanced, with the Dinosaurs dominating every time, but once you understand how to use very character, things become much easier. Certain characters can call down air strikes and dive bombing Pterodactyls rigged with explosives to clear objectives, one character can drop a jackrabbit on the ground, distracting enemy Dinos to gain the upper hand, and then there are your usual characters, the medic, the heavy, the sniper etc.
Every map is highly entertaining and they all offer a unique playstyle and aesthetic. Some maps allow players to become the T-Rex, which mows down every enemy in it's path with it's machine guns, and other maps require lots of stealth and strategy. Needless to say, every map, combined with the diverse roster of characters provides a new experience every match.
Overall, I would say that Dino D Day is one of the most entertaining shooters I have played in a while, providing laughs, scares and tears left right and centre. Buy this game

Gone Home is less of a game and more of an interactive story. You come back home from your year long trip to Europe only to find your parents and your sister gone. As you explore the house you find clues as to where they are along with journal entries from your sister describing her experience with the house.
The game has a creepy tone, but it's just that, creepy. Nothing ever comes out to get you, but you do hear your fair share of creeks and knocks.
The story (accompanied by surprisingly good voice acting) is engaging and enjoyable. At times it is angst ridden, but having been a teenager before I could relate.
Even though there are exact duplicates for a LOT of items, it's still cool that you can interact with everything from a pen to each individual drawer in the refrigerator. Most of the items don't offer any significane to the story, but that didn't stop me from picking up a bunch of them and flipping them around looking for some secret note or easter egg.
Clocking in at around two hours, Gone Home is one of those you should keep an eye on during a sale. I paid a couple bucks for it and I don't regret it at all, but I would have probably been disappointed if I spent the full retail price. Overall it's a very atmospheric game that you will probably beat in one playthrough because you just want to see what's behind that door at the end of the hall.

Nazi Dinosaurs with Cannons and Machine Guns on their backs. What more do I have to say?
Dino D-Day is a humorous WWII Multiplayer FPS about what would happen if not only did Adolf Hitler's science teams brought the dinosaurs back to life, but also gave them nerve controlled weapons, the intellegence to comprehend language, ideology, nationality, and not eat their masters? You get this silly game where Dinosaurs have cannons, machineguns, their own claws and abilities, and even suicide bombing mini dinos; I'm not kidding. The game got it's start as a single player mod for Half Life 2, but it was scrapped apparantly and it's assets turned towards a multiplayer game.
There are two teams, The Allies, and the Axis. With some memebers of either having special abilities to use.
The Allies are John Hardgrave (The Leader), who uses either the M1 Garand or the M1 Carbine. His ability is when he gets three kills, he can go into a Patriotic beserk spree! Punching facists with his super fists high into the air!
Then there's Joe Spencer, he uses either a Tommy Gun or a Grease Gun, his specialty is calling in artillary strikes onto a part of the map, which is useful for either clearing a certain chokepoint of enemies, or dealing damage to critical targets.
Up next is Nigel Blythe, English Gentleman with a Shotgun, and his choice of either a rocket launcher or a flame thrower to light those jerries up!
Supporting from the rear is Ilona Vike, cute as a button but sharp as a razorblade. This Soviet Rose is the sniper of the team and utilizes her rifle, her revolver for back up, and a dead rabbit to distract certain dinos into losing control and eating, leaving them vulnerable to either Ilona herself, or her comrades.
Supporting at the front is also Camille Brun the medic, she heals nearby teammates with her special or can chuck heal oozing medpacks for teammates to gather around.
Finally, there's Trigger, the wonder dino! Liberated from the Nazi Army, Trigger is the only Dino the allies have, and he's as deadly as he is cute, getting revenge on the long long hunt from carnivores millenia ago, Trigger uses his nerve controlled, swivel mounted 30. Browning Machine Gun on Facists, wether beast or man.
The Axis forces only have three humans, being mostly comprised of Facist dinosaurs!
Kurt Streicher is a simple soldier with no abilities to speak of, Armed with his rifle, his MP40, and some grenades, he does good on the front on his own.
Karl Hissman is the more interesting German, being a falconer, he's trained explosive, suicide Pterosaurs to fall onto where ever he points at, killing anyone nearby (Did I mention you can, if lucky, lock the Pterosaur onto an enemy?). Aside from that, he serves as the team's sniper against Ilona.
The final Human is Don Graff, the Medic and Vetrinarian for the Axis war machine. be wary that even though he is a simple medic, he is armed with an STG44.
The Facist Dinos include the classic Velociraptor, who can use his speed to surprise and overwhelm enemies, and even pounce onto them to rip their throats out.
The Dilophosaurus can pick up one of the many goats (did I mention there's goats in this game?) and lunge them at enemies for damage and laughs, as well as the ability  to knock down enemies, pick them up, and toss them for a double kill!
The Desmatosuchus is a walking tank, armed with a medium but still powerful tank turrent, he can supress enemies and kill with splash damage. Be mindful that he and his spikes are big, so it's not easy to get through certain doorways.
The Stygimoloch is the Desmatosuchus, but more mobile, agile, less bulkly, and has a MG34 Machine gun instead of a cannon. He is the German Trigger.
The Microraptor can do it all! He can fly, claw people to death when they don't know it, and blind people with a deadly acid spit, while clawing them to death!
The Compsognathus, or Compy for short, is a suicide bomber dino, though small and his bomb is just a stick grenade, he is still fanatical, and with three kills from his claws, turns his grenade from a weak firecracker, to a powerful bomb that can kill many, and set others aflame!
Finally the grand daddy of them all, only avaliable on certain maps, The Tyrannosaurus Rex! You can't spawn as him, rather there's a "waiting list" on the Axis team where a random player gets selected to become the Rex until either the end of the round, or death where upon another player is randomly chosen. He is nasty, Armed with two MG42s on the sides of his head, able to pick up and toss airplane bombs, he also uses his might roar to knock down enemies and if they're unlucky enough, The T-Rex can pick them up and eat them for health! His only problem is his pure size and slowness, making him a target for everyone.
The game comprises of three modes. Team Deathmatch (First team to 50 kills wins), King of the Hill (The side that controls the hill point for 3 minutes wins.), Control Points (First team to capture all points wins.), and Objective mode. Otherwise the game is your typical FPS combat, with the Allies being more for group tactics and shooting, while the Axis Dinos are more arena shooter.
Overall this is a fun cheap game, I got this for $1.99 when it was on sale the other day, and it's worth the money if you can find a crowded server. The game is active with a couple of players, so no worries about finding a big game. I would indeed reccomend this game.

You run through the trench, find the perfect spot, poke up your head, and begin firing. After landing 1 or 2 kills in the eighty seconds left on the defensive, you hear the command. The command to attack. You rush onto that battlefield, trying to dodge bullets and artillery shells. You jump down into a crater, but not before getting shot twice with a Chaucat. You wait in the hole, healing up. A body falls in next to you. You climb out of the crater and begin to fire. Suddenly, a bullet pierces your head. You didn't make it.
Sound good? Then get Verdun.
Completely authentic weaponry, realistic battlefields, intense scenarios, and anxiety controlling your every move. In Verdun's main mode, Frontlines, you must defend your trench and attack the other team's. The game is very well balanced: The stages give an advantage to both attackers and defenders. There will never be a dull moment.  The difficulty is perfect, making the game fairly difficult to get good at but not impossible, and it makes kills feel incredibly rewarding. While I do have a bit of a grudge against the whole points to upgrade your character system, this is remedied by making points easy to get. There really isn't anything to complain about. Verdun is a great game that everybody can enjoy.

Gone Home has an amazing premise. You arrive home one rainy night from a trip to find your family missing. The player must then search their humble abode trying to piece together the mystery. As you find things like your sister's secret diaries or your dad's porn collection one thing becomes clear: your family is fairly low on the priority list. Gone Home is an interesting little game that I gets a lot of hate that may or may not be justified. Gone Home is a primarily a story telling game based on your character coming home after spending a year in Europe to find out that no one is home, and you explore this house searching for clues as to what has happened to your family over the year that you were gone.
Somethings that I liked about Gone Home is that I like this style of storytelling in games, where you slowly uncover what is going on and what has happened. You get updated little by little with a narration from your little sister as you go through this house. If you are a big fan of storytelling in this manner, I think you'll like this game. I also found the story itself to be pretty interesting, and the developers have done a great job of letting the player put together the pieces of the story themselves, which I think makes the narrative a bit more interesting.
However the biggest problem for me is just how short the game is. I was able to complete the story in a little under 2 hours. Now this shortness issue wouldn't be a problem if the price matched it's length. I was able to get this during the Summer Sale for $3 and looking back even that seems to be overpriced for what this game is. The developers must have been taking crazy pills when they set the regular price at $19.99. I can go to the movies and buy a bag of popcorn for that price and get about the same amount of entertainment value. And it's not like I'm going to play it again either. The fun was putting the pieces of the story together, and since I have already played it, there really is no point. I may go back and take a look at the developer commentary, but that isn't very likely.
Even with this issue, I am still going to recommend Gone Home, since I was thoroughly entertained for that 2 hours, but I'll give the caveat that this game needs to be at bare minimum 85% off in order to make the amount spent more appropriate for the amount of time spent playing. It was entertaining, but not $20 entertaining.

A pestering pile of cheap tricks and clunky mechanics.
I am fan of hardcore games, and play tons of roguelikes with permadeath. Permadeath would make more sense than the mechanic in Dark Souls 2, which is; if you die, you become crippled. Slowly and surely your maxhp depletes, and so what's the point? Start a new game.
You're continually torn between objectives; go back in order to spend souls, but at the same time erasing all progress? One goal nullify the other one.
Combat is all about repetition until you find the "cheap trick" that make the fight 100% safe. Very little intuitive action, or sensible planning - simply: repeat and exploit.
Another cheap trick which makes no sense that caused me many a death is the fact that many barrels explode...but hey, only if YOU (the player, remember this is a game) touch it. If enemy destroy the barrel, nothing happens. Makes sense right? Nope.
This is how you MUST play this game: Grind souls, spend souls, grind some more. Repeat, repeat, exploit. Rarely is the experience satisfying.
The world is non-linear, but PROGRESS is linear; another mechanism where one nullify the other. It is not satisfying with an open world, when there clearly is ONE path you -should- go. Again, repeat and exploit.
If you insist on playing the game, go watch a walkthrough on youtube and try to copy it - makes no sense to do all the meaningless mistakes yourself when someone else already did it for you.
This is not a game, it's a chore.

9/10 - Gone Home is not your typical game, its more of an interactive story. I never read the reviews on the game, but I did get recommendations from friends to buy and play this game.
The game revolves you controlling Kaitlin Greenbriar as she returns home from her travels in Europe. When she gets home she finds an empty house and a unnerving note from her sister on the door. The game is played in first person view and their is no shooting, killing, or intense action to be found in this game. Is that a bad thing? NO, not if you are a fan of point and click adventure games, visual novel games, or interactive stories.
The game is short and can be finished in an hour if you speed through it, but if you are an explorer like me it will take you between 2 and 3 hours to finish this. This game is not for everyone as there is no interactions, but exploring the house, reading notes, and listening to journal entries and cassette tapes.  As I explored the Greenbriar home and found the notes and clues, I was fearing the worst outcome for this family. That is what made this game so compelling and the story so well written. The true story of the game and the ending was not what I was imagining in my mind.
Was this game worth $20? Probably not, but due to the cost of developing a game I'm sure it was considered a fair price. I bought the game during the Summer Sale and paid $5 for it, but after playing through this wonderful story I would gladly have paid more.
I would love to see The Fullbright Company make another game like this with a longer story. Do I recommend this game? HELL YEAH I DO!

A lot of people would roll their eyes if one were describe Gone Home as "A different kind of horror game" or having "Mature Themes". But this is the sort of game and scenario that earns that sort of accolade. Originally the game suggests a big pay off with how you are all alone in a semi-familiar space, once or twice I felt something was wrong and did get an eerie sense of being followed. But as the story progressed, these feelings gave way to a sense of dread as to what I was inevitably going to find, especially given the foreshadowing early in the story.
I feel a lot of people will be angrered that the pay off wasn't as spectacular as other games. I think that would have cheapened the experience however in that the game touched on very real fears people can have without relying on supernatural phenomena or a bogeyman to achieve.
Unlike walking simulators like "Dear Esther", the game gives some gratification for exploring. Following the breadcrumbs will only lead to one of the stories, where at least three or four others are going on around the player. All of these stories together create a more complete and satisfying conclusion when everything plays out in the end.
I recommend getting this game when it is on sale. It is a satisfying experience it lacks much replayability if you are thorough. Play it when you're alone and you want to try something different.

Summary: I recommend this game at or below the current price range of about $20. It's fun, has some unique mechanics, but also has some notable flaws and poor gameplay decisions.
Verdun is a WWI shooter, and it feels that way. The primary game mode is fighting for control of a series of parallel trenches, with teams taking turns to attack and defend. For the most part this is great, though a few maps have a few trenches that are significantly more difficult for one team to attack or defend than for the other.
If you live on the west coast, ping will kill you. I cannot get below 100 ms. This is unacceptable in 2015 for a twitch game. Seeing and hearing my rifle fire first but getting shot without getting a kill is a routine occurance. This easily happens three or four times every game. I am frequently killed after ducking into cover or around a corner as well. It is incredibly frustrating when your failure isn't the result of skill.
The system for calling morter strikes, gas attacks, and recon planes is abysmal. Squad leaders are forced to stand out of over and aim with their mouse. It is basically impossible to target anything at a distance reliably, and you can't aim over hills because you can't target what you can't see. The current system needs to be replaced with a map that you can use to target a grid reference. This is both more realistic from the simulation angle, and much less frustrating from the gameplay angle.
The squad gameplay is good. Players are encouraged to work together during games, and to regularly play with each other across games in order to level up the squad. One of the flaws here is that squad leaders serve as forward spawn points for their squad, which means that often the best tactical decision is for the squad leader to just sit in a foxhole near the enemy trench instead of actually advancing. Even the best player will eventually die if they attack, so squad leaders are basically discouraged from doing much, which sucks.

Hello. The following review is a comparison between Dark Souls 1 and Dark Souls 2, so it will assume that you have played the first one. Just so you have the full picture, I played DS1 first, and I haven't played Demon Souls. I've played both DS1 and DS2 on PC with KB+M.
Cons:
- The plot is almost non-existant and straight-away. Kill X things, kill big bad. While well-hidden, the first game plot was beautifully crafted and spawned many theories.
- The localizations don't seem as well connected. They generally follow a branching scheme, unlike the convoluted circle that was the first one. There are 1 or two exceptions. This in general makes the game easier to navigate (you can also teleportto any bonfire you have activated, right from the beggining), but gives a sensation of a less organical world. The areas don't seem to have a pourpose or related to eachother at all, they just are there.
- The enemies are a bit same-y. Hollows, rats, armed hollows, knights, bigger knights. And a couple of the ones already appeared on DS1, like basiliks.
Pros:
+ This time KB+M is native, and it shows.
+ The UI and mechanics (leveling up, estus, improving weapons, etc) have been greatly polished, while remaining the same scheme.
+ The covenants are great. There variety for pve, pvp, both invading and being invaded, dueling, jolly coop... Even one that summons people from a different covenant to protect you when you are invaded.
+ The connectivity is much, much better and there's tons of people playing at every level. You can easily find 3 helpers to fight pretty much any boss. Same for invading.
All in all, while DS2 is worse on the aspect of story and ambientation, it has on the other hand greatly improved mechanically, making it as enjoyable as the first one. You're certainly going to die, too.

These characteristics are reverberated throughout each of the Counter-Strike games and thus makes it one of my most favourite series of all.

When you buy it you'll die a lot and rage.
One day you'll play and realize you're dying and raging less than before.
A few days later you realize you've got the hang of one of the classes and start using it.
You're now ready to fully appreciate Verdun.
This ain't your grand pappy's fps. No sir. Verdun is a game that doesn't try to appeal to a broad consumer base, it's a rather interesting attempt to translate the horror of fighting in the First World War to something we as gamers can experience and maybe have some fun with and I think that from that basis, the game does that 10/10.
The squad based gameplay is really something to be enjoyed, when you have a proper organized squad that fights as a group, the battlefield is your playground. You'll progress together and unlock more passive bonuses that only apply when it's you playing together. You'll unlock powerfull artillery that can pound the enemy team and win you the game and later war uniforms that make you a known visually on the battlefield as Elites.
Verdun forces you to play as a squad and a team. A key part to enjoying this game is learning your role in that mix and making a real impact in the outcome of the match. Feeling that victory when it was YOU who held the line and allowed your team to retake the trench in the last 30 seconds of a half hour stalemate is something you won't find in COD, Battlefront or any other fps.
I'd really reccomend this game if you're a gamer that really enjoys historically based games and casually plays an fps from time to time. You might also enjoy it if you're suffering from COD exhaustion and need something fresh because it really is fresh. At the end of the day Verdun is value for money and the Devs are continually releasing more content that makes the enjoyable experience already there even better.

Another point-and-click storytelling game. I'm a huge fan of this genre, though it repeatedly seems to be not worth the money.
Gone Home creates a truly believable world and realistic characters. However, the manner in which the story is told is frustratingly obvious. The first time you are given clues about certain aspects of a character's personality or problems they are facing, it is interesting to guess the subtleties of their individual situations. But any fun derived from figuring out these mysteries is shortly ruined by being bombarded with obvious hint after obvious hint until finally, you are basically slapped in the face with the all-too-obvious truth. This made me feel like it was further simplifying the story, which was already far too short and simple in my opinion.
The game mechanics themselves are also a bit flawed. Almost every cabinet and drawer door is able to be opened, and there are lots of cloned objects that serve no purpose but to get in the way of certain objects that are actually important to the story. It says I have logged 2.5 hours on this game but a good 45 minutes of that was probably wasted on picking up rolls of toilet paper just to see if there was a key hidden underneath them.
The graphics and objects were fairly glitchy even when I turned my graphics on maximum settings.
In terms of sound, the background noises were too repetitive. The first time certain noises like thunder happened, it took me by surprise, but eventually I wanted more variety. The random cassette tapes you can play are a fun addition, but the sound was not balanced properly and the music plays WAY too loudly, to the point where I had to keep adjusting the volume every time I even saw a cassette player as I entered a room.
Overall, I would say this game is worth the $2.99 I spent during the summer sale, but paying more than $5 for this would be unwise. It will last you only about 2 hours even if you take a long time and pore over every detail. I guess it's still a relatively "indie" genre and can't be compared to much else, which explains why some critics loved it. While I can't say I completely hated it, the game was too frustrating in too many ways to make it a truly enjoyable experience.

The most prominent feature of the Souls game is how they narrate their story. They make you scrape off the surface to find crumbles of the gloomy past... Of the gloomy kings and kingdoms. Souls games are only known with their difficulty, but there is more to it than that. It's its enviromental story telling, item descriptions, obfuscating, yet tactfully put level design. Although this game is directed by Tomohiro Shibuya and Yui Tanimura, and not Hidetaka Miyazaki himself, the legendary director behind Demon's Souls and Dark Souls, it's still quite something, and almost (!) as striking.

A lot of negative reviews come from people not realizing what this game was. It's a short story in an interactive format. You explore a house and uncover information about what you missed while you were abroad.
I found this game really relaxed (although at times a little creepy!) and I really found myself caring about what happened to my sister, Sam.
While this game is very much a 'walking simulator' it tells a simple story very well. It's a story that many queer gamers can surely appreciate and relate to. It resonated exceptionally well with me and I loved every bit of it. I only wish there was more I could learn abous Sam and Lonnie, I want to know how their adventure goes!
Despite my praise, I do agree that the price tag is too high for the ~1-2 hour playtime. I'm reccommending with the understanding that if you buy it you should definately try to get it on sale!

Well. Just finished the game in just 45 hours. I haven't yet done the DLC material but overall this game has been a huge disappointment so far. As a big fan of Dark Souls 1  (over 800h played) this game just felt totally inferior to it almost every possible way. I felt bored almost all the time playing this game. I felt like I had already seen everything in Dark Souls1 that this game tried poorly mimic. I think atmosphere was way off during most of the game. Bosses were boring and generic and even the soundtrack was lacking this time. Some mobs just spammed one single attack, how lazy is that !? The overall expression was that this game was a bit rushed and lacked polish. It also felt just as a safe product from the B team that it didn't really provide anything interesting for the old souls fan.
Pros and Cons
+Majula is overall better hub area than Firelink Shrine
+Castle Drangleic area and Shrine of Amana were some of my favourites
+Long enough main quest
+Brings many new weapons in the game
+Backstabs are made harder->PvP much better than in Dark Souls 1
+Encouraged new fighting stances and styles
+Pretty good graphics
-Not memorable soundtrack, outside of few outliers.
-Crappy Bosses, some of them were very lame. Not memorable...
-Map design felt gimmicky and tiring, some areas felt half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and soulless
-Branches of yores ( You will get stuck often with no good reason)
-Not interesting NPC
-Not hard enough, though-
-Deaths were sometimes unfair and unavoidable (Swarm Bosses, cheap ambushes)
-Not very memorable game for an old Souls gamer to sum it all
If you haven't played other Souls games, this game would be more interesting experience though. Its not a bad game by any means, it just compares quite badly to other Souls games in terms of personality, polishment, quality and overall atmosphere. It has this overall design thinking of "quantity over quality" imho. It tries to create this huge world with more bosses than ever but fails to deliver the quality that is expected from the series and leaves me with  a very bad taste in mouth.

Verdun is a buggy, but maintained and enthralling mess.
The dev team seeks to keep improving the game from what I can tell, although I've only had it for a short time I've heard how far the game has come. The gameplay (I've really only played the frontlines mode) is quite addicting. Verdun put a sort of co-op spin on the game that I haven't seen anywhere else and I thought it was well done. Your squad levels up as a whole, and this is done by playing together. So if you play lone wolf all the time, you'll be using bad gear your entire gametime. If you get some friends, you can upgrade everything from your reload times to whether you call in a mortar strike or full fledged artillery. Also, as a mark to how good your squad is, your uniforms get better with leveling your squad as well.
As far as gameplay goes, as I said previously it is addicting. Don't expect to Rambo it, as this is a world war 1 game so there's a good chance you'll get your cranium exploded while walking out of the trench. The fighting actually feels pretty nice, although the game itself can be a bit clunky at times. The melee system is currently a bit hard to use successfully but I have faith that that will be fixed later on. The units, weapons, and maps are all historically accurate.
The community of people who play the game is relatively small, so you can expect to see the same people around now and again. Usually they mean well and will help newcomers out if possible.
I was gifted this game, but if I'd have known how much fun I'd have playing it, I'd have paid the full release price. I'd give it an 9/10.
