TL;DR Buy Verdun, just speaking of some major flaws of the game.
I don't need to speak for the positive reviewers. They've emphasized plenty about the goods of the game, and although I'll dabble in that a bit, I'm mainly here to talk about Verdun's flaws.
For starters, I reccomend buying Verdun, especially on sale. It's even better if you have friends and microphones. But I'm marking this review as negative because I think the devs will be more likely to look for criticism in the negative reviews than in the positive reviews.
When you boot up Verdun, the game briefly touches on the main gamemode, Trench Warfare. It teaches new players how  pushing and defending works, but that's about it. It hints at squad bonuses and more, but it is in no way comprehensive. While there are plenty of steam guides teaching about the game, a better way to teach new players and make that newfound knowledge stick is to make an ingame tutorial! Unfortunately, we have no form of this. This leads way to another problem, tooltips.
The tooltips in this game are ♥♥♥♥ing
. Let's imagine a scenario.
Welcome little Timmy to the frontline! Unfortunately, we have some incoming tear gas which will incapacitate and eventually kill you! Luckily, Timmy, we have gasmasks as standard issue to every soldier on the front! We even go so far as to tell you how to equip it! When gas spreads out over your location, we give you this handy tool tip! Look!
Press [Gasmask] to equip gasmask
Did you catch that? No, that's not me substituting a word for a key, that's just what it says. Or like this helpful tooltip!
Press [Sprint/Breathe] to breathe
Another, more major complaint I have about Verdun is the barbed wire. For one, it is too deadly. Barbed wire should not kill on its own, because in real life barbed wire did not kill on its own. It cut and stabbed and hurt like hell, but it wasn't enough to kill a man. It's main purpose was to discourage and to slow down or trap an enemy. Please devs, make barbed wire slow or render victims immobile, until they can free themselves after an excrutiatingly lengthy period. They'll probably die that way, and its less frustrating when you know you deserve that death.
Also, for crying out loud, can we fix all the little pieces of
barbwire that is merely a stray strand, but can trap and kill you? This kind of thing is completely unacceptable. While the devs do ask for screengrabs of these strands, You have to realize they included these in the map when they built them. It's also ♥♥♥♥ing impossible to get every strand in a screenshot, because there is no offline mode. Rather, there is no way to start an empty map without players or bots and be free to explore without being executed for desertion. If the devs would include this incredibly simple feature, we could have a breakthrough in bugfixes and finally have a chance to hunt all those pieces of♥♥♥♥♥♥out there. This is also a way to give your newer players a way to dull the sharp edge the ol' vets have against newbies. New players could have a chance to learn the map without dying, exploring the passageways and hiding spots.
Speaking of desertion, the mechanic is so poorly done its pathetic. There are two instances where you can be executed for desertion, both of which require you to be out of a permitted zone for an amount of time. You can be executed for not retreating (quickly enough) and for stepping out of bounds, be it out of the map or out of your trench when defending. Stepping out of your trench is cool - I think its appropriate and stops players from making no man's land completely, insanely deadlier than it already is. But often, if you aren't eyeing your radar like a hawk, you'll accidentally step into the out of map zone, usually to the side. In No Man's Land, where you are going to die if you stay in the open, Suddenly being caught unawares and having FIVE SECONDS to respond while also being gunned down is unacceptable. At the very least, increase the out of bounds time to 10 seconds, but can we make the boundaries more clearly established? Some fences, maybe make it physically impossible or very difficult to reach the out of bounds?
And then we get to retreating. This timer is meant to prevent players from camping in no mans land after a failed assault and ambushing pushing players, but as a side effect it forces retreating players to run irrationally because if they don't flat out sprint to the trench they'll be executed. This forces players to retreat stupidly and often get killed through no fault of their own. I don't suggest that the timer be extended though -- this would undo the very problem it aimed to solve -- but maybe do something more innovative -- imagine the no man's land area in layers. Now, imagine the retreating team slowly reeling back these layers all the way to their trench. Force the players to not be past a certain point, starting from the furthest up player of the team and ending at the trench. Maybe make a visible line that clearly indicates that its time to go, and make it a speed that allows players to retreat without being guaranteed to be picked off.
Moving on, though, there is a surprising lack of real teamwork in the game, with little to no players with microphones. This is not a fault of the game itself, but it is something to consider before buying. However, the voip that IS available can be downright atrocious at times -- as to which I cannot offer an explanation nor solution.
Something I can offer solution to, though, is a detail of the hud. The hud in Verdun is simplistic and does the job, however on some maps the nameplates can obscure major angles and render you practically blind to the enemy, namely the long tunnel in Fort Douamont. Please, make the nameplates not appear after a certain range, or stop them from showing up through walls. This has a real effect on gameplay and the ability of the players, and its something so stupid and simple.
Nonetheless, Verdun is a shooter to be reckoned with. It's got many flaws, and seemingly obvious ♥♥♥♥ ups, but its a great deal of fun. I reccomend buying it, especially at a discount. Its bolt action rifle gunplay is unique and demanding of skill, lacking the cheap run and gun flavor of call of duty. Enjoy it.

Unfortunately Warface was tarnished by lackluster reviews and a confusing business model upon release. Regardless, as the game stands now, it is my favorite modern multiplayer FPS! Let me fill you in on why I think so, and also go through a few cons:
-The gunplay is precise and eschews the contemporary fps trappings of drastic bullet drop and flinch mechanics, which leads itself to a more twitchy arcade feel than most modern FPSes. Dig 90s fpses? You’ll probably enjoy Warface!
-There are over 130 guns that are available so far in the game. These items are not re-skins but unique items that have different properties. And the majority are fun to use! The game also features the same in-game gun attachment editor that the Crysis series has. The devs still regularly add brand-new weapons to the game.
- Warface has the most satisfying feedback I’ve encountered in an FPS. The garishly large hit-markers, propensity for shotguns to ragdoll players backwards, and powerful headshot mechanics are visual-aural crack.
-Maps tend to be game-mode specific. For instance, Free-For-All levels are not available to be played as Team Deathmatch maps. This isn’t a problem as the level design is well designed for each respective game-mode, and the variety of environments on display are impressive. Warface has an absurd amount of maps for a f2p game and the devs are constantly adding new ones.
-The game features a 5-player co-op mode with unique levels of varying difficulty.
-Graphically the game hovers between decent and mediocre. The Cry Engine lends itself to some extremely pretty lighting effects in a few of the levels; Farm Sunset and many of the co-op and domination maps come to mind. Some of the simpler levels, such as Oil Depot and Dock, look dated. The game is optimized extremely well though!
-The load times can be pretty wretched.
-This game is stingy as hell when it comes to currency. All non-default weapons and equipment will degrade in effectiveness as you progress and require costly repairs. This often means it’s unfeasible to wear multiple pieces of premium armor and use your fancy new gun without eating into whatever money you have left. My advice would be to be constantly mindful of how much money you’re making per match versus how high your repair costs are; it’s easier to get the hang of after you play for a bit. The devs have made some major strides recently to address these issues; currently you receive non-rare weapon unlocks for free, and it’s possible to purchase any of the guns or equipment you could otherwise with both premium and non-premium currencies. Warface is definitely not pay-to-win despite what other reviewers have said.
-There is an issue with high-ping players and cheaters dominating matches especially if you are in the U.S. trying to find a decent match late at night. These players often will blink out of existence, teleport, not take damage, and/or aim-bot you. The community is stretched pretty damn thin. Be aware that you might not have the best experience unless you’re playing during the evening or weekend. This is the most glaring issue with the game, but can be somewhat circumvented by finding pockets of folks to play with who aren’t jackasses.
Regardless of these cons, the satisfying gunplay, vast abundance of gear and weapons, fast-paced combat and emphasis on headshots keep me coming back for more! The End.

Pros and Cons
+Majula is overall better hub area than Firelink Shrine
+Castle Drangleic area and Shrine of Amana were some of my favourites

Five Nights at Freddy's 2 is a Twitch/Thriller adventure pretty much what you get in the first game you double and increase the difficulty and force the player to face their worst fears from the first game, in Five Nights at Freddy's 2, you're brought right up close and personal with the things you're so afraid of in the first game.
Unlike in Five Nights at Freddy's, the pizzaria has been re-opened and is now "child friendly" and here is where you chose to work, in a safe & family friendly environment right?, ahaha yeah think again. The game spans out exactly the same as the first it's a very simple and very easily playable & basic designed game the mechanics have been slightly changed and tweeked and new enemies have been brought to the table with different behaviours.
What you believed to be really simple & safe work turns into one of the most horrific & difficult but 100% worth it times of your life.
The story is really simple & i basically explained it above, you're a job seeker who found an ad in the paper about a really easy job being a security guard at Freddy's Fazbears Pizzaria doing the late shift of a night that's a Monday - Friday job with minimal pay (YAY).
You're to spend 6 hours a night in your little office doing the night shift at Freddy's Fun Farm as a Security Guard, the premise of the game is very simple, make sure that nobody intrudes into Freddy's during the night while trying to avoid the strange & earily creepy Freddy & his robotic friends as they roam the building during the night.
Not everything is as peachy and friendly of a night time though as you'll soon find out because you're running on a timer during the night as power is scarce & you need to save the power as much as you can so that you can keep an eye on Freddy & his friends as they happen to be quite afraid of new people & tend to... well kill people who aren't familiar to them.
Each night becomes increasingly difficult & not only that but it seems to take longer to complete each night, of course if that's not bad enough then you'll find comfort in the fact that Freddy & his friends become more and more active through the week & require a lot more thorough checking in order to avoid winding up like so many other Secutiry Guards before you.
This game really relies on you to be 100% alert at all times & not only is hard to do that because you're constantly switching between camera's & checking outside your office doors but Freddy & his friends tend to just randomly screw with you on certain playthroughs by disabling the power of the lights or by disconnecting your cameras, not only do they do that but sometimes they completely obscure the camera vision with their evil smiles or to make things worse sneak into your office & while you're busy watching the camera's feel the need to scare the living ♥♥♥♥ out of you!
Enemies in Five Nights at Freddy's 2 don't always follow the same set path either, enemies will often pop up in different corridors and come from differen't angles as to always keep you alert.
There are SOOO many good things i can say about this game but i don't have enough characters to type all of these things, and very few faults i can pick at with this game.
Although this game is designed solid & it's scares are not those small little "Oh i saw that coming but it still scared me" scares they're truly terrifying when they happen because you never really know when you're going to get caught by Freddy or his friends & whenever you do it's generally off guard they catch you.
The AI in this game although very simple is Flawless an it always manages to be challenging even if it's so simple & due to the randomization of the gameplay you never experience the same thing over and over.
Sometimes the game can feel unfair when you're almost finished and the robots all gather around you in your office, or when Freddy & his friends turn off the power to the lights and leave you in the dark but it never feels 100% cheap it is just the game really screwing with you and tormenting you, wanting you to continue but at the same time showing that you'll never be guarenteed a win even if you're so close.
The setting in this game although simple is designed perfect to be creepy even if it is a few different static backgrounds quickly slapped together, it's a flawless attempt at making a horror experience and it works 100% without a doubt.
I give this game a 9/10.
And i give it this because there's really no flaws in it, it's just designed perfect in every way, The game is meant to be difficult & it achieves that by occasionally putting you in situations of intense thrills & other times you breeze through without even seeing Freddy or his friends
Even though the game is very much the same each time it makes the experience different each playthough so it gives it replay value & then there's the thrill of beating the levels and knowing that you've overcome the odds and made it through to the next day!
Yes i do recommend this and i suggest that people buy this game because it's so damn cheap and a well worthy experience.
If you're on the fence about it try playing Five Nights at Freddy's 1 and see if you enjoy it as they're almost the same except with new and improved enemies & a few more hard challenges.

War can be absolute hell. Few demonstrate that with the same level of authenticity, ferocity and historical accuracy like Verdun; a World War I first person shooter set between 1914-1918 on the Unity Engine. Here, you get to experience what it might have been like as a footsoldier of nations such as France or Germany; fighting repeatedly for the same trenches and fortifications in absolute hellish conditions. Here, men do not hide and squawk orders from a rearline garrison but lead by example on the frontlines with their squadmates. Here, a single well-placed bullet, grenade or mortar strike can make all the difference between total victory or costly defeat. And here, only death is a certainty; you will die many times over before you secure that trench you are later expected to defend against impending counterattacks.
Among my list of top recommended First Person Shooters to date. Anyone worth their salt who wants a rest test of their mettle, this is an absolute must have!

If you can pick it up for $5 or less, Gone Home is a no-brainer. Without spoiling anything, its story is several notches above what you normally get in videogames, and you're kept in suspense a lot of the way: as you find bits and pieces about your family, it feels like things could spiral in any number of directions, and even when the plot becomes clear, you're never sure what kind of ending you're in for until the very end.
That said, keep in mind Gone Home is really short: it might be the size of one Half-Life level, is more interactive story than game, and even if you examine everything, you'll be done in 60-90 minutes. Unless you're specifically looking to support the developer, it's hard to recommend spending the full $20 on it.

Alright, first let me clarify that I do not object to the gameplay of this game. So many people are accusing this game of not being a "real" game because it's a narrative that you explore. They're wrong. This game brings to mind the world of Myst, which was a game released in 1993 that single-handedly made the CD-ROM format popular. Anyone who claims that Gone Home isn't a game doesn't know what a game is.
Gone Home puts you in the shoes of Kaitlin, a girl who has just returned home from college to find her parents new home completely empty. Her sister, Sam, has left a very spooky note on the door telling Kate that she has left. This early narrative and the overall atmosphere of the game (night setting, thunderstorm and heavy rain, etc.) leads the player to believe that there is a supernatural element at work here. In fact, through various notes and diaries that you find throughout the house, you are further encouraged to foster the idea that Sam and her "friend", Lonnie, have been hunting and speaking to the ghost of the former tenant of the home, Oscar. Among items in the house, you find a Ouji board, a safe filled with old pharmacy equipment from the days before Oscar died, and a particularly creepy crucifix that is scripted to shut off the lights when you look at it. Other than these things there is zero horror or suspense in this game. There is an obvious bait and switch tacked onto the surface of this game from the screenshots to the art style and early themes of the game. After the initial mentioning of Oscar, he isn't mentioned again at all until the very end, after you have endured countless audio diaries of Sam moaning on about her girlfriend, Lonnie. It's almost as if the game was created to draw in players wanting a driving suspenseful story only to let them down with a lesbian romance that is mind-numbingly boring. Putting aside the annoying Riot Grrl and Feminist trash littered throughout Sam and Lonnie's hang out spots, there are some interesting items that help you put together the story of the Greenbriar family. This gameplay mechanic was actually pretty fun and reminded me of Myst. Since this was the best part of the game to me, I won't spoil it, but be sure to savor it, for it does not last long.
At the end, after it is revealed that Sam and Lonnie have kissed, Kaitlin discovers that her sister has left, not to escape any poltergeists or demons, but to participate in one of the oldest cliches in romantic fiction. She's left to go after Lonnie. And that's it. Sam mentions in one of her audio diaries that she and Lonnie went up to the attic to say goodbye to Oscar, but other than that and the early hints at ghostly activity, there are no other paranormal elements to this game. The game never attempts to explain why there is a ghost, a noticeably unrealistic plot device, in a seemingly normal and mundane game setting. It doesn't explain what Sam and Lonnie did to make peace with the ghost. It's a meaningless story element that seems to exist only as a decorational gimmick to draw in players.
The above fact added to the price tag of TWENTY dollars serves to imply that this game was thrown together to make a quick buck. The story is unimaginative and the the playing time is a mere two hours. I played through with the developer's commentary tracks on a second play through, so I spend a little over four hours playing the game. It's probably the shortest game that I've ever bought on Steam. It MIGHT be worth $5 at the most, which is what I paid for it. But honestly, even at that price, the story is lackluster and relies on shady bait and switch tactics to draw you in. It CERTAINLY isn't worth $20. DO NOT pay that kind of money for this game. Wait till it goes on sale or play a friend's copy to test it out first. Don't reward these kind of business tactics with a full $20. I would have felt robbed if I had paid that much money for this game. Steam doesn't give refunds, so you should put your money to better use.

I wish there was a sideways thumb for this title. I am a lover of spooky horror games and I feel like this had potential but managed to miss the mark for me a bit. While I thought the journal entries with the LGBT theme were a very sweet and endearing part of the story, I felt like it detracted from the spookiness a lot. It ended up sounding less like a scary story and more like an oppressed teen running away with her girlfriend. Made me wonder what the point of the whole thing was.
The atmosphere was decent as far as 'horror' games go. In the end, I had a hard time figuring out what the big mystery was. Exploration was fun at first but then quickly became sort of tedious as I meticulously gone through every room and encountered a locked door that I couldn't open. After searching the entire house without finding a way to progress, I decided I didn't want to spend any more time on this title.
I really don't like when games are arbitrarily long with no substantial filling. You can't just hide a key in a giant house where nothing is happening except the sound of thunder. Even all the lights work properly, so you don't have to be scared in the dark. There are seemingly useful bits of information everywhere but half of them are useless filler.  They didn't explain anything or help me figure out how to progress in the story. Most of it was random drivel.
So if this game is supposed to be scary, FAIL! If the game is supposed to be a new exploration/mystery type genre, not so fail, but deff not for me.

Trying to write a review for this is a bit on the tough side, as there's no sweet cheevos, no leveling up, and by the time you get to the end, there's no brofist waiting for you at the end of the credits. Instead what you have here is a game that is built off of the more old-school exploration senibilities such as the Activision Zork Titles, or much of Myst and The Journeyman Project, where your experience is more built off of exploration that allows you to unlock the full narrative. This type of gameplay is more slow-trodden than your normal games, but the reward is much more satisfying. I do have to say the makers of Gone Home have very much accomplished these ideals even in a game that on average should only take 2 hours for one to complete. Some may say that's a ripoff, I call it storytelling effencicy.
The basic plot is that you've been away trodging through Europe for a year, and you've made it home finally in the soaking rain. I should say the rain does act as a means of keeping you on your toes, but there is a soft humming tone that also blends  in with the storms, urging you to keep going forward while also maintaining a sense of urgency. You arrive home to an empty home, and the main plot is trying to figure out where everyone is, mainly your sister. I'm not going to go any further on the plot, but I have to say it's been a while since a game's narrative actually moved me, I was actually in a pretty good shock for a while there when I got to the end.
Graphically it's not going to be Crysis, but that's missing the point. The visuals are there to serve the narrative, and considering that your are exploring through a house I don't think you need Nvidia Titan Powahhh to enjoy this game. The music was also well done in the snippets that you find while wandering around.
Basically, buy this game, and even more I would say play this with your loved ones.

Dark Souls 2 is a fantastic RPG with a treasure trove of content. But that's by default, without considering all the improvements and DLC included in this particular edition! This is one of those games you'll never finish in one sitting, so prepare to spend at least a whole month attempting to beat the game, and that's if you just follow the main path!
Dark Souls 2 is a challenging fantasy adventure RPG with a very dark and forboding atmosphere. You'll find treasures, secret areas, and fight impressive bosses as you seek out the reason for your existence as an undead human. During this journey, you'll die a lot, and get caught in traps of all kinds. It doesn't hold your hand, and you'll often find yourself getting lost in Dark Souls 2, but that's only if you are a fairly new gamer. A lot of this game relies on you reading between the lines and understanding what to do based on careful environmental observation or talking constantly to key NPCs. A lot of what makes the game so great is that the difficulty is entirely based on mechanics, so YOU choose the difficulty by enlisting the aid of other players/NPCs or choosing to be a spellcaster for an easier time. You might get lost pretty often, but it's a challenging world worth getting lost in, and you might just find a legendary item for your exploration efforts! There is no "class restrictions", so you can be whatever you want to be when it comes to equipment and abilities, but you are free to roleplay as the class you start the game as. After that, you might just find yourself creating new characters just to experience the game in its entirety!
Beating the game is just the beginning, so if you're looking for a game that's worth every penny, then please give this game a try! It's fantastic!

Already invested a good amount of time into Dark Souls 2 with the DLCs? Then by all means, you're not going to be missing out too much if you don't get Scholar of the First Sin. If you only enjoyed DaS2 vanilla without the DLCs or haven't even touched DaS2 to begin with, then be sure to pick up Scholar of the First Sin whenever its on sale or you have the cash to spare.
Played a lot of vanilla DaS2 on the 360 and SotFS actually gave me a significantly more refined and enjoyable experience. Enemy placements have been improved by a huge margin and I felt that you could branch out to different areas much more easily once you got pass the Forest of Giants. DLCs also contribute a large amount of content to enjoy but not necessarily a brand new Souls experience.
Granted, SotFS improves a lot on Dark Souls 2, but it's still Dark Souls 2. The Agape Ring that stops the in take of Souls doesn't really stop Soul Memory from being terrible, so matchmaking is much more stunted. That and nothing was done about the active discouragement of invasions; invaders still can't heal without spells and no perfect Eye Orbs for either the Brotherhood of Blood or Knights of Blue. So if you really want to invade consistently, be prepared to either spend a lot of time gittin gud at the arena or burning all your pumpkins at certain bonfires.
TL;DR
Scholar of the First Sin is only worth it if you didn't enjoy the DLCs yet, but I'll give it a Yes.

I played this game for about 3 hours. Judging from the other reviews for this game, this seems to be around the average playing time. I like the game, although the end left me feeling unsatisfied.
While it was a very interesting way to tell a story, the plot was pretty predictable. By the end, I was disappointed that I was correct in my assumptions about why the family was not at home to greet Kaitlin. I was hoping there would be some sort of twist. There were also a few questions that remained unanswered by the end. Maybe I just missed a "clue" or two the first time around, although I'm not sure if I am willing to replay the game to find it.
I enjoyed exploring the creepy house, but you can only use the controls to look at objects (and throw them) instead of actually using them to do something. I feel that would have added to the experience and made the game more realistic.
I was also disappointed to find there were no achievements you could accomplish for this game. There are so many binders, pens, soda cans, and cups that I thought you could have been able to do something with them, like dumping all the cans from around the house in the recycling bin.
I really enjoyed the graphics for this game, and I had no trouble navigating through the house. I also got this game on sale, which I highly recommend doing. I feel like the original price is asking way too much for such a short game.
Overall, while I enjoyed making my way through the mansion and reading through the Greenbriar's personal documents and all, I was disappointed by the ending - I guessed it from the beginning, and one of the major plot points was never resolved. If you enjoy just snooping around in people's things and exploring creepy houses, I would definitely recommend this game (for the sale price). If you are looking for a game that you will want to invest hours upon hours in, I'd steer my attention elsewhere.

More Dark Souls is never a bad thing, and Scholar of the First Sin more Dark Souls 2 with better graphics, less bugs, better matchmaking, and more content.
That said, it still suffers from the overall dryness that the original release of Dark Souls 2 did. I just don't care about Drangleic or its history, and the game doesn't try to make an effort of making me. In Dark Souls, Lordran was steeped in lore and dripping wth atmosphere. I got sucked in to it and found myself scrambling to get every item I could just to read the descriptions and find another tidbit of info about the land I was in. On top of that, the game made me care about the history of the land. I wanted to find out more and more about the Dragons and the birth of the Age of Fire, what motivated Gwyn, and who his mysterious enemies were. The game was filled with Mystery that I wanted to uncover, and exploration was often met with another piece of the puzzle. Dark Souls 2? It has none of that. I don't care about Drangleic, I don't care about Vendrick, the NPC's mean nothing to me, the curse of the Undead feels like it doesn't even play a part in the story and is just there because the series demands it, the lore is secondary to the challenge of me beating the game as opposed to being a reward for overcoming the challenges up to beating the game.
All in all, Dark Souls 2 feels like Halo 2, in that it's a great game and worth playing, but it's fairly weak on its own strengths and its faults hit it hard because of that. It feel slike a test game, with FromSoftware looking at the success of the original Dark Souls and trying to see how they could change it up and improve, but without actually knowing what the outcome would be. All that said, I feel what the devs learned from community feedback on Dark Souls 2 will result in Dark Souls 3 being just as good if not better than the original Dark Souls.
All that said, Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin is a great game and well worth the money. If you are a returning fan of the series, you will be a little disappointed, but intrigued just the same. If you are just joining us then you are in for one hell of a journey, but I highly suggest you go back and get Dark Souls: Prepare to Die Edition as well as this. You'd be doing yourself a favor.

This was one of the most unique gaming experiences I've ever had. And that is exactly what it is, an experience. This game received a lot of criticism for it's 2-hour campaign and limited content. But that's like saying that a rollercoaster sucked because you couldn't derail and go bomb Russia. Gone Home is a breath of fresh air and really pushes the limits of creative and immersive story telling. If you have ever had troubles with family, identity, or have ever been a middle child or the black sheep, you will love this game. You will connect to this game. I sternly reccomend that you buy this game at whatever price it is listed and then find the time to sit down for an uninterrupted session and play the story all the way through. Take your time, explore, breath in the lives of the deeply detailed characters, and search for all the secrets in every nook and corner. You will not regret it. It is an ground-breaking experience that exemplifies the unique skill that video games have as an expressive art form. This game is one for the history books. Gone Home is now easily one of my favorite games that I suggest to everyone, whether they game or not. I hope you can enjoy this pleasure too.

I don't know how on Earth Scott was able to do it so quickly, but Five Night's at Freddy's 2 almost immediately raises the bar in terms of scariness from the origional. I haven't even played 20 minutes and I immediatly quit the game after getting no farther than Night 2 at 2 A.M. One thing that makes this game a lot scarier is how much different the game is than the last one. The origional formula of Five Night's at Freddy's did seem flustering at first, but it wouldn't take too lang to get used to it. Here, there are a whole slew of new things we never saw coming: No doors? What is this music box? OMG SHE'S STANDING RIGHT THERE WHAT DO I DO I HAVE NO DOORS!
The confusion is all the more dumbfounding when you find that listening to our good friend the Phone Guy is a lot harder when you are acquainting yourself with the new mechanics, a bit intrigued but all the more terrified. You will find yourself quickly spamming through cameras, trying to focus on the music box, and putting on your new Freddy Fazbear head if you feel like you are in danger. That's another perk of this game, the fear of an approaching monster in the origional game was quite terrifying, but it is quite tame compared to the sudden, horrible appearance of an animatron staring straight at you in your office. If you get your Freddy head on in time, you get to witness the sight of lights flickering as an animatron sits perfectly still in your office, watching you until it thinks it's a good idea to leave. I still have that horrible memory of seeing Bonnie right up in my face with practically nothing else other than the flickering lights. This is only scraping the surface of what is problably a very horrifying iceberg filled with tricks traps, and new horrors lurking inside your vents.
Five Night's at Freddy's 2 is an outstanding game on it's own, but if you liked ythe origional Five Night's at Freddy's, I promise this game won't dissapoint. Just be careful, and don't play this at night like I did, otherwise you can bid farewell to any chances of a good night's sleep.

Let me think about how to put how awesome and fun this game is. You can drive any vehicle you see, pilot any ship, fly any plane (civilian or military), and steer any helicopter you can grapple onto. Guns range from simple pistos you can dual wield to sawed off shotguns and rocket launchers, machine guns and sniper rifles. The fighting is fun enough, i can spend tons of hours just killing off the military bases and achieving 100% of government property destroyed and upgrades collected. There are thousands of collectables than can improve your character, vehicles and weapons. What makes the game unbelievable is how beautiful the scenery is while youre zipping along with your unlimited parachutes as you grapple onto the ground or a passing car or a tree with your grappling hook (that has some serious range on it) to maintain your velocity. The map is huge, seriously huge, and it covers everything you would find on a modern island with resources and tourists. Deserts, mountains, swamps, villages, city capitals with lots of skyscrapers, plains, jungles, resorts, refineries, even a frozen lake at the top of a volcano's caldera. There is always something to find and each location is unique. I love this game so much that I purchase multiple copies to give away so that other people that have no idea what Just Cause 2 is like, can experience for themselves. Once you beat the game, get some of the DLC for even more fun. The DLC i use the most is the rockets that strap onto your parachute to help get you where you're going even faster, or to jet out of the line of fire and then climb a skycraper with ease.

This is a very well constructed game that unfolds like a good book. Which is probably a good analogy, as the game would be best appreciated by those who enjoy reading books - if you find you don't have the patience for books then you won't enjoy this game and that probably explains some of the negative reviews.
All that said, I picked the game up for $5 in the Summer Sale, and that is a fair price - I would have felt ripped off if I'd paid full price ($20) for the less-than 2 hours it took to finish the game.
Saying too much about the story that unfolds would quickly lead to spoiler alerts, but suffice to say the writers have done an excellent job of layering emotional, sinister, and mystery storylines. There are times when the game guides you too obviously - many of the notes left for you to find are just too unrealistic and a just pushing you in the direction to go. Most "puzzles" have only one solution, so judged purely on game mechanics it's pretty basic. But as an interactive story, with a well thought out environment it's great.
Just don't pay retail.

A game that gets pretty repetitive over time unless you actively go out of your way to play in a ridiculous way. This game doesn't necessarily hold your hand and force you to participate in stunts, so the player must plan out different ways they'd like to complete a mission. So this game can be either ridiculously fun, or repetitive if the player does not try to do stunts. When it works, it becomes a James Bond like experience with great locations for missions and ends with one of the most ridiculous video-game conclusions. The final mission (I won't spoil), is the summation of all the ridiculous stunts you may have performed in the game. This is a great game to come back to once and a while, and it is not essential to complete in order to actually enjoy the experience. The open-world elements are worth the initial price, as you'll find yourself parachuting out of cars and latching enemies to vehicles so they are dragged behind. Lots to do, and there aren't many other games like it!

On the surface, Gone Home may seem to be nothing more than some kind of indie horror game. Then you dig a little deeper and it starts to sound like a "game" which is not really a game. No combat? Minimal puzzles? Why didn't they just make this a short film or a book? Rest assured, however, that Gone Home is a story which not only benefits from the interactivity of this medium, but thrives on it. You control Katie, but Katie is not really part of the story. Katie's solo adventure through this house, experienced as your own solo adventure, has you uncover the story piece by piece. A Wikipedia summary does this story no justice. It's the little things. At the beginning of the game, nothing makes sense, you're just reading letters, finding photographs, and listening to audio journals. But as the story comes together, its emotional beats hit hard. I can't say any more without spoiling anything but several days after completing Gone Home's three hour story, I can't get it out of my head. I can still see the book on the table in the TV room, the photo in the locker, the letter on the back of dad's book... This is not a game for everyone, it definitely requires you to be a certin type of person from a certain background. If you are remotely interested, stop reading about it and go play it. You may not be as completely in love with it as I am, but rest assured that if you take your time and really put yourself in that house in small town Oregon in 1995, you will leave that house having had an unforgettable experience.

I would give this game three out of five stars if I could.  For as much as I liked about it, there was a lot that I didn't.  If you can catch it on sale for under $3, I recommend purchasing this game just to try it for yourself.  Trust the reviews section - most of the praises and the criticisms I read there before making my purchase were spot on.  I picked up all of the Journal entries on my first play through to the end of the game.  It took about 5 hours for me (I'm not a fast gamer, I did stop to look at a lot of irrelevant game objects, and since steam is telling me my play duration is a lot shorter than the amount of time I was up playing, I think that has something to do with my resetting the game a few times.)  From here, I'll go ahead and point out some of the things I liked and disliked, and I'm not necessarily going to keep it spoiler free.
PROS:
* The young ladies in this story are genuinely loveable characters.  If you have a heart and an open mind, you'll find yourself wanting happy endings for all of them by the end of this story.  I hope you like love stories.
*The setting is immaculate.  The designers really put a lot of detail into the number of objects you can handle in their environment, and for a house, it is an exceptionally large building to explore.  If you grew up in the mid 90s or ever wondered what it was like to do so, you'll get a kick out of the setting.
*This game is entirely story driven.  There's nothing to fight.  There's nothing any more creepy than the feeling you get when you walk into your own home or basement when the lights are out and nobody else is there and it happens to be night time and stormy.  The challenges in this game all involve figuring out where keys are located to open doors and safes in the house that might further explain the absence of your family's presence there.
*I'm not aware of too many games that address coming out/getting outed or even being the new kid in school, so kudos to this one on targeting whose issues.
CONS:
*There are not many Steam achievements to unlock for this game (5 I think).
*From a technical standpoint, while I liked having control over the environment, certain tasks became menial very quickly.  Specifically, opening unlocked doors and turning on light switches that are near the doors.  There are a lot of doors and a lot of light switches in very obvious places in the house.  You'd think the developers could have automated the actions of turning on the lights and opening doors as the character approaches doorways, but nope.  You'll have to do it yourself every time.
*The first con was exacerbated by the fact that, at least for my old system, the game was a bit laggy.  I didn't want to take extra time on menial tasks because my system was having trouble keeping up with the demands of the game.  For a game that is so short and seemingly simple, it sure does take up a lot of resources.  Check your specs before you buy.  I saw some improvements in the lag on my system when I optioned the game out of full screen and played it in a window instead.
*What's with the journal?  Sam's narratives are basically the basis of the game story, and they come in the form of Journal entries that you hear periodically through Sam's voice as you explore the house.  But you don't ever "pick up" this journal when you walk into the house, and who would leave 20 pages of a journal scattered all over their house anyway?!  You're just expected to swallow and accept the idea of the phantom journal if you want to enjoy the game.  Maybe the ghost Sam was worried about found her journal and is relaying it to us telepathically somehow.  Uh...sure.
*Back to the characters and the worst of the SPOILERS:  I loved the characters, but for a game that is riding on its story, I wanted both the story and the characters fleshed-out more by the end.  Mom and Dad are exactly who you'd expect them to be and you have to wonder why your lead couldn't at least hazard an educated guess as to why they weren't around without having to poke around the house.  Do you know when your parents' anniversary weekend is?  The character you play is not well developed either.  She is obviously well loved by her sister and enjoys travel, but beyond that, she's just a vessel for obtaining the story of the real lead, her sister Sam.  We get a good idea of who Sam is: a 3rd year high school student with a vivid imagination, a closeted lesbian with a new-found love interest, and the new kid in school whose peers would rather know rumors than know her.  We get some good development there, with the parents finding out about the love interest, and the stolen clothes in Sam's room, and Sam running away from home, but then we get lost because the story ends just a short while after we find out Sam has run off for good (as if we didn't guess at that way before the end of the game).  For a game that seems to be tugging at our heartstrings about how parents relate to their LGBT teens, this was a really poor way to wrap it up.  Sam's parents haven't gotten upset enough to put Sam out of the house, and even the love interest Lonnie is still allowed over to the house (albeit with the same no locked doors rule my parents enforced when I was a teen).  So if Lonnie called crying to be picked up, why wouldn't Sam just bring her on over to the empty house for a while and sort things out before running away?  And if Sam thinks her parents trust her older sister's judgement more, why wouldn't she try asking her sister to speak up on her behalf and work things out with them before over running off?  And why did Sam steal those clothes again?  So this is the part where we get to leave the house and go find Sam, bring her home, and talk sense, right?  Nope!  The game's over, and I still want to know what happens next!  That's no good!
At the end of the night, I got my $3 worth of entertainment out of Going Home, but I would have been disappointed if I had paid any more than that.  It had a cute little love story that kept me playing, and I'll admit to having a soft spot for LGBT themes and kids who don't fit in in school, but if none of those things draws you in, this could be a very boring game that you'll never care to finish.

I can't describe how I feel about Verdun without describing how I started playing it.  I bought the game, loaded up my first match, ran out of the trench, and died immediately.  Wash, rinse, repeat.  But then you start learning, when to crawl, when to sprint, when to aim and when to fire blindly.  This is not Call of Duty (though the community seams surprisingly similar), you need to think about each shot, down to when you reload.  This is not Battlefield, squad members really need to work together, not just play in a similar vicinity.  I would highly recommend playing with a full squad complement of friends, or really learning how to play your role (though only half the community seems to play to squad rather than just play it like every other shooter).  It's also really refreshing to see a game being constantly updated, for FREE, with new content and engine overhauls.  The devs are constantly showing off new stuff they plan to add, with at least a vague timetable as to when they are trying to implement it.  I love this game, but I hesitate to recommend it, at least for the moment.  The devs certainly deserve love for all their work, but with what's promised, the game will be truly amazing in a while, just not right now. Gone Home is a beautifully crafted tech demo of walking through a multi-level home, and picking up various 3D objects. There are a few notes scattered through the house, which tell an interesting love story of in the style of the classic "Juliet and Juliet." While I really did enjoy the demo, and would gladly recommend it for the low sale price, I did find two notable flaws. First, the non-sale price is much too high for what you get. Second, this is being sold as a "game", which is a bit misleading. It has almost no classically defined "game" qualities at all, unless you consider clicking random things and hearing audio feedback to be a game. I do that everyday with the apps I use at work, and they certainly don't provide any entertainment value. I really do hope that the developers decide to get into full-blown game development, there seems to be a lot of promise in this demo.
TLDR: This isn't a game in any real sense. The story is decent, but nothing earth-shattering. I'll forget I ever played it in a few weeks. Unless you can buy it on sale, I would pass. If there was a neutral rating I would take it, instead I will give it the thumbs up solely for the graphics and fair story.

So I don't usually review games, because I am any combination of busy or lazy depending on what day of the week it is. But I noticed that this particular game had a lot of negative reviews, and I don't really feel it deserves them. I actually thought Gone Home was a great game. Sure, it's a bit short, but it's got a lovely, heartwarming story to tell, and the detail with which the environment has been created is really impressive. Graphics are quite nice, too. Don't get me wrong, it's not worth 20 dollars, it's just not long enough, heartwarming or not. But it's easily worth 5. If you can get it on sale, get it.
I will say one thing about this, though. I feel this game was originally meant to be a horror game, and that idea was scrapped at some point, because the atmosphere is as thick as a brick wall and there are all kinds of horror elements in it, it just ISN'T a horror game. I'd love to see this studio actually MAKE a horror game, I think it'd be AMAZING, because they clearly know how to build atmosphere and design an environment that makes the player really WANT to explore it.
tl;dr
+Great graphics
+Phenomenal environmental detail
+Awesome atmosphere
+Beautiful heartwarming story told expertly through both narrative and environment exploration
-Really short
*IMO this studio should stop trying to be heartwarming and start trying to be terrifying because they'd probably be really good at it.

What made the first Dark Souls an epic game?
It was a challenge. You could make mistakes, pay for them and then fix them.
If you were careful you could beat the game easily without dying.
It created, alongside a beautiful atmosphere and universe, a wonderful experience.
The whole world was connected, making it feel like a real world, a dying and rotting place where everything wants to kill you.
You couldn't teleport, making it a more immersive experience
You could try, die and try again knowing that this time you would make it right.
The only thing that makes
rage everytime is the Bed of Chaos' fight.
It's a "let's try it and hope for the best" fight.
You have to know the moveset and where the holes will be to do this boss flawlessly, and the trial and error concept it's not part of this game, it is like that only if you're living it wrong.
And it's completely out of context.
This game is like a Bed of Chaos fight all the time.
The only reasons that makes this game hard are:
- Lots of enemies at the same time
- Enemies hidden around the corner that will go full Al-Qaeda
- Enemies that spam the same move endlessly
- Enemies with movesets that are like a Nikita Rocket Launcher that will follow you even in the grave
- Enemies can hit you through walls
- Enemies can hit you while you roll
- Enemies can land hits even if the weapon didn't hit you
- Projectiles follow you everywhere, even making an S shape.
In this game you can't make mistakes because if you get hit it can end in only 2 ways: you get one-shotted, or you get stunned for a sufficient time for the enemy to chain another attack and stun you again. And 3 enemies, even if they deal only 2% of your life per hit, will get you permastunned and dead. Considering that you will NEVER fight less than 5 enemies at the same time, this happens frequently.
These factors doesn't make it a challenge, they only ruin the experience and the immersion.
Another great idea the designers had while creating this game was to re propose some bosses as regular enemies.
Pursuers. Ruin Sentinles. Dragonriders. Flexile Sentries.
The whole game is full of these bosses scattered randomly around the map.
The problems of this game aren't only the mechanics, it creates no feeling, no connection, it's just fan servicing.
Gaming is about experiencing. And with this game you experience

Putting that aside lets get to the good parts first. CO-op is fun, complex. Missions offer variaty in objectives and scenery, great weapons customization, also a lovely progresion system to unlock various weapons,  atachements  armors and so on.

Now to the bad...Considering that it's made by crytek, a developement studio that actually has years of experience in making FPS, it leaves you head-scratching-confused as to why they employed such awkward gameplay ethics, in the multiplayer versus domain, making plenty of their features become redundant, like class type importance is nullified, as well as tactics and strategy. Death has no weight in multiplayer, as you will revive almost imediatly after dying, leaving the medic jobless, since it is faster to respawn than to revive somebody. Utilising a classes' ability is slow and clumsy, discouraging a more support-type aproach toward your team's objective in a match. Except for "planting the bomb" matches all else feel more like cluster-F@cking with soldiers, banging helmets and winner being the one with the most helmets bangged. An old issue that still seems to plague the game is relatively low ping sensing a 0.2-0.3 lag.
Verdict
CO-OP fun and fullfilling in it's purpose (only reason I'd recommed this game to anyone)
Multiplayer versus, a  second thought, slapped together to make the game look more "whole", best method to employ in achieving victory, is to zerg like "YOLO!" (perhaps the game would be better without it?)

Although imperfect and still finding its feet, Verdun is perhaps one of the most original first-person multiplayer shooters ever made in that it is an immersive and believable rendition of the excitement, fear and horror of the First World War trenches. Incredibly, this monumental armed conflict, which can still even now be termed as a reasonably recent and modern war, has rarely ever been tackled as a first-person shooter.
Perhaps the reason is due to the challenges developers have faced in creating a level playing-field for the attacker considering the fact that in the actual war itself, for most of the time, the defender usually had the upper hand. In addition, trenches themselves are linear creations ,yet a good designer needs to incorporate that linearity in an exciting manner to entertain the player while also attempting to stay faithful to the conflict itself.
These challenges have been marvellously met in this game and it can be extremely exciting.
The maps themselves are absolutely incredible in their depiction of trench-systems covered with barbed-wire surrounding a frightening no-man's land pockmarked with shell-holes. Teams play in squads where communication is important. The thrill of actually making it into an enemy trench is marvellous, and the occasional hand-to-hand fighting especially so.
I have the highest admiration and respect for the game designers for doing an excellent (though of course not yet perfect) job, especially due to the fact that they have got to grips with depicting a war which FPS computer games have until now rarely had the courage or the imagination to tackle.

Five Nights at Freddy's 2 has been a long awaited sequel...well long awaited for me I have been very excited about this!!  Does it live up to its predecessor though, did it do things differently to make the formula seem newer?  Well, yes and no Five Nights at Freddy's 2 is a mixed bag for me but make it well known that I have enjoyed what I have played but there are some things that I do not like about it either and maybe it was because it was rushed out, then again maybe it wasnt and creator "Scott Cawthon" was very satisfied with the current build and good on him for that.  But anyway here goes my review of what I have played so far.
I love how Scott decided to change it up a little so that we had the same type of game that we originally loved.  Getting rid of the doors to me was a great idea and added a new type of tension and stress initially starting, trying to figure out when to put on the mask and when not to.  Additionally, the addition of another element that requires you to interact can make things alot more stressful and when put in a bad situation where that element needs attention but you cant do it...ADDS alot of stress to the element and I loved that!  I havent delved into the story yet let alone go out of my way to search for it like we had to with the original but I am hoping Scott added more to this because the way the story was hidden in the last game was fun to read.  Now, having said that there are a few things wrong with this game that bug me from the moment I was playing about 10 minutes in...and that was the death animations.  The animations on the animatronics have seemed to have taken a nose dive in quality and polish and that really saddened me because the way that the animatronics were animated in the original it was really good...I mean it was awesome!  Maybe Scott got too excited releasing this game to us and let it get to his head that they were fine, or maybe he was very happy with the way it was.  Either way I do not like them and I hope he may patch that in and give them (mainly Chica and Bonnie) better death animations to you.  Another animation issue I had was with the animatronics showing up at your desk while you have the mask to show there presence to you was....not what I expected.  I actually wanted them to be hulking over you, singing songs, or using their animation that they would employ as if it was them performing in the day time then the lights flash off and they disappear and reset to a different area.  I don't think it was done well and again..I hope that maybe he will patch that and add it into the game.
Overall, I am satisfied with this $7.99 purchase.  It is not perfect by any means and this game leaves room for patching and I am hoping Scott does do it.  I love the game Scott and I really hope that you read this and take my criticism as a productive way to improve on this already well done game.  I recommend this game for everyone, but I want others to play the first "FNaF" first then move on to this one and see the effort that has gone into this game.  Well done Scott and heres to a "FIVE NIGHTS AT FREDDY'S 3".  Thank you again Scott for making this sequel.

- Animations for when the animatronics enter where you reside are just...not good...like at all and I was left very disappointed on how that was executed
- Death animations seemed less polished than the deaths on the original 'FNaF' and I was also disappointed in that as well.

This game is a HUGE improvement over the first one and the first one was fantastic!  I was a little worried that it would kind of turn out like Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs where it just was hyped up too much and didn't live up to it predecessor especially when images of the new animatronics started coming out.  Then the trailer dropped and my hope was renewed but still confused and interested as to how all of this was going to work.  Well I'm here to tell you that Scott made it work.  He made it work REALLY REALLY well.  This game not only lives up to its monster predecessor but it SURPASSES IT BY LEAPS AND BOUNDS!  Scott really mastered the art of suspence in this game.  One of the number one complaints that I saw with FNAF1 was that it was just jumpscares.  While, personally, I thought the game built up suspence well, after the initial shock of the animatronics getting nearer, the suspence quickly dicapated and they were somewhat easy to keep under control.  In this game, not so much.  The no door and flashlight instead of power mechanic gives you a much greater sense of dread when they start getting close because they will inevitably get uncomfortably close and you have to act accordingly (and react in time) to make sure you survive.  Meanwhile your heart is beating out of your chest at how close that was.  There are also 10 animatronics to keep track of all with different patterns and the player must use different methods to get rid of them which makes the game a lot more hectic and suspenceful.  Some of these deturent methods also leave you wide open from a spontaneous attack from one of the other animatronics and if you think they will have mercy just because you are fending off one of the foxies (that's right I said one of) you could not be more wrong.  That feeling of dread when they get close to you does not go away until you either die or win unlike in the first one where its gone as soon as you shut the door in their face. The difficulty level in cranked up to 11 here and even veteran players of the first will be finding themselves struggling on only night 2 and it only gets crazier.  The sound is also put into use a lot more in this game and helps amp up the creepy/suspense factor.  You will be able to hear audio clues as to where the animatronics are moving to and how close they are which really adds another level of suspense and terror because there is already so much going on.  All in all, it is a very suspenseful and terrifying game to play and I feel like this game fixes a lot of issues that people had with the first one.  Even though jumpscares are still a core part of the formula here, this game builds the suspense MUCH better than its predecessor and it is a lot more hectic and challenging even for veterans of the first.  I'd say if you didn't like the first one because it was only jumpscares, give this one a try.  It is an incredible improvement onto the FNAF formula and is almost guarunteed to put you on edge.  I'd definitely recommend this to anyone who enjoys horror games.  Even if you didn't like the first one, I'd say its worth a shot.  Its SUCH a huge improvement and it feels like they took the old FNAF formula and patched up every little hole they could find and made vast improvements to the good stuff that was left over to the point where its a whole new experience while still staying true to what made the first one great.  Definitely give it a try.  Its worth it for only $8.

Gone home is a interactive story in which you uncover the story in pieces as you wander about the new house your parents have moved into. You wander the house in first person view and the story is narrated by a voiceover as you pick up items. Of course that's only if your following the main story about your sister, if you want to follow the mothers, fathers or previous homeowners story you have to read letters left around and piece together what visual clues are left around.
The controls are standard FPS controls except the button that would ordinarily shoot is now a pick up/activate button.
The story itself is a great one, I thoroughly enjoyed it and found it heartfelt. But if your looking for a long story I'm afraid you've come to the wrong place. This game is at best 4 hours worth of content, there are no puzzles to solve particularly, just an engaging story.
I definitely recommend this title, if and only if, you are interested in narrative and story over everything else. Sadly I do not think it's worth it's £14.99 price tag, there just isn't enough there. If you see it on sale, for say less than £4 then go for it!

Gone Home is a first person, story driven exploration game. You are left to uncover, investigate and piece together the events of the past 12 months by examining the house that has been abandoned by your family. The player is given the freedom to explore and uncover the story at their own pace, gleaning information from items such as notes, letters, pictures and everyday objects. What is so striking about the story telling in the game is how the player is subtly led to uncover and piece together the events in chronological order. As you move through the house room by room, you almost feel as if you are living out the events of the past year, month by month. Managing to do this within a relatively open game world filled with inanimate objects is astounding. The story is immersive, compelling and hard hitting. This is a gaming experience that stands out and will stay with you.

Edit:
So after 100 hours I'm still having a lot of fun playing Verdun, finally got my "Trench Eye" The best way to improve is to learn the maps and stick with your squad, going Rambo will just get you killed quickly, at least with a squad (meatshield) your enemies have a choice of targets.
The weapons are pretty well balanced, although getting killed by arty can be frustrating, the only problem tends to be people quitting if it looks like their team will lose or sitting back/camping hoping to be carried to victory.
Best advice: keep rolling forward, keep your NCO alive (you can forward spawn on your NCO) and remember that having a rifle does not make you a sniper, hanging back taking long range pot shots without a scope on your rifle is likely to annoy the hell out of your team/squadmates.
Edit 2.
Playerbase still friendly and helpful, new bug fixing patches every month or so, and Devs still active on the forum.

It's common knowledge that Hidetaka Miyazaki did not took a big role in the developement of DS II - all while he had to pick up the original game from the previous producer. DS II Scholar of the First Sin does a lot of things right, that DSII did obviously not - Features that were used rarely are know appearing more frequently (Traps, Magic Walls and many more).
I
finish the original game - due to the way it was produced and how it presented itself to the costumers. While Dark Souls was hard to play (until you master each moveset of bosses/enemies) - Dark Souls 2 just tried to desperately
- by decreasing the maximum Life of your character - which, i think is the main reason many people didn't receive a warm welcome and stopped playing the game before grasping the whole game.
In terms of storytelling Dark Souls II does a rather weak job. In Dark Souls all items and equipment had an original story - something that i missed completely in Dark Souls II.
In my opinion, if you didn't play Demon Souls/Dark Souls or Bloodborne you probably enjoy the game without a second thought, if you can overcome the start. For experienced Players: I'd recommend playing the game as well, but as soon as you can: start with the DLC-Areas (which are a part of the Scholar of the First Sin Edition already) - they were produced under supervision from Hidetaka Miyazaki
I'm still recommending the game to anyone.

The concept is an interesting one. Very little games persue the WWI experience so kudos to the developers for taking this on. Sadly I couldn't get past the games technical issues to get into it. Great concept spoiled by a terrible engine. The render performance of the Unity engine is rubbish. Barely scrapes more than 55FPS on a 980 Ti and that is at its absolute best as well. Most of the time it chugs along at 44FPS which I wouldn't mind but the graphics are not exactly out of this world. Other issues I have are mainly down to the controls. There is no lean function and for a game that takes emphasis on realism there is no free aim and you are allowed to use crosshairs. Other games such as Red Orchestra 2 take on this genre much better despite RO2's limited trench maps. Maybe the developers should look at using Unreal Engine 4 moving forward.

It's easy to compare this game to Goat Simulator. Both cost approximately $10, both feature goats as main gameplay features...and both games are fun for approximately 10 minutes.
Now, most faults with this game can be overlooked. The visuals, for instance, are dated but otherwise not a problem. There isn't a wide variety of gamemodes, but that's to be expected. However, the biggest problem with the game is the balance issue.
Now, when you hear that this game is about World War II with dinosaurs, I'll bet your first thought is "Oh boy, I get to play as a(n) *insert dinosaur here*!" And you do!...if you join the Axis at the beginning of the match. The Axis has a total of 6 dinosaur classes, including a Velociraptor, and Ankylosaurus thing with a grenade launcher on it's back, and even a little raptor whos' sole purpose is to suicide-bomb the enemy. The Axis also have three human classes, which are essentially assault, sniper and medic.
Meanwhile, the Allies have...one little Triceratops thing with a machine gun. All the other 6 (only 6!) classes are all human classes. While the Allies have their own assault, sniper and medic like the Axis, on a class-to-class comparisson, they all fall short of the Axis equivalents (I mean, come on, the Axis sniper has an AIRSTRIKE!). Worse still is that it seems like very little thought went into designing the Allied classes. For example, one Allied class comes with a BAR machine gun, a pistol and frag grenades. Another completely separate class has the exact same loadout, except the BAR is replaced with a single-shot rifle, and they have a melee rage meter. Considering the Allied "heavy" can choose to bring either a rocket launcher OR a flamethrower to the fight, it's baffling why the decision was not made in development to combine the two aforementionned classes into one and MAKE ROOM FOR ANOTHER ♥♥♥♥ING ALLIED DINOSAUR? In fact, the entire Allied team seems like a designer afterthought after they perfected the Axis.
But let's get back to the Axis dinos. Yes, there's a decent variety of them. Yes, it is enjoyable to kill people with them. Yes, you will laugh the first time you find the "pee" button (it's F btw). However, you'll likely soon find that they aren't as much fun as you hoped, regardless of your team. Most of the dinos are pretty short, i.e. below waist height. They have human amounts of health, though their melee attacks are all very powerful. A perfect example of this is the tiny Microraptor. It's stupidly tiny, yet can kill an Allied player in 3-4 hits, it has a unique poison spit attack, and it can GLIDE. As you can imagine, it's very difficult to hit one of these as an Ally. Playing as one is not particularly fun either, because the class feels ridiculously overpowered in terms of speed and damage. And remember what I said about most dinos being approximately waist height?One such Axis dino is the aforementionned Ankylosaurus with a cannon turret on its' back. One common trick used by players with this class is to hide behind knee-hight walls, so only their turrets are exposed. Since the turret is gunmetal grey, it makes the dino very difficult to spot in dark areas, thus creating a perfect camping situation.
One last thing: health. Players cannot regenerate health, there are no health pickups, dinos cannot regain it by eating things, and the only possible way to get it is if a friendly medic just so happens to lay down an area-healing medipack right next to you.
So, tl:dr just like Goat Simulator, it's fun for about 10 minutes until you realise how much better the Axis are. Not worth your $10, but try it if it's on sale and/or free.

Verdun takes me back to the good old days of minimal system requirements and fun attitudes. This game, while it is definitely a first-person shooter, breaks the norm somewhat by making all of its weapons true to the era, along with the battlefields and uniforms.
It can be difficult, initially, to figure out who your allies are, especially when you're fighting along British and French troops who wear different uniforms. But this is something that can be quickly learned and becomes part of your understanding of the game. The same goes for the following...
The battlefields are very difficult to navigate on. From cover it's very difficult to tell where you'll be able to find cover again if you go over the top. The trenches are a treacherous maze of shooting angles and cover that is difficult to get used to. There's barbed wire everywhere that will literally kill you if you don't notice it and don't react fast enough to being tangled.
Initially, wide-open spaces look like death incarnate, because your enemy is looking to shoot you if you go there, but with some practice you can learn to spot your enemy first and shoot him (serves him right for trying to cover such a broad field!)

Gone Home has affected me in a very deep, permanent way.  At first, I was drawn in by the nostalgia.  Since it is set in the mid-1990s, it directly targeted my childhood and the average way of life during that time.  All over the house, there are cassette tapes with underground punk rock on them and VHSes labeled with classic films, obviously recorded from TV programs/  There are magazines and 'zines (remember those?) that feature music and politics of the day strewn about the coffee tables and desks.
This game makes me remember how much we actually WROTE back then.  There are hand-witten notes and typewriter-typed letters all over the place, each revealing a little bit of what was going on in the family of the house's lives.
After I got used to the nostalgia and the 90s setting, I became focused on unraveling the mystery of why this huge, beautiful, spooky house is empty. The story is mostly centered around Sam, your character's younger sister.  She is a rebellious, intelligent, and creative soul.  Any teenager that went against the grain will immediately connect with her.
I didn't exactly know what to expect when I loaded this game and I think that uncertainty really helps the narrative.  I will say this: there is no combat, no monsters that will jump out at you, and no bloody or gory scenes that will pop out to shock you.  In those respects, it is very tame.  Emotionally, it is probably one of the most mature stories I’ve ever seen in a video game.
I urge you to give this a shot.  Be open-minded, though.  You never know who you are going to hurt by not being so.

I got this game when it was being offered for free by PC Gamer, and - considering the frequency of free games recently - this has easily been one of the better-quality ones.
If you like first-person shooters (FPS) and WWII and/or dinosaur themes (as odd as that sounds in combination), then you will really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are very good - the detail in the environment and different character models is well-done. I have, however, noticed that there can be some graphical tearing - in particular when you are in any sewer area and approach the water. This happens infrequently, so it is not too big of a problem. The sounds are great, you can hear footsteps and - with practice, can distinguish the distinct sounds of different unit types. There is isn't much music, but it can play as ambient background noise from time to time - it fits appropriately with the WWII theme. At times, a publicly-broadcast radio will play, and some of the things being said are quite comical (ex: in one of the maps, Santa gives an announcement of his struggle against the dinosaurs; you can also find his sleigh on fire if you look for it).
The controls are basic for a typical FPS and easy to familiarize yourself with. There is no tutorial, but reading the manual and playing against bots will help you understand the game a lot better. I personally do not recommend you to create a server and play against bots because jumping right into the heat of battle can still be very fun, regardless of your experience. The game borrows a fair amount from Team Fortress 2, right down to the unique noise it makes when you die and it zooms in on your killer (you are also shown your "best" and comparison statistics whenever you die). Like TF2, the game is a balanced blend of casual and competitive gameplay, being receptive to all types of players - so long as you give the game a chance and put in some effort to learn.
There are to sides you can choose to play for - Axis and Allies. The Axis has a good number of dinosaur units, while the Allies only have one dinosaur unit and specialize in unique human characters (the flamethrower and jack rabbits [stun-lock any applicable dinosaurs if used near them] are hard counters to the more close-ranged dinosaurs, like the Velociraptor). Playing and experimenting with both sides is encouraged and important, as you will auto-swap sides frequently. There are some changeable items, however, there are no "loot" items as seen in TF2 - you play with the same loadouts as everyone else.
The maps are very well done and do not suffer from the symmetrical-design seen in some FPS games, and this makes it fun to explore and find the best spots for ambushes and hiding. You do not regenerate health (unless you have a medpack/medic nearby), so knowing where the medkit spawn points are is critical to survival.
There are different game modes like straight-up Deathmatch (first team to 50 kills wins), Territory Capture, and a really fun game mode where you have to first capture points, then kill the Axis' super dinosaur (T-Rex or other powerful dinosaur) that is susceptible to explosives. A member of the Axis will control the super dinosaur, however, I am still unsure how the player is selected. The time for the game to end also seems to freeze (or is bugged), and I do not know how the game calculates when the Axis wins (because the Allies have failed to kill the super dinosaur).
If you try this game, I strongly recommend you try out each unit type at least once, to fully see what the game has to offer. The dinosaurs on the Axis side are my favorite - one dinosaur is basically a small, fast, suicide bomber (blast radius increases with melee kills); another rams people onto the ground and can throw them at other people (or pick up goats and throw them for one-hit kills; and another can fly (sort of) and shoot acid spit that temporarily "blinds" the victim (it lasts for quite a while). On the Allies side, the flamethrower is absolutely deadly in close-quarters, and the BAR can make short work of units charging straight for you.
Anyone who enjoys FPS should find this game to be very fun, especially if you play with friends. Try it out if you are interested (especially since there are many WWII FPS', but not many WWII + Dinosaurs FPS').
