Scholar of the first sin is supposed to be the definitive version of Dark Souls 2. However, I have played both and I much prefer the base version. I will explain some of the bigger changes that was made and then I will explain why I believe the original Dark Souls 2 is better.
Changes:
1. While there may be some added enemy spawns they also swapped some enemy placements. Some of the enemy spawns are very unique while others feel like a total copy paste. Some new spawns make sense while others feel very out of place.
2. They also moved some of the NPCs to new areas. You will still see them in the same maps as before but the will be in a new room. There is no clear reason why they did this. Also, there is no new dialog for them.
3. There is a new option to summon an additional fighter. So you can summon up to 4 people.
4. A bunch of new NPC summons have been added along with better AI, damage, and defense. The new NPC summons will emote and do other silly things like spam their binos. Even some of the original NPC summons have been given a buff. (Like Lucateil)
5. A huge addition of Pursuer fights. You will fight the Pursuer more than 5 times. He has also been given a little bit of a new look. His eyes glow red now, and he can cast a hex that sends multiple homing, balls of darkness. Although, if you quickly run behind him as he is casting you can just spam him with R1.
6. New clothing options. Like a solid Auros Set.
7. A Pool of Blood. A place where players have died in the same area. You can watch a group people die.
Why I believe Dark Souls 2 is the definitive version:
Although SOTFS had its moments of awe I still feel like it’s a bit of a novelty game. Sure you may see passive Hyde knights in Hyde’s tower or passive dragon keepers in Dragon Shrine, there is still something it lacks. For one thing SOTFS is way easier. Seriously, they took out all the challenging parts. Like in the crypt they took out all the Syan guards and replaced it with a dragon rider and in Dragon Shrine you only have to fight a single Dragon Keeper to get to Ancient Dragon. I can understand why people who haven’t played the base game have been down voting the game.
Dark Souls 2 had a subtleness about it. There was a certain uniqueness to it. SOTFS just feels out of place and over designed. However if you have not played it yet and you have played the base game then give it a try. SOTFS is just an excuse to play the game again. Also, the game felt like it was made for people who have played the base game. The reason I say this is because it constantly made me question what I knew about the original game. Any time I went into a new area thinking I already knew the layout I was punished for it. It’s great if you have the original. However, If you have never played a souls game or even dark souls 2 don’t play this one first. Go play dark Souls 1 and then Dark Souls 2(maybe Demon’s Souls) and wait until this game is on sale. Don’t buy this game expecting it to be amazing, you will be disappointed.

Buy it if you have played the base game and if it’s on sale. Don’t if you have never played Dark Souls 2 or a soul’s game.

Here's an old one, from the formative years of my account when I owned nary five games - indeed, I believe it was the second game on Steam I ever purchased. I still remember how I picked it up: Steam Winter Sale of 2010, and it only set me back $4.43. Just looking at my hours on record now, I must say, what a deal it turned out to be, and what an overdue review this is!
For the year that gave us a title like Battlefield: Bad Company 2, there is both something nice about Just Cause 2's visual fidelity, and at the same time something left to be desired. It has aged fairly well, all things considered, though the jungle is nowhere near as dense as one might hope and the city can feel somewhat bland and grey from all the concrete (though I suspect the latter was intentional). The ground textures look rather uninspired and there is a lack of 'depth' to them. However, the water is surprisingly good looking, vehicles crunch up nicely as they are damaged, and if there's one thing Just Cause 2 gets right, it's explosions.
The audio design in Just Cause 2 manages to go in two opposite directions at once: Voice acting and dialogue writing alike in Just Cause 2 are decisively marginal, like a B-list movie in game form, and the soundtrack is nothing to write home about, but it does get the job done and doesn't sound bad at all. Meanwhile, while vehicle sound effects are decent, weapons and destruction sound fantastic, and if combined with your favorite high-tempo track really does make for a great experience as you rip through the jungles, hills, and cities of the Panauan island archipelago.
Even on my outdated, battered old rig from back in 2007, Just Cause 2 still managed to chug along respectably on normal settings, and on my current system it performs splendidly on any, as I would expect. I have also encountered very few bugs or glitches along the way, and the game has never crashed on any of the systems I tried playing it on. Shouldn't be any problems here.
At first glance, Just Cause 2 is a run-of-the-mill third-person shooter with vehicles in a large open world; at another, you'll come to realise it does something special that not many open-world third-person shooters can do. Attaching a vicious little gauntlet to your left wrist, Just Cause 2 immediately makes it abundantly clear what it wants to do, and what it wants you to do: Take your physics-defying grappling hook, and Scorpion-spear people towards you (or yourself towards them), paraglide across the country by hooking along the ground, hijack vehicles while they're moving at breakneck speeds, destroy entire military bases in the span of two minutes - or less - and liberate the island by destroying every piece of infrastructure or machinery with a red-white star on the side that you find. It's stupid, it makes no sense, it can't be justified, it doesn't try to justify itself, and it's fantastic.
The story in Just Cause 2 is relatively simple: You are Rico Rodriguez (not the actor), an American agent and ace in the hole working for the titular Agency as you attempt to overthrow the malevolent dictator of the Panauan islands. The writing is terrible; this is quite possibly on purpose. The entire story screams B-movie turned satire, and indeed the American exceptionalism is cranked up to such a high level that it is hard to interpret the plot as anything but the average American citizen's view on foreign dictatorships, and indeed a little bit of American foreign policy, in written form. It's no Verhoeven, but the game still does better than I expected here, whether the satire was intentional or otherwise.
Yes, that's right. Multiplayer, in a game like this. I still remember the beta tests of the Just Cause 2 Multiplayer Mod: Four hundred square miles of island nation, up to one thousand players, and an open-world "team" deathmatch game-mode that prompted nothing but insanity and hamartia across the entire terrain. Nowadays, it is admittedly more tame, but the capabilities have expanded further and are even more impressive: Building servers allow impressive custom creations, while the Battlefield conquest-style game-modes serve as an interesting take on the standard advance and secure game-mode of larger scale first-person shooters.
You were no doubt wondering if I made a typo before when I wrote "multiplayer mod." It was not a typo. The multiplayer 'free DLC' on Steam is a mod, semi-officially supported. Most other mods are rather primitive, but they are nonetheless available and can improve on your experience greatly - depending on your definition of improve. Suffice to say, they can result in some
. I approve, I most certainly approve.
Just Cause 2 is ridiculous to the extreme, it simultaneously makes no sense and makes perfect sense, and it is one of the most fun open world third-person shooters I have ever played. This game has a certain soul that Just Cause 3 couldn't replicate no matter how hard it tried, and it costs barely fifteen dollars to boot. If you ask why (why you should get it, why it tries what it tries, or any number of other questions), there's only a few words left to be said after all this: just 'cause.

Scholar of the first sin is supposed to be the definitive version of Dark Souls 2. However, I have played both and I much prefer the base version. I will explain some of the bigger changes that was made and then I will explain why I believe the original Dark Souls 2 is better.
Changes:
1. While there may be some added enemy spawns they also swapped some enemy placements. Some of the enemy spawns are very unique while others feel like a total copy paste. Some new spawns make sense while others feel very out of place.
2. They also moved some of the NPCs to new areas. You will still see them in the same maps as before but the will be in a new room. There is no clear reason why they did this. Also, there is no new dialog for them.
3. There is a new option to summon an additional fighter. So you can summon up to 4 people.
4. A bunch of new NPC summons have been added along with better AI, damage, and defense. The new NPC summons will emote and do other silly things like spam their binos. Even some of the original NPC summons have been given a buff. (Like Lucateil)
5. A huge addition of Pursuer fights. You will fight the Pursuer more than 5 times. He has also been given a little bit of a new look. His eyes glow red now, and he can cast a hex that sends multiple homing, balls of darkness. Although, if you quickly run behind him as he is casting you can just spam him with R1.
6. New clothing options. Like a solid Auros Set.
7. A Pool of Blood. A place where players have died in the same area. You can watch a group people die.
Why I believe Dark Souls 2 is the definitive version:
Although SOTFS had its moments of awe I still feel like it’s a bit of a novelty game. Sure you may see passive Hyde knights in Hyde’s tower or passive dragon keepers in Dragon Shrine, there is still something it lacks. For one thing SOTFS is way easier. Seriously, they took out all the challenging parts. Like in the crypt they took out all the Syan guards and replaced it with a dragon rider and in Dragon Shrine you only have to fight a single Dragon Keeper to get to Ancient Dragon. I can understand why people who haven’t played the base game have been down voting the game.
Dark Souls 2 had a subtleness about it. There was a certain uniqueness to it. SOTFS just feels out of place and over designed. However if you have not played it yet and you have played the base game then give it a try. SOTFS is just an excuse to play the game again. Also, the game felt like it was made for people who have played the base game. The reason I say this is because it constantly made me question what I knew about the original game. Any time I went into a new area thinking I already knew the layout I was punished for it. It’s great if you have the original. However, If you have never played a souls game or even dark souls 2 don’t play this one first. Go play dark Souls 1 and then Dark Souls 2(maybe Demon’s Souls) and wait until this game is on sale. Don’t buy this game expecting it to be amazing, you will be disappointed.

Buy it if you have played the base game and if it’s on sale. Don’t if you have never played Dark Souls 2 or a soul’s game.

I played several FP-shooters in the past. It started with the Counterstrike legacy of the late 90s and ended with the recent Battlefield-crap.
Verdun beats them all.
This FPS, despite being of rather simple gameplay, surpasses all the other modern FPS games by far. You don't have to unlock gazillions of equipment, you also don't care for kill/death fame.
It is about teamplay, and although most FPS claim to be about teamplay, this one is one of the few which actually achieved that goal.
The scenario of WW1 is also unique, you will experience how few value your live has, compared to the advance of your team. You will die a lot.
This is actually the only game in which you are allowed to die frequently but at the same time can achieve great rewards.
You will die a dozen times until you manage to reach the enemy trench. Your heart will beat like a hammer when you feel the excitement radiating through all your body in the moment you jump into that trench. What will await you there?. There is that guy in the distant, covered in a gas cloud. Is he friendly or the enemy? You don't know. He also doesn't. Decent tension.
You will experience how rewarding it feels to be the only one of your team who managed it to enter the enemy trench. You will pray for your team mates coming to your help. Or will the enemy find you first, covering behind a pile of sandbags?
Imagine yourself walking freely among the enemy team in their trench. You wear a different uniform but in the heat of the battle, somehow nobody takes notice of you. All of them are busy staring across the berm towards the trench of your team. You stab those poor guys one by one with your bayonet. And clear the whole trench. Endless excitement!
Imagine you playing dead on the floor when those hordes of intruders killed all your mates and spread into your trench. Will they notice you? Or will you manage to stay alive so that your entire squad can spawn around you?
Verdun is never boring. There is also a decent community playing this game. Probably because all the kiddos are busy with CoD and BF, you will meet mostly gentle and adult people in Verdun. So the chances to find some guys in your team really willing to act as a team is remarkably high.
Also the devs are very present. You might even meet them on the servers and shoot them from time to time. I play Verdun since July 2014 and experienced the devs in constant dialogue with the community since then. Thus the support has been of ongoing quality and a calm down of issueing patches or the implementation of new maps, weapons and other ideas is not in sight.
Verdun is easily the best FPS experience I ever had. I don't even like FPS any more (growing old) but I will play Verdun until it ceases to exist.

This game is underated. This is warface, where heros are trying to fight terrorists that suck contries dry of wealth, leaving the people and the country to die off. You engage in tactical firefights, MASSIVE boss battles, escort missions, and infiltration. You can fight anywhere from a Simple village in africa, to the tallest skyscrapers in a city. Now here is the quick stuff.
Pro's:
-Really fun for people that like quick tactics.
-Huge firefights.
-Large choice of guns, armor, and utility.
-Medics can revive dead players within a time limit, and yes they are also very powerful packing a shotgun.
-Grenades do realistic damage.
-C4 Does pretty realistic damage.
-GREAT for playing with friends.
-PvP is great most of the time, with tons of bullets flying around, and different ways to dispatch your enemys.
-PvE is also quite fun, as they update the missions a lot and 1 mission never has the same set of enemys. (snipers might be swtched with and RPG squad, ect...)
-Sniping is balanced with other classes, as they are at risk at close and medium range, and are bad for taking out multiple enemys.
-C4 can be avoided and used agaist the person that put it, for a very humiliating death.
-TONS of attachments availiable, from red dot sights, to grips, and many other tactical attachments.
-Bullet damage is realistic
-You get to flashbang everybody in your helicopter while extracting.
Con's
-It can be very annoying trying to get a gun, because you have to get it thru research.
-If you dont own the gun, most of the time you cannot by permanent, you must research it.
-Some knifes (and SHOVELS) are very powerful and are OP.
-The Camping is really bad in some spots.
-'Nades from friendlys can blind you, and even though the Frag cannot hurt you, it throws off your aim a TON.
-Shoot the medic sim 2015
-Teams can be unbalanced
-When medics try to revive people in PvP, they often respawn JUST before he is revived, because he hit spacebar. (WAIT FOR THE MEDIC, YOU GET POINTS AND HE DOES TOO.)
Overall, I say this game is vey, very good. It has lots of different things you can do with each class, and its also quite fun in firefights.

Sigmund Corp. uses a technology that can create artificial memories. They offer this as a "wish fulfillment" service to people on their death beds. Since these artificial memories conflict with the patient's real memories, the procedure is only legal to do on people without much time left to live.
Sigmund Corp. employees Dr. Eva Rosalene and Dr. Neil Watts are tasked with fulfilling the lifelong dream of the dying Johnny Wyles. Johnny wants to go to the moon, although he doesn't know why. The doctors insert themselves into an interactive compilation of his memories and traverse backwards through his life via mementos. With each leap to an important moment in Johnny's memories, they learn more about him and what brought him to his current position in life, including his largely unhappy marriage to his childhood sweetheart, River. Upon reaching his childhood, the doctors attempt to insert his desire to go to the moon. Supposedly, Johnny's mind would create new memories based on that desire, and Johnny would die believing he lived without any regrets.
However, Johnny's mind does not create the new memories as planned. Dr. Watts and Dr. Rosalene must solve the problem to fulfill Johnny's dying wish of going to the moon.

Admittedly, I have not logged tens or hundreds of hours playing this game, BUT I still know what I like when I see it.  I like Verdun.
IMHO:
Where Verdun succeeds is two-fold.
First, the graphics are not cartoon-like, as they tend to be in so many other WWI games, or even FPS's.  The motion of aiming is slightly laborious, as it would be were you to be lugging around a heavy firearm, fighting trench warfare and trying to not die every moment of your day.  The lighting of the game is glorious, with the shadows being a major component to the visual realism.  I had the distinct pleasure of hiding in a destroyed tank's shadow while trying to lay down fire and not die!  Didn't work out so well, but it did lend to my immersion of the battlefield experience.
Second, the sounds on the battlefield are very interesting.  The guns have their own "life", lent through not only the operation (reloading, bolt action, etc.) of the weapon, but the sounds it makes in said operation.  I get the distinct impression the creators of the game went to some pain to ensure the sonds were "true", if not unique.  I am reminded of BF1942, in which the creators went to similar extents, and we know how that effort paid off!  Also, the changes of sounds of footfalls from dry ground to wet/muddy ground really brings me into the experience.
Verdun is not perfect (yet), but its designers are continually making it better, and for that I say THANK YOU for a job well...progressing [done comes later]!

This game, Fits my catagory as fun. The insane plot, and the humor to go with it, makes it worth buying. If you like TF2, You will like this game, the humor from that game, can be found in this one, but it's still a different kind of humor. What I mean is that, It's not directly copy and paste. But that alone, should make someone want to play it. But, No, The gameplay is great as well. First off, This is a multiplayer game. No single player. HOWEVER, there is an option to face bots, if you want to play singleplayer, And you can customize the bots freely, Such as the difficulty, and What class they spawn as, But the fun can be found in the multiplayer in my opinion. I just like the fact they added the bots. You play as 1 of 2 teams. Allies, or Axis. The two powers in World War II. And each has some unique classes, Of course, You have your standard soldiers, for standard FPS gameplay, But they can be limited in what they do. Some are more close combat oriented, and others prefer long range. And you are stuck with the weapons they spawn with, you cannot pick up others. I like that idea. Of course, The most unique aspect of the game, Is the Dinosaurs. They are fun to play as... Extremely fun... At least for me. Others might have fun killing them, i like playing as them. This game is about as indie as it gets: it fills all of your wat jar and overflows enough to make your shoes wet. My disdain for this sad existence of an 'experience' makes me cry at night.
I was never a fan of the artsy hipster better-than-mainstream feeling that early indie titles had (mainly Braid and Limbo) but those games were at least fun, challenging enough to keep playing, and worth their price tag. Gone Home is only one of these things, and it's definitely not fun or challenging or worth the price in any sense of the terms.
I guess if you were a huge fan of Fez then you won't mind searching every inch of this mansion to unlock the secrets, small, bland, short, and boring though they are. I will admit my favorite thing about this game was how you could zoom in on papers and posters and see visibly clear text with an actual message instead of a low resolution scribble to give the impression of writing (mainly like in Mass Effect 2). That's the only thing I appreciated, everything else made me want to uninstall. But how could I? I already spent $20, I had to see it through.
The atmosphere was also good. In fact some parts were creepier than Amnesia.
If you don't like romances, don't buy this game. I hate romances. If there's a grand story with lots of characters in an epic setting, then a romance between two characters is fine. That's natural. A story, movie, or book that is only and foremost a romance is not what I like in my media. Had I know this game was just a romance, I wouldn't have bought it, but unfortunately you don't realize this until the end of the game and by then it's too late. Did I mention the end comes within two hours? I beat this game in less than the time it takes me to watch a good movie, and I could have rented one for a lot less than I paid for this. Video games are not movies, the experience has to be directly related to the cost of the game, and $20 is way too much.
Would I recommend it for $5? No, I wouldn't, but if you want to see what all the craze is about then I guess the only time I would say you should buy it is for 99 cents. Better yet make your brother buy it and play it off Steam Family Sharing, at least then you won't have to stare at it in your own library.

I've decided that I'm never playing a friend-recommended game again. Ever.
So you can tell that I don't like this game, and trust me I could write a very snarky and sarcastic review about why I don't. I've done it before. However, this game doesn't even deserve that in my opinion and I'm left in complete anger and confusion. Go ahead and get angry over this opinion, go ahead and string me up in the streets and sacrifice me to From Softwares B-Team (which is an inappropriate name because these schmucks aren't even the D-Team). Before you do, Dark Souls 2 fans, either explain to me why you would crusade the holy land for this game or let me write out my list of grievances, Declaration of Independence style.
- This game's design is amazingly uninspired compared to all From Software games, before or since. This culminates into several things: level design is confusing, conviluted and just plain drab, there are segments that make no sense given the context, and the enemies and pretty much everything else in this game look like lesser-versions of their Dark Souls 1 equivalents. Speaking of level design, I can recall a segment where I went to strike an enemy, but because my character has to use an entire football stadium to initiate the backswing I end up striking the walls that are an inch to either of my sides. The enemy then proceeds to maul me.
- You can either have a very cut and dry 'this is what the story is now get at it' kind of plot or a very shifty and sneaky kind of plot execution that souls games are known for. You cannot, to any stretch of the Eldritch imagination do both. I'm speaking of the opening cutscene. Lets continue to talk about that.
- This game begins at a pace a snail would find laughable. Not only is it long and drawn out with an opening cutscene, but it then proceeds to lead you to a 'Retirement Home for Mystical Women' that houses a group of ladies that I'm told are called the Fire Sisters or something like that, but I've found my name for them to be more appropriate: The Mystic Babble Sisters. I originally called them the Cryptic Babble Sisters, however if they didn't tell me so much about the plot then I wouldn't have had to make the change. Corporate was furious with the proceeding paperwork do to the merger.
- While the previous game and then Bloodborne had environments, animations, enemy design, and player movement and attack executions that felt very real (or at least as real as they can in games with settings such as these), this game falls short. In fact it went off the ski ramp, pizza'd when it should have french fry'd, and then fell of the ♥♥♥♥ing cliff. I don't feel sorry for the family. I feel like I'm driving a tank off the 20 cliffs I myself have fallen off of instead of feeling like I am controlling a human being and the enemies seem to have the same issue. Feels like I'm on a crusade to put the country-side out of its misery at this point.
- In Bloodborne (yes I'm comparing the two again!) what an enemy attack does to you is easily telographed. I mean, if you get caught in a grab you are then hoisted up like a baby bird and effectively shattered as such. It took me 10 minutes to understand that that lack-luster, stabbing...motion I think it was that the enemies were doing was a stab move and that that was the reason I was slowing down during an attack that happened at the same time.
- The souls games are known for very intense and awe inspiring moments of gameplay that send the player into joy or terror without having to do a cutscene or stop the gameplay in any way. Its very organic in that way and the people in the produce isles (yes isles) like it that way. However most of the very neat enemies in this game were either out of reach or had the option to just check out if they wanted to. I remember enemies in this series where I had to fight them and then mulled it over in my head what to do. Then they would just stare back at me with those dark, retched, soul shattering....eyes. Not in this game. I did the same thing with a knight that was airlifted into my medieval hot LZ by a friggin' eagle and then decided to port to the Void when I wasn't going fast enough for his lazy♥♥♥♥♥ I swear baby, I wanted to tangle with you. I just...I just had to think about it first. No, don't go!
I could go on..and on....and on about why I don't like this game and go over every one of its design flaws, but I'm getting a bit ranty now and had to resort to a sex joke in the last paragraph. If you read through this whole rant, then congratulations, you win the prize. If you did so and are a die-hard (and I know you die hard...heh) Dark Souls 2 fan, then please explain to me why this game is so loved, because I don't see it.
EDIT: The same friend who had bought me this game informed me that the game 'gets better as you play it, the beginning is kinda bad'. While I already find this to be a gargantuinly stupid thing to have in a game (I'm talking about a slow and terrible beginning), I went and tried again. It only got worse. I put this edit in here for nothing else then to explain my perplexion with this game. I find some nit-picky stuff to complain about in games, but its only because I love them and can generally find a silver lining to even the worst games. I mean hell, I even liked Valkyria Chronicles for the art style at least. However I find nothing, absolutly nothing good about this game and that saddens, angers, and confuses me. While I like games that are challenging, I want them to also be fun. Bloodborne is the perfect nirvanic example of the harmony between challenge and fun and interesting gameplay. However this is just a massive road trip of everything wrong you can do in a game. Worst of all I seem to be the only human being on the face of this earth who agrees with has the same thoughts without being overly pretentious, so I guess if I could ink out some kind of silver lining from this game it is that it has shown me that I haven't yet crossed over into being a complete pompous ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Thanks Dark Souls II!

Verdun is a browser based shooter, that is free to play...oh wait...
Verdun is a poorly optimized unity based WWI shooter that is severely overpriced and SOMEHOW finished???
PROS:
-weapons, maps and sounds are authentic really bringing you into WWI
-WWI is an often unexplored time period for video games and i applaud the effort to be different
-very gritty and unforgiving combat makes u feel like u really are in war
CONS:
-this game begs to be a realistic shooter with its high damage weapons and gas mechanics but instead the game has fast paced movementsand aiming, grenade hotkeys and even "drop shotting"
-load times on maps are ridiculously long without an ssd and seerver join times are through the roof
-the ui is terrible showing little info on how squad systems, class systems and progression works...overall confusing, clunky and hard to navigate
-optimization is awful, i have a gtx 970 g1 gaming and an i5 4690k, i can barely run this on medium settings on a full server
-too much lethality in tight playable areas, these often large maps are cut into tiny playable areas at a time with 32 players that have 1 hit kill weapons along with grenades, gas and airstrikes!!! it gets to a point where you will view the respawn screen more than play

For a indie game to tackle something as big as this, the game is incredible.
Its not your regular run-of-the-mill shooter where you're a bullet sponge or some sort of super soldier.
This game is the most accurate representation of the great war, with historically accurate weapons, soldiers, maps. And unlike a certain other game. It has the trench warefare, the staple of the first world war.
The developers are not only game developers, but really dedicated historians, they give historical facts on the war and the guns in the game and hold events like the christmas truce event and many different charity events.
The game isn't for everyone. This is more in the lines of the 'Arma' games, where they go for accurate representation of war, even if it means you can be a little clunky at times. You're no super soldier who reloads in a second, you don't have your grenades on quick stand-by etc. I really enjoy that with this game though, the developers are clearly passionate and they bring updates and features to the game very frequently.

Gone Home isn't your average game.  In fact, some people will even stuggle to call it a game, and that's probably why the developers choose to call it a "story exploration" video game...because that's really what it is more than anything: a story.  That being said, if you have an open mind as to what is enjoyable in gaming and can find this game on sale, it is most certainly worth your time.
The time and attention the developers at Fullbright put into this game is astonishing. You gain a real sense of nostalgia while playing, and the appropriate music choices and subtle nuances won't be lost on someone that grew up in the 90's.  Admittedly, this game feels like I'm slightly too young for it (currently 25), but the themes and emotions this game aims to convey are actually kind of timeless, so anyone can really relate to them.
Couple that with the fact that most anything you find in the game you can examine, pick up, turn around, and then eventually throw across the room is pretty spectacular.  Especially when you consider that this is an indie game.
Now, to be fair, the storyline is a little obvious. You can sort of see where the whole thing is going right from the start.  And if not, you'll quickly discover it as the game is only about 2 hours long (if you really take your time). However, don't let that deter you from what is, no doubt, a moving and nostalgic piece of art.

Having over 100 hours in the original game, i wanted to download this one for the extra DLC and "updated graphics". All i got was major disappointment. I played Dark souls 1, and Dark souls 2 religiously but this game just gives me a sour taste with the series. The updated graphics is just a lighting change, to the point where if you enter an area where you cant see, you better start praying you have enough torch to get you through. Though that is not a complaint, it makes a mechanic of the game more useful.
Having just over an hour in the new game i already see what they're trying to do to players. The "Artificial Difficulty" that the souls franchise has never reigned true, it only punished for new players. An example of this would be Sens castle is dark souls 1. Punishing the player for not being observant of his surroundings. In the ORIGINAL dark souls 2, you learned how to dodge in Heides tower of flame, through the slow attacking behomeths. Which ultimately helps you with the Halberd wielding boss fight.
These two seemingly minor part of the game, set you up for the rest of Dark Souls. The first two areas in the original Dark Souls 2 were meant to teach you how to play the game through basic mechanics, but with scholar of the first sin, they threw it out the window. They implemented "Artificual Difficulty" into the game, adding numerous enemies that are unneccesary in the beginning areas.
Having only been an hour in i am discouraged to keep playing. The swarm of enemies that are unfair to the player is enourmous. With the small miny bosses "Heide Knights" roaming everywhere it's hard to work around them, or with the forest of the fallen giants, their are foot soldiers in the original dark souls 2 which are easy to manage if you play strategically, but now they replaced them all with Hollow Elite Soldiers. Not only increasing the difficult when they did this, but the sheer amount of extra enemies they inputed was phenomenal.
Walking into No-Mans Wharf i was amazed by how much you needed a torch to move around. Forcing you to utilize it in that area. I have no issue with this but, No-Mans Wharf already had numerous enemies to handle while trying to light the lanturn in the middle of the levels. The reasoning of adding more is beyond me. In the original their are maybe 5 Vangarian Soldiers around with a few foot. Now theres at least 3 more and dogs that surround you so quickly you're already bleeding.
To someone who has not played a Souls game before i would not recommend this, unless they wish to use a guide to help them with horde control in a non-horde control centered game.

Most definitive edition games are just graphic updates and light on new content, Scholar of the First Sin is the opposite.  Besides the new lighting system, the graphics are about the same.  But the PVE restructuring is so well done in Scholar of the First Sin that it makes the original Darks Souls 2 feel like it wasn’t the final draft.
For brand new players, the path layout is more user friendly because of obstacles that block harder routes until your character has better gear and stats.
For returning Dark Souls 2 players, you are in for a treat, the PVE is harder, certain paths have been rerouted, some enemies have been moved or altered, more NPC invasions, and there are lots of surprises that will catch you off guard.
Other notes: the dark areas are really dark and torches are a must, the new lighting system is great, and there is more enemy and weapon variety.
Overall, I still feel that Demons Souls has the best PVE experience, Dark Souls has the best boss battles, and Dark Souls 2 is a hybrid of good, but not great PVE and boss battles, while providing the best PVP content.

Verdun! Literally my dream game. I love World War I, and no, I don't love killing people, unless of course it's a video game about trench warfare with squads and serious team based strategy and historically accurate weapons and uniforms and battlefields and ohh... please excuse me as I go to the bathroom.
AHHH I'm BACK!!!
Verdun is a first-person shooter that immerses you in the trench warfare of the Great War. You play in 4-person squads on teams of 16. It's the Allies versus the Central Powers, and as of the time of writing, the Allies consist of Canadian, British, and French (vive la <3) squads, and the Central Powers consist of German squads. Each team has different squad types, light infantry, stormtroopers, and basic infantry. There are machine guns (like the chauchat woot), submachine guns, scoped-rifles, ohh it's amazing.
The game requires players to advance as a team, through only allowing a team to attack OR defend at once, and work with their squads, by giving bonuses when you are close to your squad leader. It really works, and it's only gotten better. The community helps with this a lot too, maybe since the only people who are CRAZY enough to buy a World War I video game love World War I.
AHHHH
If you're looking for a new fps for your library, if you love history, if you like teamwork, if you for some reason hate Canadians (why?), then pick this up. You won't be disappointed.
I've literally dreamed of a World War I fps since I was 10. And it's here. At the time of writing, they even added a new map, the Marne! It's, like, the most beautiful trench warfare you've ever seen. The developers are consistently updating the game with bug fixes and new features. At the time of writing, the only frustration I have with the game is that it currently refuses to use the dedicated video card, but the developers are aware of this problem and are working on it.

Everything that should be openable or liftable in real life is openable or liftable, and rotated to look all around it. The other part is how much I enjoyed listening to the very well-voiced letters to the protagonist, Katie (nominal protagonist. Alright, so let me start off by saying that I've read many of the reviews for this game, and I agree with most of the points made, whether they be positive or negative.
First, the cons of this game, though they honestly don't bother me and I think will serve more as a warning for other people. This game is rather short (it's taken me around 2 hours for each playthrough). The amount of time it takes you to finish Gone Home depends entirely on how in depth you get with your exploring of the house. For me, it seemed pointless to breeze through it, and so I looked at as many objects as I could. The good part about doing this is that it gives you the opportunity to really immerse yourself in the lives of this family.
Another thing I feel I'd warn those debating buying this game about is the lag. Honestly, it really isn't bad (I've played a few games that have horrible amounts of lag); just a little bit here and there. This didn't bother me, and I found myself too into the game to notice it much. Still, those expecting absolutely perfect movement with no lag whatsoever may find themselves a little disappointed.
Now, on to the fabulous aspects of Gone Home.
The amount of thought and detail put into this game is astonishing. I feel the creators have really tried to make it to the best of their abilities. You can examine almost everything in the house, even the little objects that have absolutely nothing to do with the story. This feature helps to make the entire experience more realistic, and in my mind, a little more personal.
Finally, I'd like to mention the true reason I find myself drawn towards Gone Home time and time again: its fantastic storyline. I'm not going to get much into the plot itself; I feel it's already been explained plenty in the other areas of this store listing. Rather than talking about its contents, I'd like to discuss how said content made this game into something magnificent. Everything about the story discovered within the empty house is absolutely amazing. This game has made me cry both times I've played it, and I felt a connection to the characters I wasn't neccessarily expecting. Also, the voice acting is breathtaking. I've fallen for this game, for sure, and continue to do so with each extra minute I play it. I honestly feel Gone Home can be played multiple times through (as I've done it without a problem), though I wouldn't recommend doing so without putting some time between each play through. Of course the first time playing it is the best, so do try to make the most of it.
In conclusion, this game isn't one full of action, fight scenes, etcetera, though I'm sure you've already heard that. If you are looking for a game like, you're in the wrong place. However, if you are looking for a game that challenges the concepts of most video games, one that holds a truly beautiful story, and acting so brilliant it will make you genuinely laugh and cry, then you have found yourself the right game, because Gone Home will deliver those things.

GREAT Game.  Needs more players though.  Verdun is an underrated gem that needs to be played.  World War I is an undertouched subject for video games and I believe Verdun has hit the head on the nail when it comes to the time.  You can play as the Entente (allies) or the Central Powers (Axis), each having a unique type of gameplay.  The game is surprisingly balanced with the way it works, and no faction really has a massive advantage against the other.  The French are just as good as the British but both have their ups and downs that each player will figure out for themselves.  The gameplay is simple, you start by either defending or assaulting a trench held by the enemy, you have a limited amount of time to attack/defend.  If you/the enemy has men inside the hostile trench by the end of the countdown, the game goes into overtime and your team has a chance to still advance and capture unless you/the enemy is killed in your trench.  If the trench is taken, an enemy IMMEDIATLEY goes into a counter attack and the newly capture trench MUST be defened to advance.  So on, and so forth.  The maps are detailed, the guns feel amazing, the graphics are great, the sound is nuts, and this game is immersive as all hell.
There is a squad system that is somewhat confusing to figure out.  The way it works (I believe) is that if you and 3 other friends play in the same squad for some time, you can level that squad up to get slight perks (ie; mortar shots, mustard gas, late war uniforms, and some personal perks etc).  These don't effect the game in a massive way but it is some incentive to play with your friends I suppose.
SHORT VERSION:  Play this game for an intense, gratifying, and immersive game.  From trench to trench, its not a fight, it's a bloody WAR.  Everything feels and looks good and is definitley more fun with a group.  Play it now.  NOW.

Just finished "playing" Gone Home. The reason for the quotes is because it's not really a game as much as a guided interactive narrative story. You are a 21-year-old girl who's gone home (heh) in June 1995 from a lengthy trip across Europe to find the huge family home empty with a note on the door to not look for your younger sister.
As you walk around you can pick up objects (most are irrelevant) and read many, many notes and letters; listen to cassettes; hear what seem to be audio diaries from your sister as she tells a tale of her falling in love. As you discover secret passages and learn about supposed ghosts, the tension builds and the "game" frequently gets spooky.
While game critics have fallen all over themselves to shower Gone Home with effusive praise, a LOT of gamers are hating on it pretty hard. Part of it is because many gamers are caveman mookheads who are used to shouting profanities at their Madden Warfare peeps and a story where you aren't the real protagonist that deals with grunge-era riot grrrls and middle-aged marital and life troubles doesn't interest them.
A greater part though is that it is an extremely short experience, taking no more than 2-3 hours to complete. For a game that retails for $20 - it's currently $5 on Steam; I got it for $3 on a Flash Sale - that doesn't really have you do much more than walk around looking at stuff, that's a hard sell. (The excellent Spec Ops: The Line is another example. It takes about 6 hours to beat and at $60, that's a terrible deal, regardless how good the story is. However for the $6 I paid on sale, it's a must-play.) Other than a couple of locked areas that need combinations to open, there's almost no "gaming" in Gone Home.
I was fascinated by how they laid out the story and understand why screenwriters I've heard talk about it enjoyed it. While it sets out a clear trail for you to follow, it relies on you to pick up the crumbs and understand the loaf they fell from. (OK, that's a yellow card for terrible metaphors there.) I think I missed a few things judging from the reviews and videos I looked at elsewhere; I never found one safe's combo. The way some things are scattered around are clearly for storytelling than logic's sake and the way the sister's journals are presented doesn't make sense until the very end and even then doesn't make total sense.
That said, if you can pick it up for cheap (like $3) and you understand what you're signing on for (i.e. not a GAME game) and you want to hear some Bratmobile, then you might want to give Gone Home a home in your home's game collection. (Suck it, Gene Shalit!)
EDIT: I just realized there's a Commentary Mode. I'll have to cherk that ert.

Katie is a 20 year old woman that has just returned home from a trip through Europe.  She has come back at 1:15 am and hopes to find somebody home to welcome her back, but her house turns out to be eerily empty.  She then starts to search around the house for clues as to what happened to her family.  This is the basic plot of the game “Gone Home” by The Fullbright Company.  The main character is Katie, and the game centers around her discovering what happened to her family.
The game is rather simple.  I did nothing more than walk around and interact with the many objects that I found.  The explanation for how the game functions can definitely be seen as boring, but what The Fullbright Company does with the house is actually rather astounding.  Firstly, the house is extremely detailed.  As soon as I walked through the front door of Katie's house, I immediately felt as if I entered the front door of a real house.  Something that really helps this feeling is how there are many, many objects scattered around the house that I could interact with.  Every lamp can be turned on or off, every phone can be picked up, every drawer can be opened, etc.  This really helps the house feel real.  Not only that, but since I could interact with more objects than I needed to, it made the game feel very mysterious.  I felt like the next object that I needed to pick up to continue the story could be anything in any room.
That's where the charm in this game lies.  The game starts with a few locked doors, but it's definitely not a linear experience.  The game allows you to explore a majority of the house right away.  In fact, if you know where all the right objects are, you can skip right to the ending in a matter of minutes.  However, that's exactly what makes the thrill of discovery in this game so potent.  Everything was already laid out in front of me, but I had to use my investigative skills to find the end of the game.  In addition, every discovery I made felt important.  The story of this game is slowly revealed with every discovery made, so every discovery felt satisfying.
Not only that, but every discovery let me become more immersed in the story.  Immersion isn't a very hard thing to accomplish with a video game, but this game immersed me like no other.  By the end of the game, I felt like the house wasn't just a house anymore.  I felt as if the house was a house that I had lived in for my whole life.  I felt as if the family I was hunting down was a family I actually cared for.  Most of all, I actually cared enough about the solution of the game to feel as if all the discoveries I made were worth it.
However, that's where one problem I had with the game lies.  Although every discovery felt satisfying, I realized how few of them actually mattered.  I was constantly finding notes detailing everything about the family I was trying to find, but a lot of those details didn't matter in the end.  I won't reveal what those details are, but it made it feel as if a lot of the discoveries that I made simply could've been left unrevealed.  It could be argued that the unnecessary discoveries helped the immersion, but I felt like they were less immersive and more intrusive.  Those unnecessary discoveries didn't stop the game from immersing me, though.
A great example of how immersive this game is would be how scary it is.  I don't scare easily because I tend to fear the unknown as opposed to things popping out at me.  The Fullbright Company definitely understands how to actually scare a person.  The atmosphere in this game really got to me multiple times.  I was constantly afraid of stumbling upon something evil even though those fears were rather silly.  The developers even acknowledge those silly reasons with humorous dialogue.  For example, lights are constantly flickering in this game, but I stumbled upon a piece of paper very early on that gave a logical explanation as to why the lights kept flickering.  There was no reason to be scared by flickering lights anymore, but that didn't stop be from looking around nervously whenever a lightbulb blew out.
Most importantly, the climax of the game actually had me on my toes.  There's no doubt in my mind that other people wouldn't have cared at all about what happened during the climax of the game, but I cared a lot.  I was so immersed in the game at that point that I was actually afraid to continue due to what would be waiting for me at the end.  I have no doubt in my mind that some people will find what I'm about to say ludicrous, but the ending to this game was actually one of the most intense experiences I've ever had in a video game.  With that being said, the resolution is rather disappointing.  Once everything had been explained, I couldn't help but feel underwhelmed.  I had to look back through everything I did and see if everything truly mattered.  Like I stated earlier, a lot of it didn't, but the experience was definitely worth it.
Overall, “Gone Home” is a very good game to those that welcome the idea of house exploration.  There will probably be people that see this game as a waste of time, but this game can be refreshing to an open mind.  There is definitely no other game like this on the market, so I would recommend giving it a shot if what I've said interests you at all.  Even though the ending is unsatisfying, the experience is worth it.  You may even say it's worth writing home about.

I really, really enjoyed playing this game. That said, the first thing you need to know is that this game is literally just you walking through a house, finding keys and examining objects to move forward and piece together the story. There's nothing to fight, nothing to run away from, just you and the story and lots of walking and clicking.
If that doesn't immediately turn you off from this game, keep reading.
The year is 1995 and you play as Katie, a girl who has returned home after a year abroad to an empty house, with a note from your sister tacked to the door saying she's sorry she couldn't be there to see you, but it was impossible to stay. The note says not to look around for anything, so of course that's what you begin to do right away. From there, you explore the house to find objects, notes, and journals that all piece together to tell the story of your three family members. The story itself is quite endearing, as well as very, very human.
While the graphics are certainly nothing to write home about, the little details that were put into the game are excellent if you take the time to look. Everything in the house adds to the story, from the big things like notes left lying around to small things like ticket stubs and post-it notes. There's also tons of fun 90's references that really set the time period.
If you're the kind of person who can take time away from the action of a game to just look at all the little details, then give this game a shot. If you like visual novels, give it a shot. If you want action or something with a challenge, then this isn't the game for you, and that's cool too.
It's a quick playthrough, and doesn't have much in replay value aside from going back and looking for anything you missed, or replaying for a new perspective on things once you know the whole story. If you just want to try it, wait until it goes on sale and get it then. While I think it's worth the full price tag from a people-should-be-fairly-paid-for-things-they-make standpoint, it's a hefty price for something fairly short that you may not like.

In summary! This game is awesome. This game is not known for having a great story. But if you follow the lore carefully is quite interesting. But we know what made Dark Souls series famous, you will die! and a lot. Some people complains it is not as hard as the first one. Maybe, maybe not. This is a game where your own skills can affect everything so much. I have seen people finishing the game without leveling without saving without using bonfires. So the community probably master this game so far. Still, this game has online, the best of it! You can co-op, you can PVP! you can do all you want wherever(or at least in most places) you want.
I have been so addicted to this game that this became the first game I actually did 100% of the achievement! And I am still happy playing it!
Lets talk about the game itself:
Story: This is not a story driven game, but the lore of this game is amazing and very interesting. You should totally see the youtube videos called "Dark Souls 2 Lore" and support if you like them.
Gameplay: Simply great. You know that a game is good when you have overpowered gear, a walking tank, and tiny fellow kill you with a dagger, skills and poison. The game is full of haters, cheaters, hackers etc. But most of the community play the game fair and square. Mob is not extremely hard. So some people may complain it is too easy compared to DS 1. I love the game if you want it more hard simple join the covenant of the champions and shup up!
Graphics: This was supposed to have outstanding graphics. I don't think the graphics are bad, but texture are not so good. Also Dark Souls 1, with DsFix looks prettier than this. So it could be improved for sure. I think the issue is that the main core of the game was made to run in last gen consoles.
Audio: I have a really nice audio setup(7.2) And when my sister came to me for something and I rested in a bonfire, she said, there is something burning. She was tricked totally. So I will give the audio a better grade than graphics.
Difficulty: This game is made to be mastered. You cannot play 10 hours and dream to be "gud"(referring to the community) It is easier than DS 1 I think but just burn some aesthetic on the bonfires and voila! I like this game the wait it is.
In overall, this is currently my favorite game so far so I totally recommend it!

My first thought of Gone Home when I saw it on the Steam Summer Sale was that it looked like a type of Amnesia I'd actually enjoy; no jumpscares, monsters, or death, and a calm environment to solve puzzles in.
Not only did Gone Home offer this (okay maybe there could have been more puzzles but I'll go onto that later) but it added a huge (yet crammed into a short amount of time) storyline, and a huge amount of feely feels.
A lot of people complain about the shortness of the story, and yes, I completed it in one sitting, but I made sure to look at everything, find everything to be found and just immerse myself in the story, which at the end of the day, I like to do.
I'd describe my gametime almost like that of a film, there was an introduction, a climatic mid section, and the feely finale.
As I mentioned before, there could have been more puzzles, and you spend a lot of the time just following linear paths to your next location, however, what this game lacks in puzzles it makes up for in narrative.
Gone Home may not require you to think hard and solve puzzles, but you can still examine the beautifully created world (with amazing sound, graphics and voicing) and group together all of the little extras that they've hidden around the world, such as hints towards the parents' life rather than that of Sam.
Overall I would recommend this game to almost anyone, and I have to admit, it's possibly the best game I've ever played, and for anyone with a bit of time free on their hands, I'd tell you to go and download this game, and just play it, and enjoy it.

In summary! This game is awesome. This game is not known for having a great story. But if you follow the lore carefully is quite interesting. But we know what made Dark Souls series famous, you will die! and a lot. Some people complains it is not as hard as the first one. Maybe, maybe not. This is a game where your own skills can affect everything so much. I have seen people finishing the game without leveling without saving without using bonfires. So the community probably master this game so far. Still, this game has online, the best of it! You can co-op, you can PVP! you can do all you want wherever(or at least in most places) you want.
I have been so addicted to this game that this became the first game I actually did 100% of the achievement! And I am still happy playing it!
Lets talk about the game itself:
Story: This is not a story driven game, but the lore of this game is amazing and very interesting. You should totally see the youtube videos called "Dark Souls 2 Lore" and support if you like them.
Gameplay: Simply great. You know that a game is good when you have overpowered gear, a walking tank, and tiny fellow kill you with a dagger, skills and poison. The game is full of haters, cheaters, hackers etc. But most of the community play the game fair and square. Mob is not extremely hard. So some people may complain it is too easy compared to DS 1. I love the game if you want it more hard simple join the covenant of the champions and shup up!
Graphics: This was supposed to have outstanding graphics. I don't think the graphics are bad, but texture are not so good. Also Dark Souls 1, with DsFix looks prettier than this. So it could be improved for sure. I think the issue is that the main core of the game was made to run in last gen consoles.
Audio: I have a really nice audio setup(7.2) And when my sister came to me for something and I rested in a bonfire, she said, there is something burning. She was tricked totally. So I will give the audio a better grade than graphics.
Difficulty: This game is made to be mastered. You cannot play 10 hours and dream to be "gud"(referring to the community) It is easier than DS 1 I think but just burn some aesthetic on the bonfires and voila! I like this game the wait it is.
In overall, this is currently my favorite game so far so I totally recommend it!

My heart pounded as I looked around the cramped, muddy hole I chose as a hiding spot.  Every one who charged with me had been killed.  But I knew I had to do my duty to Deuchtland. "For the Kaiser.", I quietly muttered to myself the crouched down and started moving through no mans land.  Suddenly a bullet grazed my arm and hit the dirt next to me.  I froze, had I been seen?  But no more bullets came.  I let out a sigh of relief, it was a shot meant for someone else, I just hoped none would ever find them. I then crawled a bit longer when I saw the unmistakeable blue coler of a french soldier's helmet.  I then realized there were five of them.  I quietly took my rifle out and aimed.  I fired the gun quickly killing one then I slowly took them all out.  I then felt a metal blade pierce through my chest.  I had been killed.
Such is the way in Verdun.
Verdun is a game taking place in WWI in the horrid trenches during the battle of verdun.  The point of this game is to shoot down enemies (with one-shot-dang-insta-kills) and level up and obtain points. You'll be leveling up in whatever way you want/can whether thats you making surgical headshots on your friends, or shooting down countless hordes of Germans, British, or French. All in all the only thing I dislike about this game is the fact that there is no tutorial or bot training mode which, as you may assume, leads to you getting shot down again and again until you know the controls.
Just remember soldier, this isnt Halo where some shield will hold your hand, so keep your dang head down!

I have not simply not reccomended because I don't think it is a game. As a matter of fact, I love "The Stanley Parable", and many claim that that game is not a game as well. However, the reason I disliked this game is because of the massive build-up and pretty much no payoff at the end. The game introduces tons of creative ideas and tons of things that you have to figure out by yourself. However, none of it is ever explained in any way. For example (spoilers),

Honestly, as I went through the game, I got more wrapped up in the Dad's story than in Sam's story just because Sam's story is just really stereotypical and something we have all heard before in a basic love story.

As for the gameplay, I did enjoy looking around the house and trying to discover the mystery of why the family members left and about the previous owner of the house, but the only story that wasn't compelling was the character whose story was focused on the most. However, at this point, I still felt that Sam's story could be really interesting
At this point, I finally felt that the payoff was going to happen, as I finally saw a twist that I could never have seen coming and was about to sing the praises of how good the game was and how it manages to make me think for at least just a bit. However, it completely psyches you out and delivers a stereotypical ending that leaves more questions about the story and let me down completely. Yes, it was a twist, and yes, I didn't expect, but that doesn't make it a good twist. It would be like if during "Jurassic Park", instead of the T-Rex making the water ripple, it was a giant clown. Yes, I didn't see it coming, but that doesn't make it good.
Overall, the game was fun when you were collecting things at the beginning and for stories such as the Dad's story, but the game never risks anything and simply delivers a basic love story that was not that interesting to do.
Also, I forgot to mention: I beat this game, explored a bit after winning to find the logs I missed, and only missed 1 audio log in total, all in 88 minutes. That means I can essentially beat this game 100% in probably a little more than 1 hour and 30 minutes without a walkthrough to find the other audio logs. All in all, 2.5 out of ten.
Afterward: People gave this game a perfect score, and some even gave it a "Game of the Year" award. It just goes to show that critics arn't always right, and while you should consider the opinion of a critic, don't base your interest in a game on that only.

If there were a better way to experience a story other than reading it, Gone Home would be it.  Not once did I feel like I was playing a game or watching it or reading it. I experienced the story as Katie did.
In a nutshell, Katie returns home after a long absence, thinking her mother, father, and sister will be there to greet her. They’re not, and she has to explore the house to find out where they are. That’s selling it short, though. What starts out as borderline horror point-and-click (complete with a thunderstorm and flickering lights) turns into an overload of emotions: pity for your father, shame for your mother, fear and courage for your sister.
It all builds to one final scene, where I found myself standing at the entrance to the attic holding back tears.
In other words, just go play the damn thing. Seriously.

As a Narrative Designer, I've been studying this game to find out what's working well for it and what's not.
After perusing the reviews page on here, it seems that most people were expecting this game to be something it wasn't. It seems a lot of them mistakenly believed it was a horror adventure game with spirits or dead bodies. The spookiness of the house stuck constantly in a severe storm answers why that happened. If this took place in the day time it would be a much different atmosphere. Traveling through the dark house by yourself can be very daunting if you've played a lot of horror games. I found myself a little jumpy, even though full-knowing there is no combat, no ghosts, no other presence in the house. Part of this is the Oscar subplot in which Sam believes his ghost is haunting the house. That little bit may have also encouraged players to expect supernatural activity. There's also the creepy voice-mails left by Lonnie which sound like she may be in danger. Then there's the "blood" (hair dye) in the bath tub. It seems really unnecessary and compounding the problem of making it seem like a game it's not.
So bearing that in mind, how do we approach this game? Reading through the store page, it's clear. This is a story exploration game. You're given a house full of clues and you have to put them altogether to view the story as a whole.
Many people will not enjoy this. They need something faster paced that has traditional gameplay elements. For me, as a writer and an explorer at heart, I absolutely love this game.
Have you ever wanted free reign to explore a house from top to bottom, searching every nook and cranny to get a view of what a family's life is like? Then this game is for you.
Personally, I felt like a detective and had a blast scouring each room and hallway for clues. Some of them were hidden in plain sight, but there were many hidden secrets that made my efforts worthwhile. I really enjoyed the story in its simplicity and focus on characters. Actually, for me, I wanted more story! I was expecting a huge blow-up between Sam and her parents. I'm still not sure why they left the house - I suppose it was for the couples retreat, but it's never very clear what day it is in the game (or perhaps I didn't put enough dates together from all of Katie's data).
I'm a fan of point-and-click adventure games from the 80s and 90s, so this was like a 3D version of that. Whenever I played those games I would try to click on everything just to see what the game would say or how the player character would react. This had a ton of personal touches like that.
<Spoiler ahead!>
Perhaps the most frustrating part for me was when I found a note in the basement. I had only been reading it for a few seconds before the game threw it back on the floor and Katie said "Nope." I couldn't pick it up again. Now I get they're trying to inject character into the game, but at least let me read it completely and THEN have her not pick it up again. I thought I had missed something important but didn't want to play through the entire game again just to read one note. I looked the note up here on community and it wasn't even vulgar or explicit at all. I'm not sure why they wanted to take it away, but I guess it's an artist's choice.
</End spoiler>
All of the vocal content is well-acted, but it's strange that we're hearing Sam speak when we don't have the physical diary entry to read, so it's just like her disembodied voice is automatically coming through your brain. How do we know that's what she was thinking? At first I thought it was Katie speaking her thoughts, so that was a little confusing. However, once you understand it's Sam and accept a bit of suspension of disbelief, it's very thought-provoking and haunting. At the very end we find the entire collection, so one could suppose the game is delivering them so we don't have a giant exposition dump at the end of the game. In which case, that's very appreciated.
The ending disappointed me a little. I really wanted to actually meet another character in the game, even if it was just over the phone. I really wanted to call Sam. Judging by her last note, it seems that I missed her by only a few minutes. Why wouldn't she call back again? Afraid to get the parents - no, they're on their trip and it's the middle of the night. I suppose that's part of the meloncholy-ness of the game. She's gone and there's nothing you can do about but come to terms with it. Poor Katie gets to deal with all the backlash from the parents complaining about Sam suddenly leaving forever. I would imagine Katie would move out herself soon afterward. It would be too awkward to be there.
It's interesting to watch other people play. Some people tend to put things back where they go (me), some people gather items and orgranize them. Some people leave all the lights on and all the secrets wide open. It makes you wonder if Katie wouldn't just leave after experiencing this. Would she leave all the answers open for her parents to view, or would she reset it and make them go through the same process. Would it be any easier for them? Probably not. I'm not sure they could. I tend to think Katie would keep Sam's secrets hidden, especially because of the note saying "Don't tell them" or something to that effect on the door.
I also wanted to find a photo with the girls and Mitten the cat, haha! We never see what Mitten looks like, just find its collar.
Overall, this game isn't exactly innovative with its simple find the combinations and the keys to unlock the doors, but the story is really strong and for me it is a lot of fun to have full control over the house and just do what I want with it without having to worry about another character stopping me.
The story itself is very simple, but the sincerity in how it's delivered and all of the intimate details really make it come to life. Sometimes all you need is a simple story. Those are the ones people remember the best.
My favorite narrative items were the stories of Captain Aurora and the First Mate. Reminds me of the fiction I used to write as a teenager. You can really tell a lot about a person in the stories they write. I almost wanted to see some writing from the father as well. We found some tidbits of Oscar's and his was very interesting in a "Flowers for Algernon" short-of-way.
Overall, I really enjoyed this game. I stayed up late last night playing it and wanted to finish but was falling asleep at my keyboard and bumping into the walls, haha! This morning I was much more refreshed and able to finish it properly. Turns out I missed one door and a whole section of the area with the laundry room and the conservatory.
Okay, so TL;DR?
If you like exploring and digging through endless chunks of subtle backstory, this is your game. If you want something more exciting, filled with action, don't bother. This is a simple slice of life story, not some supernatural action adventure.
A Lesson for Developers: Don't brand your game as something it's not. Present it in an honest way.
To the people who complain about the price: People tend to really devalue games nowadays because there are so many you can get for free. Remember, this is an indie developer. They worked hard on this game, and it cost money to make - especially with the costs for having studio-quality audio and paying their employees. They also put their hearts into it. Don't expect them to sell their work for cheap because some AAA studios can. If you're really tight on money, wait for a Steam sale.

While I didn't want to write this until I complete it, I have to say I'm really excited so far and incredibly blown away. Story narration based on small notes and voice clips all over the Greenbriar home. Which means no matter where you go, you discover so much about your (Kate's) family during short duration in Europe. Greatly appreciated it that three sections of the home is locked up completely, so there is no way you could skip major plot of the game. While the story (so far) is based around three members of your family, the parents are not as significant as Sam's part in the story. What makes that even more interesting is that, dependent on how much you discover and look around in the house, you could potentially focus on the story about Sam without delving too much into what is going on with the parents.
This was a very thoughtful, intuitive and heavily detailed story. I'm horribly slow so I look and inspect everything because not everything you learn about the Greenbriar family comes from Sam's dialogue. So much more is understood or felt when you can apply your personal understanding of the world and connect how item A would somehow be associated with story C. A lot of the story of the game can be expressed without words since a lot of symbolism and association is very utilized.
On the hardware side, I'm very impressed that the Dev team put together this work of art that can run successfully on a system that barely plays DayZ while you are immobile in first person-view. Which means my tower is very under-strength as a quick purchase, and I can still play this game with great success and minimal frustration based speed/loading and interaction. While I tone down everything to minimal on DayZ and can't play it, I can turn everything down on Gone Home and can play it to the fullest. So another great seller idea by the Dev team who put this together with the mindset of minimalist computer power.

The game in essence is nothing new or unusual, but the athmosphere changes everything. Firstly I'm tired of all games about WWII and frankly I think it's overrated. World War 1 was the one that made the world tremble and changed the vision of war, but I guess we're not here to discuss history.
The game is diverse, it has plenty of factions (such as canadians, british, germans or french), each one having different clothing, different voice commands, which are in the native language of the faction and weapons. Unlike other games where there is a big loading screen filled with either nothing or simple tips, there are various information about the events of WWI here and there, so when it comes to history and research, the homework was done.
The environments are beautiful and by not being simple hallways with boxes, it does give the actual war impression. You can be mostly in open land, which leaves you vulnerable, thus need to find a trench or a pit, but you're not safe there either. But this also leads to a thing that bothers me: the maps are incredibly huge. At least when playing deathmatch, if I'm in the middle of the map, two steps later I'm told I left the battlefield. There is no border between the actual battlefield and the irrelevant part of the map, which on one hand is nice because hey natural environment and not game forced at all, but also annoying that you don't know where to go.
Verdun is also pretty much the only game I like playing deathmatch. True, while nothing more than kill, die, respawn cicle, unlike in other games where you find yourself a nice place to camp or run around shooting, here you must explore the map, find the enemy and eventually (if possible) find a place that it is possible for the enemy to come, but not spot you (which makes camping a little more fun than on other games, where you're set in a corner and let the kills flow).
Worst part of the game? Lack of players. Like seriously, most of times there is 1 server at all with a handful of people. Go get the game folks.

I purchased "Gone Home" after reviewing many positive reviews and  with the game going down in price for the Summer Sale, suffice to say, it was time for me to try this game out.
For its price, the game is rather fascinating.  You play a young woman who has come back from Europe and to visit her family who are not there.
The game focuses on the younger sister Sam and piecing together what happened while you were gone.
The game is not very challenging.  If there was any challenge, it was trying to find locker or file cabinet combinations.  Or secret rooms in a massive house.
But aside from finding and discovering things about Sam and the main character's parents, I enjoyed the music and the voice acting.
The graphics were good and the game ran smoothly on my PC and Mac with no problems whatsoever.
These are the positives, if I had a negative, I would say the game was overhyped and my expectations were set to high.  I'll tell you right now, don't set it to high, don't even read reviews.  This is a game that is subjective to the user, it's a game that can be beaten quickly and there are some lingering questions about the characters that definitely don't give you complete finality.
Aside from that, for its price, for its non-banal approach, I give it a positive recommendation.  Not a very high recommendation (more like 82%) but I do recommend this game for casual gamers.

If ever there was a game that completely punctuated the difference between those who critique games for websites/magazines and those who actually purchase and play those games, it is Gone Home. The critics absolutely adored this game and the gamers despised it. Hmmmm. This tells me to never trust a metascore ever again and to stick to the reviews written by those who have actually purchased the game and played it. (Thank heaven for Steam reviews!)
The description of the game states, "No Combat, No Puzzles: Gone Home is a nonviolent and puzzle-free experience, inviting you to play at your own pace without getting attacked, stuck, or frustrated." And I am usually OK with games of that sort IF they can hold my attention and are somewhat engaging. Gone Home was neither attention holding nor was it engaging. Walk around, read notes, listen to a story that clearly has an agenda to it, and that's all. The story line felt rather forced and unnatural and perhaps even a bit silly. After an hour I began to get bored with trying to reveal this preposterous story by digging through every drawer in the house in the hope that there might be another bit of info that would help the story progress a bit, I just gave up. No amount of vodka was going to make this game interesting for me. Glad I bought it on sale.
