Gone Home, an adventure game that the critics love due to one clever trick. You play the older sister of a teen girl who's just fallen in love, and you arrive home after a year abroad to an empty house. You point and click to read notes and examine objects to find out what's going on. As you play a GIRL who is looking out for HER SISTER and the game's plot is PITCHED AT FEMALES, you can't possibly criticise or badmouth this game without looking like a MISOGYNIST. That's the game's clever trick.
It's set in the mid 90's, a time of teen angst and grungy music. So instantly it appeals to us old folk, who grew up in the 90's and are up for a bit of nostalgia. And it's appealing to teens today who can relate to the themes of love, misfits and rebellion. However it somehow manages to be both banal and overly dramatic, like a cheesy 90's show... so you never really do engage. Just more overwrought stuff that happens to somebody else.
The story is well written and well told, and it does hit impressive highs, but the game as a whole isn't all that. If you liked the art of storytelling in "To The Moon", the slice-of-life world building of "Photopia" by Adam Cadre, or the whole games-as-art tightness of "Braid", then you'll like this. It's not as good as any of those games however. And it's over in 2 hours. But they're worthwhile hours.
Recommendation: buy, but only with a hefty discount, 'cos 2 hours man.
N.B. I picked up Gone Home the same night as Sniper Elite V2. One a slow methodical game of even pacing broken up by unimaginable Nazi gore and violence. The other was Sniper Elite V2.

Note: I'm reviewing Gone Home after buying it for a whopping three dollars during the sale.  Had I paid full price, my review would likely be negative.
Gone Home is an interesting experiment written by a handful of people that still vividly remember what it's like to be a teenager, that chaotic time in everyone's life in which they come to grips with who they are and feel everything with an intensity that is forever lost as we get older (for better or worse).  It is about family in a jarringly real way, with all the baggage, joy, frustration and sadness you're likely familiar with when dealing with your own.
Sadly, I feel it can only be recommended to a very few with the patience and open-mindedness to unravel its secrets.  It is something to be contemplated, and most will find it tedious and/or pointless.  It is worth the gamble if you happen to find it at a discount.  With a running time of 2-4 hours and with little replayability, the full price of $19.99 is likely to leave most feeling burned.

I really enjoyed Gone Home. It's a shame that it is so controversial to like it. It was a wonderfully human story about a family's issues, specifically focusing on a troubled late-teenage (17 year old) romance. Wandering around this slightly creaky old mansion, I definitely felt like I was interacting with the belongings of a very normal, very real, family. VHS tapes with hand-written labels, evidence of some crushed dreams and uncertain futures, hints at childhood trauma, the desperate search for self-identity of a teenager... I enjoyed meeting them.
I played through at a very relaxed and calm pace and finished in about two-and-a-half hours. I can't imagine it lasting more than four hours with the most thorough of players. There is no real reason to replay it, aside from experiencing the story again, like a favorite book or film. The developers recently introduced a commentary mode with some significant commentary track time (supposedly an hour and a half of new audio), which I will play through after I let the initial experience settle in my head for a week or two.
I had no real frustrations with the interface, game design, graphics, sound, stability, performance, or purpose. I think it achieved exactly what it meant to achieve (to tell a warm, inter-personal story in an interactive format), and did so in the best way possible for its purpose. There were a few moments I would have liked my character to move SLIGHTLY faster, but really, I could stand to be a bit more patient.
As for the very strange controversiality of the game, I don't really know what to say, because I don't really understand what the problem is. The things I see mentioned the most just sound like players misunderstanding the entire premise, or not putting the same value on the storytelling aspects that I feel the developers had hoped. Or, unfortunately, just pure negativity and disgustingness.
As for purchase price, that's up to you. I bought it at $10 and I felt very satisfied. It's definitely on par with going out to a really good movie that resonates with you.
So overall, I do recommend it. With the application of (what I think are) obvious conditions: If it doesn't sound interesting to you, you probably won't like it. If it seems too expensive to you, wait until it's cheaper. If you don't feel like having a smaller, more focused game experience, you probably won't enjoy it.

When playing Gone Home, it's best to remember that the adventure is in the journey as much as the conclusion. The game has you start off with nothing, but it makes you leave with a load of knowledge that transforms the house into something else. The game does an incredible job of building tension, developing mystery well enough to also let the player formulate their own ideas as to what could be happening. It's these speculations and thoughts that develops a certain anxiety in the player, which can make something as mundane as the sound of thunder ominous. It is these effects, the pacing, and the feelings that the player experiences that creates a surrounding feeling of uneasiness.
In essence, the player exaggerates the meaning of simple items, turning a note on the fridge into a chilling note that could only lead to another hypothesis set by the player. In other words, the sense of terror is brought on by the player, themselves. And that's the great thing about this game, it will have you immersed, and before you know it, an empty house can seem like an eternal source of secrets, dark memories, and fear.
The common struggles of different people are explored, showing how much depth exists in the average human life. As more is found out about your family, you find a story of love, forgiveness, and pain. And would you believe it--this is your driving force to continue exploring the house.
All of this happens to answer a simple question: where is everyone?
If the game is on sale for a good price, I see no reason why you shouldn't experience this game.

I'll be totally honest, i wasn't anticipating Dark Souls II to be so... fulfilling.

Well to start this off, dark souls 2 has got some amazing gameplay mechanics. They've added multiple combat features that weren't  in the first dark souls game. This adds to the intensity of combat. Another thing to note is the intelligence of the AI, they really upped their response speed since the first game. Now its pretty hard to memorize movesets and attack patterns. Dark souls franchise is known for being to have complete control of character stats. Whether you want a mage, archer, tank or a combination of these, its all possible.
This game has really made AI a pretty interesting thing. In the first game, you could easily parry/ dodge almost every enemy after fighting them enough because you memorized their attack patterns. But here, most generic enemies could quickly change their movements based on how you attack them. Also, Sinh's boss fight sucked.The coop in this game is rather unpleasant; this is because of two things: Soul memory and the splitting of the PC community. If you don't know, soul memory(the amount of souls you've collected on that specific character) is basically the new way of distinguishing whether or not your level is good enough to coop with someone else. This could be irritating because if you die a lot while possessing many souls, it will still add to the list and make coop harder. The community was also split because DkS2 and the Scholar of the first sin edition split up the PC community as they are not directly compatible.
While the first game had a not-so-obvious story, dark souls 2 more or less shoves it in your face multiple times over. Though its not the most interesting of stories, it is a good reminder that every great kingdom shall fall. This was also the story of the first Dark Souls game. The game does have some amazing soundtracks,
. I do feel like the final boss was a little weak, but i guess that's why the scholar of the first sin is their to add a second ending and a pretty tough boss fight. Also, Madjula is beautiful and so is the area's soundtrack.
To conclude all of this, I would definitely recommend this to anyone who didn't get the original Dark Souls II with its dlc or anyone who has spare cash to dish out.

It's surprisingly difficult to find a WW1 game out there, and even more tough to find a good one. Verdun defies expectations with its historical accuracy when it comes to trench warfare, and its realism where one shot can be fatal.
Verdun is a Unity-based game, and as such, it runs great and looks great. Battlefields are detailed enough to create a decent environment, however they still aren't as great as other games (such as Insurgency). You play as a soldier fighting on the front lines in World War 1, where much of the war is fought in trenches dug into the ground and gas attacks are common. You and your squad need to work as a team to cover all angles and play well. Here are some of the pros and cons.
+ Good community
+ Team-based gameplay
+ Few performance issues
+ A different kind of FPS, not generic whatsoever
- Environment could be a bit more detailed
- Few full servers
- Lacks return-appeal
- Multiplayer
Is it worth it? For sure. I would recommend buying it on sale though, you can snag a great deal.
So, long story short:
Verdun is excellent at bringing a long past due change of pace to the FPS genre, but has a few caveats which you should be aware of.

*THIS GAME IS NOT FOR EVERYONE*
*This review differs greatly from my review of the DX9 edition*
That said, I do not label Dark Souls 2 or even its predecessor as "hard". I do label it as challenging, and testing at times. It fearlessly rebels against the steriotypes of roleplaying games, but has a charmingly cliche theme of knights, wizards, dragons, corruption and a wide range of others. DX11 has definitely revived this game in my eyes.
Pros:
-The lighting enhancements are lovely.
-Some textures are sharpened.
-The new enemy placements make much more sense compared to DX9.
-New NPC friends and foes breathe new life into the game, creating a brotherly theme at times, and almost rivaling at others.
-Some new items to obtain, and others are adjusted to be obtained at more sensible points of the game.
-Increased maximum player count. Originally 4, has been upped to 6.
-Game breaking bugs fixed. Most notably the durability glitch.
-Exellent optimization.
-Access to a wider range of weapons and armor can help balance things out and give many players a fighting chance against twinks, and other degenerates.
-Tightened security, what was once a game where editors and modders ran unchallenged, now has frequent ban waves, thus creating a much more balanced environment to play in, since everyone has access to the same things.
Cons:
-Harsh community, chances are you'll be invaded by other players who have heavily twinked inventories, do not expect to make many friends.
-Co-op matchmakes are scarce at best.
-A few new item and enemy placements are questionable.
In the end, the pros outweigh the cons, but that is only in this version.

Insurgency set in WWI. This is a  game about WWI, as you may already know, but it's probably the only realistic WWI FPS game ever made. While the game is named after the battle of Verdun 1914-1918, it actually takes place across many battles of the Great War, such as the Somme.
Pros:
-Friendly Community. All people below 16 I've found on this game are actually respectful, can be helpful, and don't scream on the mic every time they're killed.
-Communication. This isn't like other WWI shooters out there, FPS or not. It has easy communication options such as typing or talking, and it allows you to easily plan out your moves. Also, not everyone on the server can hear you talk, only your squad, so you don't have to worry about that one annoying guy on the server playing music over the microphone because he thinks he's an entertaining one.
-Reasonable Stamina. This isn't CoD or Slender. You can run more than 4 seconds without collapsing. The stamina is reasonable and you don't run like a 300 lb old man in a muddy field. You run like a fit, 190 lb. man in a muddy field ;)
-Realistic(ish) Damage. You're not a bullet sponge in this game. You can't take a quarter of a clip/magazine and keep on running. Rifles are one shots in this game (to anywhere. The reason for the "Realistic-ish") most machine guns are 2-3 hit kills (odd, since most of them used the same caliber as the rifles at the time), and all pistols besides the Webley (One shot. What? It's .554, did you expect to survive a shot like that?) are 2-3 shot kills also.
Even if you survive a shot and keep on going, you can recover from the pain, but you won't be able to take another shot no matter how long you wait.
-Bullet Physics. This isn't a Source Engine game or CoD WoW, bullets take time to travel and will drop at long distances. Don't expect to find a man half a quarter of a kilometer from you, have your sights on him, fire, and then the bullet to just travel instantly. You'll have to aim a bit ahead of him (if he's moving) and above him to compensate for the drop. Unlike Red Orchestra though, there's no zeroing on any guns, so it's a lot harder to aim at long ranges. Also, bullets will go through thin and/or weak cover such as fences or, with heavier calibers, metal.
Cons:
-It doesn't matter where you get hit, whether it just be your toe or your heart-area, you'll still suffer the same amount of damage.
-No rearmament. If you run out of ammo, your only hope is to melee or kill yourself. You can't pick up people's weapons or find an ammo crate in this game to rearm.
-Falty-ish hit boxes. Yes, sometimes the hitbox will be with you or against you, regardless of how well you can dodge a bullet or aim. Yes I've seen people aiming to their left, and then hit someone they just turned away from (although that might latency, and there's been no way to solve it yet), I've sprayed people with an entire pistol mag and still miss, but my sights traced on them...
-Clunky-ish movement. Even though you move at a reasonable speed for a human-being, it still feels like you're not running as fast as someone should go. It feels like there's dumbells in your character's backpack or whatever.
-Last but probably not least: Bad-ish melee (at least for me). Melee feels stale, and unbalanced. It doesn't actually feel like you're hitting the person or object you've targeted, and unless you have a bayonet then melee is almost entirely useless. You can't get close to people 99.99...% of the time, and even when you do, they'll most likely notice you, turn around, and shoot you. There's no physics to melee either. No one loses their balance, there's no stopping power to melee, and there's no animation at all for getting hit by melee. The same goes for getting shot. You just hear bones crack, flesh tear, and then your character just ragdolls to the floor, as if they've just collapsed from a sudden heart attack, nothing more. (That one was a bit harsh.)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
That's my review. Verdun has some of the largest potential of any game I've ever played, but the developers are a bit more concerned with adding new weapons and teams than fixing these minor, but annoying problems in the game. The game is highly-playable, don't get me wrong, and you can have a good time if you learn how to play properly and have a good team. The only problem with this game is that I hear it was made on the Unity engine, so obviously trying to push it into an advanced client game rather than a simple 3D, casual shooter on some website like Kongregate (which, BTW, hosts the demo of this game) is a bit tough. 7/10

I recommend this version of Dark Souls II if you don't already own and play Dark Souls II vanilla, without the DLC. If you do, just buy the DLC and be happy.
My only reasoning behind upvoting this version of Dark Souls II is, merely, because it's Dark Souls, and I love the Souls games to death, and will fanboy over them every single time, and throw my every last penny at the developer to make more games.
Basically, the gist of this game, aside from what gave the original DkS2 it's charm, is that they moved some items around, inserted/moved/deleted some enemies, included all DLC seamlessly, and improved graphical quality. DkS2 original, on my old crappy graphics card, still ran like an optimized dream; DkS2 Scholar of the First Sin, however, lagged me out every time I stepped into a fog door or sat at a bonfire. Sure, it doesn't do that anymore, but it told me that Scholar of the First Sin had indeed changed the graphical quality enough to make my old graphics card squeal in pain.
Granted, some of the design decisions of this game over the original don't make much sense. Some items were moved, or removed, in illogical ways. For example, I got used to logically looking for a key to a door to a bonfire located ahead of the path. However, some were moved way away, or were put in a different area altogether. Some bonfire keys I couldn't even find anymore. That kind of ticked me off, but hey, it's Dark Souls.
Scholar of the First Sin is rife with artificial difficulty. "Let's just add two or three enemies here, one here, two there, and one there to make it more difficult and surprising over the vanilla copy." No, it didn't achieve either of those. It only lead to more frustrating circumstances. Make each enemy HARDER to fight. Don't be lazy and copy/paste. That's just poor mechanics design.
Also, the illogically-placed petrified NPCs are just... what? I don't even know what that was supposed to do. Make me spend more souls on Fragrant Branches of Yore? It made me stop and scratch my head and say, "What were they thinking?"
As per my old Dark Souls II review, I still confirm that the environment looks empty, dull, and stale, especially in certain places around the first area (the name eludes me). In the distance, I could see repeated textures on the ground, 90 degree angles and clipping problems where the ground suddenly juts out of itself with a seamless flat edge. I don't know how else to describe it. The environments were just not up to snuff.
All that said, I can only barely recommend purchasing this, just because it's Dark Souls, and it is still pretty fun. Infinitely more frustrating (which does not = difficulty), but fun.

And there's a bilingual bonus if you also speak Malay/Indonesian, since pretty much all the place names are in Malay, and they're occasionally hilarious in how literal it is - the nuclear power plant in the game is called "Awan Cendawan Power Plant" for example.
Outside of game content, the game runs very smoothly on my laptop, while still looking quite great. JC2 is quite cheap nowadays, too.

This game... Truly there are no words that can fully describe how amazing this game is.
Most of us can agree, the original Dark Souls II was easy, and some of us hated it.  I got this game again to play with friends, not truly knowing if I made a mistake. Purchasing Scholar of the First Sin was the best "I don't know" buy I have ever done.
Pros:
Graphics are fantastic, not as cartoony as the original version felt. +
Gameplay, FROM has most certainly improved the game mechanics. Dark Souls II now feels as it should have felt on release, fighting is fluid, dying is fluid (and common) FROM has really remade the gameplay to near perfection. +
Challenge: As I said before most of us remember Dark Souls II as being pretty easy, it had challenging bits, but not many.  Scholar of the First Sin lives up to the challenge that the Souls series is known for, while still keeping it fun. Mostly. +
Desert Sorceress +
Cons:
Challenge: Some of the things that make Scholar of the First Sin more challenging is pure annoyance. In many areas there are new enemies that should not be there. These enemies mess with the lore, assuming that you're big into that. Other areas are now just swarms of enemies that can easily kill you in a few seconds, even faster if you're using a build that can't even hit the enemies. (Looking at you Caestas) -
Bonfires: Some bonfires are honestly useless, enemies will waltz right on in to the only place you think you're safe. (Other than Majula) -
Overall this game does have its fair share of flaws, but I find it incredibly easy to overlook these flaws. The game makes up for them. Whether you play it with friends or by yourself, you're guaranteed to have an amazing time. Assuming this is a type of game that you like. I had a friend tell me this game was almost a carbon copy of Skyrim. I have a carbon copy of his face in my fist now.

I can certianly see why many people don't like Gone Home. It's not what most expect with a game, and the focus and emphasis of it is entirely different. There is no action sequences. There are no fail states. Perhaps most importantly, there are no real sucess states. You can "beat" the game in the sense that you can reach an end state where the credits role but to do that while ignoirng the entire context of the game is irrelevant.
I truly enjoyed Gone Home. I thought it was interesting and well-written. I enjoyed the ability to just peak around through someone's life. It's of course incredibly voyeuristic, but at the same time in an age where massive sandbox games are being released, it's interesting to see someone take the same concept and apply to a single building. What would it look like if just one building was fully modeled? If it really told a story and you could find all the tiny little details?
The game is short. It took me 1.5-2 hours to complete. I would not consider playing it again. The "gameplay" so to speak is so integrated into the story that even if I might have missed aspects of the story, to jump back in for the sake of completationism would destroy the experiene which demands a holistic interpretation.
The story itself is perhaps not the most interesting of things. It is a tale that progresses along via audio diaries you unlock. Yet to me that is not the main attraction. It is the sense of understanding and majesty that can be provoked by truly investigating the details of one building. It's all the silly references and callbacks to the '90s. It's the exploration and levelbuidling craft displayed.
I liked Gone Home. I think most people would. If you think a game cannot be a game if it lacks action, or if the idea of a short game bothers you, or if you think games are antithetical towards story then I would not see the sense in buying this. I do not think that detracts from its merits though.

Reading all of the other reviews that complain about cash-grabbing From, the graphics not being far superior, or complaints about playing on a keyboard still being difficult (seriously, this isn't a game meant for mouse and keyboard), it frustrates me that people seem to miss the point of this re-release. It was intended to package everything together, improve on some things, change some things out of hindsight to improve the experience of the game. If someone didn't own the game, it's a good opportunity to buy a package. However, if you're looking to good chunk of the game (enemy placement, item placement, etc), changing the game overall is going to upset fans. People won't like the change to the game, it's just how people are. So why not update the game a bit, improve some graphics, add support for more players, and do more? This wasn't necessarily intended for people who already owned the game, it was intended for people who are looking for a different experience with the game, or who didn't already previously own it.
Having played Dark Souls I for nearly 500 hours on PC and Console, and Dark Souls II for near 300 hours on PC, you could say I am a fan of the series. So it's no surprise that I ended up getting Dark Souls II, DX11; this totals my Dark Souls 2 expenditures to approximately $110. I run a higher end PC as well, so performance isn't really ever a problem for me, so I am writing this from the perspective of someone who works, and has a nicer PC.
While I may be partially biased towards the upgrade, please hear me out on this one. If you played Dark Souls 2, felt content with the game, then I would not advise purchasing the upgraded edition; there simply is not enough to warrent purchasing, in my opinon. However, if you are looking to get a refreshed feel to the game, take on (in my opinion) more difficult areas, or play Dark Souls 2 for your first time, I suggest getting the upgrade.
Performance hasn't changed much for me between the two versions, which is fine because Dark Souls 2 ran well enough for me on the DX9 version. Loading times are still the same (maybe even a small bit faster), netcode is same or better, and I really like the multiplayer additions, which includes having 3 summons and 3 invaders as well. In terms of how the game runs and feels physically, it all handles well, though there are no significant improvements. More NPC summons, better enemy AI, more NPC invasions; they're all really cool, and a lot of the NPC summons and invaders feel like they actually have a personality.
A big complaint I see is that people have a huge issue with not being able to transfer over old characters. While this is a minor nuisance at most (seriously, just make new characters), playing through the game anew is a great experience in itself. New builds to try out, new playstyles, building new characters is a fundamental part of the replayablility of the game. Having seen as many people as I have complain about not being able to transfer over characters, I question how people miss the bigger picture here. It's really not that big of an issue, sorry you can't transfer over your SL 300 character to do whatever with. Build a new character, get over it, move on.
While the graphics haven't changed much (of course, they won't change much at all if you were like me and ran GeDoSaTo), the areas have all had fairly significant changes. And while there haven't been areas added, there are slight changes to existing areas to accomidate for new enemy placement. The new enemy placement adds SO much more depth to the game, adds a lot of new challenges, and so far, have not diminished the feel of the game at all; it only adds to it.
All in all, the game is fairly the same. Very slightly better graphics, no new weapons or armors, just moving and adding the enemies around for a more challenging feel, and moving items around. It's a really cool experience playing through this time, and seeing what has been changed. Again, if you don't own the game, this is definitely the version to get. If you really enjoyed Dark Souls 2, I would heavily suggest getting the upgrade. If you are on the fence about it, or you were content with playing it the first time, don't buy it.

Gone Home is the very definition of story exploration. You are Kaitlin, a girl who comes home after a year abroad to an empty house. Your sister, Sam, has left you a series of notes that you find by exploring your large mansion home. The atmosphere immediately makes you think you are about to walk into a horror game but there actually isnt any kind of combat or scares. The goal in the game is simply to explore and find clues.
Let's get on to the more critical things. The graphics are pretty good and I didn't experience any bugs or glitches in the game which was nice. The story sucked me in from the beginning and I found myself trying to put the pieces together and wanting to know more about this family. The characters are deep and all have something about them to be discovered. I didn't find any characters that didn't serve a purpose.
The only negatives that I found is that the game is incredibly short. I finished in under 2 hours and I explored all of the mansion and I am assuming I found all of the letters because the story progressed in a way that made sense. The ending leaves you wanting more which wouldn't be bad if this were the type of game that you could get DLC for and keep playing from where you left off but there isn't any replay value to this game at all.
Overall for the price I payed which was 3 dollars the game delivered what I would expect from a game so cheap. During sales I would recommend this game because it is a nice break from the stressful games that require strategy and good timing. It is as I said simple exploration which a good story. However, if it is much more than 5 bucks I can't say you are gettting your moneys worth out of it.

Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin is my first experience with Dark Souls II. I played Dark Souls: Prepare to Die extensively, with 200 hrs on it. The first thing that I noticed about DS II: SotFS is the difficulty.
To me, DS II:SotFS is very difficult in the early game. The AI is very good, and the tracking on enemies' attacks are very good.
I started as a Depraved Undead, which may have not been the most easy class to choose for the early game. Starting at Lvl 1, He is the lowest level of the classes on start up. His stats are average and the equipment he can effectively use at Lvl 1 is very limited. He does have available to him an item that allows him to ``respec`` or respecialize his statistics later, which can be helpful when deciding to ``reroll`` your character if you have spent some attribute points mistakenly.
Starting class aside, the reason why I found the game difficult than its predecessors was melee combat.
I would like to take a moment to discuss the various changes in combat.
Melee striking is pretty much the same. There are different animations of course for swinging your weapons around, including some new additions to weapons that you might have grown accustomed to using. I am still discovering new weapons as I have not quite finished my play through. In fact I believe that I am far from completing it actually, but I think my experiences are worth sharing.
Damage is a little bit different. Divine damage is no longer (?) as it seems to have been merged into LIT damage. I have not seen any indicator of DIV damage in the game. Magic / Fire / Lightning / Dark is still here. Pyromancy / Dark can now scale with INT / FTH. Poison seems to do much greater damage than in previous games, while Bleed seems to do less than it did before. However, Bleed also damages Max Endurance now and stamina regeneration, among a host of other things, other than straight damage. It has more of a combat debuff feel to it now.
Everything hurts really bad. This goes without saying to anyone who has any experience with the Dark Souls franchise. With Light Armor on, one should play extremely cautious, as multiple enemy groups are common and numerous. Expect to get stunned very easily. Shields help reduce the damage, but starting shields (the ones you get for free) do not reduce 100% physical, so it is best to purchase one that has at least 90% reduction, until you can find something better or unless you are practicing parrying with a smaller shield.
Poise can be gained through attribute points now, so that's a bonus. :D
Parrying is much harder, imo. While many of the attacks are parryable in Dark Souls:SotFS, it is unlikely to parry them without a shield / offhand that is meant to do so. The parry frames have been adjusted for each offhand item such that Kite Shields (Regular Shields) are FAR WORSE at parrying than they were in previous games. The parry frames have a delay on these shields and I have not the patience to even learn to parry things anymore in my short time with the game, nor has it hindered me.
I have gotten far with my 100% physical blocking shield and stamina management alone, and along with rolling every odd attack or two, I believe it to be a non issue outside of PvP.
Ranged aiming is better. Using items for combat is about the same (limited throwing distance). Throwing weapons have greater damage and bows have greater damage. Ammo can be expensive and hard to stay stocked up on. If you are relying on Bows a lot, it is best to gain access to Steady Hand McDuff and his bonfire. He has unlimited supply of iron arrows. These are my preferred choice of arrow atm and for 30 souls per, they are not too expensive.
Rolling is a little bit different than Dark Souls in the way that your weight adjusts something of a slider, instead of going from Fast / Normal / Slow as you would in previous installments. Now there is varying degrees of Fast / Medium / Slow Rolling speeds. The variance lies within the distance rolled and the speed. Test it out in game to find your preference.
Rolling has a lot fewer invincibility frames in this installment, imho, without upgraded Adaptability. I have yet to see a significant increase in invincibility frames through upgrading my ADP, and can only say that learning to use roll and using it at the right times (just before the swing) is very important here to avoid in taking damage.
*UPDATE*
I had a brief look at the Dark Souls Wiki and discovered that I had 85 AGI, which is lowest.. I had 6 ADP. For a DEX build this is really bad, as I am reliant on staying mobile and avoiding damage. So I am currently boosting my ADP to about 30. That should be enough as it will increase my invincibility frames by about 250%. There is a chart explaining it here:
. Videos on the AGI page as well.
*/END*
I really cannot comment on anything relating to spells. I haven't cast any spells yet in game, and probably won't for quite some time. I have had spells cast on me by invading NPCs (of which there are many!) and they seem to function quite well. I will have to update later if / when I do have more experience with the spells.
One thing I can say is that I do miss KICKING THINGS. From Software has decided to replace it with a bashing motion. It interrupts shield block, but has none of the knock back effect of kicking. :'(
Oh yes, backstabbing and critical hits. They are still very effective when you can pull them off. However the enemy tracking does not allow you to easily backstab every mob in the game anymore. I can see why they wanted to change it and it's a healthy change overall. As for critical hits, I can't comment too much but it seems like a smaller hitbox. Its always been a small hitbox, but it seems like a minor adjustment in the enemies' position can make the hitbox miss very easily. I am not a fan considering how hard it is to parry things now.
But I am sure it will just take some time getting used to.
That's all I can say for combat. As for the rest of the game..
The voice acting is very good, level design is good, graphics are superb.. I am really satisfied with the game overall.
Movement has changed a bit (I was expecting this), however remains comfortable. Camera is a bit awkward at times, and I would warn everyone to STAY AWAY FROM LEDGES. I have fallen off of quite a few of them already.. The slopes are very slippery and I would advise to just stay away from them, when ever possible.
I like that Bonfires allow you to Fast Travel, although there is something to be said for walking a distance. I became very familiar with the area around the FireLink Shrine in Dark Souls, and found a strange comfort in traversing that area. I will say though, that the music around Majula is absolutely terrible and boring. Sorry Majula music lovers. :/
I feel as though adding more of the manual shortcuts like the elevators from Undead Parish and FireLink Shrine would have been a better idea to incorporate than teleporting, but teleporting saves time and is somewhat essential now that the Undead Protagonist cannot Level Up at any bonfire (He must talk to the FireKeeper Maiden in Majula for that).
(TL;DR)
Great Game, Worth your money, Just buy it. You can always make more money later. ;)

My husband bought Gone Home for me after playing through it himself. I let it sit, unplayed, in my library for quite a while until a couple of days ago. I am so glad I stopped procrastinating.
Almost immediately the voice acting, sound mixing, beautifully detailed art, and open-world interactivity pulled me in. Very quickly I felt immersed in the beautiful, dimly lit atmosphere to the point that exploring the house in the dark made me nervous. I found myself leaving a trail of lights on, not unlike I would in real life if I were home alone, and holding my breath as I turned corners. Thunder crashes made me jump, flashes of lightning in the windows had my mind playing tricks on me, wondering if I was being watched. But as I continued through, reading notes from my sister -who was really feeling like my sister, not the sister of a fictional character I was playing- learning more about my family's loves and fears and flaws, I felt more and more emotionally invested. I laughed along with Sam as she fell in love, and my heart broke alongside her as her trust in the people around her crumbled. Once I learned about our parents' denial of her relationship with Lonnie, I found myself throwing plates and cups and papers on the floor out of frustration. My heart raced every time I feared that this time, through this door, I would find something that would break my heart irreparably. Upon finally picking up the attic key, I questioned whether or not I even wanted to go upstairs, fearing the worst. And finally, when I learned that the whole time I was not the one having “gone home”, I cried. I was relieved and happy and proud.
Gone Home is not just a game but an extraordinary emotional experience and love story, presented through an intricate storyline, stunning graphics, and sound mixing and voice acting that's absolutely exceptional. It is entirely worth the cost at full price.

I've had a lot of fun with Dark Souls 2 so far and I have some positive opinions and some negative. What I do like about the game is first off the enhanced visuals. Overall it looks very good and I love the wind affecting objects like grass, trees and capes on armor. But there are certain details which could have been made better for example the background behind the ship in No-Man's Wharf ...it's hilarious. Mechanically the increased number of equipment slots is a no-brainer and being able to consume multiple soft-souls at once is great. The new dodging system is somewhat questionable. At the get-go you have 0.1s of invincibility during a roll making it very hard from the beginning but it can be increased. The durability system is really bad because the weapons degrade extremely quickly. Clearing an area between bonfires almost or completely break my weapon. Having multiple ones is of course a solution which brings me to the next point -- the weapon enhancing. Boss weapons are now upgraded with Petrified Dragon Bone which is an extremely rare material and fully upgrading ONE weapon requires a ridiculous
of them. The only way to obtain more is to burn Bonfire Aesthetics and farm certain areas which is boring. The same goes for Twinkling Titanite which you could purchase in Dark Souls. I didn't like only having 1-4 Estus Flasks until mid-game. Starting off with 5 and still having the 12 limit would've been better. The story is solid as far as I observed.
Now ...the multiplayer. First off, invasions. I have no problems with the invaded chugging Sunny-D and using Lifegems -- that's completely fine because they didn't choose to be invaded. The lag caused by delay for data transfer is not the game's fault but I feel like an option to only be paired with people relatively close to you would have been great so you don't have to deal with the lag. I've had invasions with one or two seconds of delay and it makes it very hard to dodge/block ...especially casuls spamming magic/hexes/miracles. "So what's the problem then?" The modders. There is nothing that will stop you from being paired with modders. At least 15-20% of my invasions have been people with infinite health, stamina, poise all running with no armor and a giant weapon. I have reported all of these players, of course but something similar to Punkbuster or a simple script when pairing is needed. I mean, you can calculate the maximum value of each individual stat with gear included so there's nothing stopping them from doing so. Secondly, duels. Anything that heals should be banned during a duel, period. I swear, most duels I've had was against casul magic casters with Havel's armor. Otherwise, it's really fun. I do not like the new matchmaking system in Dark Souls 2 because it's not based on level but the total amount of souls you've had. This can make it a bit unbalanced because I can be paired with someone who has an advantage in the total number of stats. If I choose to invade a person and I'm at level 350 (you should be at highest tier in this level) that player can be in level 838 which is the highest level attainable in Dark Souls 2. That is a massive difference. A lot of community members choose to remain at only 150 - 200. If there's another Souls game I'd love to see From Soft focus more on PvP and build it in a more competitive way.
That's my honest opinion on Dark Souls 2. I'll give it a 6/10 because I mainly got the game for PvP and can be really unbalanced (almost impossible with modders but gravity OP) at certain points. I had a great time during the story though ...but multiplayer -- meh.

I wanted to like this game, really.  And I did somewhat enjoy it.  It felt like there should have been some puzzles to solve, but there really weren't - it was just a linear walk-through "experience."  But I guess that's okay - I kind of knew that it was more of an interactive story than a game, so I'm willing to give it a pass on that.  I was pretty immersed in and interested in the story.  And I didn't HATE the 2 hours or so that I played it.  If there was a "Sort-of recommend" option, I'd pick that, but as is...
SPOILERS AHEAD....
*************************************
What disappointed me about the game was the abrupt ending and how nothing really HAPPENED.  You're running through the house investigating everything you can find to see what happened to your family, and why they seem to have left in such a hurry.  And then it ends and it turns out that your parents are on vacation and your sister just ran away - she'll probably be back before the end of the summer, if you ask me.  All that worrying about what had happened to them and why the house was so disorganized, and expecting a final scene where you actually find them and maybe help them get out of trouble or something... nothing.  Just anticlimactic ending.
From the beginning, something seems badly wrong with the house.  There's an invoice on a table in the foyer for the movers that moved the family into this house a year ago.  Looks like they disappeared shortly after "I" left on vacation.  What could have happened to them?  Boxes that were never unpacked everywhere.  Crumpled up notes from last summer sitting NEXT TO (only occasionally in) the trash can.   Not only has no one taken out the garbage in this house, but they haven't even bothered to pick up the paper that's been sitting right next to it for 10 months.  And unopened soda cans everywhere - but no empty ones in the trash.  At this point, I was pretty sure that I was walking through an old crime scene - a cold case to solve.  But no, the letters all progressed chronologically as I walked through the house, and eventually I found stuff from just yesterday.
It's a little rough on immersion when you imagine that people were living in this house yesterday, but had left a chronological trail in the exact order that I happened to walk through.  Dad's typewriter and early work on his next novel still set up in his office, but then later work on a typewriter in the greenhouse - because it wouldn't do if I found the later work mixed in with the newer.
And it seems like everyone in the house took their notes and letters to a new place every time they had something new to read, and then just left it sitting there on the table or under a binder or crumpled up near a trash can.  All of my postcards sitting, as if just read, in a different part of the house?  Haven't these people ever heard about organizing their mail?  And some documents that should have come FROM the denizens of the house but never seemed to make it out.  Not to mention the kitchen with nothing but milk and frozen peas, and no real cookware that I remember seeing.
All in all, there was so much weirdness going on, and I just hoped that SOME of it would be explained at the end when I found everyone tied up in the attic - like why they never unpacked in the last year, or why they removed all the VCRs as if the Government, in association with the Rand Corporation and reverse vampires, were going to send out mind control rays through them.  But no, at the end - parents on vacation, sister ran away to be with her girlfriend.  Yawn.  Wouldn't have been so disappointing if there was more game rather than just hearing a story, but again - I was willing to give that a pass if it had just been going somewhere...

I'd suggest Global Offensive. I used to play CS:S fairly hardcore many years ago, so I decided to give it another spin for old time's sake. There is a thriving community, but unfortunately 90% of the game has turned into flash grenade spam and campers.
If you play a normal match (no mods, no user-created content), I guarantee 9 times out of 10 you'll run into a server full of 20~ people who are spamming flash grenades and camping around corners.
Back when I played this is 04-06, everyone fought head on. Nobody stayed in one room the entire match, nobody camped doorways with an AWP or used a flashbang spam/P90 combo for easy kills. This game's playerbase has gone way downhill and the game just isn't fun anymore when the only weapons people use are the AK, M4, AWP, M91, and flashbang. I can honestly say that since I bought the game on Christmas Day, I've played many hours of it and have yet to see a single person using a shotgun, any non-P90 SMG's, scoped rifles, etc. It's all about what's OP now, and spending more time trying to cheap your way into survival instead of actually having fun.
You know what's not fun? Running in a doorway and insta-dying because of the guy in the corner. You know what's not fun? Spending 20 straight seconds stunned because the enemy has you cornered and still has to spam you with flash grenades to ensure they don't die.
Welcome to Counter Strike: Camp N' Flash.

The lag caused by delay for data transfer is not the game's fault but I feel like an option to only be paired with people relatively close to you would have been great so you don't have to deal with the lag. I've had invasions with one or two seconds of delay and it makes it very hard to dodge/block ...especially casuls spamming magic/hexes/miracles. "So what's the problem then?" The modders. There is nothing that will stop you from being paired with modders. At least 15-20% of my invasions have been people with infinite health, stamina, poise all running with no armor and a giant weapon. I have reported all of these players, of course but something similar to Punkbuster or a simple script when pairing is needed. I mean, you can calculate the maximum value of each individual stat with gear included so there's nothing stopping them from doing so. Secondly, duels. Anything that heals should be banned during a duel, period. I swear, most duels I've had was against casul magic casters with Havel's armor. Otherwise, it's really fun. I do not like the new matchmaking system in Dark Souls 2 because it's not based on level but the total amount of souls you've had. This can make it a bit unbalanced because I can be paired with someone who has an advantage in the total number of stats. If I choose to invade a person and I'm at level 350 (you should be at highest tier in this level) that player can be in level 838 which is the highest level attainable in Dark Souls 2. That is a massive difference. A lot of community members choose to remain at only 150 - 200. If there's another Souls game I'd love to see From Soft focus more on PvP and build it in a more competitive way.
That's my honest opinion on Dark Souls 2. I'll give it a 6/10 because I mainly got the game for PvP and can be really unbalanced (almost impossible with modders but gravity OP) at certain points. I had a great time during the story though ...but multiplayer -- meh.

Gone Home is one of those games that, unless you read the reviews for it, you're going to feel slightly scared when playing it. I mean, it runs off of that illogical fear with the setting in which it is placed. You come home around 1 AM, alone, and no one's there. There's boxes that are either packing up or being unpacked spread throughout the game, and sounds that make you think "OH! SOMEONE'S IN THE HOUSE!" Though it turns out, this game is not at all about that. So, for those expecting a horror game because they were playing Amnesia: Dark Descent and Gone Home is a game that came up in the recommended titles section, this is not it.
Gone Home follows the story of Katie's (Your character) little sister, Sam, and her life through her teenage years. You also learn a bit about a small side story about the house's history, the story of Katie's father's struggles, and the less exciting, slightly boring story of Katie's mother's job. The main story though, is about Sam. Without giving too much away, I will tell you this: Gone Home is a rather short game depending on how you play it. You discover the story. It's up to you whether or not you want to dive deep into the multiple storylines to this game. In my opinion, it feels more so like it would have made a better movie than a game. If you like games like that, where you discover the story, and if you like stories about growing up differently, then you might like this game. It most certainly is not a game for everyone, but a lot of people will really enjoy it. Though, my biggest suggestion for if you want this game is: Buy it on sale. Do NOT pay $20 for this game. Even though I did enjoy this, and there's a good three to four playthroughs that you can get from it and finally find everything there is to find in it, I don't believe that it should be so highly priced. Best bet for buying this game, wait until it is (at most) $6.

I'd suggest Global Offensive. I used to play CS:S fairly hardcore many years ago, so I decided to give it another spin for old time's sake. There is a thriving community, but unfortunately 90% of the game has turned into flash grenade spam and campers.
If you play a normal match (no mods, no user-created content), I guarantee 9 times out of 10 you'll run into a server full of 20~ people who are spamming flash grenades and camping around corners.
Back when I played this is 04-06, everyone fought head on. Nobody stayed in one room the entire match, nobody camped doorways with an AWP or used a flashbang spam/P90 combo for easy kills. This game's playerbase has gone way downhill and the game just isn't fun anymore when the only weapons people use are the AK, M4, AWP, M91, and flashbang. I can honestly say that since I bought the game on Christmas Day, I've played many hours of it and have yet to see a single person using a shotgun, any non-P90 SMG's, scoped rifles, etc. It's all about what's OP now, and spending more time trying to cheap your way into survival instead of actually having fun.
You know what's not fun? Running in a doorway and insta-dying because of the guy in the corner. You know what's not fun? Spending 20 straight seconds stunned because the enemy has you cornered and still has to spam you with flash grenades to ensure they don't die.
Welcome to Counter Strike: Camp N' Flash.

I would love to be able to recommend this game, and I was anxious to play it for weeks.
HOWEVER
There are far too many issues present within the game for me to be able to recommend it to others, however with attention to these issues I would hope that the game (the core of which is excellent in theory) becomes more enjoyable for others.
Pros:
-WW1 trench warfare is a niche theme, and it is unfortunate that the game suffers from several flaws that stop it being one of the best FPS available on PC.
-Sounds design is EXCELLENT on both weapons, movement as-well as ambient map sounds.
-Well designed maps that appear to be historically accurate.
-"Hardcore" gameplay style is appropriate and well-implemented.
-Texture quality is decent, but doesn't hold up to a number of modern releases.
-Suspenseful gameplay that immerses you in the setting.
-Ranged combat is engaging.
Cons:
-Lacklustre tutorial that leaves a lot to be wanted.
-Filler game-modes that don't add much to the core experience.
-Frequent sounds cutting, similar experience on multiple PCs with different audio receptors.
-Jerky movement system that appears to have a mind of its own, tested with multiple keyboards.
-Annoying tendency to automatically set the crouch to prone or crouch on spawn or entering trenches and craters.
-Cycling crouch, standing and prone is a tad tedious (minor gripe as there are separate  controls available).
-Lacking certain animations.
-Retreat mechanic is poorly implemented, and ends up being "run away and get shot in the back or hold your ground for 10 seconds and get executed.
-Constant respawn adds a lack of meaning to peoples lives; this results in the experience becoming too arcade-like with people constantly neglecting teamwork due to a lack of penalty for "lone wolf" style gunplay.
-Hitboxes are occasionally rough, which degrades from the overall experience.
-Grenades and clubs constantly not working, reported across multiple players.
My biggest issue however is with the squad system that makes you feel more like part of a special forces squad than a small part of a larger battle. The lack of consistency in equipment and imbalance of roles detracts from the overall experience of the game. For example having (in a game of new players) 2 squads with only an NCO and then 2 full squads leaves you with the following:
4 NCOs
2 Flankers (armed with revolvers)
2 Riflemen
2 Raiders (armed with revolvers)
This then leads to a game focused on monotonous close quarters combat that has very little weight behind it, usually devolving into a dull kite-fest.
-Game-breaking bugs:
For example after less that 10 minutes of play I was no longer being credited for kills, and couldn't be killed by enemy gunfire, artillery, gas, wire, or execution. This occurance was not enjoyable for me or for the enemy. Especially the enemy. Multiple instances of bugs similar to this have made the game frustrating during my admittedly short amount of playtime.

"It can't possibly be over..." That was what first came to mind as the credits started to roll upon "completion" of the game.
"Letdown." That was next.
It's simply not worth the money. I'm glad I only spent $3 on this game instead of full price. Boring, one-track, and ultimately pointless... this is hardly a game. It's more like a narrative that plays if you're lucky enough to click on something important.

However, as anybody should know, a game isn't just about raw playtime. Gone Home fully deserves its increasinly rooted place in indie gaming history for an experience that delivers in subtle atmospherics, scraps of paper and whispers. This is not a game illuminated by the flare of a smoking gun or a complex crafting system of survivavl through open world exploration. Instead, the bells and whistles are stripped back, the HUD is made redundant and the intonation is on total immersion into a well-structured story experience.
There are many better in-depth and impassioned views and reviews above and below this one regarding the story, but to add a point of practicality and precursor to the mose-click 'add to shopping basket;' a few things to follow up recurring themes in the wake of this quiet all-conquering indie development:
1) Gone Home is an intricate story told in an intimate way through its methodical and meditative rhythm. Its tension and atmosphere is generated from the very grace and pace with which you traverse this strange and abandoned home, uncovering it's secrets and exploring its nooks and cranny's in the slow development of multiple characters that entwine the story tapestry. As hinted, you dictate this pace; the player, so try to ignore the negative reviews stating nihilsim, boredom ad banality, as it is the indiviudal players preference that has made this so; not the game. If you are an all-action, all-killing quick thrills gamer, you will hate this game- it unfurls slowly and languidly to nurture narrative. If you are a strategic, statistical, survivalist gamer, you will hate this game- there is no threat, no zombie apocalypse and no crafting system. To save you the trouble of listing off all other alternatives, in basic terms, if you are looking for a game that tries something different, that is built on story instead of story built on top, give Gone Home a play, for it is a quiet, expanding tale that is formukated through fragments and observations. The rain falls in the black expanse outside the home you explore, distant thunder rumbles, light and shadows grow as you move through rooms and corridors and the night- the game- lasts as long as you want it to. The true detail is in the jigsaw of story; not any graphical majesty of this small-scale Unity build.
2) Gone Home also shows where this renaissance in story telling games is heading, so there's no harm in owning a piece of indie development history. The story is by no means the most intense, emotional, intricate tale ever told- it did not bring me to tears, but the quiet majesty of its execution is worth experiencing from the perspective of simply enjoying the game experience. Once you have finished this game, been told the story, I find little cause for instant replayability. It's like reading a good book knowning that one day you will pick it up and have a second look. For this point alone, the price at time of writing (£15.00) can be seen as a little steep for a 2-5 hour experience, but any cut in a steam sale should be an instant snap if you are slightly interested. Be willingly immersed and you will enjoy your time in the house of Gone Home.

A final thing, while Gone Home has rightly been applauded and awarded since release as a watermark for indie gaming with a storytelling soul, there are many other great small-scale devs left in the shadows of its glaring hype. If this experience sounds  like your thing, make sure you scour the Steam indie section and greenlights for similar projects with similar narrative heart and soul. To the Moon, Kentucky Route Zero, Dear Esther, Home, Trauma etc etc...The best stories all deserve to be told.

Gone Home was a controversial release when it first arrived. For some, it was the atmospheric story driven first person adventure they were waiting for; for others it was a disappointment, offering less than anticipated, concentrating on the image of things unseen rather than right in front of you.
For me, I feel I fell somewhere in between. I expected a ghost story, to be honest, but what I got was far more surprising. The relationships of the characters the game creates for you to envision, as well as to interact with through their notes, letters and thoughts scrawled in journals, is not just a step forward for the medium of games as an artistic expression, but it also lets us evaluate the significance of how small the littlest of objects can be, yet still tell us so much. It reminds me of the thoughts I've had about someone close passing away, how the most fleeting things, a gift they sent for Christmas a long time ago meaning so much more than what it is on the surface.
You get to know these characters, and while the game is not long, I do not see that as a weakness, and I see it instead as a means for the developers to avoid the oversaturation of their ideas, the same way a film would have you fill in the blanks and only tell you a piece of the greater puzzle. Forming your own convictions for the characters, feeling what you feel, is what makes this game remarkable.
I've spoken with Steve Gaynor in email before and he is a very polite, creative individual, so I would highly recommend supporting Fullbright with this game and the future of their games to come. They are going to do great things as a studio and I think with Gone Home they have invented a template that will give players many amazing experiences to come.

Gone Home is a sweet, short and a simple game. I enjoy the slice of life genre across many mediums, but it is rare to find that genre in a videogame. The motifs of punk rock, military, travel, pirates, and family were not only familiar to me, but also made me invested in the story.
It's a first person game, where you play as the character Kaitlin Greenbriar who has returned home after travelling a year abroad, finding her family missing. In her absence, her family has moved to a large mansion that presumably Kaitlin has never seen before. You snoop through your family's belongings to get to the bottom of the mystery.  The game takes place on a dark and stormy night, which furthered my amusement because the evening I played was during an extremely loud thunderstorm with no internet connection (that last bit was the scariest part!).
To those saying it is not a  game; a game is any amusement or pastime, which Gone Home certainly is. However, it is  nowhere near as epic as Mass Effect or as funny as Team Fortress, and I could see for people who view videogames as a genre rather than a medium for story telling would be disappointed. This game is for the patient (I got frustrated during some lulls), and those who like simple slice-of-life mysteries.
For a game I finished in roughly 5 hours, the full price seems a bit steep. Luckily I bought it on sale for $5. Do the same and you will be glad.

Gone Home is a sweet, short and a simple game. I enjoy the slice of life genre across many mediums, but it is rare to find that genre in a videogame. The motifs of punk rock, military, travel, pirates, and family were not only familiar to me, but also made me invested in the story.
It's a first person game, where you play as the character Kaitlin Greenbriar who has returned home after travelling a year abroad, finding her family missing. In her absence, her family has moved to a large mansion that presumably Kaitlin has never seen before. You snoop through your family's belongings to get to the bottom of the mystery.  The game takes place on a dark and stormy night, which furthered my amusement because the evening I played was during an extremely loud thunderstorm with no internet connection (that last bit was the scariest part!).
To those saying it is not a  game; a game is any amusement or pastime, which Gone Home certainly is. However, it is  nowhere near as epic as Mass Effect or as funny as Team Fortress, and I could see for people who view videogames as a genre rather than a medium for story telling would be disappointed. This game is for the patient (I got frustrated during some lulls), and those who like simple slice-of-life mysteries.
For a game I finished in roughly 5 hours, the full price seems a bit steep. Luckily I bought it on sale for $5. Do the same and you will be glad.

I first came across Verdun a couple of years ago after I saw people talking about it on TWcentre. Back then it was still in early beta and was not very impressed simply because of how primitive the game was. However a couple months ago I saw it and bought it on one of the steam sales and decided to give it another try.
Pro's:
-Frontlines (the main game mode) is a fun and exciting game mode, it is also particularly addictive. Pushing the enemy back and staving off enemy counter-attacks is often a thrilling experience and the half hour time limit often disappears very quickly.
-The Maps are beautifully crafted and you can tell that the developers have taken a great deal of time in making sure that these maps are both immersive and authentic as well as functional. The trenches are also particularly well detailed. The selection of maps also offer interesting and surprisingly different views into the First world war on the western front. From the lush Vosges and Aisne, to the Muddy, grimey and blasted landscapes of Flanders and Artois. The Maps themselves are probably this games strongest point.
-Aesthetically the game looks great and will definitely not age any time soon.
-Gunplay is satisfying and classes are well balanced.
-Different squad types offer interesting and varying playstyles.
-Developers interact with the community constantly and roll out very regular updates
-The sound design is also very well done. Guns sound meaty, explosions and the general ambience are very immersive.
-Realistic and Hardcore Gameplay.
Cons:
-Feels clunky at times.
-Player limit of 32 feels a little on the small side.
-This game requires a surprising amount of teamwork for your team to be successful and I feel the game doesn't really emphasise this enough.
-Doesn't quite have the polish of other shooters in this genre.
-Map rotation is confusing and seemingly random.
-Squads currently lack much depth in the progression system. In other words there isn't much reward for slogging away and working your levels on a particular squad.
Verdun also has a particularly steep learning curve. You will die. A lot. While this is neither a pro nor a con, it is certainly worth mentioning. People who have experience in FPS games like Red Orchestra and Insurgency however will fit into Verdun very quickly. Persevere with it, and you will learn.
Overall, I am blown away at how far Verdun has come and I throughouly reccomend this game to anybody who is interested in their hardcore FPS games. Verdun does a fantastic job of exploring what is a horribly overlooked time period in the game industry. I look forward to seeing more from this game.

A lot of reviews about this game are conflicted, rightly so. This review will be as neutral as possible, and in my honest opinion after playing the game and reading many reviews, I feel like this game is worth playing (for $5 and under).
First of all, the story is very short. The game can easily be accomplished under an hour if you have experience with games of this genre (Dear Esther, Myst Series) and less than 5 minutes if you have a guide. However, the short story is compensated by how real and deep the story is which is enhanced by the fantastic voice acting and Stereo sound. This game is a coming of age story that will give you shivers in how real and relatable the story is. Some reviews comment on how the game makes you feel like you are solving a murder mystery or the house is haunted with certain hints (red hair dye in the bathroom, ghost games in the closet, satanic ritual pentagrams etc.) yet these are all explained by the story, the very real story. If you expect horror and mystery, this game isn't Sherlock Holmes, nor Amnesia. Ultimately this game will entertain those who love the point and click genre, as it is a very simple Dear Esther and has a similar feel to the newer Mysts, yet the game is universal in how understandable the story is, even if the game is shorter than I would like it to be

The game is addicting. At first. Why do I suggest you not get it then you ask? Community interaction/mechanics reasons.
The PVE is good enough, but the game has many blatant problems when it comes to the other half embedded within the PVE experience, PVP. For example, you can invade someone with two or three other players helping them, kill all the extra players except the host and then the host pulls out his ethernet cord to save his humanity. He loses nothing because the punishing mechanic meant to stop that doesn't work. It's supposed to stop them from summoning people when they do that, but there's an item you get to cancel that effect called the bone of order. The bone of order comes back every day, so people can pull their plugs out or alt+f4 all day every day. They stand to gain a free human effigy if their phantoms kill you, an item that makes you human and thus able to summon phantoms, while you lose an orb for being disconnected when it doesn't go their way.  They lose nothing, you lose something. On top of that, the orb you just lost needs to be farmed back or bought for 10k souls each on NG+. I've been DCed from host when I was winning more times than I can count on all of my hands and feet.
Then there's the cheaters. Not as common as DS1 was, I'll admit. But they're still around. The game needs to have servers instead of P2P connections because this community can't be trusted to not do the worst of the worst to itself. Only buy this game if you plan on playing completely offline. The mechanics just aren't up to par when it comes to player interaction. This game comes across as though the B team at FromSoft really hated invaders and put every mechanic in the game against them.

Minor update for the Steam Awards 2017:
Dark Souls 2 is my favorite Souls game out of the 3 because it tried to be different. Lots of imperfections, sure, but the gameplay is very good.
BANDAI NAMCO Entertainment, and FromSoftware, Inc. is charging $20 for the DirectX 11 upgrade with changes like enemy placements, reworked online experience, tweaked item placements, tweaked areas, improved graphics, two new weapons, and an armor set. Is it worth spending $20 for a very simple patch?
No.
The graphics are tweaked and some areas look good now, especially Shrine of Amana, but the overall improvements are barely noticeable. The lighting patch was lazy — you still see pre-baked lighting, no dynamic shadows when you light up majority of the scones, your shadow is not present in some of the bonfire locations, you cast no shadow when you're near big light sources, some rooms are well-lit despite having no light sources, etc. The dark areas are indeed dark, and like Dark Souls 1, your character glows. It feels so disconnected when your character glows in the dark, but casts shadows on their body when you light a torch. Again, lazy job and they asked 20 dollars for this definitive edition.
The difficulty is somewhat a bit harder. After reaching the Lost Sinner, I only died five times, two of which were environmental deaths (I forgot the default jump was clicking the right stick). The new enemy placements range from good, great to what the hell. Forest of the Giants has tons of undead foot soldiers and they will gank you if you're being an impatient fool. You can still cheese some of them with arrows and some will not aggro if you provoke an enemy near them, so the bow and arrow tactic still work. There are some areas that are outright sadistic, but manageable like Dragon Sanctuary. Aggro one guy, you'll aggro all eight/ten of them at once. I think the part where FromSoftware ran out of ideas is Drangleic Castle because you got a horse and assorted enemies that are out of place.
Despite them claiming Scholar of the First Sin is more difficult, it's very easy to new players due to more summoning per session and a ton of NPC phantoms during tough situations. This is also a bad thing because the NPCs made certain boss fights very easy. You can summon Pate for the Last Giant boss battle and you can summon an NPC with dual greatshields and Havel gear. The Lost Giant didn't stand a chance.
The new NPC summons are great, but they're inconsistent. The new ones have better AI (they give you clues, they can heal, dodge properly, etc.), but the old ones, especially Bernhart and Lucatiel are dumb as before. The new Forlorn invader was disappointing because his AI is simple and dull. He can dodge, parry and back stab, but he lacked that certain charm that made the DLC NPCs great. Maldron was a prick, Aurheim was an a**hole, but they're fun and the encounters were memorable.
Overall the update is okay, but paying 20 dollars for features that can be easily patched like any other game for free is a rip off. For owners of the original Dark Souls 2, I recommend you wait until the patch is around 5-7 dollars, and you better migrate as soon as it happens because the original will be more and more deserted thanks to FromSoftware splitting the user base. New players will love SotFS and it's slightly cheaper than the original.

Most of us can recall the experience of stepping foot in a friend’s house for the first time. The first visit is often an overload on the senses but after a few minutes you refocus and start to notice things: smells, furniture, books, movies, hanging pictures (and my God, all the cool stuff they have that you don’t). With all these items you start to piece together a picture that tells the story of the people who live in that house.

“Gone Home”, is a first person exploration game created by a small team of developers who formerly worked on the DLC for BioShock 2, and the game replicates the feeling of piecing together the story of a house’s inhabitants through their possessions. In the game you’re put in the shoes of Kaitlin Greenbriar who has returned home from a trip to Europe. On arriving, Kaitlin finds the house empty and it’s up to you to figure out why.
Exploring the house at the beginning reminded me of the first time I explored the infamous mansion from the original Resident Evil. But the sprawling house in “Gone Home” only shares the mansion’s spooky and ominous atmosphere (and locked areas). There are no zombie dogs waiting to jump at you through the window, or shambling undead, and you won’t find any weapons or ammo. This minimalist approach however manages to make things slightly creepier and more immersive.

As you explore you’ll feel like you’re on the set of a David Lynch film. From the pouring rain striking the windows, to the sudden flicker of lightning, the house is drenched in atmosphere. The minute attention to detail shows that a great deal of love went into designing the game and examples that show this are scattered throughout the game. From lighting illuminating a postcard in real time, to a record player that lets you listen to a whole album, the attention to detail is striking.
Speaking of attention to detail, the game could very much be considered the forerunner of a new genre. The house you explore is much like a time capsule of the early 90s-- hell, you could even call it a virtual museum. Gone Home takes place in the 1994, and the developers put all sorts of things into the game that were popular at the time. Throughout the house you’ll find playable mix tapes featuring real life riot girl bands, magazines, books, posters, even Super Nintendo video game cartridges. In one room I even found a shelf lined up with VHS tape recordings of the X-Files, all which gave a sense of real lived-in house.
As you explore further you’ll also find items that belong to Kaitlin’s younger sister Samantha, a high school senior. Samantha is central to Gone Home’s plot, and finding her objects will trigger short monologues narrated by Samantha, similar to the monologues encountered in the very similar first person exploration game Dear Eshter. But while Dear Esther’s monologues never fully painted a concrete story, and left a great deal open to interpretation, Gone Home delivers a concrete narrative, albeit in pieces you must put together yourself. I don’t want to give too much away but I will say it’s a beautiful and haunting story that left me genuinely moved.
The game’s principal design is based on paced exploration. You won’t find a run button to move faster which may annoy impatient gamers, but the game is so immersive and pulls you in with such force that you won’t mind playing by its rules. Clocking in at about 4 hours, Gone Home isn't a long game, and once you've beaten it there really isn't much incentive to go replay it. But what it lacks in quantity it makes up for in quality, offering an unparalleled level of immersion. Those who play it will be rewarded with a unique and immersive story-driven experience that few games offer.

First thing to get out of the way, this is much less a game than a sort of passively-interactive story experience. That's a hard sell already since it's so easy to fall into the trap of pretense that confuses itself for depth, and there are few examples within the genre that work that well. Dear Esther is similarly set up, and likewise beloved by critics to the point of impossible standards for the average player to meet, and while this game adds more interactivity and active exploration of the environment, it still falls through some similar pitfalls.
Without any puzzles to solve or zombies to punch, the story itself becomes the entire thing then, and frankly it's not all that compelling. I ended up getting more wrapped up in the player character's post cards, the stories of the family's past, the father's book deal and the mother's co-worker, than I did in the sister's difficulties with love. It says something remarkable about the game's authors that the background stories are fresh, curious, and fascinating, while the primary narrative tastes like a re-heated leftover that doesn't really do anything new with the genre of "I'm 18 and found my soul-mate."
While the subject matter of teenage romance has been retread numerous times already, the game's main problem here is the pacing and setting actively interfering with the story. At times where keeping track of the order of events becomes necessary, it got difficult to keep tracking of life events for the family, and I had forgotten what the date was that I, the player, was meant to be exploring the house, until finding a calender in the locked off kitchen about 90 minutes into the story. Further, the atmosphere of the game, a big, creaky, un-lit house in a thunderstorm, alongside the frequent mentions of a past tragedy and possible hauntings, exploring long disused basements and the "secret in the attic" end up putting you in a mindset where you're anticipating something quasi-horror-tragedy-ish the game never had any intent to provide. The result is a story that builds up to a "everything coming together" climax, and that ends with me asking "...what, is that it?"
And yet, at the end of the day, I still appreciated what Gone Home is trying to do, and the moments when it works to bring me deeper into subtler stories that inform the background white noise of the narrative, and still manages to immerse you in the lives of this family, even though the focal story, while not exactly bad, is much less than captivating. I certainly wouldn't say it's worth $20, but if you can get it on a good discount (as low as $3 during the summer sale) it's definitely worth your time, and arguably, for all it's flaws, one of the best examples so far of interactive environmental storytelling.
If you want to play a simple shooter game, but that's also fun and entertaining, this is definitely the game I would recommend.
