Gone Home is a story driven exploration game that lives up to its description. Returning to an abandoned house after a trip to Europe, the protagonist will set out to explore both the house and the secrets hidden more or less thoroughly within its walls. The game design is atmospheric, and will draw those players willing to go slow and explore in without a doubt. Whereas it is possible to interact with a great variety of objects, it is for the most part not necessary to do so -- there are (with a few exceptions) no puzzles to be solved, no objects to combine, and very few secrets to discover on the map or within the gaming world itself. The exploration of the house is, therefore, heavily depending on gathering the puzzle pieces of the story centering almost exclusively on the protagonist's younger sister, Sam.
For a game that depends so heavily on relating a story, however, I find the narrative of Gone Home to be disappointing. While Sam's story is narrated in a charming way and interspersed with items, notes and similar paraphernelia that will send teenagers of the 1990s down a trip on memory lane, the narrative itself is neither shocking nor spectacular. While I would not subscribe to the ubiquitous criticism that Gone Home is a dream come true for only militant, feminist lesbians, I perceive the main storyline as slightly cliché and lacking in depth (particularly for a game that relies heavily on the narrative as a propelling force). Furthermore, the narrative feels incomplete: there are suggested sub-plots which are never explored and, towards the ending of the game, entirely abandoned in favour of Sam's narrative. The game's ending is predicatable, and only answers questions tied to Sam's disappearance while the overarching question of why the protagonist is returning to an empty house remains unanswered. This is not to say that the narrative of Gone Home is not enjoyable -- it is an emotional, intimately related story that will appeal to those who enjoy coming-to-age stories. It is, however, not a spectacular or particularly innovative narrative that will stay within the memory of the player for a lengthy period of time.
While Gone Home is a pleasant passtime, the game itself is short even if the player is willing to take their time exploring the house. I looked into every nook and cranny I could find and finished the game in under 2 hours. Furthermore, the game has little to no replay value. As soon as the story is complete (or rather: as it becomes clear that some strands of the plot will remain untied), there is no more incentive to play the game. Had I gotten the game for its full price, I would feel cheated. It was, however, well worth the roughly 3 Euro I spent -- a ticket to movies, which would keep me entertained for about the same amount of time, would be more expensive.
If you are a player who enjoys slowly exploring the gaming environment, or one who likes to actively unravel a story, this game might be for you -- if you are a gamer who likes their games with a good dose of action, give this one a pass. In general, I would recommend giving the game a shot at a discounted price -- it will keep you intrigued if you allow yourself to get immersed within the world of Gone Home.

My first review (and only because the game so kindly asked me too) do please be kind,
I've been playing Verdun since the Beta was a new release and free on Steam, when there was only two squads total to pick from. Verdun has come a long way since then and it pleases me to see that they will go further with more weapons, squads, and maps.
Verdun is not a twitch shooter and is not a run and gun game. It is a game where keeping crouched in a trench and prone out in nomansland is not only recomended but neccesary to advance more then 10 yards. Verdun is a very unforgiving game and it will punish new players until they learn that this is a different sort of FPS. I see a lot of negative in game comments complaining of missing a target or picked off by an unseen sharpshooter or failed mass charges and spamed arty barrages. All of which I say man up and get over it. Its World War 1 and nothing more and certainly nothing less. Hour long games can easily end in stalemates instead of clear victories.
Communication and teamwork are vital to gaining ground and a awesome K/D isn't important to winning a match (unless you play on attrition) Verdun is brutal and holds nothing back, its unforgivingly hard and often seems unfair, but again that was the 1st World War where a Division sized force would advance approximetly 10 yards over the course of six months. Everything from the Phosgene and Chlorine gas attacks to relentless arty strikes can make or break a victory.
It will kick your♥♥♥♥♥one match...and make you feel like a bad♥♥♥♥♥war hero the next. A skilled Lewis Machine Gunner can shatter a coordinated German attack until a ever watchful sniper can draw a bead, a Canadian Raider armed with nothing but a few grenades and a club can infiltrate a trench and blugeon a German NCO calling in artillery to death. The line between killing and being killed is very fine. It forces you to play creatively but carefully too and it can easily make you realize the futility and hopelessness of everything about it.
It is a hard game...and that's why I love it.
Hope this review helps.

Gone Home is a two to three hour game that has you returning from an overseas trip. As you navigate the late 80's / early 90's scape, you find that something has happened while you were away. Through exploring your suburban home, you find notes left by your sister as she reflects upon her rather typical teenage life. And that is the premise of Gone Home in a nutshell.
The reason I do not recommend this game is because I found the story to be rather cliche, the gameplay terribly basic, and not at all challenging. It would be one thing if there was something interesting to discover, but ultimately I cannot take Gone Home seriously, nor will I herald it as a unique and inspiring experience. I won't spoil anything, but the ending is completely predictable, and for me personally, not really that enjoyable. Because the game focuses on a single narrative with little depth, you will only be playing through Gone Home once. Perhaps, eventually you may feel the urge to return to see if you missed something, but chances are you won't bother.
As a child of the 90's, I understand the nostalgia of record players, cassette tapes, and life without decent internet. However, that hardly makes Gone Home a more fulfilling experience. No doubt the game is well polished in terms of graphics and design--the home seems real enough, and the detail on the objects is fantastic. But is it worth the price? Absolutely not.
I will end this review with a grain of salt. I am somewhat bitter about paying a full $20 for a game I was rather excited for. If this game is on sale, maybe it'll be worth it for you. This game has gotten many rave reviews, and I have read some of them, and disagree entirely with their points. This game may invoke a sense of nostalgia, but maybe you should visit an antique shop, or your attic instead?

For some reason this game doesn't know what it is. It could be very good but there are many issues that I feel like are a direct result of the developers not knowing what exactly they want this game to be. I will go over all of them in detail in this review.
First and formost, dinosaurs. They are hard to control and can one-hit all human characters while their hitboxes are so small and they move so fast that anyone who finds themselves on the allied team, as you most often will, is not going to have a good time taking down their enemies.
Secondly, the movement in this game is very clunky and heavy as are the weapons, to a fault. It's not "different gameplay", it's bad gameplay. It feels like Quake but slower and heavier.

Honestly, I cannot reccommend this game even at the price of $2.49. If you want a dinosaur game go play Orion: Dino Horde, but be sure that you can run it because it's not well optimized. Also remember that it goes down to 99 cents during almost every sale.

If you haven't played the original release of Dark Souls II, then my recommendation is a BIG RECOMMENDED. If you have played the original and are thinking about buying this re-release then you can read on.
SPOILERS AHEAD!
The good:
- The lighting in this game is better because now you actually need torches to be able to see in some dark areas (The Gutter).
- Invading and Co-Op NPCs are much better and feel more alive. Hell, they're even mocking you if they manage to kill you and they also have other surprises ready for you…
- Better enemy placement: In some areas the enemy placement makes more sense lore wise and gameplay wise.

The bad:
- Some areas have become optional or even meaningless. Exp: Before you had to kill the Gargoyles to get the key to light the fires in the Lost Sinner boss room. Now you conveniently find the key on your way to the Lost Sinner. Where I have to ask myself: Why do we even take the hassle now to kill them? There is no real rewards for them anymore. They even made Dragons Aerie optional, why?
- Better graphics are not that noticeable for the most part and where they could have improved the graphics by simply improving the details (or even adding any details at all! I'm looking at you, Forest of Fallen Giants King's Door courtyard) they didn't.
- Enemy placement (again): What is a good point for Dark Souls II: SotFS is also a negative point. In some areas the new enemy placement is ridiculous! To a point where it is plain annoying and not really harder. I'm looking at you Heide's Tower of Flames.
- Arbitrary road blocks: Now you have petrified statues everywhere and quite often they don't even make any sense from a lore perspective.
The game is still awesome in it's own right but I simply think in comparison to the original a downgrade. Still I will manly play this version now as it will probably be the reference point for Dark Souls II discussions in the future….

Good god where to begin.. this game, has the most epic, most intense atmosphere i have ever witnessed. Playing this game, you're scared, all the time. One shot is all it takes for the most part, with a few small exceptions where you might take one and live to tell about it. Sitting in the trenches, you peek your head over to see what goes on, only to see a seemingly empty no-mans-land. There is no hud, there are no enemy markers, you use your good ol' mark one eyeballs. Then, as you have a false sense of security, you start aiming around to try and spot something and all of a sudden your worst nightmare comes true, a gas attack. The trenches are filled, you don't see♥♥♥♥♥♥ literally maybe a meter infront of you, unable to identify friend from foe, it's a mess. Some of the gas might move a little, and then there it is.. a bunch of huns, gasmasks on, charging like the devil out of the gas and into the trenches screaming god knows what at you whilst baraging you with accurate rifle fire. The suppression system makes itself known by then, the screen goes bleak, your aim is off, and your character is frightened and unable to properly fight till the effects wear off. Cowering away and turning around, even more of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s keep going at you, not stopping their charge and sprinting with all they have, shooting and stabbing whatever they find. Every single kill is so worth it, it really gives a sense of satisfaction. This, is the darksouls of the shooters. You wil die. Over and over again. But then once you catch on, you start returning the favor, learning to lead properly as it is VERY tricky at the start to do so. Couple of hours later, you yourself wil be the one instilling fear into the enemy as you charge the trenches, jumping ontop of players and stabbing/shooting them with all you have, maybe lob a grenade or two if you have them. This game is great, the graphics are wonderfull, not over the top but pleasing to the eyes. The sounds make you think you are there, the artillery blowing everything to hell around you, bullets whizzing over your head and into the mud surrounding you, comrades screaming their warcries which honestly for me only inspire me to attack even harder. The weapons handle great, each and every one of them have their own 'manual' so to speak, they really are very different in how they handle, how they aim, reload, clip size. Teamwork is almost always present, there's always a bunch of chaps in the team that direct others and most respond. For example the left side of the trench gets breached, they wil direct the forces in that direction, or when they spot a large group charging like mad they'll notify the team and again most can and wil respond. This game is anti-noob at it's purest, it discourages the CoD players and such, leaving only players willing to be a part of something greater, there's very few solo players as those get rekt, hard. And the balancing, good god it is beautifull. Nothing is OP, though admittedly the german MP18 does get close to being it, luckily there's one or two of them being used at most and i am sure this wil get nerfed sometime as it does have a rather incredible range for a machine pistol. The devs are active and responcive, they DO listen to the players, take suggestions into account and work out the best way to use them.
TL;DR, GET THE GAME ALLREADY, it's like the baby made when darksouls and arma mated, and NO P2W AT ALL, it simply does NOT exist in the game.

Scholar of the First Sin is essentially Dark Souls 2 if you gave the game back to the dev team a year later and let them tweak all the little things that bugged them and a large portion of the community initially without giving them enough budget to really rework them. While there are some interesting changes in the way certain areas react to your presence there may not be enough new content to justify buying it if you've previously finished DS2 and all it's DLC. For players who missed DS2 though this is an excellent place to jump in...if you’re okay with SotFS being a tad more sadistic than DS2 already was.
While much has been made of the graphical upgrades for next-gen consoles the DX11 version here on Steam looks very similar to last years original release. Some textures have been improved and upscaled but the most notable change comes in the lighting and post-processing effects. They certainly are pretty and, in the odd moment when I wasn't about to be disemboweled by a monstrous horror from beyond, I quite enjoyed taking in the scenery. Certainly the "Gorgeous View" message will be dropped a few times throughout each playthrough. One significant visual change that affects gameplay though is that the darkened areas of DS2 have been made...well...darker. This means that using a torch in certain areas has moved from being “a good idea if you have an extra pair of hands on standby” to being all but a necessity for clearing certain areas. Whether that's good or bad will come down to your personal preference and for new players will likely make the torch feel more like an integrated part of the game than an optional add-on.
The most notable change however is the complete rebalance of enemy and item placements from the original DS2. If you're a newcomer to Dark Souls 2 this next section will essentially be white-noise. For newcomers the only relevant thing to say about the rebalance will be that Scholar of the First Sin is, arguably, harder than the original Dark Souls 2 and for a series that's built a reputation on being ball bustingly difficult you might want to take that as a warning.
For the seasoned veterans of DS2 however...the changes will come off as something of a mixed bag. Some areas such as Heide's Tower of Flame have placements that make a great deal more sense in terms of lore than they used too, for example the previously rare and unique Heide Knights that were found sitting scattered around Drangleic now account for about half of the population of Heide's Tower. So while the old stone knights remain they are now supplemented by proper Heide Knights whose attitude will change depending on your actions within the area.
On the other hand some of the changes in placement and balance feel a bit more...odd, like From Software wants us to pay more attention to certain areas. A good example of this would be the Lost Bastille which could previously be accessed from two different points via the Forest of Fallen Giants or Dead Man's Wharf. This played into the Lost Bastille being a fairly non-linear area as keys from one side were required to gain access to bits of the other and vice versa. Now however the entrance to the Ruin Sentinels boss, and thus the main body of the area, has been arbitrarily walled off by requiring a Fragrant Branch of Yore. Given that you don't encounter one of these normally for quite a while into the game this means that you're essentially forced to backtrack and take the path through Dead Man's Wharf.
In all the changes are significant, no doubt there, however they sine wave between sensible changes, irritating diversions and slightly sadistic ambushes in previously safe areas. I'd say overall this makes the game slightly harder as, even if you memorise all the new enemy locations, there seems to just be generally more hollows between you and becoming a true monarch.
The main draw to SotFS for veteran DS2 players however will be that all of the DLC packages were included in this re-release and many of the enemies from those areas now appear around Drangleic proper. For fans of the original DS2 that may have missed the DLC this gives a substantial new chunk of content to digest. So take this recommendation with a grain of salt as your mileage will vary depending on how much of the original DS2 you played.

Yeah, it's a short game, but hell, I spend more than its full price when I go to see a movie which lasts about the same amount of time and which I garner the same amount of entertainment out of.
Look, if you're a homphobic neckbeard who haunts chan boards, or a teenage Call of Duty player, this game isn't for you. But for some of us, it's a wonderful piece of art and nostalgia. For fans of games like Dear Esther or The Longest Journey, that wrap you up in the story of the inhabitants of their worlds and leave you wanting more when they're over , its a must buy.

There are no enemys in this game.  No one is a bad guy, no one is a good guy.  You are not a noble knight, nor are you a badass anti-hero.  This game barely tells you who the character you are playing is outside of name.  There is no shooting, no platforming, no puzzles.  What this game does have, is a story, an enviroment, and a soundtrack, which in my opinion is everything it could ever need.
You experience this game through the eyes of Katie, a 20 year old returning home to her family from a year-long European trip.  Strangly however, she finds that no one is home. Not her mom, dad, or sister Sarah has left any obvious signs of where they have went. As you move through the house, you find notes, letters, pictures, books, folders, binders, and practically anything else, that all slowly answers questions about your family, while raising other ones.
I finished this game in a bit less then 3 hours, and that seems to be the about of time you can expect as well. Its a fantastic game to sit down with and enjoy in one continuous session. However there isn't all that much replayability if you play the game throughly on the first playthrough.
Overall, this is a fantastic game, that I would recommend to anyone looking for a story and exploration driven experience, and is not looking for a high level of action, or over the top adventure.  This is the most natural game I've ever played, and truly feels realistic and human in a way few other games ever manage to achieve.

If you have not played the Dark Souls II "main game" (campaign) at least once, then consider this a "Recommended" review. This review is mostly for people who know Souls games and are at least mildly interested in PvP.
Note: I bought Dark Souls II on its Spring 2014 release and have over 600 hours combined in Dark Souls II and SotFS edition. This review is not just a single's day rage & rant—it is the culmination of systematic and consistent rage & rant. I both love AND hate this game.
If you want to PvE, Dark Souls I is more fun (imo, mostly because the campaign feels more like an adventure and less like a checklist).
If you want to PvP, Dark Souls II has better PvP but still remains highly flawed. Expect lots of running, healing, ganking. You can try the arenas or the Dragon Remnants covenant, but this still doesn't fix the fact that the Souls series combat mechanics are ill-suited for PvP. Pretty much any MMO I've ever played seems to understand that massive breadth in content requires specific fine-tuning of the content for PvP because the whole premise of fighting someone else who is also making active choices under opacity makes PvP completely different from PvE.
Granted, some patches have fixed the occasional glaring error or two, like the brain-dead Tanimura Rush (fittingly named after the combat designer), overpowered cheese builds (dual Avelyns early on, Helixadon, Bat Staff, etc.), poorly balanced 1-shot backstabs, healing items in arenas, etc. but overall they dodge around the primary issues arising from the fact that THERE IS NO PUNISHMENT for players who intelligently utilize defensive mechanics like summoning multiple phantoms, dodging correctly, healing at the correct times, etc. This skill-ignorant reward/punishment mechanisms would not be bad IF the game had proper PvP settings to counteract these issues (even the arenas are far too big and reward super defensive gameplay—the only truly small one, the Red arena's bridge, has the fall death gimmick). But the poorly implemented (although original) design choice to attempt to mostly integrate PvP into PvE prevents Souls PvP from being anything more than a gimmicky bauble to spice the whole package.
The straw that breaks the camel's back is the long, random queues. Unless you are playing with a friend, you don't get to choose who to play with (most importantly, you can't ban/communally downvote unpopular players). There's no rooms/hosting systems like pretty much any game with true PvP. The "fun" factor of PvP is too infrequent and too dependent upon enemies not playing the "run, dodge & heal" game all day. Every 2-3 hours of PvP, I get maybe <25% of my matches being any fun whatsoever.
The depressing part is that many fixes can easily be conceived. Take the Bell Tower for example: by removing most of the monsters and placing phantoms and invaders in queue and summoning them in at the same time to maintain 1v1/2v2/3v3 ratios (and, say, booting leftover phantoms after each wave of up to three invaders is defeated) the Bell Tower goes from "the place which 90% of players only go through once and the other 10% (try to) enjoy PvPing in" to "that place for team PvP." Also, healing might need to be disabled—especially because of spots like the floating platform above the stairs or using the railing to prevent backstabs/long combos. These changes are minor, but would make a marginal area much more fun (don't even get me started on the Rat Covenant).
Unfortunately, as I said before, Dark Souls II PvP is mostly a gimmicky bauble. Even changing PvP area mechanics won't fix the skill-ignorant defensive favoritism in PvP.

A long time ago, when Call of Duty 2 was all the rage, I remember getting into a discussion about why there were so many World War 2 games but no World War 1 games. “It would just be the same,” was the general consensus, “but with worse guns.” For a while I accepted that analysis, but the argument overlooks a critical difference which didn’t occur to me until years later: trench warfare.
Okay, so, a disclaimer here: I am a huge WW1 buff. I am thoroughly obsessed with “The Great War”. So right off the bat Verdun earns a special place in my heart. Even though I generally don’t play multiplayer shooters, I love Verdun because of what it accomplishes. The game transports you right into the bleak hellscape of the western front.
Almost everything about this game is downright perfect. From the weapons to the classes to the back and forth nature of trench warfare, where the advantage always lies with the defender, the game is as wonderful as can be. There is nothing like running across no man’s land, watching your teammates be mowed down by machine gun fire, trying to make it into that crater for cover. Nor is there anything like the adrenaline rush of standing knee-deep in filthy water in a godforsaken trench, seeing frantic movement in the distance – the rifleman to the left of you falls, your commander calls in a mortar shot, and suddenly the entire trench is filled with posion gas. You have to struggle to put on your flimsy gas mask, and over the sound of your own labored breathing you can hear them coming.
Verdun is like no other first person shooter I’ve ever played, multiplayer or otherwise. If you are a fan of the bloated genre, you owe it to yourself to pick up this game and experience an entirely new form of warfare. If you’re interested in World War 1, then this is a no brainer.
So come visit the western front, won’t you? The trenches are lovely this time of year.

While this game is certainly not for everyone, it was very very much for me. Game might perhaps be a misnomer in terms of the actual experience, however. It's more an interactive exercise in immersive storytelling. You walk through your family's empty house, gradually picking up clues to what has been going on in your life, and along the way discover where exactly your little sister has run away to through diary entries she has left for you.
Sam's (your sister) narration ties the whole experience together beautifully, as you wander the empty house with the sound of rain ever-present in the background you get a sense of the isolation she must have felt. Her wry, thoughtful commentary on her life rings true for me as an ex-teenage girl myself and the correspondence of hers you find was always delightful and even managed to startle a few laughs from me.
Basically, while I certainly wouldn't recommend this looking for a straightforward mystery game, someone looking for a novel storytelling experience would be in good hands with Gone Home.

I love exploring in games. I was born in the 80s and grew up in the 90s. Honestly, the most interesting thing for me about an apocolypse scenario would be exploring people's houses and seeing the things they left behind. Because of all of that, I was sure this would be the game for me.
The Positives:
Creepy game. The sounds constantly had me turning around to make sure there was nothing behind me
Remembering the 90s tech was pretty fun
Great music
Simple controls
The sister's story is interesting
The Negatives:
The graphics kinda suck, for a realistic game
There's a lot of filler. Repetitive items, and very few things matter at all
If you moved fast you could easily complete the game in an hour - hour and a half
Other than the sister's story, nothing else is really going on
You feel like the story is kind of leading up to something, I found the ending was disappointing.
All in all I think they had a cool concept, but didn't put nearly enough work into it. They could have expanded on the mom and dad's stories. They could have made more items that matter. It could have been replayable, exploring the history of the house and the people who died in it. They give you tastes of interesting stories but you never get to explore them further. It's too bad, could have been a great game.
I honestly wouldn't recommend buying this for more than $2. It's like reading a crappy book, too much filler and the ending isn't worth it. Save your money for something better.

If you are interested in the Great War then you should definitely look into this game.  It is not a run and gun shooter anything like Call of Duty.  It is a gritty, tactical, crawl across the mud into no mans land under fire from the enemy and fighting trench to trench.  You find yourself gaining ground and losing ground fighting up close and personal once you get into the enemy trenches.  If you pop your head up for more than a few seconds an enemy will most certainly snipe you.  Instead use cover to block your body and watch diagonally across no mans land to catch the enemy charging across the fields towards your trenches.  This way you are mostly covered but still have a field of view to catch the enemy.  Commanders spawn the 4 man squad on top of the them and call in mortar strikes, gas, and scouting planes.  MG's go prone and riddle the enemy full of bullets.  Riflemen take accurate shots close and far with the help of scopes for snipers, grenades for grenadiers, and bayonets for the riflemen.
You get to learn all about the terrain and different battles fought in Verdun.  The developers went to great lengths for historical accuracy.  The attack and defend system works well and creates a good structure to simulate a feeling what trench warfare must have been like.  You are not allowed to run randomly around the map when defending, instead you must defend your trench and the land behind it.  This structure keeps the idea of trench warfare in play.
You owe it to yourself to pick this up if you like tactical shooters and WW1 era themes.

-Graphics were greatly improved. Shaders and illumination have grown extremely in quality, while textures also got an increase in quality but without having much of an impact as the new shaders/illumination have.
-If new to Dark Souls 2, this edition has the same price as a new game (and less than the standard 60 USD mark) and comes with all 3 DLC, which many claim, and I agree, are even better than the base game (not to minimize the quality of the base game).
-New audio touches, many of them add to immersion, while being something small, it adds to the whole experience.
-New enemy placement: there has been many changes regarding enemy placement, in some places there are even more (thus effectively making the GAME HARDER), in others the enemies are in different spots, there are even some new variants of enemy (say, a Hollow Royal Soldier two-handing a Estoc). These changes make the game harder at points, while at the same time help veterans get some feeling of fresh-ness.
-Maximum players online increased from 4 to 6 (3 invaders and 2 Phantoms (helpers) + the Host).
-Better Optimization.
-DLC keys used to access the DLC areas were blended into gameplay, being found as one plays instead of being given right away to the player once he starts playing. This makes the transition and access to the DLCs more natural and intuitive.
-Better AI takes smarter decisions when it comes to combat and pathfinding, this paired with the fact that at many times you will be outnumbered by enemies (and take into account this version adds even more enemies) makes the game effectively harder, but not unfair.
Overall, I consider this version to be better than the original Dark Souls 2, while the graphic improvements may not be that astonishing, the new illumination its beautiful enough to notice, while the textures improvements are more discrete. A recommended buy for newcomers into the series and a must-buy for fans of the Souls games for it has enough of a fresh feel.
Note: the patch that original versions of the game (PC's DirectX 9, PS3 and Xbox 360 editions) doesn't contain all the things this edition has. In fact, the most important change that adds to the feel of being fresh, the new enemy placements, are exclusive to this new version, and let me tell you: they are worth it.
DISCLAIMER: I have 150 hours on the original Dark Souls 2 on PC and about the same on Dark Souls: Prepare To Die Edition, but I have close to 10.000 hours on Dark Souls 1 and around 700 hours on Dark Souls II for PS3 (I moved to PC later).

This game was completely worth the $2.99 I spent on it. Heck, I would have spent full price if I had known that the story would have been so gripping and beautiful. Most people would say that this is not a game, and they are too right to a degree they would be correct; the game is more of an absolute masterpiece or literature spread out through a 3D world. The time that I have spent with the game has been amazing in many ways, the ambience of the house is creepy at times, and the way that Sam's voice actor pulled us into the world was unprecedented compared to any recent game. You could feel every pain, every joy, every regret. I hope that more games like this are made in the future, because there are not many story driven games these days (Wolfenstein: the New Order being the most recent). I think that as a follow up, the developer should have a game from the perspective of either one of the parents or Sam herself, though that might be ruined by the fact that the story was so well done in this. For someone looking for a great story done in a relatively short time, you should consider picking tthis up if it is on sale.

Would definitely recommend to any FPS or historical warfare fan.

I just downloaded this game a couple nights ago and it immediately had a feel that Combat Arms had a baby with Call of Duty.
There are some problems with this game. For instance, in PvP the spawn system is horrendous. You can easily spawn camp the enemy team if they get behind, and it will basically drastically force the other team into turtling if you're any good. Another problem is the fact that the PvP maps are so small. Some maps you can literally walk 3 feet, throw a grenade and get a multi-kill, or you can just walk up two more feet and kill someone with your gun.
The game is an arcade shooter, it's super easy, pretty fun, and pretty enjoyable. If you're any good at other FPS (2.0+ KDR in CoD, BF4, CA, CS:GO) you'll basically be the top 2 every game. I think I average about 35 kills per game.
The maps, again, are very readable to where someone will go (they really only have 2-4 paths a person can take to get to the enemy spawn) and it's pretty easy to tell when someone is about to go around the corner.
There are cool novelties in this game, which is the helping vault, crouch shooting and sliding. Sliding is pretty fun and little overpowered for some reason because it's so random when someone does it. Helping vault is a little cheesy when you have like 4 people in a game and one dude is sitting on a wall waiting for someone to help him vault up.
The microtransactions are pretty fair, I guess. I bought $50 worth (I've played this game 12 hours in the 2 days I've had it so I felt obliged to give something) and bought basically the best gear in the game which is the Warlord set. Even though regular people can get the items (The full set is around $40000 in-game dollars) you won't see it often because it's so expensive. The armor is OP as ♥♥♥♥ though. If I don't get damaged for 5 seconds it basically regens all my armor and HP. ??? why?
Then you have the dumbest thing about the game, which is weapon purchasing and repairs. A weapon costs around $40000 in-game cash to buy permanent. So with that money you probably think that you don't have to spend anymore money on it, right? WRONG ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥! You have to repair that♥♥♥♥♥♥every time you play a game. You're basically buying a gun to spend money on it. You don't have to repair the items you rent, and you can rent guns for $7000 in-game cash for 7 days.
Anyways, the game's free so who gives a flying hoot. It's a good time waster and it's fun for the time being. 7/10.

Dino D-Day is a fresh breath in the unfortunately stale age of Call of Duty. Like all games it has it's pro's and cons, but I feel the pros far out way the cons. The community is friendly and the game is simply entertaining. Over all I give the game 7.5/10
The Pros:
The community is friendly.
The game's loading screens let and trailers let you know the game doesn't take itself seriously and the community seems to reflect the "It's just for fun" attitude. Newbie’s are always asking for help and the Vets are off to the rescue with quick replies.
The Dino-factor.
Adding in a handful of random dinosaurs with machine gun attached to their head makes it fun to play other characters for a change instead of the running shotgun or the always camping sniper, although those characters are open if that’s your style.
The game offers a multiple maps and game play options.
This is often taken for granted, “it's an online multiplayer game, of course it is going to have options!” Yes, but these add a certain flavor to each game and game play.
The Cons:
There is no tutorial and the manual is not always helpful.
The game gives you some hints on the loading screens, but more often than not the Newbie’s, like myself, have had to take a break from chowing down on an Allied soldier or shooting dino's to ask for some help.
The maps are often cluttered.
It makes for great fun on some places but other maps just feel like they were thrown together quickly so that there was an extra map. One map even has two towers that allow you to spawn camp rather easily.
The graphics aren't too modern.
This one isn't a large concern of mine, I remember Goldeneye, still have it in my N64 and this is a large step away from the age of Doom. Still, I understand why some people could be put off by the raw graphic.

It's a better game than vanilla Dark Souls 2, but now, more than ever, you need friends to play with, or at least NPC summon to combat the tedium.  I don't want to be a part of that crowd that gripe about artificial difficulty, but it does get quite tedious from time to time, and I'm lucky to have played through this remake with a friend that turned tedium into sufficient challenge for 2 players.
But for the Souls series virgins out there, buy this game. Maybe buy and play the first one first, not because there are story plots that you would miss out on.  It's because this game is a better one in terms of variety and mechanics, and undoubtedly has the best Player versus Player in all 4 Souls-like games (DS1, DS2, DeS, BB).
To be honest, I'm a bit burnout at this point in my Souls career, and I crave the control that is Soul Level matchmaking in Demon's Souls and Dark Souls 1.  But you will be fine.  Go forth and get beaten to a pulp by the game, git gud, then get beaten to a pulp by the online communities, git gud there too.  Start complaining about Hex and Havels.  Go watch some yami tamashi.  Learning to parry and fight without lockon. And after that 100 awesome, infuriating, ocassionally ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic hours.  May we meet again by the bonfire.

Gone Home is an adventure game similar to classics like Gabriel Knight, Zork: Grand Inquisitor, Monkey Island, or King's Quest.  The player takes a first person perspective to explore a location, examine clues, or carry items from one location to another to figure out some type of mystery.  Despite appearances, this mystery has no science fiction or supernatural elements.  It is a relatively common storyline that deals only with the main character trying to find why she has come home to find her family missing.
Gone Home continues the fine tradition of those classic games in look and style.  The graphics are nice and there is an impressive number of objects that can be manipulated or examined in some way.  Programming is meticulously neat and I found no bugs at all while playing it.  Sound effects are functional and work well within the game.  On all technical aspects, this game passes beautifully.
Plot, characters, and writing are generall well-crafted but there are some rough edges of game play that I found distracting.  One is that often times, a simple real-world solution to an obstacle would be to smash or use other physical force the game does not allow.  For example, the most expedient way to open a locked file cabinent is simply to jimmy it open with a pry bar but the game instead forces you to find the combination.  Another is that running and jumping features would have saved time when moving from one location to another.  Also, there are numerous "red herring" objects that contribute absolutely nothing to advancing you forward towards the conclusion.  Lastly and most importantly, is that I found the ending to be very anti-climatic.  I felt through most of the game that a dramatic twist was just around the corner.  No such thing ever materialized.  It was revealed at the end that the mundane and obvious explanation I had surmised early in the game was indeed the correct one.  I was disappointed to see the end screen show up right after that particular piece of information was plainly stated in a journal entry.    There is a lot more to this story that could have been told.  It would have been a more satisfying closure if I had been able to resolve the issues between the other characters and bring them all together again.
I would love to see the author make more games.  There is definitely a lot of talent here combined with a dedication to quality work.  To borrow a phrase used for one of the character's writing efforts: "You can do better."
ADDENDUM: There is some screenshot evidence and anecdotes that show the developer is banning those who post negative reasons.  Let me be clear: THIS IS NOT COOL.  I was on the fence on whether or not to give this game a thumbs up, because I did like the programming, but the story is a boring and unsatisfying drama.  In light of the development that bad reviews are being silenced, I am changing my recommendation.

A lot of the user reviews bash two things about this game: the story and it's pricetag. While I would agree that $20 is way too much for only about 2 hours of gameplay, I have to very strongly disagree about the story. The story is AMAZING. You play as a girl who has come home after backpacking in Europe to find her house empty, and notes and clues scattered about explaining where your sister has disappeared to. People seem to be in a huff because they were expecting some creepy horror game or something, which is not what this game is meant to be at all. It's a point and click story-heavy game about your sister and her girlfriend. The story was extremely interesting to me and it's one that you rarely hear discussed in video games, which was part of why I loved it (not to mention the awesome 90's riot grrl and pop culture references). My best advice is don't go into this game thinking it's going to be scary or that there's more to the gameplay than just picking things up and reading and looking at stuff. Expect a good, interesting story and leave it at that and you'll walk away satisfied.
Especially now with the summer sale going on and this game being up on flash sale pretty frequently, I strongly suggest buying it. But again, the game only lasts about 2 hours on your first run through, so I probably wouldn't suggest paying the full pricetag.

If you've been eye-balling this game I'd recommend that you pick it up. It's not in your standard faire of ARPGs. This game does not hold your hand and it's a challenge for the sake of the challenge, and I love it.
Combat is almost puzzle-like. You need to learn and understand what each of your moves do and how to best use them. Then you need to learn what your opponets move set is and how to counter, parry, backstab, block, and generally move through their attacks.
This game is difficult in the sense that their is so many skills to master and so much to take in. Nothing is automated so you could potentially play through most of the game before you realize that different types of shields have differing movesets, etc. You could also go multiple playthroughs without fully understanding how your equipment load effects your stamina, rolls, run speed, etc etc. This game encourages trial and error. Whether that means falling off cliffs to see if you can get to a secret area, walking along stretches of wall and tapping your action key looking for secret passages, to figuring out whether poison works on what bosses. There will never be a popup saying go to this area next. It's all on you. Each time you die you also lose all your souls, which is a combination of currency and XP, with a single chance to go back and reclaim it or it'll be lost for good. You'll probably backtrack a lot trying to figure out what's next. The story isn't spoonfed to you. It's found through talking through each NPC's dialog, reading equipment descriptions, and observing the environment & your enemies. If you kill the enemies enough, they respawn everytime you rest to regain health etc, they will eventually stop respwning potentially making an area easier. This allows you to farm for souls and equipment.
There is also a metagame referred to as "fashion souls" among DS players. There is so much gear and equipment to collect, and potentially upgrade, that you can darn well look like whatever you like, using whatever weapons you like. Cosplaying is common.
Then you get PvP/CoOp. Co-op is done through leaving summoning signs or joining covenants that summon you to other players worlds (to aid them against PvP'ers). Co-op is helpful for getting through an area or challenging a boss. PvP is done with summoning signs, joining covenants that summon other people to your world or you to theirs (territory defense style), it's also done with items that allow you invade someone else's world. PvP/Co-op is useful for advancing levels in covenants which provide gear/spells, but it's also bring new dimensions to this game after you put in dozens of hours messing around PvE.
The Souls game all have a New Game+ mechanic. After you beat the game you can restart it with your gear, but everything is more powerful and difficult. DS2 has a mechanic that allows you to NG+ and area after beat a boss. There's a cap on how high it can go (I've never reached it but I've never tried to either), but I've seen people on their Original NG and having one or two areas NG+8. A quick warning, if you NG an area and then beat the game and NG the whole game, that area that has already been NG+ will roll over to the next difficulty (e.g. NG+ overall, but that one NG+3 will roll over to NG+4). Each NG+ will introduce new equipment and enemies (and more enemies).

You can be invaded by people that hack anything from invincibility to superpowers to even having different skins. This causes some major frustration, especially for me. Fromsoft does rebalance gear from time to time.

I think that the primary complaints of this game stem from a few points, which I'd just like to quickly address.
1. Length:Price
I'll be completely honest here by saying that I think the notion of paying $20 for a game with the amount of content of Gone Home is unreasonable. About two to three hours of content for that price is just unfair. WIth that in mind, though, a full sale price of 85% off, around $3, is more than acceptable for what Gone Home provides. The length of the game can completely vary depending upon the player (a true speed run clocking in at under a minute), so if you truly explore everything the game has to offer, the ratio of length to price evens out significantly.
2. Plot Simplicity
I'll be completely honest again. The main narrative that the player follows in Gone Home is a bit subpar. The story follows Kate Greenbriar as she returns home to an abandoned mansion, exploring the house to pick up clues of what occured in her absence. Primary bits of text just follow her sister and her love story that although breaks uniformity in some ways, does it in the shallowest of senses. It gives a resolution is an astounding mix of closure and anticlimax. If that were the only element of story, I would say that Gone Home is a let down, but so much more is delved into. Numerous subplots evolve and progress as more information is discovered about the family. Some of those subplots are much more interesting than the "Main story" and receive enough time to develop as their own entities. In fact, if the love story weren't passed off as the main focus, as Gone Home tries to do, the game would be all the better for it. Despite this short coming, the inclusion of the subplots provides a MAJOR redemption. To judge the entire game based on what's used as the main story is down right unfair.
3. Flase Atmosphere
I'm just going to hit this one quickly, because for the most part, I agree with the complaints. I knew going in that nothing actually scary was going to happen in the game, despite the conflicting environments. To say that the psudo-spooks created by the game leads to a bit of misdirection in the player, that's fair. To say that it ruined the game as a whole is more than a stretch. I've heard the counter arguement that the dread created by the game can lead the player to think the worst occured as a result of the love story, which is fair, but I'm not sure is a full excuse, so I won't use it. In other words, the environment didn't really hurt or improve my experience as it may for others, but either way, saying that it would lead to a polar view shift is ridiculous.
So, in conclusion, is Gone Home deserving of Game of the Year? Not in my book. Is it deserving of the rain of pure scrutiny that it's getting on its Steam page? I don't think so, either. I'm going to be blunt. I haven't reviewed a single game prior to this. I just wanted to give some defense to a game that I think is getting more flak than it deserves. I know that most of those reviews just exist to counter what many would see as undeserved praise, but I can guarentee most of them are played up just to provide contrast to that big ol' 86 Metacritic stamped at the top of this page.  At the end of the day I'm just tossing a single poorly writen positive review in a sea of negativity. Basically, I don't think this is the greatest game I've played by a long shot, but I also spent the last 20 minutes writing this monster about it, so you be the judge. Thank you.

I really loved this game!!
I loved how it managed to maintain a really intense atmosphere; there were times when I was certain there'd be some sort of jump-scare, and every time the lights flickered I freaked out! my heart was pounding right up to the end, certain I'd find something too spooky even as it was clear that the game was coming to an end. To carry that all through the telling of such a powerful (in a non-frightening way) story; that's really amazing. There were also moments where I just found this intense peace as well, which was really great for a wuss like myself. For instance, I noticed that Sam had glow in the dark stars on her ceiling, and I turned off the lights and looked at the glow of the stars and the light through the window- it was a  truely serene moment (there was a noise outside the door immediately afterwards though and I was just like NOPE lights on again please and thank you). The artwork and little details like that in the game really made it for me (I highly recomend looking at all of the nintendo cartidges; totally awesome!). The sub-plots of the parents' lives was very interesting as well, and it was a really cool way of bringing you closer to understanding those characters, while still keeping them as distant, mysterious, faceless figures.
This was a really intense form of story telling, and really it felt completely new, I've never experienced something quite like it. The replay value is interesting as well, I completely see myself going back and playing this again very soon! and there are plenty of little things that I still want to go back and double check/discover. For a closed-world game, it has a very open-world feel.

A single tear flows down my cheek before losing itself to gravity and bursting into a million smaller pieces as it finally hits the ground. Through blurred vision I am watching the white lettering on an otherwise black screen as the melancholic tones of the credit theme flow past me.
I have just played through Gone Home. Scratch that. I have just had the privilege of *experiencing* Gone Home. Common terminology that we associate with videogames seems to fall short, and indeed, do a disservice to the emotional cornucopia that is this work.
It is safe to say that my views on what contitutes 'proper' videogame design, as well as the entire concept of artistic expression have been irrevocably shattered. Gone Home is a transcendental experience. We can finally silence those who would claim that videogames will never be art. This is it. Our Citizen Kane. Our Hamlet.
I look back at myself 80 minutes ago just after I started my journey through this virtual experience and can't help but laugh. How naive I was. I recall thinking "this♥♥♥♥♥♥is gay as hell", "So where are the monsters, this is a horror game right?". The cruel irony of the fact is that those assumptions were eerily accurate. Just not in any way that I had expected.
Gone Home is indeed a horror game, but not in any conventional sense of the word. Our fear does not come from any external factor such as ghosts or demons but from the fact that Gone Home challenges our innermost prejudices and assumptions. It bares our soul to ourselves. It holds up a mirror, forcing us towards introspection. And what we see in that mirror is perhaps the scariest thing we will ever see.
Gone Home casts us into the skin of Katie, a 20-something year old who returns from her journey around the world to her parental home. The house is strangely deserted, but through strategically placed notes and letters, Katie quickly finds out everything that happened during her absence.
Naysayers might point towards the verbosity and lack of variety in the narrative, as well as the contrived way in which the story is presented, but in doing so miss the point entirely. Gone Home is more than a game, so to provide it with proper criticism, we have to free ourselves from the trappings of critical discourse against videogames. We have to judge Gone Home on the intimate, emotional character painting it so delicately crafts that challenges our every notion. Everything else is secondary.

Verdun is the best and most realistic World War 1 shooter in my opinion.
You can play 4 Maps:
Teamdeathmatch
Everyone against Everyone
Wave surviving ( computer ememys)
The Trench war ( the main and best mode)
You can play as a German or the Entente (The French, belgian, canadian, Usa, british) soldier. In this part of the game you play on the West front.
I want to describe you the main mode, because that is the main reason why the game is really good (:
In the trench war you have to run into the enemy trench. When you have more players in the enemy trench as the rival have, you need to hold this position for a couple of min or seconds. When you win the trench you win one point, so it could be that the result is 1: 0 to example. So you have to protect youre own trench and you have to make a assault on the enemy trench. This have a real character, because you lose a lot of fighters before you can enter the other trench as it in real happen. stand is deadly and you have to crouch or lie almost all the time when you want to survive. Another good point is the team play. This is a real team play game, because you can't win without team play, so you need to use strategic plans. This game needs a lot of skill. The weapon handling is nice too, because you haven't a lot possiblitys to shoot the target. With a normal weapon you only have 5 -10 shot before you have to reload the weapon, unless you have a machine gun (: . but you have to find a really good position because you can't shot while you running. The bullet fall down in a longer distance, and so you need to calculate the shot before you shoot.
The only weakpoints in this game are the teambalance and the movement, because you can't change the position very fast. But I can recommend this game, and it makes a lot of fun. You shouldn't give up when you die a lot in the beginning, because this game need a lot of practice. You should have a FPP over 30, that you can play the game in a good movement. Even with a low graphic chip is this game playable. Then you have to use a low picture mode of course.
800 -600 and even then it makes fun.
You can use gas, smoke, arti, reconnaissance aircraft , a telescope and comands as commander. You can play a sniper with a sniper telescope or soldier with granates, a flamethrower and much more classes to example. In my opinion it is not boring to run from trench to trench. It is more difficult and diverse as you think. Every situation is different and it is really hard to enter the trench alive. You also have to survive in this enemy trench for a while too.
And when you get a good team balance, in a lot of battles you get an end with a result of 0:0 after a half hour (: It is like in real you lose a lot of soldiers for one trench. You can't run around like a crazy chicken as in other shooter games when you want to survive.
Of course it is allowed to run around like a crazy chicken. but then you are fried chicken (:
When you like games with skill, thinking and teamplay. And when the game should have a bit of an real character, then Verdun could be the right game for you. Especially when you like sniper games, because in the defending everyone needs good snipers.
The Game is worth playing and I give 8 from 10 Points for the current version of Verdun.

A marvelously huge, varied adventurous sandbox.  Get your hands on a huge variety of vehicles on land, sea and air, get your hands on one of about a dozen different weapons, upgrade yourself as you like, take over locations and bases, drop out of the sky whenever you want.
Honestly?  This game is great fun.  The mission-related stuff is a bit weak, as missions are often a bit repetitive, but the side-quests can get pretty wacky.  Don't get this if you're a person who wants to 100% games, because it will eat your life.  There is SO MUCH to find and do and pick up, not much of it requisite, but it's there.
The graphics are fairly good, not to mention somewhat demanding.  But, if you like scenic, this offers excellent scenery of a fairly wide variety.  The music is nothing of note, but also avoids the grating rap or pop that plagues modern-setting sandboxes.
All in all, a rather good game, and a marvelous sandbox.

Trench warfare is probably the most inovative and the most effective way of fighting eachother...im just joking, Trench warfare was boring, fustrating and...well...not that effective as it took ages to advance on the enemy. Considering this is what it was like in real life, it was boring but if we turned this ww1 style into a game, we would be getting somewhere. Welcome to the early access game of Verdun which in the whole backfill, was a largebattle between the German empire and the french which seemed to be a pivotal part of ww1 and one the would have effected the whole war. Verdun in a brief description is historically correct on how it sets itself. what i mean by this is that you will see real weapons in their like the British lee-enfield, which everyone can agree is superior to any other current ww1 rifle. Verdun is amazing for me as it put me in the shoes as one of those lingering, scared soldiers in the trenches at the time, this was accompaned by some beautiful graphics, sound and mood. I really enjoyed being a trench sniper out in the famed "no mans land"picking off german or french soldiers popping their heads over the parrapet. Verdun is Multiplayer only but this is why it strives. the ammount of people on the map is incredible which adds more immersion. there is a class system and a level up system which rewards you for doing heroic things such as killing lots of people. Overall i enjoyed verdun from my first impressions, it really made me feel like a trench soldier in ww1, i just wish more games could be more stylised and fresh just like this, i think you should play it!. SCORE 7.9/10

I played this for around 800 hours on ps3, and for first playthrough I thought "Woo, yeah! Another souls game!" and to a lesser extent, my second playthrough. But after the first couple times with the game, you start to take a second glance, and realize just how wrong it is.
The first mistake the game makes is the intro cutscene, its really edgy and self aware, something the souls games are definitely NOT known for. Outwardly using Namco's marketing of "it's a hard game xDDDD" and "ur gonna die git gud xDD",  in the cutscene (that is fairly inaccurate, and seemed like they were just like, "Make something brutal and cool :D" and threw random stuff in there) was a terrible choice that gives me a bad vibe and makes me kinda angry even today.
Later on you find out that what they said is true, that they actually focused the game around dying a bunch and being frustrated, as if that was an intentional thing that the series aimed for. Even after Miyazaki outwardly stated that difficulty wasn't the focus of Dark or Demons, here we have a game aimed for it. You can tell it's this way with how seemingly every room is just one after another ambushes. There are no interesting or creative enemies in this game really, and they made up for lack of good, challenging enemies, by clustering them all in tight spaces with you so that you have to be forcefully outnumbered and die a lot. Sure Dark and Demons had ambushes every once in a while, but they were at least balanced around that idea, and the enemies often had low health and damage, Dark Souls 2 however, just says, "NOPE", and throws 5 hard hitting enemies who are fast and have a lot of health into that small corridor, because thats difficult, right? Your only option is to be lucky, hold up a greatshield and turtle, or wait for all enemies to sychronizingly exhaust their attack combos at the same time, so you can come in and strike a couple times. Fun, right? This applies to boss encounters as well, and the only true challenging boss encounters are challenging because they gank you (Other than dlc bosses[Excluding you, Ivory King boss]).
Another major downside is the level design. In addition to the layout of enemies just essentially being ambushes of mobs the level design is mostly just a small hallway leading to another one with some random items that are out of place lying about. Levels are seemingly dissassociated from one another, with each one just making no sense or having any correlation from another, and some just being outright geographically impossible (Going up an elevator in earthern peak to end up in a sinking castle surrounded by  lava). And the world design pretty much checks out too. All places are very limited branches that don't really reward exploration. Most levels you'll find yourself just thinking, "I must have missed something... right?"
In terms of combat I'd like to say its improved, but... I don't know. Theres plenty more variety for pve and stuff, but they've completely nerfed quality builds and messed up the way buffs work. Instead of it being a temporary way to make damage closer to normal as a caster, it makes your weapon far greater than a melee characters. Say you have 50 strength, and wield a greatsword which has amazing scaling in strength, you should always outdamage a person who buffs right? You've deticated stats to having powerful melee and close up attacks, while sacraficing the option of being able to cast spells or use miracles, you should at least be more powerful right? Nope. Something who has bare minimum stat requirements to two hand a greatsword (12-14) and has it infused with dark, buffs with dark weapon using minimum requirements (16 intell, 14 faith), will at least make even with you, if not completely outdamage you, which has lead to a bit of a problem, you're kinda pressured into using magic, as theres no downside. You outdamage melee people in melee and ranged attacks, so why not? Powerstancing is a nice thing they've added for combat, which is often overlooked (as a lot of combinations are worthless), but they've kinda messed up armor. Naked vs fully upgraded alva is the difference between being four shotted or five shotted, so is it really worth it? The last thing about combat I'd like to say is that they linked i-frames in rolling to a stat. It's a bad idea. Instead of having to be skilled at rolling and sacraficing armor in exchange for rolling well, you have to artificially increase your skill level in rolling, by leveling up a stat.

Before I start, I just want to say that I LOVE the orginal Dark Souls. I bought that game like 6 times already on Xbox and on PC. I actually even bought Dark Souls II for Xbox and PC as well. (I couldn't wait till the PC launch)
Dark Souls II didn't even hold a candle to the first one. Sure, it had a lot of improvements, but overall it went a lot of steps backwards. So like a dummy, I bought this version as well.
Now that that's out of the way, hear me when I say that everything that was wrong with Dark Souls II was amplified like 3 times in Scholar of the First Sin. It's just a badly designed game. Smple as that.
Example:
Rember that Bonfire in Brightcove with the spiders next to the bonfire? I had just gotten near it when I started thinking "Hmm. Maybe they finally removed those unnecissary spiders.". What did they do? They didn't remove those two spiders... They added like 6 more! WHAT? Those two spiders were a terrible design choise in Dark Souls II. Bonfires are suppsed to be something that your heart leaps at the thought of seeing, and Dark Souls 1 gets that right.  Whoever was making the decisions for Dark Souls II and Scholar of the First Sin just didn't know how to make a good game.
Is Scholar of the First sin harder? Yep.
Is it fun? No.
You know what made the orignial Dark Souls so amazing? Rushing into monsters would make them mob you, so you had to plan your attacks and only try to fight them one at a time. Single combat was amazing in the fist game. What did they do in the second one? When one enemy notices you, ALL of them notice you. Fighting multiple enemies is unavoidable and not what Dark Souls was about. Especially since the mechanics focus on single combat. THATS WHY THE LOCK ON WAS PUT IN THERE IN THE FIRST PLACE! Iron Keep Alone has like 3x more enemies than it did previously. And they ALL want to fight you at once.
You thought the archers were annoying? Now there's MORE! And they're facing each other as well.
Don't even get me started on the phantoms. Phantoms in Dark Souls 1 were something rare. They were there to add to the lore and a way to get a player to expereince some of the multiplayer mechanics at the same time. Dark souls took that idea and misunderstood the entire purpose. They're used pretty much like extra enemies. What does Scholar of the first sin do? THEY ADD MORE. It's like whoever was working on this game had the thought process that adding more stuff meant the game would get better, even though the stuff they were adding more of was terrible in the first place. Adding more terrible stuff to the already terrible stuff doesn't magically turn it good.
Did they fix the durability bug that happens at 60 fps? No
Did they fix enemies having terrible hitboxes that hit you even though they barely started swinging? No
Did they fix enemies having pretty much instant attacks that are impossible to predict? No
Diid they fix certain enemis having pretty much unlimited stamina so you pretty much HAVE to sacrifice health to attack? Nope
If you actually liked the things I think are wrong in Dark Souls II and thought more of that would be good, then you'll probably LOVE this game. If not, it's actually much worse.
I don NOT recommend this game and this is the game that made me vow to never buy a game before it's out again. No more preorders for me...

Silly sand box fun. With a ridiculous story that is meant to be taken on the cheek. Just Cause 2 is a sand box game to the letter. Your main goal is to 100% each of the cities, military bases and settlements by collecting and destroying stuff. With over 400 square miles to explore with over 100 vehicles, there is plenty to do. Aside from collecting/destroying things, there is a range of missions to complete, which in turn unlock other races and missions to attempt. All of this goes towards causing CHAYOS. As corny as this sounds, it works as a way of unlocking new stuff to buy and upgrade with your collected goodies like: upgraded health, weapons and vehicles.
Aside from conventional weapons you also have a grapple that allows you to get around easier and also use as a hilarious weapon. Have you ever tethered a man to the base of a gas canister, to then set it off and watch him get dragged through the air until it exploded in his face? No? Well that’s Just Cause 2 in a nut shell.
The community made multiplayer mod is also free on steam. Allowing friends or strangers to team up and cause more CHAYOS than a single man could ever achieve. Tether 8 guards to the wings of a plain and take of so you look like an aerodynamic Australian cork hat? I think so!

Although i can see there's a lot of hate in the game. i would still recommend this game.
The game is about you "Katie" coming home from a trip, and arriving at the new house your family just moved to recently. the strength of this game doesn't come from it's gameplay or superb soundtrack. The strengh of the game is from the subtlety of how it present the story to you, the player.
Yes, the game is really really short, around 2 hours long. (recommend you to grab it during sales) However, with just 2 hours of gameplay you feel like you want to get to know these characters. It's a story that's relatable and easy to understand.
p.s:- I can't really give a synopsis of any kind, as that will spoil the story.
Pros:
- The story is really good, it makes you wonder sometimes to what happened to the character after the story ends.
- Interesting way to tell the story of the game, via notes, letters, etc.
- The game was set in the 90s, it gives a sort of nostalgic feel to how people communicated last time when social media didn't exist.
Cons:
- The house itself is a bit eerie, but i guess that's to give the mysterious feeling.
- The walking speed is quite slow in the game, which makes it annoying when you're trying to get to 1 point to another.
- The lighting in the game has some error, for example, i went inside a cloesetroom, close the door and switch off the light. i was still able to see the items inside. While in reality, it should be near pitch black.
TLDR:- The game is worth grabbing, however!!! it is not for everyone, get it if you enjoy a good story that will be revealed to you slowly. It is slow and short journey, but it's a nice one nonetheless.

Gone Home isn't a game so much as it is an interactive experience.  It has great sense of atmosphere that helps you become immediately invested in the story.  Though it is rather short (my own experience clocking in at around three and a half hours), this is one of those times where you'll walk away from the ending with a feeling of satisfaction while at the same time, your mind will continue to spin, thinking about what you've just gone through.
There are a few negatives like the fact that drawers/items that you can open or pick up seem arbitrary.  You can open a drawer in a dresser, but the next two down you can't.  You can pick up a wrapper from the ground but not certain bulky times left on a desk.  While this is no means a deal breaker, it would have been nice to be able to either be able to open/manipulate every drawer/item, or at least have the expectation set that nothing can be manipulated in/on certain types of furniture.  Again, not a huge misstep, but it did tend to pull me out of the experience when it would happen.
While not for everyone, if you want something different; something a little slower paced but still a shorter experience, do yourself a favor and try Gone Home.  Easily one of the best purchases I've made on steam.

Gone Home, as the user-defined tags suggest, is a 'walking simulator' and an 'interactive story' and not really a game, per se. Gone Home is atmospheric and moody, with a compelling plot that hints at (and reveals, if you pay close attention) a much deeper story than the one presented superficially. It is certainly a title worth playing for the few short hours it will take to complete.
However, though it won a ton of critical acclaim and awards, in my opinion Gone Home didn't quite deserve all of the accolades thrown its way. There is nothing really new about Gone Home. In fact, it's based off the Japanese game 'The Royal House Haikyo'.
There weren't any moments where I went "Wow, that was really neat!" or "Never saw that before!". It's actually quite predictable and quite plain. Don't get me wrong; it executes very well. But I was playing point and click adventure games similar to this in the 1990s. I think it primarily gained it's attention from being such a refreshing change of pace rather than being anything revolutionary, though those with younger or shorter memories may have a 'New To Me' experience.
Do yourself a favor and play Gone Home. But do yourself a bigger favor and temper your expectations.

It amazes me how harsh people can be on a game simply for it's length. Even more bizare is how negative people can be on a story-based game simply for it's gameplay style. But the thing that bugs me the most is that for those simple and closed minded reasons, people can overlook something special and unique.
"Gone Home" is that kind of game. It's not a horror game. It's not an action game. It is nothing more than a story reveal overtime and your part is revealing that story. My favorite type of story seems to always deal with a mystery. The reveal piece by piece to the truth to that mystery is in itself hauting but also rewarding. And this game is just that. It's a well crafted mystery styel story play through interaction, well acted voice work, and if you are willing to pay attention, listen, and embrace the story, You will find yourself moved.

And no, moving enemy positions doesn't make it moreso, because all that says is that your game's lore and enemy placements weren't well thought out.
I don't care about the price tag, that'll change, I care about an actual challenge. So when I see a turtle night ballet dancing around for an overhead slam, or bosses that just look like big humans, or bosses that spawn multiple enemies because "Why make it interesting when we could make it hard?" I get irritated with the design. And that was a glaring problem of the first release, how they managed to rerelease it with the same issues is beyond me.
Blocking off an opening area with a petrified enemy because the area might be too difficult is laughable, throwing a pile of Heide knights into the tower not only doesn't make sense, but having them aggro you makes it ridiculous and unfair. Which is the problem- the fairness. Dark Souls was always a fair challenge, and despite it's issues, the design of that game overcame many issues you might have, and was a clear improvement over it's predecessor. Whereas here, it feels like the difficulty was shoved into your face, as opposed to the intrigue of a cool fantasy setting.
This game is good, and I'd recommend it over a lot of games, but I'm holding it in the Souls games regard, and when you think about how Dark Souls 1 is available, I'm sad to say that I can't recommend it. I heard they're fixing the durability issue at 60 FPS, but that doesn't change a game that isn't individual, but one that's derivitave. Any good idea in this game was lifted from the first game. Even some bosses were flat out copy-pasted into this.

When I booted up "Gone Home" for the first time, it was late Monday night/Tuesday morning, around 3:00 am.  My plan was, I'll boot up and play around a few minutes to see what this is all about.  After a couple minutes of tinkering with my perferred settings, I started the game.  I had planned to go to bed soon after, but soon found myself so engrossed in the experience, I couldn't stop until I finished the game.  I hadn't looked into what specifically the game is about other than you arrive home after a year abroad and your family is not there, forcing you to piece together the reasons why.  In my opinion, that's all the information you should know going into this game, so you can truly appreciate it the way I did.
The first thing I noticed about the game was the atmosphere.  The ambient sound effects, the raging storm outside the home, and my God, the music in this game is perfect.  Once I began to pick up objects and examine them, I noticed how fantastic the graphics and art style were (at least on max settings).  The strong narrative and the mystery behind it, coupled with the simplistic controls and atmosphere make for an incredibly memorable experience.
I totally recommend this game, and I don't want to say much more about it because it should be experienced with as little spoiler as possible.  Suffice it to say that, despite the games simplistic controls, there is a fantastic sense of exploration and piecing together the narrative in your head is both challenging and dynamic.  Just when you think you have it figured out, a new piece of information changes your mind.  My only knock on the game is that there is really no replay value, but the core experience was so memorable and enjoyable that after awhile, I'm sure I'll be playing through this again.
