Verdun proves to be a realistic simulation of World War One's battles, with even the gunfire actually created by players.  In the game, so much as popping your head out of the trench could land you sniped, or gunned down by MG fire. It is quite unforgiving, yet still extremely fun to play. With the game's squad system, it promotes teamwork and co-operation, and the career points system is equally good, as with it you can unlock new classes for your position in the squad, and how many career points you earn is dictated by how well your squad does and how well YOU do, which also promotes teamwork and strength-in-numbers.
Overall, it makes this game quite a solid experience. However, the game does have a few flaws.
Right now, at least, it only has 3 gamemodes to play in, which, although fun, can get a little boring after awhile. Very few people play Rifle Deathmatch anymore with the addition of Attrition, so really, it's just two gamemodes, which takes away from the game's experience. Also, it has its fair share of glitches, such as guns not actually pointing at you, yet you still being shot (which really messes up gameplay due to you thinking he's not looking at you.)
So my final verdict for Verdun, with all of the above facts included, is 8/10. A good, solid game, that I would recommend to World War I and even World War II genre fans.

Verdun is an excellent WW1 game based on trench warfare. It has some fantastic maps and is an extremely atmospheric game to play. The online community is of the highest standard that I think I can honestly say that I've played with.
In many games it feels slow and painful to level up (unlock weapons etc), but in Verdun it always seems that I have spare points up my sleeve any time that I want to try a new weapon. :) (Maybe I'm just too frugal with those points in the first place, but I digress)...
As a criticism, I have only experienced 1 bug, when I kept spawning in 'no man's land' and was executed for cowardice (many times in a row), but after leaving and restarting the map it all seemed to work ok.
When I first started playing Verdun I was the only one running around on maps. I just started games to see if people would join and they usually did- even if it was only for the last few minutes. Then I realised that I could change my server region and the Aus server is generally more active than the Asian server. (At least it was when I first started). So if you can't find any games to play and can't afford to run around by yourself much, check out some other servers.

Scholar of the First Sin is the director's cut version of Dark Souls II, pure and simple. And just like any other director's cut, the product has been polished and updated. It's same product as the one that came before but with small additions. Certain enemy placements are different, certain item locations are different, minor tweaks has been made here and there, and the inclusion of the mysterious "Scholar of the First Sin" adds some more lore to the game.
If you haven't bought DS2 yet, then this is the definitive version and it's worth every penny. It is a great game and it's well worth your time.
But what of the people who already own DS2, what should they do? It's a director's cut, it bears repeating. All the extras, tweaks and changes are nice but ultimately it all comes down to this: the original Dark Souls II version is still great. Speaking as a big dark souls fan, I'm glad I bought it, but it wouldn't have been a big loss if I hadn't.

Blah blah payed patch blah blah.. Everyone pretty much declares this instantly whenever I bring this game up, even I myself felt this was really.. Dirty and underhanded of FROMSoft.
But in just 9 hours, I've come to see, that it's actualkly a really good remix, that goes beyond patch content. Looking at it as a whole, a lot of the encounters have changed, not just in the types of enemies, or the number of enemies, but it also changed the amount of thought I had to put into an encounter, a perfect example is.. *Spoiler*
When you're going through the forest of the fallen giants, the base encounter isn't much different, there's undead trailing along the path like usual, but they've added an Ogre, which on the surface is a really shallow way of changing things up. But it gives more of a decision than you had in DSII, on top of how it forces a change in how you handle the enemies, then going on to the next half of the river encounter, enemies are identical, an archer on the upper path, shielded hollow on the lower path, off the bridge they added an undead with a bandit knife, and made it so when you get close, an axe hollow will fall from the boulder, (the one you can jump off of from climbing up, and heading to the right, for some throwing knives) and attack you, it actually changes the dynamic a bit more slightly, as when facing it normally, you go from the sword and board hollow, to the archer hollow, then deal with the sleeping axe hollow, get item from river, while now there's multiple, active threats, with one activated threat (The axe hollow on the boulder) that you have to deal with, making you deal with the archer hollow last, (if you go for him first, I've found there to be a tendency of getting rekt, as there's an axe hollow by the ladder I believe) where it gets a bit interesting is once that encounter is dealt with, you climb up to where the Heide Knight usually is, and for starters he's gone, no big deal, he wasn't aggro, but now all the undead up there, are laying down, they replaced the upper rampart hollow with a firebomb soldier, while the lower soldiers, despite 'sleeping' are now higher in number, and threat. (more sword hollows) if you rush ahead, and don't think about the situation, you end up surrounded by 17 or so hollows, and you get decimated, while in the original it was more so action-gamey, reaction battle for this segment.
There's several other moments like this so far, where the encounters just seem to require different skills, and a bit more thought, they feel more threatening, but not in the higher-numbers sort of way, but in the amount of things you need to keep track of.
Over all, just based on the remix'd encounters, which are not just copy pasted, some thought, and even destructable objects were used in order to create said encounters, I'd say the content is DLC quality, and required DLC tier work to be put in to it.
As for seperation of DS2 and DS2SFS, do I think it was necissary? Well, looking into it, yes, the remix is a complete revamp of the encounters, re-thought, and everything, which I think money should be thrown at (19.99 in my case) the increase in summonable players is also required in order to handle some of the new threats, and having players invade into a completely different encounter area, where SLs will probably be different compared to the original game, or for these players to be summoned into these areas with new encounters, would create issues.
Also, I feel as though there's enough differences, to keep DS2 and DS2SFS as two seperate games, I'd feel a bit annoyed if they remixed the game to this degree, then disallowed returning to DS2 the original, for as much as I like SFS's new encounters, DS2 is still a unique experiance to it.

It's same product as the one that came before but with small additions. Certain enemy placements are different, certain item locations are different, minor tweaks has been made here and there, and the inclusion of the mysterious "Scholar of the First Sin" adds some more lore to the game.
If you haven't bought DS2 yet, then this is the definitive version and it's worth every penny. It is a great game and it's well worth your time.
But what of the people who already own DS2, what should they do? It's a director's cut, it bears repeating. All the extras, tweaks and changes are nice but ultimately it all comes down to this: the original Dark Souls II version is still great. Speaking as a big dark souls fan, I'm glad I bought it, but it wouldn't have been a big loss if I hadn't.

I got this (upgrade version) free from a friend, we have something akin to 1000 DS2 hours between us on various platforms so have basically played the Souls series to death. (don't take my 'played' time as a given on Steam).
Let's get the bad stuff out of the way first, and maybe add a sprinkling of good stuff too, just for balance.
Most, if not all of the bugs and glitches from the original are still here, including the 2x durability loss bug that occurs at 60fps.
My musings:
The much touted graphical changes aren't really an upgrade, just a few tweaks to lighting (makes some areas a little darker or a little lighter but not much else), and textures (SLIGHTLY less muddy than vanilla).
The gameplay remains the same as vanilla too apart from slightly different enemy locations (some actually make more sense within their respective levels now) and unfortunately a ton more gank squads.
Personally I've never been a fan of artificial difficulty with regards to placing more and more enemies in an area to ramp up the difficulty, I would call this lazy and uninspired to the nth degree, totally shameful.  I would much rather have less enemies to fight but in more interesting and dangerous locations, for example, fighting a 2-hand weilder on a narrow bridge with no rails over a sheer drop, or an archer in a tight coridoor etc.
The durability bug is the deal breaker for me though, it's been there from the start and FS have done NOTHING to even address it, even after all the exposure it's had. It's like FS live in this tiny bubble that no outside influence can penetrate.  It's disheartening to the extreme, especially as Bloodborne is so much better in this respect than DS2 will ever be due to B-team's lack of care and attention.
There's no doubting that DS2 is fun, but, for me, not for the right reasons and the same thing applies to Scholar.
If you don't own Dark Souls 2, or own it but NOT the DLC then this is an ideal purchase.
If however, you own Dark Souls 2 AND the DLC avoid like the plague, as for my money, this hasn't enough changes to justify being paid content, only a cash-grab from a severely floundering B-team.

At the writing of this review I'm 20 hours in and has completed about 1/3 of the game. I'll try to make this a review of the game itself, not a review on the business practice of Bandai Namco which is basically what every reviewer is talking about.
First of all, the Dx 11 upgrade is definitely noticeble. The texture and details is definitely sharper especially on charactors and enemies. You can recognize enemies from much farther away instead of a big blur in the distance. The lighting is much better and overall contrast and color saturation is much more beautiful. It is definitely a step up from Dx 9 version.
The game support up to 4 players coop now. For me it is the biggest problem with this version. The staple of Soul games is the sense of dread and loneliness. You walk down empty dark corridors, facing giant monster by yourself. That is what make Soul games unique and attractive. Now if you walk down the environment with an army of four, all these sense of dread is gone. 4 vs 1 Boss fight feels epic at first, but soon you realized all bosses fights now become mindless hackfests. No strategy is needed, it is always 3 people hacking away at the boss and each player taking turn back off and heal. You fight one such fight you've seen it all. No you don't have to play the multiplayer portion of the game but unfortunately this version has steped up the difficulty to geer towards MP that it is going to be very difficult to go solo this time around. I recommend you limit your summoning to only 1 phantom each time, and maybe 2 max at a few particularly difficult sections.
The new enemy placements means the game guide you more to go on a more linear route. It used to feel a lot of freedom, as well as confusion, in the initial part of the game to try many different area. But now in the attempt to guid the player more, a lot of these areas have much harder enemies as some kind of soft "road-blocks". For new players it does offer better direction as to where to proceed and where not to go. But it does make the game more linear, more scripted. As a benefit of this I do find the game now paces better and challenge is more even throughout every environments. Definitely less down-times.
Overall though it is still a very well designed and crafted game and it is very enjoyable to play through. I do find there's an effort on the developer's part to make it a worthwhile upgrade. Again, I'm not here to judge the pricing and the way they release this upgrade. But safe to say, if you don't have the original or if you haven't bought the DLCs, it is definitely worth buying this version.

Gleich zu Beginn wird man im 1. Bossgebiet auf eine harte Probe  gestellt,d man mit schlechten Waffen sich bis zum 2. Leuchtfeuer dort durchkämpfen muss und man definitv  Taktik benötigt und genau wissen muss wie man Vorzugehen hat! Im Orginal gab es einen kleinen Miniboss gleich am Anfang, der hieß Heideritter und hat einem ein ziemlich gutes Schwert gegben, dies ist nun nicht mehr der Fall, da er nicht mehr an der Selben Stelle ist. Aber auch mit schlechteren Waffen lässt es sich überstehen und Spätestens am 2. Leuchtfeuer könnt ihr euch bessere Waffen holen, diese upgraden und den Bossen ins Auge schauen. Alle die Zweifel haben ob das Spiel lohnenswert ist, JA! Gott ja! es ist das beste Spiel seit langem. Meiner Meinung nach ein mega geiles Spiel. Also von mir gibts ein Däumchen hoch! :D

When I finished this game, I wanted to immediately run through it a second time.
The game is short, but also poignant, interesting, and beautiful.
Most importantly however, the game highlighted for me the fact that game stories still try to be Hollywood movies. Video games are an interactive medium. To limit games to the types of stories we have limits the art form immensely.
Gone Home has no combat, no puzzles, and no central conflict. But it is a shining example of what we can do with this medium. I have played video games for nearly 20 years. The fact that it took this long for me to experience something like Gone Home saddens me. But the existence and success of Gone Home give me hope for the future of this art form.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who is invested in video games as an art and believes there is something truly powerful about games' interactive nature.

HOWEVER, this game is a story, in which you immerse yourself into the world of a young girl named Kaitlin as she tries to piece together the circumstance of her empty home.
If you come into this game with the mindset that this is a game that can be beaten you will be sorely disappointed. I would most liken this game to a personalized movie that provides satisfaction to those who take their time to explore the rich world and story told via scattered notes left by Kaitlin's sister.
In the end I highly recommend this game to anyone who is willing to sit down for 3 hours and enjoy the experience and story the game provides.
Likewise I would not recommend this game if you are looking for anything other than being told a story.

Dark Souls returns as a remastered and repolished nightmare. I obviously mean that in the most positive of ways. I have been a fan of this series since I grabbed Demon's Souls in the $15 bin at Walmart all those years ago. Once you lose your souls to the monsters in this universe, you just can't stop coming back.
I absolutely did not hesitate whatsoever to buy Scholar of the First Sin. I bought the original Dark Souls 2 around Christmas time when it was cheap. Got the game and all three DLC for about the price of the game at a regular price. I had so much fun, ranking up to about 600 hours. That is, until Scholar of the First Sin came about. I wasn't entirely sure if buying the game a second time was going to totally be worth my money. Didn't really want to spend $60 for something I already owned for the most part. But I honestly planned on doing so anyway. I completely support Fromsoftware and all of their endeavors so that they can continue to make this franchise larger and larger. But to my great surprise, The game was only $20 since I owned the entirety of Dark Souls 2 already. In all honesty, the people saying not to buy this if you own the full game and the DLCs because it's a "waste of your money" are just finding a reason to complain. If you own everything then it's 20 bucks. Calm down and play the new stuff.
Scholar of the First Sin is noticably different from the get go. It's prettier to look at by far. The graphics are absolutely gorgeous. And while running Things Betwixt as if I've never been to the tutorial zone before, I noticed several basilisks in the area where you need to knock down a tree to use as a bridge. Even more to my surprise, you aren't able to even access that area of Things Betwixt until you find a Fragrant Branch of Yore. I literally said "That's freakin' awesome." outloud as I ran into the petrified Hollow in the way of the fog to that room. I immediately knew that playing this would be a blast.
Due to spoilers, I avoided taking Heide's Tower of Flame first, seeing as how it is literally the "hard mode" path now that it's swarming with Heide Knights and a Dragon blocks the path to the Cathedral. But even if you head to the Forest of the Fallen Giants, you find that it's much harder, very Demon's Souls-like in it's execution; The large tree where, in Dark Souls 2, the first Heide Knight was sitting, there now are about double the amount of Hollow Infantry and if it wasn't for the fact that I literally have been constantly playing Souls games for the better half of this year, I would have totally been destroyed by that LITERAL AMBUSH AHEAD.
Some changes are subtle, like some enemies aggroing you from a better distance or being moved a couple feet to, at the very least, surprise you a little bit. Others are rather large changes. Like the petrified Hollows being placed all around the game, both blocking your path to areas you literally need to get to and some of them have just been placed in places so that all the branches you get can be used for something. It's absolutely wonderful.
Almost all of the rare gear from the original game can also be easily obtained or found in the game now. Making it feel more like the other games. Farming one-time spawning black phantoms is rather frustrating and should not have been a thing to begin with. Also, the new gear, the Forlorn set and weapons. They are very nice to look at, and the Forlorn themselves are a very amazing NPC. They show up randomly in nearly every area of the game at any given time. Functioning as a real player would. You could be playing offline and forget you were for a moment because you kept dying in the same place and eventually you get invaded while in battle and you don't know how to react. "YOU WEREN'T THERE BEFORE WHAT THE HECK"
One of the biggest "WOO. YES." points in this game has to be the thing that everyone has enjoyed. The Pursuer. He does as his description implies. He pursues you to the ends of the earth. it's almost as if he invades you in his own Pursuing fashion now. I absolutely love it.
I have already said more than need be, and there's a whole lot more. To say the least, I love this game. And it is my favorite game in the Souls franchise so far and I hope they continue to make masterpieces like this and bring in more fans to steal the souls of. Join our covenant, brothers and sisters. Be branded by the Dark Sign and have your souls taken from you. Just remember... Dying is not failure. It's a promise. Just don't give up. Don't let them kill your confidence. Don't. Go. Hollow.

After having bought this game five times (once for myself and four times for my friends), played on several tournament matches, and generally mastered the game since acquiring it in 2015, I am deeply unsatisfied with the new updates and the state this game is currently in.
The nerfing of rifles from one-shot to two-shot kills at a distance are needlessly irritating and bring down the level of realism to Battlefield 1-standards of gameplay. But more annoying is the almost-permanent curse of clunky gameplay, stuttering, and lag. Got bad internet? Then I've bad news, your ping will spike up to 300, enemies will teleport over to whatever foxhole you're hiding in and kill you, you may shoot someone right in the face but you'll miss anyway. I'll go as far as to say that these updates have needlessly broken the game while avoiding the very real problem of absent fluidity. Whatever new benefits brought about by them are cosmetic at best.
On my part, it's almost as if I'd turned back to square one. Verdun has become infinitely more frustrating than enjoyable for me to play, and so I will no longer recommend it.

As I'm sure you've heard, Gone Home is not a game.
It's essentially an attempt at non-linear storytelling, which holds up reasonably well at first, but ends up resorting to voiceover explanation along a linear path.  Ultimately it gave up partway through because it (understandably) became too difficult to convey their story without resorting to sequential ordering.
It's an experiment.  An interesting experiment, but ultimately a failed experiment.  Charging money for it is insulting.

UPDATED:
Years of promises only lead to disappointment after disappointment.

When the devs knew about problems in hitreg and did not fix it but only putting workaround like allowing tradekills, you know these guys can not put a consistent quality throughout their updates. When they keep changing mechanics of the game, it clearly shows they know they can't please everyone so they took a selfish decision and didn't even considered voice of dedicated ppl who play this game for thousands of hours, ppl who keeps this game alive. Thousand of those hours has been put by community to resolve balancing regarding loadout and map, but yet the success of BF1 and WW1-themed game and most importantly influx of new players (players who don't want "battlefield's arcady style" gameplay) has derailed them to be one of those copycats promoter of "realistic" gameplay, which is wrong.
If you are new player and trying to pick this game up, don't expect anything true about the game description, English is not their main language.
. Weapon handling is not realistic (nothing realistic about pressing melee to cancel reload), movement is arcady (jumpshotting is by all means necessary and allowed), nothing realistic about respawning and press a button to call arty.
Developer who can not treasure their own original community and basically going-with-the-flow type of developer, is the one who will make the playerbase stagnant. If they had believe in their philosophy rather than trying to please everyone, this could be one of the best gem in indie world, but sadly it is not. M2H clearly understood how to develop a game to be decently successful, but they did not know how to translate it to their development going forward. Without any continuation in their mind, it translates to their playerbase and the overall satisfaction of the game.
Now they moved on to Tannenberg and gonna change the mechanics (again) and start all over from scratch, no more signature style thug-of-war, no more arcady-style of character movement so basically will be a copy of RO in WW1 skins.  So heavy-heartedly I have to change my review, as this is a bitter truth of once a good indie game with clunky but flawless movement and mechanics, not to mention how crisp the weapon handling before the Horrors of War Update. Overall, I'm disappointed with the development of this title, not because the community but rather about how they handle problems in their game. Thank goodness I can make some friends and enemies from this.

The story pulls you in and grabs hold of your soul. It crashes into some heavy themes so don't go in here expecting generic storytelling. You, as a player, are constantly hooked up to the very end, with a strong and satisfying conclusion. By the time the story is over, all the plot points are seamlessly connected, as if you flipped a page in a book. Gonne Home is a must buy.

If you don't own Dark Souls II, this is the definitive edition. It's a great game and a rarity. Dark Souls is one of the last true learning experiences in gaming, one of the last RPGs with real character customization, and one of the last satisfyingly hard games.
The gameplay itself communicates tone and atmosphere. The souls mechanic creates a beautiful tension between caution and exploration. Items feel finite and resources scarce. Story, if you want it, is uncovered through snatches of soliloquy and descriptions on items, not desperately put on display as if the game is a film. The limited and obscured multiplayer interaction reinforces a sense of isolation that is ever-present.
Visually, the game is stunning, not through impressive graphics, but through artful juxtapositions of light and dark. A well-lit ruin on the verge of collapse into the sea serves as the game's main hub. Taken by itself, it's a drab, depressing little town. And yet within the context of the game, it's a bright and beautiful home, safety and sanctuary. The darkness of your journey has the power to make the bland beautiful, which the game's artists understand well.
Spells and weapons represent worlds of varying playstyle, especially in PVP. PVP is faction-motivated and unapologetic. It is avoidable for those who refuse to tolerate it, but the default game takes no measures to sterilize PVP into a separate mode. A variety of builds, an unattainably high level cap, and the ability to start the game over at a higher difficulty all contribute to replayability. Dedicated PVP is equally addictive.
Some people will tell you the first Dark Souls is better. They're probably right. But I still cannot recommend this game enough.

If you already own Dark Souls II, this rerelease is underwhelming. It's more expensive than the previous DLC packs but incomparable in content. Monsters have been reshuffled in all areas, but nothing is substantially challenging or different, except that the torch is required in certain areas now (admittedly, a good change).
The improved graphics are unimpressive, often indistinguishable. The only obvious graphical change is that lighting has been turned up, which actually makes some areas look worse. The shoddy backgrounds, the blurred movements of distant enemies, the excess of tiled textures, and any other eyesores you'd hope would be eradicated in an HD rerelease all remain unchanged.
The durability bug is still present. Still. Your old characters will not transfer over, and you won't be able to play with people who stuck with the old version of the game. In fact, if you buy this, you'll have two copies of Dark Souls II in your Steam library, one old and one new. You're literally buying the same game a second time. And no, you can't give the old version to a friend.
Unless you desperately need to follow a PVP community to this version or can't live without the most complete game possible, don't buy this. Or at least wait for a sale. Any other developer would have released this as a free patch to users who had already spent $80.00 on their game. As much as I love this studio's work, it's apparent to me that From Software has no idea how to sell games for the PC.

I like to imagine the look on the CoD fanboys' faces when they hear of a low budget, indie FPS set in World War 1. How they scoff. Well, they can keep paying £40 for the same retextured s*** every year. Verdun is proof that the FPS genre has not hit a dead end.
I have to admit, I was dubious as well upon hearing about this game. Surely a setting in which people ended up getting killed as soon as they popped their heads up from their hidey holes doesn't exactly make for very exciting gameplay. In fact, that's part of what makes the game so good- the atmosphere. There's a kind of buzz that you get from not knowing if you'll wind up getting a bullet through your skull, and that is exactly why Verdun is so thrilling.
For a low budget game like this, the multiplayer is executed almost flawlessly. I did experience one glitch in which I kept getting warped back to the spot where I was 5 seconds ago, but that happened to me in Battlefield before, so I wouldn't class that as a massive problem. There's no real bonus for high level players other than skill, and there's no real way to dodge a bullet in no man's land, so new players will easily get the hang of it. The squad system improves the experience for groups of friends playing, but doesn't hinder those playing alone.
I'd say the area in which the game really shines, though, is its immersion. The panic when you miss the shot and you have to reload, but your foe has his sights set on you, the genuine fear you feel when all your squadmates are lying dead beside you and you don't know where the enemy is, just that they're coming for you- that's something you won't get from the triple A franchises. That's what makes Verdun the best FPS in a long, long time.

If you don't own Dark Souls II, this is the definitive edition. It's a great game and a rarity. Dark Souls is one of the last true learning experiences in gaming, one of the last RPGs with real character customization, and one of the last satisfyingly hard games.
The gameplay itself communicates tone and atmosphere. The souls mechanic creates a beautiful tension between caution and exploration. Items feel finite and resources scarce. Story, if you want it, is uncovered through snatches of soliloquy and descriptions on items, not desperately put on display as if the game is a film. The limited and obscured multiplayer interaction reinforces a sense of isolation that is ever-present.
Visually, the game is stunning, not through impressive graphics, but through artful juxtapositions of light and dark. A well-lit ruin on the verge of collapse into the sea serves as the game's main hub. Taken by itself, it's a drab, depressing little town. And yet within the context of the game, it's a bright and beautiful home, safety and sanctuary. The darkness of your journey has the power to make the bland beautiful, which the game's artists understand well.
Spells and weapons represent worlds of varying playstyle, especially in PVP. PVP is faction-motivated and unapologetic. It is avoidable for those who refuse to tolerate it, but the default game takes no measures to sterilize PVP into a separate mode. A variety of builds, an unattainably high level cap, and the ability to start the game over at a higher difficulty all contribute to replayability. Dedicated PVP is equally addictive.
Some people will tell you the first Dark Souls is better. They're probably right. But I still cannot recommend this game enough.

If you already own Dark Souls II, this rerelease is underwhelming. It's more expensive than the previous DLC packs but incomparable in content. Monsters have been reshuffled in all areas, but nothing is substantially challenging or different, except that the torch is required in certain areas now (admittedly, a good change).
The improved graphics are unimpressive, often indistinguishable. The only obvious graphical change is that lighting has been turned up, which actually makes some areas look worse. The shoddy backgrounds, the blurred movements of distant enemies, the excess of tiled textures, and any other eyesores you'd hope would be eradicated in an HD rerelease all remain unchanged.
The durability bug is still present. Still. Your old characters will not transfer over, and you won't be able to play with people who stuck with the old version of the game. In fact, if you buy this, you'll have two copies of Dark Souls II in your Steam library, one old and one new. You're literally buying the same game a second time. And no, you can't give the old version to a friend.
Unless you desperately need to follow a PVP community to this version or can't live without the most complete game possible, don't buy this. Or at least wait for a sale. Any other developer would have released this as a free patch to users who had already spent $80.00 on their game. As much as I love this studio's work, it's apparent to me that From Software has no idea how to sell games for the PC.

There's many negative reviews, targeted at the game's currency system and about it being "pay to win". Well, there are some aspects of the game that I see could be leaning a bit toward the pay to win idea. Some of the better weapons cost over $10,000, and ever co-op mission or PVP match I do, I get about $400-600 on average everytime. So, to aquire some of the better weapons, you need to grind a decent ammount. However, leveling up gives you money and gives you VIP status, so the money you earn is increased by %75. Also, if you complete a co-op mission and you succesfully complete it the first time, you get $600. You also get weapons and gear at certain times you level up. Plus, everyday you log in, you get a new weapon/item, which aren't bad weapons either. The default weapons aren't bad either, they're actually pretty good.
Now, onto the real gameplay.
PROS+
-Gameplay mechanics are smooth and easy to learn
-Nice variety of weapons, skins, and accessories.
-New Co-op missions everyday which at least 4 players complete objectives with you. (Teamwork is GREATLY needed)
-Friend system allows you to invite people to play PVP or Co-Op Missions with you. (If you don't have friends who play the game or you don't have the chance to play with your friends who own the game, the first time you play co-op, just ask online if anyone wants to play co-op missions, since you need 4 people to start a mission.)
-Clans allow you to make friends and do clan wars with other clans. (like Clash of Clans)
NEUTRAL
-Vendors allow you to select either a weapon, accessory, or scope that you earn by earning %100 toward that item. (In other words, every time you play you earn a percentage toward your selected item, depending on how well you do in that mission/match. Those percentages add up, and once you reach %100, you earn that item. However, for the gun, you have to buy the gun for the permanent price, although it costs less than what you would pay for a permanent gun in the shop. If you don't buy the gun, you can buy it at any other time.
CONS-
-Hackers are found in about %40 of the PVP games you play. None that I've found on Co-op however. Some people just shoot through the walls and kill you, randomly shoot you, even if they aren't looking at you, or just headshot you way more often than heashots should occur. (A sniper in a game I was playing, got 89 kills, with 82 or 83 headshots. All in 10 minutes. I hate to call the blame game, but it was clear that he was hacking.)
-The cost of 1 day, 3 day, 7 day, or permanent use of guns and that the guns you earn, you only get to keep for a couple of days.(excluding vendors) Any weapon you unlock by leveling up or buying the Class packs, (which cost from $10 to $40) you don't keep permanently. Only for a couple of days you keep them. (not a huge problem however) Also, the ammount that you spend for a gun to keep for 7 days, should be the permanent price. The interval between the cost of owning a gun for 7 days and permanently, is pretty high. The permanent cost is rather high, but not to the point of pay to win.
Overall though, I enjoy the game. If you have friends to play with you, the replay value greatly increases. The mechanics, unlockables, missions, and social system are nice. However, the hackers and the cost of and time you own guns, are the downsides that the game has. Overall, I'd rate the game an 8/10.

Is this a game? Is it art? What is a game, anyway?
Years ago, Greg Costikyan made an early stab at defining "game", by distinguishing between games, puzzles, toys, and stories. By way of example, point-and-click adventures are mostly "puzzles" (they are solved, rather than "won"), Sim City is a "toy" (it has no inherent goal, beyond what fun you make with it), and something like Civilization is a "game" proper (it involves struggling toward a goal, almost certainly in competition with one or more opponents). The categories are somewhat fluid; any given work may have elements of any/all of them. But by those definitions: No, Gone Home is a "story", not a "game". All of these are forms of "art" (whether good or bad art is a separate question).
But those categories can all exist in different media: Civilization is a game, but so is, say, Agricola. One is in the medium of "video games" and the other in the medium of "board games". It is unfortunate that we are saddled with the term "video games" for the medium, when in fact the medium is not limited to games, per se. Myst is a puzzle, Sim City is a toy, yet both are within the medium of "video games". I think trying to radically re-name the medium is not really possible at this point, so for this reason, I personally have taken to compoundizing the word to "videogames", in an attempt to de-emphasize the "game" aspect.
So what is Gone Home, then? It is not a game; it is not a puzzle; it is not a toy. It is a story, told in the medium of "videogames".
Is that the best use of the medium? Probably not. Every medium has its own unique strengths and weaknesses. As a narrative medium, videogames' primary strength is probably the audience's empathy with the protagonist. Getting the audience to identify with and care about the protagonist takes effort in most media, while in videogames, because the audience is literally in the protagonist's shoes and controlling their actions, that identification happens virtually for free, and can be much stronger than in most other media. Something like Amnesia: The Dark Descent uses this fact to great effect. Gone Home arguably does not make full use of it, except in a couple of scenes.
Personally, overall, I found the story in Gone Home stronger than many of the other reviewers here, but possibly that's down to expectations: I basically knew going in that this was a "story", not a "game". There are hints at a supernatural occurence that never materializes, but I never found these hints to be distracting, or even particularly emphasized.
In the final analysis, Gone Home seems to me to at least be a worthwhile experiment: Can you use the videogame medium to tell a story, with essentially no "gameplay" elements whatsoever? Yes, you can. Is that a good idea? Probably not, but it was worth attempting in order to answer those questions. And the story told in this particular videogame is decent enough; I'm glad I played it, didn't feel my time was wasted. As a videogame, it is absolutely worth playing if you are interested in videogames as an art form, if for no other reason than that it does something that has maybe not been done since the 1986 interactive novel "Portal".

In a world where crappy fps games rule the market and companies such as Activision release the same game every year one game stands above the rest, Verdun. I find it difficult to describe my love for this game but I sure as hell will try.
TLDR: For those of you with lives who don't want to read my ridiculously long review let me give you a summary:
Verdun has great performance, combat, level design, historical accuracy, a large array of classes with variants for each and only it's only con is the French. Buy this game. (Plus there is some possible free dlc that will add a huge amount to the base game which is already huge).
PROS:
1. PERFORMANCE: Verdun is very well optimized I play the game on a pretty crappy rig with an integrated graphics card and even I can get 60fps while playing this
2. COMBAT: The combat in this game is fantastic! Rifles are one shot kills with each rifle from the two factions feeling different and unique to handle. Pistols, the bane of my existance, or two shot kills but obviously have a higer rate of fire able to clear a congested section of a trench rather easily. Machineguns can be devestating but are easily out manuevered by a coordinated squad. There are even trench clubs and shovels for one hit melee kills as well as bayonets, knives, and grenades.
3. THE SQUADS: For each of the two factions there are three squads each with four positions that are unique to that squad. Each position has three variants to appeal to all players. The officer, or NCO, uses a combination of pistols, grenades, binoculars, and if you're lucky a rifle. They inspire their nearby men giving statistical bonuses to members of their squads who remain in their aura. Also, officer can have their squad mates "forward spawn" allowing a squad mate to spawn on their officer. An officer can place down markers to tell his squad where to attack, defend, or move. Every officer has one of three devestating strategical abilities depending on the squad they belong too. These abilities include a devestating gas attack that blinds the enemies providing cover for your troops to advance and if you're lucky some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ will choke on it. The mortar is pretty self explanatory you blow people up with bombs from heaven. And last but not least is the recon plane which reveals enemy positions in a given area. The rest of the squad members range from machinegunners with various loadouts to snipers and crazy berserkers who go into battle with nothing but a shovel and 5 grenades.
4. ACCURACY: This game is one of, if not the only, WW1 multiplayer fps around. It is extremely well researched from the uniforms to the design of the maps.
5. ATMOSPHERE: This game makes you feel like you are fighting in WW1. Everything about it is makes you feel clastrophobic, paranoid, and just downright terrified. Gas attacks unman you causing your voice to sound like a helium balloon was just shoved down your throat. And nothing, and I mean NOTHING, is more terrifying then being the last man alive in the enemy trench.
6. LEVEL DESIGN: I kind of already touched on this but the maps in this game are fantastic. The maps are huge and logically designed with multiple stages. Just the other day I had played a map I had played probably 20+ and we were able to push the Frenchies back to their second to last trench. I started to see parts of the map I had never seen before including a huge well fortified bunker and an isolated section of the trench that acted as a last foothold for the defenders if they were overrun.
CONS:
1. THE FRENCH: Nothing angers me more then those silly blue uniforms. I mean come on BLUE?! They stand out like a sore thumb
2. PLAYER BASE: It saddens me to say this but rarely do you see more then 400 players on Verdun at once so do expect to meet the same people in battles. However, if you are worried about this affecting game sizes do not be dismayed. Verdun has an excellent drop in and out system so a game that starts 2v2 can end with a full out 16v16 battle.
Overall I love this game and I recommend you buy it if you're tired of jetpack soldiers and laser guns corrupting the fps genre.

Gone Home is amazing. It's a gentle, slow-paced revelation about a family full of people struggling to find themselves and their happiness in a complex world. There are creepy elements to it, akin to the masterful scare tactics of the Bioshock franchise, but  that creepiness is accompanied by the same incredibly in-depth attention to detail that the team is known for, and in the end the creepiness comes down to the real-life feeling of walking through a strange, empty house in the middle of a storm. Nothing jumps out of the shadows, nothing attacks or confounds you, nothing happens at all, in fact. The game doesn't force thre story down your throat; on the contrary it guides you only very subtly and lets you find out everything on your own. You never actually meet another character and only hear from them in recordings and notes left scattered around...and yet, all the characters (even the one you never hear from directly!) still burst with life and personality, still have complex stories that beg to be told. In the end, there is a deeply touching story laying there waiting for you to discover it...you just have go to looking! It feels very, very real (almost uncomfortably so at times) and very personal. If you're pushing for a straight-line story and trying to get to 'the end', the game is only a couple hours long. If you allow yourself to experience the game as it was meant to be experienced, in a leisurely fashion, exploring and investigating every nook and cranny of your new home and gathering all the little details that really enrich the experience, that stretches to six or more hours. Personally, I love this game in a deeply emotional fashion and recommend it to everyone I know - the story is so near to my heart and so skillfully woven that I can't keep it to myself. It's not as thorough or as expansive as some of the other FPS games on the market, but in a way its restricted focus is precisely its charm: it's a game that makes you appreciate the humble six shot revolver as a potent assault weapon and the bolt action rifle as a deadly longe range killer.
I also find the balance fairly well-done; sure, there's a career system where you level up to open new weapon ugprades, but frankly most of these upgrades have more to do with play styles than power ups. For example, the difference between many level 1 and 2 Corporals is whether they trade in Binoculars for two Grenades. This is actually not such an easy choice to make because each has useful trade-offs (Binoculars help you focus your Mortar ability at long range, Grenades are obviously more useful at close quarters.) Some of the level 3 upgrades I probably will never bother unlocking because I don't play that way (e.g. Corporal with Rifle with Bayonet). So the point is, even a newbie doesn't need to be too worried about being outclassed by veterans in terms of gear: eventually everyone masters their weapons of choice, and that may well be level 1 load-outs!
It's a niche game that won't appeal to all, but it appeals to me. :)

Great game.  Really captures the spirit of the era.  I was excited to finally have a first person shooter set in WWI.  When I began playing, I took my bolt action rifle and charged over the top of the trench only to be killed several times within yards of my own trench.
After a few hours of heroic yet fruitless charges trying to take the enemy trenches, I started sticking closer to my squad and discovered the true fun in the Verdun.  We were sprinting from crater to crater combining our unique skills and weapons to breach the enemy defenses.
I quickly realized that my own evolution in methods was very similar to what actually occured during WWI.  Shifting tactics from bloody mass charges to more efficient fire and move combined arms tactics.
As a someone who greatly appreciates the history of World War I, this has quickly become my favorite game.  To the best of my knowledge, Verdun accurately captures the scenary, emotion, and ferocity of the conflict that introduced the planet to modern warfare.
I have found the gameplay to be smooth and easy to pick up.  While there are some technical glitches, I cant remember a game that doesnt have any.  This is a game that gets straight to the point.  It portrays World War I accurately without any of the bells and whistles associated with many of the other games on the amrked these days.
If you are someone who is interested in the World War I and wants to appreciate the intense emotion combat that occured I highly recommend this game.

This is an extremely contentious game for a variety of complex reasons, but ignoring all that for a moment, I found it a lovely game about telling a short story through the system of an in-game environment. There's no action, no spooky ghosts, and there aren't really puzzles in any conventional sense. Just you, and a house filled with stuff that all tells a nice story.
My only complaint is that the main narrative kind of relies on pseudo audio logs as its central storytelling device, whereas the side-stories are told exclusively through notes and objects in the environment. While it kind of betrays the concept of a story told entirely through the environment to have audio logs tell you exactly what happened, they're incredibly well voice-acted and do a great job conveying the story's emotional center.
The original price of $20 could be argued as a little steep for a very short game, but for $5-10 on a sale price, you might just discover one of the more pleasant experiences out there.

I bought the original Dark souls II on the Xbox 360 a long time ago when it first came out, played it (practically) offline and got about halfway through, and ended up dropping the game. It just didn't feel right. I loved the first game, but the second just didn't click. All the areas were filled with reskins of player sized enemies, recycled ones from the first game, and sometimes a new one that was more often than not just another thing wielding a sword. Invasions were scarce, thanks to the vanilla networking system, while some people might like not being invaded at every turn, I like the occasional tussle with the redfriends.
Now I see that theres essentially a Dark souls II: GOTY edition, available on steam. I figure, why not pick it up?
Boy, that was a good decision.
I'm instantly greeting by a big, happy 60 FPS, improved graphics, improved lighting. That's a good way to start off. As I progress through the pretty looking enviroments, I see that the place is filled with those player ghost things, messages, and bloodstains. The game feels almost bustling with activity.
I notice as I'm cutting my way through the levels, that almost every single one has been redesigned, the most notable change is the enemy layout. Instead of always being a steady flow of generic warrior folks that die in one or two hits, followed by a small group of the area's unique enemy, everything is spread out and tweaked into a glorious mix of enemies that always has you on edge. Oh, theres completely new enemies too, and the layout of items has been changed so you are very less likely to miss out on "crucial" areas of the game like a blacksmith or boss soul trader and not being the wiser to it. They no longer hide a pretty important item in some hard to reach place. For example, there was an ember you had to get in the lava fortress place to wake up a blacksmith, That's been moved.
All in all, with the revamped layout of everything, it almost feels like a new game. I can't speak for the DLC, but I would imagine they would have tweaked some things in there too.
Heres a Pros and Cons list for those who love TL;DR
Pros
-New enemies
-Improved layout of everything from enemy postitioning and compotistion to items
-Minor geographical changes
-Dlc included
-Improved netcode, you never feel alone
-Improved graphics, and I'm sure mods will come out to enhance them further.
Cons
-If you bought the original version and the DLC's paying another 30 bucks feels pretty steep
Even if you own the original version, I still reccomend upgrading, as the new layout of the game is so much better, it feels like a new game almost. The price point will sting a little, but at least they didn't make you pay the full 50.

Gone Home is a game that makes you think, and then re-think what you've just experienced. Not many games can do that, and Fullbright shines when it comes to telling an excellent narrative. Stories told through items you find in your home often are far more intriguing and captivating than a story told linearly. It's often the times between finding objects you begin to question why, how and where are things going with the unseen characters in the story. Who are these people? What are their own stories: the ones that are being told when you read between the lines.
Gone Home captures atmosphere, mood and everything that was the early 90's, a time period I look back on that was full of childhood wonder. In this game, the reason for why rooms are the way they are, some in shambles, with curiosities littered everywhere create a verbose tale of intrigue.
The soundtrack in this game is incredible, the atmosphere is thick in sparseness, with subtle audio cueues and music that define the characters even more. Chris Remo's score is perfectly paired with the ambience of the house. An ambience that is befitting a rainy Friday evening.
Gone Home is everything I've ever wanted in a gameand a story, as it provides an incredibly intriguing, multi-layered, multi-faceted experience. Even on the second playthrough, I look forward to the commentary tracks, and stopped to analyze more of what I had thought I'd seen.
There is no other game like this one, it is an incredible experience and a work of great craftmanship. I give it my highest recommendation.

So, from what I've seen, there are two widely "pushed" stances on this game (and the way I see it, it does qualify as a game, and more so than something like Dear Esther, to use the other commonly contested example... but I'll get to that in a second). The first stance is that the game is a masterpiece, a beautiful work of art or whatnot, etcetera. The second stance is that it's a pile of dung, not worthy of anyone's time, completely overrated, preachy, etcetera. I'll get to why I think both stances are, more or less, valid (although as usual... are exaggeratively spouted with too much "excitement" if you know what I mean).
I'm not going to spoil much more than the first 5 minutes, as Gone Home is obviously heavily story driven. The game is experienced through the shoes of a college student who has just returned from a trip around Europe, and arrives home expecting to see her parents and little sister... only to find everyone away/missing. So basically you walk through the house, finding out what's been happening over the past year or so that you've been gone. It's sort like looking at a bunch of memories, both via your interaction and exploration (although, yes, exploration is a term I use lightly) and the audio journals that are peppered throughout the game.
That's all I'm going to say. While I can't address the reasons for the "preachy" complaint without explicitly detailing the tale's central struggle or issue if you will, I will say that I didn't really get too much of that vibe personally. It really WAS just conveying a story, in my eyes. And this is coming from someone who is even admittedly a little zealous when it comes to "hipster disdain" and a dislike for these so-called "arty" games and that sort of thing. I still didn't find it particularly preachy; take from that what you will. I also don't want this style of game to become "the norm" in a million years. But hey, isn't that what it's all about? Variety is what makes this kind of game stand out, even if it's not to one's particular liking.
So honestly, both of those aforementioned stances are valid and both are completely subjective. A lot of that is really in the eye of the person playing. Personally, I'm somewhere in between, though leaning somewhat towards the former. I don't think that the game is a masterpiece, but I do think it's heartwarming, and I also think that the manner in which they chose to tell the story is well-suited *to the story which is being told*. On the other hand, yeah, in retrospect on the COMBINATION of short length and actual gameplay depth of the game, I probably would've been♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥if I'd paid full price. That's absolutely NOT to say the game should have been longer OR deeper; I think it is the perfect length for what it is doing and the story it tells. The pacing is good, which brings me to the reason or reasoning for the differences between this and Dear Esther.
Dear Esther is literally just Point A to Point B, with a convoluted narrative that, for me at least, DID seem very preachy and kind of dumb. Gone Home is really more of a interactive diorama that kept me focused, intrigued, and occupied during the two hours I spent with it. It feels properly paced, and like it actually has something worthy to say. If you, as the player, want to learn about this family through all the stuff lying around the house, you can. If not, you can just play it like Dear Esther (sort of, although you'd still get a better and less boring tale, I think). But that's the key in and of itself; you have that choice.
All in all, if want to sit down for a couple hours and have an interesting, "quieter" experience, then I'd say you should give Gone Home a shot, especially for say 5-7 bucks. But again, 20 is really just too much for this. I don't like the price to length argument or pretty much any of it's variations, but 20 bucks just really seems *kinda* crazy. Again though, good experience if you're open-minded and not having an amped-on-caffeine-ready-to-play-twitch-shooters kind of day.

This is FPS as historical simulation, not your typical shooter. The battlefields are vast and beautifully rendered, and picking your way across no-man's land can be a harrowing experience, like playing whack-a-mole as a the mole, but worth it once you and whoever is left of your squad finally run amok inside the enemy trench-complex (anyone can be a spawn point so, as long as someone made it across, you can spawn into a trench assault). Being squad-based, it is very much a team-sport, so take a minute to review squad roles before jumping in, but it's not that complicated. The main thing is, follow your NCO (and unlock a rifle if you're unhappy with the default load-out; there's a rifle for almost every class). Overall, I am genuinely impressed by the way that historically informed squad roles, pitted against each other across a huge variety of landscapes, can make for such well balanced game-play. 5 stars.

Really short game, but one of the best written games I've played. There is a lot of realism here: from the way the characters talk, to what you find as you search the house. The game delievers on its purpose: an interactive story about a twenty-year old student coming home from a visit abroad to an empty house. Where is everyone? Guess you better go look for them...
This was first recommended to me by a friend who is typically not one to discuss emotions, and he called it an "emotionally impactful story." While that phrasing might be too strong, I did find the story to be important and well delivered.
It also is a great replica of the 90s. I grew up in the early 2000s, but the mixture between "I remember that when I was 6" and "Oh gosh I remember that!" makes me think that those who were born before me would enjoy this games aesthetics even more.
While maybe not worth $20 (the writing sure is worth that, but the gameplay...since there really isn't any gameplay...not so much), getting this on a Steam Sale is worth it. Not the best replay value, though I know I want to bring my friend over who doesn't typically like video games and have her walk through this interactive story.

This game is a new and refreshing addition to the FPS market. With the WW1 style guns and mechanics, it brings originality, difficulty, and entertainment to the end user. The simplicity of this game makes it easy to dive right in and enjoy. The learning curve is very sharp, as traditional shooters tell you to run and gun right into the face of the enemy. You will learn right from the start that your life is precious, and you will be in frustration everytime you die. However, it helps you reflect on your (game) life choices and refines your FPS style and strategy. Visuals are good, not amazing, but that is what you expect from an indie game. Very proud of the developers for making so much with what little they had. As far as bugs, glitches, etc, you won't find many which helps entertainment. I would like to see 1) Squad size from 4 to 8 as that is military standard, 2) game sizes from 16v16 to 32v32, 3) Some sense of accomplishment in the grand scheme of the game (campaign mode, like in Rising Storm). Overall, in the indie market, I would give this a 9/10. As the game matures, I can only imagine the lengths it can go.

No, I didn't love the game. Yes I'm giving it a positive review. With the "buy it on a sale" caveat.
Ignore for a moment the intense polarizing views that were created mainly because (perceived) expectations were not being met and let's view this game as what it is. This is an interactive story: video and sound together with some gaming elements (walking, point&click) are exposing a simple story in small increments. The subject matter (teenager-dom and gay love, peripherally touching on friendship, relationships with parents and divorce) is not original, but still underrepresent in commercial games, and for that it deserves praise. I personally found the central story relatively shallow and cliche, but I appreciated the way the game tried to create immersion by tying the storytelling to various types of every day items and types of communication. If you are an American who grew up in the 90s there are also some nostalgia elements you may enjoy. The controls are fluid and intuitive, the graphics are lovingly detailed and the sound effects are well done (though I didn't really get the unnecessary emphasis on creating a haunted house atmosphere with the sound design). Yes, I found the full price slightly high, but catching it on a sale should by now be easy.
Interactive storytelling (really interactive, taking full advantage of the medium) is still at its infancy. This game is one more attempt at it. And while it's flawed, it's a stepping stone towards a  new genre of games. It gets a positive review from me, because it is good at what it sets out to do: create a detailed slice of the world of a specific family at a specific point in time. It is also a project of love and that shows in the details, and gets it some extra points as far as I'm concerned. So provided you don't pay full price for it and you understand what this game is, then yes, it can be an enjoyable experience.
And here's a tip: I consider Papo & Yo a more succesful attempt at doing mature storytelling in an ineractive way that fits the medium. If you are interested in seeing a different take at interactive storytelling, give that one a go too.

This is an excellent game. Even though Dino D-Day isn't that popular, the game has some good and bad thigs things about it. First of all, the different classes are very creative and fun, especially in the Axis. You can control a variety of different dinosaurs like the velociraptor and the compsognathus. The velociraptor can leap on people and will kill the oppenent and kill them if someone can't shoot it off in time. The compy (Compsognathus) will go and take out peole. If they get 3 kills, they can run at the enemy and explode with devastating power. Those are just a few of the creative dinos and what they do. The Allied classes are pretty cool too, though I thought the Allies could have had one or two more classes, but that's just nitpicking. There are some great map designs, (Other then T-rex maps, talk more into detail later.) I still haven't found all of the good sniper spots yet. The only bad things I can think of are the graphics, and the ultimate kicking-butt-and-taking-names-dinosaur, the T-rex. The graphics are meh, but can be easily overlooked after a few rounds. The T-rex, though incredibly awesome, isn't that great in game. At times he seems overpowered, but at other times he seems too weak. I think it's mostly because of the design of the maps with the T-rex. In one map there is a huge open expanse where there will either: A. Get slaughtered by snipers, the machineguns, snipers, etc. or B. Get to their base and slaughter them. It doesn't bother me much because I play the maps without T-rex, so I can't comlain much. The only other thing wrong is how unpopular this game is. When the servers start to empty out, there can sometimes be only 5 people total on one of the many servers there are. Like most other games, it's only fun when there are lots of other people. So I recommend you get this game and fill up the servers.

Overview: This game is shockingly good for a F2P game. But.......
Pros:
-Large Weapon selection
-Many in-game items can be permanently purchased with in-game currency.
-Not as grindy as most F2P games
-Classes can actually benefit each other
-Solid visuals, lots of options for low-end platforms
-Game could be best described as a cross between COD and Crysis
-Co-Op missions are satisfying and a breath of fresh air.
-Guns handle well (except for shotguns)
-Community usually manages to behave better than COD
Neutral:
-Gear unlock progression is largely randomized (my engineer gets showered with awesome gear while my rifleman still has yet to unlock more stuff)
Cons:
-Shotguns are either laser cannons or nerf guns depending on how the hit detection feels about them at that particular moment....
-Lag is not always present, but when it is, it will ruin your day.
-Hit detection sometimes feels spotty.
-Hackers exist here
-People often play like COD tools (spawncamping etc.)
-Sometimes feels too much like a twitch shooter
TL;DR
-The game is pretty solid quality for a F2P game and if you're looking for COD-style game with more teamwork and less hackers, get into this immediately. However, go in with the full knowledge that this is a F2P game and your expectations should be adjusted accordingly.

An absolutely brilliant open-world action game in which the laws of physics are thrown out the window and insane stunts occur with impressive regularity.  The bozarre story and impressivley bad voice acting leave something to be desired, but combined with the game's ludicrous action the whole thing feels like an 80s action movie, which is kind of charming.
Of course, you can also just ignore the story altogether and go explore an absolutely massive island, driving motorcycles off cliffs while shooting at planes in the sky above you, tying an enemy jeep to the ground at 80mph and watching it flip over and smash into a tree, or discovering secret bases in the mountains and coming up with perpetually more elaborate ways to blow it up.
If you're a Grand Theft Auto or Saints Row fan, this is a must buy, because it takes all the reckless driving, huge world, and unecessarily large explosions to a whole new level.

This game is out of some nihilistic nightmare.  A constant tug-of-war of malicious violence across meaningless landscapes dotted with artillery craters and barbed wire.  In a way, surviving the horror is as challenging as killing other players.  You should expect to die... a lot.  C'mon, it's WW1.  The most brutal war ever (if WW2 hadn't stolen it's thunder.)  Yet there is a sense of satisfaction in jumping from cover, slowly advancing in the face of almost certain death with your squad- and team-mates.  Pushing on because at the very least you'll make a target for a shooter which may allow your friend to get a foothold in their lines.  Diving into a crater as a split second later bullets whiz over your head.
Then, your attack fails!  The enemy is counter-attacking and you must retreat and hold the trench line.  On defense it's easier not to die if you hunker down tight, but without poking out to shoot some guys you risk being overrun.  It's better to fight the opponent when they're in the no-man's land and you in the trenches; thus it is equally worse fighting the enemy when they "share" the trenches with you.
Your death is usually not glorious.  Crawling forward up a ditch, finally making it to the enemy lines.  Inch my way around a corner only to be shot in the face by a machine gunner who's been expecting me all along.
It's fun to play as an officer and call in mortar strikes or gas clouds.  Having a scope is a huge plus for long range, but it's size makes the weapon a challenge to use effectively in close quarters.  Sometimes it's fun to play a grenadier with 5 grenades and a shovel and charge at the enemy trenches and bombard them!
The controls are a bit wonky.  Sometimes I swear I've reloaded my gun, but the animation never finished or something I did interrupted the reload.  A German solider runs over the hill. I click on him and nothing happens. Without a bullet, he bayonets me.
You don't always know if going prone while moving you might give up at crouch instead.  Thinking I'm going prone I "dive" into a crater, only to get wack-a-mole'd by a stray bullet with my head popping out like it shouldn't have been.  Actually a dive animation would be really cool (*hint hint devs*)(maybe OP though).
It also sucks when not enough people are on and I can't find any meaningful games to join, so I'm writing this instead. You should buy and play because the game only gets better with more people (50 vs. 50?! hell yeah!)  The squad and class system is really cool, and the career upgrade system works well and contributes to the variety of the gameplay.  Finally, I'm extremely impressed with the realism of the game: bullet-drop, every weapon historically researched, traditional uniforms.  The experience is both an FPS and a trench-war simulator, only adding to the unique challenge Verdun offers.

This review is based on 50 hours of almost straight gameplay (yeah, I know, I just could not get off of it).
Graphics:
- tessellation (check e.g. Things Betwixt rocks before going to Majula)
- improved textures (all NPCs, monsters and it looks to me some weapons too)
- improved lightning (especially in darker areas, you actually need to use a torch!)
- better (softer) shadows (combined with above makes some areas astounding - e.g. The Gutter)
- better effects (weapon buffs, spells, world effects, "flowing" fire/sparks from torches and stuff)
- looks absolutely amazing in 4K on GTX 970, constant 60fps (with v-sync).
Level design:
- challenging and a lot better enemy placement that makes sense!
- no "difficulty in numbers" as everyone was afraid
- better item placement
- you actually have to find DLC keys instead of having them in your inventory since the beginning
- many areas reworked with different paths to get somewhere (using petrified monsters)
- several new mechanics to get something/open something/conquer something
- tons of new challenging invading NPCs (great fights!)
- some new items (I have not found them yet myself, so take this with a grain of salt)
- new lore, emphasized especially on item description
Performance:
- generally better performance
For all this I did not pay that much (I also sold some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ steam cards of which I have no use anyway), and if it can help the appearance of some next Souls games on PC, I am glad I did.

There is no time limit, no threat, no impending doom (despite how rough that storm can get outside), and the puzzle mechanics are little more than exercises in memory. Like other minimalistic plots (such as those found in the Half-Life series and Souls series), Gone Home has a core narrative that is strong enough to carry the game, but grows stronger based on how much you invest into its exploration. Are you going to spend more than a few hours playing it? Maybe you will, but you probably won't. So buy it on sale. But try not to miss it. I'm glad I didn't.

This game is a classic, now mainly played by the older community (probably because they didnt like the changes to CS:GO)  due to things such as the original buying system for weapons etc. Changes from the original counter-strike include things like.. Improved graphics and physics. You can now smash through some crates, computers and plenty of other items littering the levels. Glass, when hit by a bullet or knife, only falls away in a small radius around the point of impact, so it now takes another bullet or somebody jumping through the frosted effect of the cracked remnants to make it through completely. You can no longer penetrate two-foot walls with bullets, and a grenade going off on the other side of a wall will no longer hurt you anywhere near as much, but you can still send bullets through boxes, cupboard doors and the like. Water now splashes visually as well as audibly, giving the defending side on maps like Aztec a bit of an advantage in locating intrepid aggressors. And hostages are now capable of following you without getting stuck so easily. Like the old game - the community is very large and extra's are available for download, such as maps/textures and mod's for those who own servers.
The best thing about counter-strike source is the gameplay, which is fun, quick and hard to stop when you are good! You can however.. easily load the game, play for 20mins and stop (but still feel addicted to come back and play again whenever you feel the need to shoot some players). The maps give you multiple but limited choices to how you approach each round and which way you're going to run, paired with the fact each time you can choose a different gun and see if your opponents have changed strategy as well! If you're reading this review - I'm suprised, it's an old game but well worth playing still, I reviewed it as it's my first review for steam and one I know the best (trying to slowly get a badge or whatever, lol).

I really enjoyed this game. Wait, "game" really isn't the right word -- It's more of an interactive experience. It's hard to write a review about Gone Home without revealing  too much, and the experience is best enjoyed without preconceptions. Here's what you need to know:
- As the protagonist, you return home to find your family's house empty, and you have to figure out what happened.
- It's short. I finished it in 80 minutes.
- Sarah Grayson, the actress who does the main voice in the game, does a phenomenal job and really brings the character to life.
- It's not for action die-hards or people who are easily bored. It *is* for those who love a good story, exploration and a mystery.
- And finally, it's a great example of how indie games are revitalizing this medium, even as triple-A games succumb to Hollywood-itis.
If all of this sounds like something you might enjoy, get it now!

This game is an experience in storytelling. There is something to bed said about a story told almost solely through items you discover, and the journal of a girl being read aloud to you by her disembodied voice. There are no characters to see, they don't exist in a physical sense, but you will be immersed in a world that is so very vivid, one fleshed out for you by small notes, cassette tapes, and Sam's commentary. I got wrapped up into Sam's story, into her life and her love, her struggles and her successes, and the ways I found myself relating to her. You won't regret becoming invested in her.
The atmosphere of this game screams 'survival horror' in a sense. Massive, old house with secret passages, a house that is vaguely implied to be the scene of some sort of horrific occurrence;  exploring, alone, on a dark, violent stormy night. In fact, I was worried most of the game of some sort of cheap jump scare, a ghost or a bloody scene, but it never came. That's, of course, not the point of the story, but my exploration was punctuated by the tenseness I felt, and the quiet, unsure fear of what each room held. There's something to be said about a game that creates an intense atmosphere, fills the world with details (labelled videotapes and Super Nintendo games? Nostalgia) and tiny things to discover, and just...lets you roam free.
Let's just say, for the second hour of the game, I was near tears. By the end of the game, I was crying. This game constricted itself around my heart in a way no other game ever has, especially one this short. It actively blurs the lines of narrative, of the ways to tell a story, and it succeeds - many games have, but this one holds a place for me because of the simplicity of the story and the masterful execution of telling it. Simply put, this game is an experience.

Alrighty, after seeing all the polarzing reviews, I think it's fair I give out my honest opinion on the game.  Thankfully, for all you Souls fan, it's a positive one.  Initially I was pretty skeptical about the changes, especially towards the beginning, as there seemed to be quite a bit of enemy spam.  However, while there is a lot of enemies, their placement wasn't there to be cheap, but rather more difficult and feel more like an army, as with the game's lore there was a battle thad taken place there.
Little things like that, are pretty consistent throughout this game, the areas feel more lived in and alive, and also the enemy placement is a LOT more exciting in many locations.  There is a lot MORE enemies as well, so there's less 1v1 with easier enemies...but more with stronger enemies, which feels good, but very different from what you'll be used to.
Now for returning Souls players, there isn't THAT much that is new in the ways of content, there's a new enemy or two and a new boss fight....that's about it, but the with the new placement the game feels pretty fresh, especially after the first area, that is different, but not as dramastic as later locations are.  Hell, Royal Rat Authority is a good boss fight now, who'd have ever thought that would be a thing?
I think I can safely say, if you're skeptical about the game, it's worth the money if you feel like re-experiencing Dark Souls II.  It's different enough to surprise you and if you're getting into the game for the first time, the enemy placement really is awesome.  Plus the game is quite long, especially for first time players.
A word of warning though, there is the Durability Bug and as far as I can tell wonky hitboxes at 60FPS.  You can limit your frames to 30 FPS (It's not as disgusting as it sounds, honest) and these aren't issues, but they are worth noting, because it does break the game in that regard.  Hopefully you found this review helpful.

So I just finished the game - I'd say it was about 2-3 hours of actual gameplay.  Personally, I really liked this (glad I bought it at sale price though).  A few warnings however - if you are under the impression that this is in any way an indie horror game or something (I know some were), you are mistaken.  This game is more about delving into the lives of one specific family, mostly concerning the younger sister of the player character.  Technically speaking, I was pretty impressed with the way the game was put together - the graphics, soundtrack, and interactability of the environment.  You're essentially wandering through your family's house (they moved there while your player character was away in Europe) and what a LARGE house it is (to me at least).  I guess the caveat about this game is that if you can't get into the story or really care about the family/characters you're learning about - you'll find it to be a snore, nice graphics and atmosphere notwithstanding.  Oh also, this game is VERY 90s.  It takes place in 1995, and I'm sure it was somewhat specifically aimed at people who were growing up around that time (that doesn't mean you can't enjoy the game if you weren't, if you like exploring huge old houses and learning about the lives and problems of a family, then you'll still like it).  I can understand why people considered it a "love letter to the gaming community" of sorts.  It is very personal, and there is a lot about it that people can relate to.  Some would say the story is "cliche'd" and if that's there opinion then I won't fault them.  However it read to me as more "relatable" or "nostalgic" with enough depth of characters to make it really enjoyable, and even pull on the heart strings a bit.  Of course, your mileage may vary, but hopefully the reviews can help you decide if you want it.
