There's something extremely uncomfortable about the experience of Gone Home, it's not executed well enough to make you feel entitled to search for your family's whereabouts by sifting through their personal items but you have to do it anyway if you want this to be anything but a walking simulator. So you are essentially forced to pry into people's lives and listen to incredibly personal, emotional confessions and thoughts. I did not respond well to this.
Another thing thaty killed Gone Home for me was the realization of how absurdly tiny the game is. It takes place in a mediumly sized two-story house with a basement, and when you actually travel from one end of it to the other it's a very depressing realization.
The game is short and the only thing that keeps you from flying from one end of the house to the other is constant the reading and listening that the diary entries, scraps of paper, and audio logs you find require. Any sense of interactivity is a total illusion, watching a youtube video for this game is almost the same as playing it.

Whether or not you enjoy this game is largely about your expectations going into the game. I had read a number of reviews before I played it, which meant I had a good idea of what I was getting into, prior to deciding to try it. Simply put, this is a first person exploration game - you arrive home after a year abroad. Your parents and sibling have disappeared and you are wandering around your empty house trying to find out what happened to them. There is no combat. Nothing is going to try to murder you (probably). You walk around and you try to figure out where your family went, based on the clues they have left all over your house. Full playtime is only about two or three hours for your first time through.
If all of that is all right with you, the game provides some really excellent nostalgia for the 90s, a great atmosphere and several engaging storylines.

Alrighty, after seeing all the polarzing reviews, I think it's fair I give out my honest opinion on the game.  Thankfully, for all you Souls fan, it's a positive one.  Initially I was pretty skeptical about the changes, especially towards the beginning, as there seemed to be quite a bit of enemy spam.  However, while there is a lot of enemies, their placement wasn't there to be cheap, but rather more difficult and feel more like an army, as with the game's lore there was a battle thad taken place there.
Little things like that, are pretty consistent throughout this game, the areas feel more lived in and alive, and also the enemy placement is a LOT more exciting in many locations.  There is a lot MORE enemies as well, so there's less 1v1 with easier enemies...but more with stronger enemies, which feels good, but very different from what you'll be used to.
Now for returning Souls players, there isn't THAT much that is new in the ways of content, there's a new enemy or two and a new boss fight....that's about it, but the with the new placement the game feels pretty fresh, especially after the first area, that is different, but not as dramastic as later locations are.  Hell, Royal Rat Authority is a good boss fight now, who'd have ever thought that would be a thing?
I think I can safely say, if you're skeptical about the game, it's worth the money if you feel like re-experiencing Dark Souls II.  It's different enough to surprise you and if you're getting into the game for the first time, the enemy placement really is awesome.  Plus the game is quite long, especially for first time players.
A word of warning though, there is the Durability Bug and as far as I can tell wonky hitboxes at 60FPS.  You can limit your frames to 30 FPS (It's not as disgusting as it sounds, honest) and these aren't issues, but they are worth noting, because it does break the game in that regard.  Hopefully you found this review helpful.

I was entertained and engrossed by this title, but I wouldn't call it a game per se, I'd call it an interactive story.  It's doesn't branch as far as I can tell, it just uses a first person perspective and an interactive environment to draw you into the story, which unfolds as you explore the environment.  It's brief, you can finish it in a few hours, but it does a nice job of making you want to finish the story.
I don't know if it's worth 20$, but as a 5$ on the summer sale, it was a nice diversion.  As an experience, it is like sitting on the porch on a Sunday afternoon, and reading a nice book. I think if it were presented as an interactive story, it'd be a much more accurate way of selling it, but I don't know if it'd sell as well as describing it as a game. All that said, I wouldn't mind seeing more entertainment like this, as I enjoyed the time I spent in the story. If you like stories, you'll like this title, but if you need your games to convey a sense of accomplishment, or grant you a victory of some sort, you may want to give this a pass.

This is a great change from the shooters we have been receiving recently. Where as other games are taking a futuristic approach to war with advanced technology and skills, Verdun takes you back to the early 1900's with an authentic feeling WWI feel.
Currently there are 2 different game modes to choose from, Frontlines, which is a squad based, team oriented game of capture the trench. In this game mode you must push the opposing team back out and away from their current holding and claim it as your own, or else they will be doing the pushing. The unique aspect of playing Frontlines is the aspect of attack and defend, and how it is handled as the rounds play out. If your team loses their hold on the trench, you are required to fall back to the previous trench and defend from there, hoping not to take a bullet in the back upon retreat. The active objective trench acts as a boundary where both sides can enter and fight for the claim by having more soldiers present (unless teams are unbalanced, this is compensated for). Teamwork is a MUST for a squad/team to succeed.
The other game type is a free-for-all Rifle Deathmatch, which it just what it sounds like. There are no worries of someone out-gunning you simply because they have bought a better gun or other concerns. Rifle Deathmatch is a true test of skills where everyone has a bolt action rifle, the same amount of ammo, and no individual has an upper-hand based on what you have in-game. There are some options, such as, the type of rifle (all authentic era styles) and very basic attachments. Would you rather have a bayonet for a 1-hit-kill melee, or perhaps a ranged scope for better distance shots? There are pros and cons to either choice.
All-in-all I rate this game very highly, and would recommend it to anyone and everyone who enjoys the FPS genre, it's a good change from the fast-paced shoot'em ups we have become accustomed to

This is not a game in the traditional sense. There is no obvious goal, there is no antagonist, there is a house, and a diary. The point of Gone Home isn't to challenge any skills that you have built up, it's not meant to scare you either. The point of Gone Home is for you to feel and experience a story. I am going to try to avoid as many spoilers as possible in this review, because I feel that it is best experienced in its entirety in one sitting if at all possible.
to be honest there is very little gameplay to be had, I would even go as far as to call it an interactive movie. Scholar of the first sin is an upgrade for DS2. The changes Fromsoft made here are significant enough, in my opinion. It resulted in a more challenging and interesting experience over the old version.
I'll try to explain why, focusing mostly on the gameplay experience. there's also a TL:DR at the end.
I'll also mention that I judge this game from the perspective of a returning player with 240+ hours spent on DS2.
This is the first reaction I had when I saw some of the new enemy placements. I'll try to avoid getting into spoilers, but let's just say that if you are a returning player you are in for some surprises. They've not just changed a few enemy locations here and there, some areas have a different layout of enemies now.
It seems that Fromsoft also tried to make some of the areas more dense, so you'll end up fighting against more than one enemy quite often. They also went out of their way in some places to hide enemies better (
)
There are also some new invaders and some of the old ones have a new place which their invasion triggers from. Also, it seems now that enemies will chase you further, so running away is riskier.
I was also happy to see some of the bosses appear as a mini-boss in some areas, for instance
and more.
All of that made me play kinda like the first time, checking every corner, advance slowly and pulling enemies with my bow as much as I can. Every zone have something new that wasn't there before, so it felt like a fresh experience going through them again.
Some of these new placements also make sense lore wise, for instance,
, which are all good additions.
All in all, these changes makes the game more challenging than the DX9 version. Expect to die more.
Another thing you'll notice that some items are not where they used to be. Some of those changes are actually great, like
. Those changes are not such a big deal as the new enemy placements, but it does help to this feel of a "fresh" experience.
The maximum amount of online players in a single session have been increased, you can have up to 5 phantoms in your game (gold/white are at the maximum of 3). I've joined the Heirs of the Sun covenant as soon as I could in my playthrough and in some cases when I got summoned the host had another 2 phantoms with him, making the boss fight kind of a joke. But it's still fun. Invaders should really watch out though as 4 vs 1 is a thing now.
Yep, the graphics are now better, but only by a slight margin. The lighting engine is better and a torch is more necessary in dark areas, but it's still doesn't look like the old 2013's E3 trailer. To be honest, the DX9 version with GeDoSaTo and other visual mods still looks better than this version (I also miss clean UI mod :-(  ).
I wish that there were more graphical options so that we could get this version to look just as good as the old version with GeDoSaTo… but the video options are exactly the same as in the DX9 version.
Fromsoft advertised this version as the "definitive edition", and as such I feel like they could have done more with it.
For instance, the 60 fps durability bug is still in the game (praise the Bracing Knuckle Ring),  the hitboxes could use some more work (I'm looking at you Smelter demon !) and some little things like more information about the covenants (information on the rewards, the ranking etc… I know it's all on the wiki pages but why it can't be in game ? ) are still missing.
But the thing which hurts the most is the fact that the two versions of the game are incompatible. You want to move to NG+ (or beyond) in this version with one of your old characters from the DX9  version ? nope, can't do that.
You want to play Coop with a friend that have the DX9 version ? nope, can't do that either as they are running on different servers.
The latter is actually pretty bad as it ends up splitting the community, which I can't imagine why Fromsoft thought was a good idea.
It really makes me wonder why this version couldn't just come out as an update to the DX9 version or at least be compatible with it. It's not like it's not possible, plenty of games give you the option of playing in either DX9 or DX11.
+ New enemy placements makes the game feel fresh and more accurate lore wise.
+ The new enemy placements and invaders makes the game more challenging.
+ Some of the new item placements are a welcome change.
+ The increase in maximum online players in a single session is fun, killing a boss with 4 players is kinda hilarious.
+ The graphics are slightly better than the DX9 version with a better lighting engine (without mods that is…).
+ If you don't own the dlcs or the DX9 version, the price is worth it.
- The 60 fps durability bug still exists.
- The fact that we now have two incompatible versions of DS2 is not good. You can't transfer your old characters from
the DX9 version to this one and it also divides the community as both versions runs on different servers.
- It had more potential. For a "definitive edition", Fromsoft could have improved the game in many other areas. From making more accurate hitboxes to giving more information about the covenants or even giving more graphical options and so on.
I enjoyed it for what it is. As i wrote at the start I feel like the changes they made are significant enough and it lead to a more challenging and interesting experience that also felt fresh. Just bear in mind that this is merely an upgrade for the DX9 version and it should be treated as such.
I'm kind of disappointed that it's not compatible with the other version and it really makes me wonder why it couldn't just come out as an update. The discount options are nice and all but I totally understand why people are not willing to spend 20$ or more on an upgrade for a game.
But I think it should be judged on whether I had fun with it or not, and in the end of the day I am enjoying it so that's why I recommend it. Make no mistake, this is the better version of the game.

What an extremely pleasant surprise. I was skeptical about this, as pure exploration games can be hit or miss. But I caught it on sale, and knowing that it included artwork by Emily Carroll made me curious enough to bite, and I'm so glad I did.
I finished it in one extended sitting, but not because it was short - though it was that. I did so because it just drew me in. Admittedly, the subtle use of 90s nostalgia was a factor in getting my attention, so people who did not grow up in the 90s may have a different experience. But even without that, it stands on its own.
Yes, all this game does is story, but it does it so well. The writing, atmosphere, and voice acting are exceptional. It really triggered genuine emotional responses in me, and I'm not ashamed to say I teared up a little at the end. That is an amazingly rare occurrence.
Gone Home is very up front about what it is from the start, it's all in the description. So if this isn't your kind of thing, you already know that. However, if you're receptive to this kind of gameplay storytelling, I would strongly recommend it.
Edit: While my feelings on the game itself have not changed, it is worth mentioning the sort of behavior the developers are known for engaging in. Banning users and deleting comments in the Steam forums for criticism and disagreement, using twitter blockbots to block out anyone who follows people they disagree with politically, that sort of thing. If that matters to you when purchasing games, be aware.

2, January 1915
Today I received my platoons orders, we were being shipped to the front just outside of a French town called Verdun to protect our lines from the Germans. After supper I climbed on one of the tables and told the lads to gather round. One by one they slowly shuffled in looking up at me in a gaze of curiousity. "Well boys, we're to be headed to the front." A round of hollers screeched out as to suffocate the fear that had just been bestowed upon my men. "Enjoy tonight. Drink hardy lads. Tomorrow we leave." I climbed down from the table and made my way out of the mess hall and hurried home to my wife.
20, February 1916
The boys are rambuctious. We can all since the fighting will start soon. We've had small squables between us and those Jerry ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. I lost my first man today in preparation for what General Petain called, "The turning point in the war." Our blood had begun to boil with all this waiting and teasing. Why havent they attacked us? Why havent we attacked them? I miss my wife dearly and cannot wait to leave this desolate wasteland and return to her warm bussom.
6, March 1916
Jerry has been flogging us hard for what seems like forever those stubborn ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s wont let up. My original platoon has been devastated. James, Robert, John, William, Jack, Peter, Roy, Louis, even little Billy are all dead. Those of us that are still here dont even bother with the replacements, they dont last long. Our trench is muddy but not from the rain. A solid two inches of blood runs from one end to the other mixing in with the soil causing it swollow anything that weighs more than a shell casing. Its lined with the mangled as they wait to be sent back to safety and leave this god forsaken place. We've become so low on supplies that to keep the trench walls up we have had to resort to the use of bodies and dead horses. The stench is so overwhelming it almost drives me to death. I could just charge over the trench and rush towards my sweet and bitter escape from here. The only thing that keeps me going is the thought of you, my dearest Mary, oh how I wish I could return to you. I long for the aroma of your hair, the touch of your oh so soft skin pressed gently against mine, will I ever return home to you? Will any of us leave this blood stained place? I can hear the sound of shelling in the distance, soon the sounds of horns and men screaming will echo throughout the line as the Germans charge towards us only to be cut down like they have some many times. Death has become such an accustomed part of life that I fear life without it. I fear so much but do not fear death. Death would be a welcoming suprise to me embracing me in its warmth and freedom. Will I leave this place? I most certainly will, dead or alive, I will leave this place.

Scholar of the first sin is an upgrade for DS2. The changes Fromsoft made here are significant enough, in my opinion. It resulted in a more challenging and interesting experience over the old version.
I'll try to explain why, focusing mostly on the gameplay experience. there's also a TL:DR at the end.
I'll also mention that I judge this game from the perspective of a returning player with 240+ hours spent on DS2.
This is the first reaction I had when I saw some of the new enemy placements. I'll try to avoid getting into spoilers, but let's just say that if you are a returning player you are in for some surprises. They've not just changed a few enemy locations here and there, some areas have a different layout of enemies now.
It seems that Fromsoft also tried to make some of the areas more dense, so you'll end up fighting against more than one enemy quite often. They also went out of their way in some places to hide enemies better (
)
There are also some new invaders and some of the old ones have a new place which their invasion triggers from. Also, it seems now that enemies will chase you further, so running away is riskier.
I was also happy to see some of the bosses appear as a mini-boss in some areas, for instance
and more.
All of that made me play kinda like the first time, checking every corner, advance slowly and pulling enemies with my bow as much as I can. Every zone have something new that wasn't there before, so it felt like a fresh experience going through them again.
Some of these new placements also make sense lore wise, for instance,
, which are all good additions.
All in all, these changes makes the game more challenging than the DX9 version. Expect to die more.
Another thing you'll notice that some items are not where they used to be. Some of those changes are actually great, like
. Those changes are not such a big deal as the new enemy placements, but it does help to this feel of a "fresh" experience.
The maximum amount of online players in a single session have been increased, you can have up to 5 phantoms in your game (gold/white are at the maximum of 3). I've joined the Heirs of the Sun covenant as soon as I could in my playthrough and in some cases when I got summoned the host had another 2 phantoms with him, making the boss fight kind of a joke. But it's still fun. Invaders should really watch out though as 4 vs 1 is a thing now.
Yep, the graphics are now better, but only by a slight margin. The lighting engine is better and a torch is more necessary in dark areas, but it's still doesn't look like the old 2013's E3 trailer. To be honest, the DX9 version with GeDoSaTo and other visual mods still looks better than this version (I also miss clean UI mod :-(  ).
I wish that there were more graphical options so that we could get this version to look just as good as the old version with GeDoSaTo… but the video options are exactly the same as in the DX9 version.
Fromsoft advertised this version as the "definitive edition", and as such I feel like they could have done more with it.
For instance, the 60 fps durability bug is still in the game (praise the Bracing Knuckle Ring),  the hitboxes could use some more work (I'm looking at you Smelter demon !) and some little things like more information about the covenants (information on the rewards, the ranking etc… I know it's all on the wiki pages but why it can't be in game ? ) are still missing.
But the thing which hurts the most is the fact that the two versions of the game are incompatible. You want to move to NG+ (or beyond) in this version with one of your old characters from the DX9  version ? nope, can't do that.
You want to play Coop with a friend that have the DX9 version ? nope, can't do that either as they are running on different servers.
The latter is actually pretty bad as it ends up splitting the community, which I can't imagine why Fromsoft thought was a good idea.
It really makes me wonder why this version couldn't just come out as an update to the DX9 version or at least be compatible with it. It's not like it's not possible, plenty of games give you the option of playing in either DX9 or DX11.
+ New enemy placements makes the game feel fresh and more accurate lore wise.
+ The new enemy placements and invaders makes the game more challenging.
+ Some of the new item placements are a welcome change.
+ The increase in maximum online players in a single session is fun, killing a boss with 4 players is kinda hilarious.
+ The graphics are slightly better than the DX9 version with a better lighting engine (without mods that is…).
+ If you don't own the dlcs or the DX9 version, the price is worth it.
- The 60 fps durability bug still exists.
- The fact that we now have two incompatible versions of DS2 is not good. You can't transfer your old characters from
the DX9 version to this one and it also divides the community as both versions runs on different servers.
- It had more potential. For a "definitive edition", Fromsoft could have improved the game in many other areas. From making more accurate hitboxes to giving more information about the covenants or even giving more graphical options and so on.
I enjoyed it for what it is. As i wrote at the start I feel like the changes they made are significant enough and it lead to a more challenging and interesting experience that also felt fresh. Just bear in mind that this is merely an upgrade for the DX9 version and it should be treated as such.
I'm kind of disappointed that it's not compatible with the other version and it really makes me wonder why it couldn't just come out as an update. The discount options are nice and all but I totally understand why people are not willing to spend 20$ or more on an upgrade for a game.
But I think it should be judged on whether I had fun with it or not, and in the end of the day I am enjoying it so that's why I recommend it. Make no mistake, this is the better version of the game.

Before I start with the negatives, it is fair to state the positives. This game is one of the few co-op games that faces you with hard enemies so you have to work with your team in order to make your way through them. I have to say, this game is one of the best team based games I've ever seen. It is an FPS (First Person Shooter) co-op based on skill and teamwork and I recommend you give it a shot by all means.
Well, the game was enjoyable which is why I invested my money in it but now I cannot recommend it. Micro transactions have taken over the game and the money and the XP rewards were cut in half; which means you have to pay for a double XP card (VIP) to get what was originally free of charge.
Also, the latest challenges are extremely hard which requires the use of tokens dah! Yea I know, it is expected of a FTP (Free To Play) game to charge you money, but then, you might find yourself spending $10 over one match against AI which I consider a crime and trust me, I hate to brag but I am considered one of the best players in co-op; after all I spent 600 hours playing only co-op matches. Back then, I used to get decent rewards out of the missions which were worth the time I spent on. But now what you get is far less than what you pay for.
Furthermore, you cannot own what you purchase for a long time. That's right, you have to pay a monthly subscription for each piece of equipment you purchase which is ridiculous.
The game has bugs and the voice chat is broken so you have to use the chat window or Teamspeak to communicate with your buddies. I mean come on! The game's most essential aspect is teamwork and you need voice to communicate!
Still, if you fancy co-op games then you should give it a try after all it is free but not free to enjoy for too long. I spent a decent amount of time in it back when the game was rewarding. Now I don't feel like paying VIP only to get what I used to get when the game was free.
I think this game was a life changer for me, reminding me that FTP games will never be perfect. From now on, I swore to only play purchased games like CS, COD or BF4 which provide 100 of weapons and mods that I do not have to rent with my hard earned money only to have an edge over my competitors.
If you like walking around and exploring places learning their story then this game is for you. If you are expecting something of a supernatural nature, maybe you should look somewhere else!

I held my hands over my head as artillery shells exploded around my trench. Dazed, I staggered forward, one goal in mind. "Defend the trench!" my mantra repeated, beating a tattoo into my consciousness. I reached my pillbox. Crouching, I blew my whistle. My men soon came to the pillbox, posting up around me. Shots rang from my gunner as he killed another enemy. "All clear!" I slowly raised myself until I could see out of the makeshift window. I saw movement in some of the underbrush. I called in a mortar shot on that position. Crouching again, I waited, each passing second an eternity.
...........
A small hiss rose into earshot. I wondered what it meant as my gunner shouted "Grenade!" The word was not even out of his mouth as a bright flash errupted just outside of the pillbox entrance. I was knocked senseless. Two things crossed my mind as I faded into darkness; my family, and how I would never see them again, and my joy as I heard my mortar shell strike home. The screams of my enemies became a lullaby as I drifted into oblivion.
10/10

Very fun game to play, reviews are pretty low but from what seems to be very early release date gameplay.  Which from what I have read seemed to have many problems.  Flash foward to 2013 when I picked up the game during the Christmas sale sometime that I don't remember, then to 2014 when I finally gave it a try.
Well even though I don't remember what I payed for it, more than likely less than $5 after a few hours in it earned at least that much in laughs and enjoyment.  Plays alot like Day of Defeat source, arcady FPS with those great rad doll physics.  Maps are small and are very open allowing flanking and spawn camping.  Models and graphics are dated but when you played Wolfenstein when it came out that doesn't really bother you too much and the fun factor outweighs any of those problems.
My initial playtime was pretty much all Allied team which to me seem very outmatched to the Germans, dinos are hard to hit and when you do manage to hit em your bullets seem to do little damage to even the poodle sized ones.  And in that time you get the gun totting dinos or the pesky kraut soldiers gunning you down while you run in circles spraying the ground in vain to kill the gnashy clawed and grenade armed compy from making haggis out of your entrials.
After getting the hang of the game the Allies still seem underwhelmed, now the Germans with the mighty dinoforce may seem very overpowered after the thrashing I took at their hands and claws.  Well I will say they take some practice to get the hang of, but after a bit steeper learning curve with the strengths and weaknesses of the dinos you can cause some havok.  After a few games with the compy I went on a hide and hit and run tear with him maxing out his grenade  damage by shredding Allies one after another using speed and small stature to hide and strike.
Now I may be biased to deem the teams unbalanced, and I don't seem to be the only one to have that opinion.  That doesn't stop me from playing either side.  Down the road it may even out with more Allied dinos or maybe up the weapon damage but the game is fun to log in and play for an hour or so.  The dinos have special abilities like grabbing a goat or downed soldier and chomping him or tossing him back at his comrades as a ranged weapon.  You can even get a chance to play as the fearsome T-rex  on certain maps.
And did I mention the dinos can pee on command, yes when ever you what at a push of the key, no more tea bagging here.  Straight up dino urine in yo face sucka!!  Is it worth buying...Yes, fun to play...Yes, are there servers and ppl playing....well as of 03-01-14, a few servers and a handful of dedicated players who love this game.  If you have a chance to get this game that will be one more person playing and by telling your friends that's a few more, unless you don't have friends then it's time to play Dino-D-Day and make some.

"Dinosaurs in my WWII shooter?" is something you might say upon reading about this Source Engine FPS, but aside from solid gameplay and interesting playable "classes" the dinosaurs are fun in more ways than one. In a world full of WWII shooters there is seemingly no end in sight. While Dino D-Day might not be the most interesting game ever, it's alternative universe brings to us a Nazi army equipped with dinosaurs with various methods of lethality. While this prehistoricly altered timeline offers an interesting twist on the old Allies against Axis formula, some of the game seems a bit unbalanced (which could just be me plainly not being terrific at Source games). Regardless of some seemingly stronger dinosaurs, Dino D-Day provides a skillful and fun experience which always seems to come with the use of the richly endowed Source Engine.
Through the hours spent playing this game I found that I had two favorites and luckily they were split between teams, so I did not have to worry about being stuck on the more historicaly "accurate" Allies. Maps are well detailed and supply alternate routes to remove standoffs and suicide pushing, but much of the time these routes are overlooked for the high traffic areas. Overall, this game shows us a roaring good time, and who could say no to playing as a T-Rex with machine guns strapped to it's head?

Dark Souls 2 is a arpg game where your go on an adventure and explore a mysterious and dangerous world.
You will die often. But its okay.
The game want you to learn from your mistakes and will reward you for playing carefully.
The difficulty of the game may seem high for new players, but the more you play it, the easier it get. There is also some in-game mechanic that allow you to decide how hard the game will be.  Things like classes, or conveent will change that.
A Melee character may struggle where a ranger or a mage could easily destroy all his foes.
And Some conveent will allow you to receive hel from Npc/ Other players. While other will make you a target or will disable help from others.
There is a very high amount of weapons and armors. also Magic, Pyromancy, Miracles, Hexes.
All of these options give you infinite combinations possibilities.
You could be a Heavy Two-handed sword mage, Or a Fireball throwing Theif with a dagger.
The choices are infinite.
Sadly, some weapons are outright better than others and while they don't really disturb when you clear the main game. It can be a problem when you want to play only to pvp. You will often see people all using the same weapon, for instance a katana, because it is simply the best option to win.
But in Dark souls. Skills Beat Stats. So a skilled played should not fear an overpowered build.
Story in darksouls is scatered and vague. Most of the explanation you will get it from Item description in your inventory.
It doesn't shove its story down your throat. You follow it if you want. and ignore if you don't care about it.

To start this review off, I don't exactly approve of the way From handled this game. But that being said, the remaster, or as I like to call it, the reshuffling is worth your money in my opinion. The new enemy placement involves practically brand new enemies that were barely used in the base game. The main enjoyment comes from relearning the game, and figuring out the new AI, which is implemented on some new NPCs and enemies. Alot of items have been moved around as well to better match the environment they're located in. The item placement does allow practical easy mode, as you have access to very powerful weapons early on, should you be careful when exploring.
Map design is largely the same, which is a shame. But the few times they made a change, it is very noticeable and well needed, like a new shortcut in No Man's Wharf.  As an exception, The Gutter as I felt, is largely overhauled which is funny as it was one of the better designed areas to begin with. No changes have been made to bosses at all, no new moves, AI or anything, sigh.
Online seems to be a bit more fluid, although this might just be a placebo effect. Large scale multiplayer (3 white phantoms + invaders) works flawlessly without any sort of hiccups, so bonus points there.
Graphics have been improved as well. The game looks better of course, but you could achieve the same or better by using GeDoSaTo and an ENB with the base game. But if you're not into that stuff, it's a pretty good improvement. The most noticeable change is definitely the particle effects and lighting. Particles seem smoother and the bloom effect has been improved, as well as sprite animations. Torches have meanings in particular areas now, not as much as I'd hoped for, but still alot more than before. Many areas have altered gamma/contrast and color correction.
All that being said, if you don't own normal DaS II, buy this game. If you do, buy this game. If you own both the base game + DLC, I still recommend getting it for the new experience. I have played two game cycles so far, and there are different changes in NG and NG+.

It took me a while to 'get' Dark Souls. Having played a ton of RPGs, I found it difficult to put aside all the actions I had learned from playing them, and then having to start from scratch with a DS game. Once I realised how to play the game differently from all the others there was no stopping me. I had originally started with DS2 (dx9) but had hit the same roadblock. Now, having bought this version I'm ready to step in again, staff in hand and homing soul pew hovering over my sorcerer's head, living (or should I say hollowing) to fight another day.
SotFS in some ways is different to the original what with enemy placements, loot locations etc. The vast majority of the changes are welcome (I'm looking at you No Man's Wharf), and I only have one or two minor grumbles to mention. I'm just hoping there isn't another Sen's Fortress type of area otherwise I might cry a little.
I kind of understand the grumbles about the new version. Having said that I'm a big fan of From Software and happy to throw my money at them. I don't care if I get hate about this. We're all entitled to our own opinions.
In addition to being a fantastic game, here's a FWIW section ....
*Enemy placement. Having played some of the original I still had held its mental model in my head. So of course, I am having to start from scratch which is great. The game is keeping me on my hollowed toes.
*Music. Matoi Sakuraba is amazing. I listen to the DS music a lot when not playing and hearing the music played while fighting a boss is an amazing feeling!
*Environments. Really interesting environments with nooks and crannies to explore, secrets to find, and enemies to run away from!
*Coop. I love summoning and being summoned by other players as there's still that sense of jolly cooperation. I would also like the option to have my summon only available to friends too. To have the choice would be good.
*Meaningful NPCs. Dark Souls had the endearing Solaire, whose story (for me at least) was emotional. I feel that DS2 lacks an NPC of this calibre and would love to experience that sense of 'I must help this person!' in the game. That said, I'm only 20+ hours in so maybe there is an NPC who is as endearing as our wonderful Solaire.
*Soul memory. I just really dislike the feature. It makes me mindful of acquiring souls so I don't out-soul my friends if they are offline. Soul level would be a better indication of coop. Yes, I know there's the Agape Ring but I would still prefer the choice.
If you are new to DS2 then I am confident you will love this game. If you want tips, here are some that a DS friend told me that helped.
- Slow and steady. This is my mantra when playing. Entering a new area? Turtle up, and walk forward slow and steady.
- Try all classes. If you're unsure or finding a particular class annoying, play around with other classes until you feel comfortable with the gameplay. It took me a while to realise I love sorcery. I seriously fecking love sorcerers :D
- It's OK to cheese. It's not cheating, it's being strategic. If you played DS, remember that knight in Undead Burgh? He can't climb ladders. Try luring it out .... :)
- Leave/rate messages. Drangleic is a harsh and unforgiving world. Leave helpful and/or funny messages for your fellow hollows to help them on their way (ambush right, don't give up!). Also rating other players' messages will restore some of their health. You never know they might be fighting a boss when you are rating. More of an experiment in interactive storytelling then an actual game. It proves that complex characters can be created without a hint of a cutscene or (in the case of three of the four family members) a voice over. The mystery that drives the player forward focuses mostly on your missing sister. That story is fairly standard and without surprises, however it deals with mature issues and handles them well and with respect. However it is the parents story that was the highlight for me. The parents are more complicated, nuanced, and in the case of the Father in particular - both sad and redemptive.
For the right price, it's worth playing through to see how this experiment in story plays out. Approaching it expecting anything other then an interactive story could lead to negative reviews from frustrating players. Also, be warned that the story does focus on mature subject matter (and by mature I mean it literally, not in the M rated content that populates the games of the last couple of generations) and as a result young players will likely not be able to relate to what is presented here and find the whole exercise rather boring. Again that isn't the result of poor writing or a bad story, but simply due to the fact that 14 year olds aren't going to relate to a game that takes place before they were born, has references to the X-Files, and deals with a marriage in a slump and a teenage girl finding and experiencing love.
However for the right audience, the game will resonate deeply and create a lasting impression. A truly unique game that stands well apart from pretty much everything else out on the market. A great experience, if not a great game.

In short, your millage with SoTFS will very depending on how much you want to run through Drangleic again.  The enemy revamp and larger phantom party is the big draw but you probably won't notice the graphical update.

Gone Home has an engrossing story that's mildly depressing.
It's a short game, but worth the extra exploration of observing objects to gather an idea of what is going on with the protagonists' family and their personal lives. The central character that you gather info on is your sister, Sam, whom is supposed to be home, but is gone...home. Get it? She's gone from her home, that's why the game is called Gone Home; that, and the house is completely empty of human life, except for you, Katie, the elder sister/female protagonist.
I do commend the writing and narrative that the developers took the time to flesh out. You get a proper character examination through finding documents, how your father is a struggling writer, your mother is a newly named Forest Conservationist, and promiscuous. And your sister shares a revelation that Katie probably knew about, but shares her emotional experience through the narration.
The graphics are modest and humble as they're clearly not the centerpiece of the game, it's not drooling in high resolution textures or particles like Metro 2033, but the models and lighting and textures get the job done. The audio is near perfect, from the ambient soundtrack that plays at a minimal volume, to the harrowing narration, and the 90's grunge music played by some local Portland bands. Gameplay is about as simple as it gets, walk around and click on stuff. Really, you can pick up and examine coffee mugs and ask yourself ten seconds later, "Why did I pick up that coffee mug? Is this a dream? No, this is what my life has become."

Gone Home has an engrossing story that's mildly depressing.
It's a short game, but worth the extra exploration of observing objects to gather an idea of what is going on with the protagonists' family and their personal lives. The central character that you gather info on is your sister, Sam, whom is supposed to be home, but is gone...home. Get it? She's gone from her home, that's why the game is called Gone Home; that, and the house is completely empty of human life, except for you, Katie, the elder sister/female protagonist.
I do commend the writing and narrative that the developers took the time to flesh out. You get a proper character examination through finding documents, how your father is a struggling writer, your mother is a newly named Forest Conservationist, and promiscuous. And your sister shares a revelation that Katie probably knew about, but shares her emotional experience through the narration.
The graphics are modest and humble as they're clearly not the centerpiece of the game, it's not drooling in high resolution textures or particles like Metro 2033, but the models and lighting and textures get the job done. The audio is near perfect, from the ambient soundtrack that plays at a minimal volume, to the harrowing narration, and the 90's grunge music played by some local Portland bands. Gameplay is about as simple as it gets, walk around and click on stuff. Really, you can pick up and examine coffee mugs and ask yourself ten seconds later, "Why did I pick up that coffee mug? Is this a dream? No, this is what my life has become."
8.0/10

This is an amazing game.  You play the part of a young woman who has just arrived home after a year of travel abroad, to an empty house.  The gameplay consists of exploring the house (more of a mansion), reading things, finding things, picking apart the backstories of the rest of the family and discovering what has happened to them.  There really is nothing else like it out there.  The experience is short, but well-paced, and everything is very well-written.  Some people have complained about the length of the game, but really, it is just right for the experience.  There are many brilliant aspects to the story and storytelling that I cannot get into without spoiling them for others; but suffice it to say that it will keep you intrigued from beginning to end.  I recommend sitting down to play this game on a weekend, when you have about four or five hours of uninterrupted time to complete the story in one sitting.  If you want a mindless diversion (which isn't a bad thing), look elsewhere; but if you want an immersive, unique experience, if you want a smart, character-driven narrative that can only be conveyed in the medium of a video game, if you want to be drawn into the world of a troubled American family and their mysterious house, play this game.

Going home is a simple yet rewarding game that occupies your mind for a few hours. The story is uncomplex and the narrative is a homage to games in the like of The Stanley Parable.
It's pro's are:
Graphically the game performs well and is nicely optimised for smaller systems, allowing for a realistic gameplay that is not hindered by clipping or lack of detail.
The storyline is short but sweet, with few twists and turns, but very immersive.
The game is easy to play for all ages, but takes a more adept mind to pice together the events unfolding.
Cons:
Small amount of gameplay, it is a point and click that has a single ultimate goal, which is a shame as the game has a lot of potential.
The objects in drawers etc. lack reality, and although work seems to have been done to create a realistic atmopsphere, more could have been done.
All in all, for a cheap few hours of walking around in-game and listening to a lovely female narration, I reccomend this game for a play-through at least once, and if you are open to all types of simulation, then Gone Home should tickle your fancy.

Masterpiece No. TWO!  Praise the sun.
From Software followed a simple principle. Never give up.
It is hard to elaborate on the different aspects of this game solely as this is a remastered version.
Luckily I have waited especially for this version, before playing Dark Souls 2 at all.
Certainly this makes my impressions much more positive,
in terms of what DS2:SotFS has to offer.
But lets be fair. This remastered version is of outstanding quality.
Everyone had hope that DS2 will be as good as its predecessor.
And with this version, they defintely fulfilled this promise.
Of course, the pre-release version was graphically much more intense.
Maybe this will be possible in Dark Souls 3, someday. That is ok.
However, the graphics are this good, they make you jaw drop every now & then.
They have put so much fine-tuning into their shaders,
making DS2 sometimes looking like photo-realistic,
especially metal surfaces with the DDoF.
Instead, a lot of angry gamers seem to downvote this game. Is this fair?
Not at all.
DS2:SotFS defines CRPG at a new level. With its flaws!
It is not the mere technical aspect, which makes this game amazing.
It is how it has been put together.
Art, design, ambience, various game elements, game play, one gear fits to another.
From Software reveals a gap between its Dark Souls series and the other RPG competitors.
Skyrim looks like a uncharitable jester beside DS2.
Of course, Elder Scrolls are modable games, and thats their main premise.
They can get better, and better, but slowly, with a lot of CTDs, work and effort,
but certainly not at 60 FPS, out-of the-box, on medium hardware of today.
DS2:SofTS is even this good, just after its release, Red Project,
which has delayed its already better-than-Skyrim Witcher 3 over and over,
announced a DLC/Season Pass for Witcher 3.
Red Project feared that everyone would forget about them.
There are the Aws and Ohs.
But why is noone able to give proper credits to this game?
Imho, DS2:SotFS is far too complex to be reviewed and rated all at once. No one can.
You will need time for this game.
And thats exactly the point where I started to appreciate Dark Souls.

This is one of the best games I have played in a long, long time. There's no violence, there's no button mashing, it's just you in an empty house - and not just any empty house, a house with a story to tell. In photographs, notes, and behind loose panels lies this story. It took me a few hours to get through the game, and I enjoyed every single moment of it.
The story was... I don't have words for it. It isn't really your everyday story, it's different, and some of us might have seen similar stories around us in real life, or in movies, or whatever, but this story from the viewpoint of a third-person... it left me speechless.
It's realistic, original, and I couldn't help but shed a tear by the end of this. A certain section of people might enjoy it more than everyone else, a certain section will not enjoy it at all. It isn't really for everyone; some people won't relate and they'll dismiss it for lack of suspense or whatever, but this game has shown me that a story can be told in a straightforward manner, without turns and twists, and still be enjoyable.
Buy it, seriously, it's like $4.99 now and worth every cent.

This is a charming game that feels like a brief modern Myst minus the puzzles. It's an interesting experiment in storytelling, where your mostly voiceless protagonist explores her family's home, looking for clues as to where they went. The house is old and foreboding. Things are not what they initially appear to be.
This is a game that could easily be spoiled by too much explanation, but suffice it to say that players looking for an interesting exploration of character and the human condition will be much more satisfied than those seeking action or adventure. There is very little plot, yet the simple gameplay is always engaging. Your imagination and fear are often your biggest adversaries. I'd recommend this game to anyone who enjoys offbeat or unique games piping with atmosphere. For frame of reference, I found Journey on PS3 to be beautiful but a tad underwhelming. This provided me with more of a nostalgic sensory experience than that game, but unlike with more linear and action packed experiences, your enjoyment will vary greatly based on your mindset, suspension of disbelief and imagination.

Should you buy this game?:
>Do you own Dark Souls 1?
-If no, buy it instead. It is still the better game.
-If yes, did you like it?
>Yes:
Do you own Dark Souls 2 and all the DLC?
-If yes, don't buy this game or wait for a sale.
-If no, or like me, you don't have the DLC, this is a better deal because this is a slight improvement on Dark Souls 2.
>No:
If you did not enjoy Dark Souls 1, you will not enjoy any iteration of Dark Souls 2, as it is like Dark Souls 1 only slightly worse in most areas except for the DLC levels which are slightly better as a whole. Therefore, your money is better spent somewhere else.
What's Changed from the Original Dark Souls 2:
-Graphics are slightly better but still are a bit dated. Character models are notably improved. Some textures in the base game levels still look like cat vomit. DLC levels are downright beautiful.
-You don't have to purchase the DLC levels. However, to access them you must find keys to unlock the doors to them. Fortunately, there is a Steam Guide for that. Don't forget to get the Gyrm Shield, Flame Crest Ring, and a bow for when you descend imto the fire salamander pit of doom for the Old Iron King's key.
-Enemy placement is on the whole improved. This was a pleasant suprise because from the trailers and interviews I was afraid they'd just spam ten kajillion enemies and put random OP enemies all over the place for no logical in-universe reason just to meet FROM's annual murder quota. However, the enemy placement mostly makes sense. For example, one really can't find fault with putting Heide Knights and  a fire-breathing dragon in Heide's Tower of Flame where the Dragonrider lives. Additionally, there was generally an attempt to make the game "smarter" not "harder." For example, in the Forest of Fallen Giants in the area where the Heide Knight was, there are now substantially more Hollows, but they are all laying down and awaken when you get near them. Therefore, if you proceed carefully, you can fight them one or two at a time and not be ganked by the mob. Notably, while most areas are more difficult as a whole, the Shaded Ruins are quite a bit easier as you will no longer be ganked by Lion-O and the Thundercats three steps into it. Generic enemy AI has been improved a bit and it is more agressive, but we still aren't talking Deep Blue levels of intelligence here.
-There are quite a few new NPC summons and invaders and their AI really is good. They Fashion Souls it up, use gestures, and often use clever tactics. The new summons are genuinely useful and the new invaders can be a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥(in a good way). However, the old NPC AI hasn't been improved, so Lucatiel and Benhart can seem a bit derpy after you've summoned the awesomeness that is Bradley of the Old Guard or Sellsword Luet.
In conclusion, this game is worth your money if you enjoyed Dark Souls and either do not have Dark Souls 2, or have it but not the DLC. However, if you already have both the original game and the DLC then it goes from "good deal" to "borderline ripoff" territory fairly quickly since the core of the game remains fundamentall the same, and you should therefore wait for a sale.

I'm not going to go into too many details here - there's plenty of reviews already that point out the flaws in this game and question the high ratings it's gotten from critics. I'm just going to share my personal experience.
I watched Gone Home's price drop and go back up for awhile. Finally picked it up ($5 is a deal!). The game left a lot up to your own imagination. I would hear a creaking floorboard or thunder rumbling and panic. I turned on every light and left every door open - always worried a door I know I left opened would suddenly close.
This isn't your traditional game. I wouldn't even call this a game at all, but an interactive novel. I think a $20 price tag is incredibly steep (especially considering I beat it in less than 2 hours). To be honest I feel like $5 is still a little steep, but I found myself invested fully in the lives of this family and the question of where everyone went and don't regret purchasing this. I tend to become more emotional though in general in books, games, and movies. If you're that type of person I think you'll get a lot more out of this "game".
Take this "game" as you will. Go in empty: no judgements, clean slate and piece together this family and their troubles, issues, and attempts to reconcile their lives. I think the problems in this family - what each member is facing and how they work to reconnect with each other - people will look at and say to themselves I understand what they're going through, I've been there. While I can't say I've had to face the issues the characters have the story is brought to life in such a way you feel that emotional shift, their highs and lows. One minute everything looks bleak and dark, and than the phone rings or you get a letter in the mail and it's like the sun is shining just for you, everything comes together.
Long review short: I really can't justify the $20 price tag, but if you can get this for under $5 give it a shot. I'm sure you've spent more on far worse during a Steam sale ^.^

"Gone Home" is a simple game. You are the oldest daughter of a family that moved to a new house while you were on a long European vacation. You arrive at your house, only to find that it's completely empty. It is night, and it's raining, the house is spooky, and you have to find out what happened to your family.
While there aren't really many traditional "puzzles" in "Gone Home" I found that I didn't miss them. It is a real achievement that the Fullbright Company was able to create a game that feels engaging without a traditional mechanic outside of exploration. Honestly, as someone who was fascinated by the world of "Myst" as a kid, but who never had the patience for the sometimes arbitrary-seeming puzzles, I think there should be more games like this.
If gaming is really about becoming other people and exploring what that's like, or going places you could never go in reality, I don't see why it should be any harder to imagine yourself as a young woman coming home to an empty home than it is to imagine yourself as a "chosen one" running across walls in Ancient Egypt, or whatever. There's a lot that is really valuable in "Gone Home," if you give it half a chance.
In contrast to most games that I play, which can sometimes feel like they are sapping my life (like Civ 5, or TF2), I actually felt refreshed after playing.
"Gone Home" is short, which means that it could be played again fairly easily, but I wouldn't expect to have much of a different experience the second time around. I feel like if I did return to "Gone Home," it would be in the same way that I would return to a favourite short story.
There was a moment that made me jump out of my chair and turn my computer off—and while its memory "charges" the rest of the playthrough, "Gone Home" isn't a game about jump scares. It's a simple game about family drama, very elegantly executed. If you're a bit of a voyeur and you like snooping through people's houses (and if you love nineties girl/garage punk), you will love "Gone Home."

Should you buy this game?:
>Do you own Dark Souls 1?
-If no, buy it instead. It is still the better game.
-If yes, did you like it?
>Yes:
Do you own Dark Souls 2 and all the DLC?
-If yes, don't buy this game or wait for a sale.
-If no, or like me, you don't have the DLC, this is a better deal because this is a slight improvement on Dark Souls 2.
>No:
If you did not enjoy Dark Souls 1, you will not enjoy any iteration of Dark Souls 2, as it is like Dark Souls 1 only slightly worse in most areas except for the DLC levels which are slightly better as a whole. Therefore, your money is better spent somewhere else.
What's Changed from the Original Dark Souls 2:
-Graphics are slightly better but still are a bit dated. Character models are notably improved. Some textures in the base game levels still look like cat vomit. DLC levels are downright beautiful.
-You don't have to purchase the DLC levels. However, to access them you must find keys to unlock the doors to them. Fortunately, there is a Steam Guide for that. Don't forget to get the Gyrm Shield, Flame Crest Ring, and a bow for when you descend imto the fire salamander pit of doom for the Old Iron King's key.
-Enemy placement is on the whole improved. This was a pleasant suprise because from the trailers and interviews I was afraid they'd just spam ten kajillion enemies and put random OP enemies all over the place for no logical in-universe reason just to meet FROM's annual murder quota. However, the enemy placement mostly makes sense. For example, one really can't find fault with putting Heide Knights and  a fire-breathing dragon in Heide's Tower of Flame where the Dragonrider lives. Additionally, there was generally an attempt to make the game "smarter" not "harder." For example, in the Forest of Fallen Giants in the area where the Heide Knight was, there are now substantially more Hollows, but they are all laying down and awaken when you get near them. Therefore, if you proceed carefully, you can fight them one or two at a time and not be ganked by the mob. Notably, while most areas are more difficult as a whole, the Shaded Ruins are quite a bit easier as you will no longer be ganked by Lion-O and the Thundercats three steps into it. Generic enemy AI has been improved a bit and it is more agressive, but we still aren't talking Deep Blue levels of intelligence here.
-There are quite a few new NPC summons and invaders and their AI really is good. They Fashion Souls it up, use gestures, and often use clever tactics. The new summons are genuinely useful and the new invaders can be a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥(in a good way). However, the old NPC AI hasn't been improved, so Lucatiel and Benhart can seem a bit derpy after you've summoned the awesomeness that is Bradley of the Old Guard or Sellsword Luet.
In conclusion, this game is worth your money if you enjoyed Dark Souls and either do not have Dark Souls 2, or have it but not the DLC. However, if you already have both the original game and the DLC then it goes from "good deal" to "borderline ripoff" territory fairly quickly since the core of the game remains fundamentall the same, and you should therefore wait for a sale.
Both the base game and the mods  for it have served me several years for several hundred hours of fun.

Nevertheless... it's a Souls-game. The new enemy and item placement give this version more the feel of a new game, rather than just a simple graphic-overhaul (which it was taken for by most people, me included).
--
What else is there to say? I mentioned it already - it is a Souls-game. So its hard. Maybe not quite as hard as the first Dark Souls, but still a challenging game all in all. It is precisely this difficulty that make this series so special. Grinding yourself against a boss, learning its each and every move until you can finally take it out and gain your well earned souls, if maybe only to replenish your losses. Overcoming the obstacle and feeling the rush of finally succeeding is what makes this series so special for many people.
Also sporting a fairly obscure method of story telling, not giving away too much about the history of the country you are passing through or the intentions of the people you meet on your travels, makes for an experience you will remember. And no matter what others might try to tell you... there is a story to this game, but it is up to you to find the hints and fill in the little gaps that remain.
And remember... no matter who you meet and converse with in the land of Drangleic - they might just be lying.
--

If you already have the original release, it's worthless. The new items and enemy placement doesn't do enough to make things really fresh. But at least, is it the better version for those who haven't played the original release ? I don't know. I might be jaded simply because of how used I am to the old one to really notice how better it might be and while I do see some improvement, more diversity in enemies mostly, there are also some degradations which irates me.
The original often swarmed you with enemy instead of being difficult hrough interesting design. It was improved in some areas, such as the corridor to Velstadt, and worsened in others. In Iron Keep, players used to pull enemies with arrows to deal with them away from archer fire. Now the enemies automatically aggro to you, you just have to wait for them in line and kill them as they come, while the archer is now in front of you instead of behind. I suppose From Software wanted us to save our arrows but it doesn't strike me as good design, it only strikes me as being an admission that the level design doesn't allow for good gameplay. So does the moving of some furnitures to make the path clearer to find, or maybe it's just that From Soft doesn't trust its players. That's not even mentionning some new placements directly endangering important NPC. It's utterly ridiculous, how no dev thought some of these new placements might be problematic eludes me.
Even imagining that the changes were always for the better, it doesn't even fixes the flaws of the original. A lot of enemy still spin around like boomerang on crack thanks to some truelly ridiculous auto-tracking which forces you to abuse invicibility frames, IE go through the attack rather than evade them through smart dodges. Why is that still here ? It already bad enough that too many enemies have sweeping attack that cover too much ground to be avoided through smart placement, but they still auto-track like a compass.
The way forward from the beginning of the game is still rather obscure, I presume some still won't be able to find the Emerald Herald for she stills blends in with the goddamn tree. Licia of Lindelt still is a problem, placed where so many wouldn't think to go. These are potentially huge issues, the kind forcing players to go fetch a walkthrough to know where to go. Not fixed. The weapon degradtion glitch born from the fact that the game runs at 60 FPS isn't fixed. I presume it would all recquire too much effort. The graphical overall is rather meaningless, especially on PC. Some effects have more bloom. Some areas are made artifically darker. It's paler. It's not the trailer Dark Souls 2, it's still the gutted Dark Souls 2 with the same small areas linked together nonsensically with some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t lore making the whole atmosphere of the game much weaker than its predecessors.
Is it a good game, is it fun ? Yes and yes. Is it worth it ? Probably, if you haven't got the original. But let's not mince words here : this is lazy. Some of the changes are cute, some are dumb, in the end though Dark Souls 2 still feels like a botched job, even with this new edition. A good and fun botched job. But still not the game it should be.
I still love it though.

For the Newcomers:
Starting is tough, but as you level up and learn patterns, you will overcome things you thought impossible.
Be patient, use strategy, be aware of your surroundings.
Some areas with tons of enemies can become much easier if you approach slowly.
Tips:
- Running low on flask and durability near a boss door? Drop your co-op sign and help others win the fight, gain souls, restore flask and durability, and restore humanity, all at the same time while warming up for your own fight.
- For melee build players: dont forget to raise your ADP stat for better rolls.
- If you're overwhelmed, lure enemies so you can take them out one by one. Utilize narrow hallways, doors, walls, stairs, ladders, etc. This game will try its best to kill you so no shame in using all the available options to increase your survival.

What could I say about this game that you couldn't say about the original "Great War". This game is a struggle plain and simple. This game will test your will to move on even after you heap the bodies against your enemies trench.
You go to attack pop down a nice screening on the enemy trench of gas. You move forward with your squad bullets whizzing over you head. The craters in no mans land were a stew of waste and bloodied corpses rotting in the heat of the day. You approach the crest of the hill heart pumping the shrill call of the NCO's whistle ushering his soldiers to glory. Glory for what the Kaiser? No the personal glory of ending anothers day on this earth.
You don the gas mask before entering the trench quickly you cant be seen. Slowly crouching your way into the trench. An officer pops his head around the corner to see if his perimeter has been breached. Too late his curiosity is what got him killed. Even as you round the corner your enemy helplessly bleeding out beside you a bullet whizzes by your head from down the trench. You aim down the sites but are too late. Finding yourself looking up at the sky all you can think about is the faces of those you are leaving behind as the life drains from your corpse.
This game is purgatory for the souls of the damned. Forced to walk this earth fighting over narrow strips of land in the hopes of forwarding a greater war effort. A man better than myself said that, "It is well that war is too terrible, lest we grow too fond of it". No better words describe this game.
You are going to hate this game when you begin playing. You will think the game is a bit unfinished as you get shot by a sniper in the bottom of a hole. You will hate this game is you are locked in a struggle not to advance but to hold the line. My friends want to return this game they hated is so much. We perservered, we became a fighting unit that would be the pride of the Kaiser. We advanced time and time again through the gas and into the trenches, locked in a mortal struggle. They began to not hate this game but endure this game.
This game is not COD, Battlefield or any other AAA game you've played. This is a portrait of struggle, a game that rewards few and punishes many. Would I reccommend this game, Hell Yes.

I'm basing this review on having never played the DX9 PC version. Previously, I'd played through the game on the Xbox360. At that time, I was a little sad for DkS2; I thought it was good, but compared to DkS1 kinda, well, boring.  So, I was kinda a bit unsure on whether I should pick this up now I've dropped the Xbox for PC.
First impressions, it's better. Ignoring the graphic upgrade for the moment, which is what I'd expect from a PC game in the first place, I've already had more fun playing this version in two hours than I had in playing the origional version in, god, 80 or something. It's mostly little things, like the enemy AI seems better, the small changes to placement, the fact that, yes, there are some gank squads out there, but so far I've yet to run into one that feels unfair. There are some nice little environmental changes (additional gunpowder barrels, i'm looking at you) that you can use to your advantage. It just feels, in terms of gameplay, more what I'd expect from a Souls game.
The game runs fine, as well (better than DkS1, which, you know, is hilarious) and is nice and smooth right out of the box, although I notcied some graphical and audio stutter in the opening cutscene. Nothing horrendous, but it was eyebrow raising.
So, the graphics...... I'm sure that the DX9 version is just as good with mods, but this looks fine out of the box. The lighting still isn't as lush as that promised by the infamous E3 demo, but there are now areas that are pitch black. It's funny, but I never thought I'd be happy to not be able to see what I'm doing. I'm looking forward to seeing how the gutter plays now (something else I'd never thought i'd say).
As for the durability bug, yep, that's ~very~ obvious. Oddly, though, I don't mind it. Even weider, I actually prefer it. Having to consider the weapons you have and making sure you keep backups adds a nice, if unintended, twist in play.

However, if, like me, you've only played it on last gen consoles, or you've never played it full stop, or you bought it in the xmas sale and haven't picked up the DLC yet, then have no qualms about picking it up.
Although, do yourself a favour, and drop brightness in game down to 0.

After quite some time with this game I have come to give this review some more depth. The first section of this review will be for people that have never played a "From Software" game before and the other section will focus on the controversy surrounding this remastered version
It`s difficult but when you start to come around at the fourth boss or so and get the hang of it`s gameplay mechanics, Dark Souls 2 will drag you into the world and keep you immersed for months. The world is rich with story and detail. The difficulty is always fair and when you finally take down that difficult enemy you have been analyzing for hours you get that satisfaction only DS can give you. From an RPG standpoint the leveling , gear, weapons, dialoug...basically everything is done with such class and confidence that it will be hard to find anything flawed. I know I sound like a fanboy but when a game comes around and gives me a whole new perspective of how I play and enjoy video games. you know it`s something special.
Even if you`re scared of the difficulty I promise you it will be worth it, if you give it time. I too was hesitant about playing Dark Souls in general but oh my how glad I am I did.
Now for the package itself. I do think it`s in general a bad idea to release a remaster in the timespan of less than 2 years. It`s a cash-in, although it was primarily made for the PS4/Xbox One users who got a terrible last gen version of this game. They will certainly experience a much bigger difference in both graphics and performance.
On the PC, the graphical upgrade is nice but DS2 already looked good to begin with. Only noticable change I can see at the moment is the lighting which has improved and actually gives the torch some purpose. With that said. DO NOT buy this remaster for the graphics alone. Not worth it!
Another controversial topic has been the splitting of the community and I do agree that it was a pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥move on Namco`s behalf. This needs to stop. On console it`s fine but on PC it`s different. There are no performance differences between the versions which makes the server split pointless. Alot of my friends have the original DS2 and I can`t play with them simply because of this travesty.
Scholar of the First Sin does come with all the DLC`s which I highly recommend. Go with the cheaper upgrade version for DS2 so that you can have the great Crown of Kings trilogy, if you haven`t played DS2 yet this is the perfect time. The best version by far , but not worth it if you have finished DS2 and the DLC before hand.

Sometime during my time in the trenches, I had met a few guys who seemed pretty nice. We would often hustle a couple rations from the distributioner if we were lucky, and then take them out and eat inside one of the radio rooms. Then of course the general would come in and give us a beating, but we had fun nonetheless. At some point during this time we had to go on an offensive. So me and these guys had to head out into no man's land. And boy what a hell hole. We crawled all the way through, crossing our fingers that we wouldn't get bombed or gassed. Only 2 of us made it. Of course, there was no time to mourn, and in all the action I barely noticed. So me and my last friend, Joe, went into the trenches. We were all scared, sure, but none as much as Joe. He kept muttering something about, "He was right there and then..." I don't know who he was talking about, but I brushed it off, or as well as I could, anyways. We stepped into the radio room, because we heard a lot of talk in there. There he was, a 17 year old boy, couldn't be older, talking to his commanding officer about not wanting to die. Joe just stood there for a second. And another. As he was doing this the boy rushed for his gun. Joe didn't even stir. I quickly raised my gun and shot. He fell dead. Joe fell down into a fetal postition. I had never seen him like this. I didn't ask anything, worried he himself would just take out his gun and shoot himself, as has happened to a few of our men. I stood there for a second, and then just marched on, as it appeared Joe had no intention of going on. I continued in the war, but I never saw Joe again after that day. I always tell myself that, "Maybe he just got switched to a different squad." But I know, that in my heart, he just lay there, to this day, under a small mound of dirt. I can never forgive myself for what I did, leaving him behind, but I had a country to serve.
-Unknown Made-Up Diary

So, there are so many negative comments about this game, and partly I really agree to them.
Selling this new "definitive edition" even for customers who did have to old one is kinda **** and it also divides the playerbase.
BUT on the contrary, I am one of the people having EVERY part of the old game, and I don't regret paying the money.
The game is worth it! (people complaining just don't like Bamco's money making strategy)
Why? Well:
- new enemy placement (which really can give even expierenced players a hard time)
- ****load of new red invaders (which still, are not that hard to struggle with, but meh)
- better/more precise item descriptions (well, if you're interested in the lore, there you go)
- a new endboss plus a better fitting ending if you go that way
- some new items (which mostly look damn smexy, but some are sadly just for the looks *I look at you Forlorn weapons*)
- some improvements to graphics, especially lighting (textures are also a "bit" updated, don't expect a Crysis 3 here)
- further improvements for the multiplayer (more players can invade/coop now, BoB arena actually works like it should   with waiting times from 1-30sec, bell areas now are just sadistic...)
- new white npc summon signs (for new players especially nice, most bosses early have about 2 summons)
- new item placements for almost every essential item (kinda **** searching all those bone dusts and shards again, right? Oh and Great Lance right at the beginning? Hell yeah! Or wanna get to Vengarl early? Gimme my Claymore? Slice people up after 10 minutes into the game? Totally into that.)
- some boss improvements
- FUC*** TORCHES ARE FUC*** USEFUL NOW! (won't spoil any more of that though)
- and so on
- oh wait, did I mention ALL 3 DLC's are in the game (and are actually implemented in the game like they should be)
Cons:
- obvious money maker for Bamco
- some controller problems (for small part of the community)
- weapon durability still has its problems (but really, you can avoid that)
- devided playerbase (but I always am able to connect to people for PvP and Co-Op - even faster than in the original)
So, From did a good job and it really is a "definitive edition". New players definitely should grab this version, and even experienced players will like and should try this.

Finally a good World War 1 game! Experience the great war with all the bolt action, trench warfare, chemical weapon fighting you want! As of this review there are a deathmatch and Front lines. The Front lines game mode requires a little bit more explaining. I am going to quote the wiki here for you guys new to the game.
"Frontlines is the most popular type of match played in Verdun. It is a competition between two teams, one French and one German. Each team has up to sixteen players. Bought this game for my brother who is a huge WWI buff. Have to say it is quite hard starting out, and spotting enemies is a pain to get used to, but after a solid 9 hours of training we figured it out and now we are running headlong into the battle like pros!
Graphics are solid, I am running on ultra settings with my GTX 660 at 70fps average.
The squad system is simple and fun to play with, and the class system is easy to level up and gives a wide range of weapons and tools. Wanna be a sniper and troll unsuspecting runners? Yep got that. Wanna be a camper and mow people down with a machine gun? Yeah got that too. Wanna run screaming across no-man's land with a shovel? HECK YEAH!
There are two gamemodes, Frontlines and Rifle Deathmatch. Frontlines is a tactical nightmare of trenches, explosions, and countless snipers. You really need to think while you fight, or you WILL die fast. A little advice, stay low, keep your head down, stay with your mates, stay low, and did I mention? STAY LOW. Basically just prone the whole time :P.
You shouldn't go anywhere near Rifle deathmatch until you are comfortable with the game, if you just jump in there with no experience, you are basically a free kill for all the l33t snipers.
Ok I guess I have to throw some cons in here somewhere....
Gameplay is a little confusing to start with, and there is no in-game tutorial, just a steam pop-up with a TON of reading.
Picking out enemies on the battle field is seriously hard to master unless you are a god at finding tiny unmoving snipers across the map...
All in all, this is a great game to play with friends and enemies alike. I rate it an easy 9/9

It is important to note that, as many expected, it is - not a sequel to Counter-Strike, but rather the next step in the development of a series of weapons and original game mechanics, gently moved to a new Source engine from Valve.
