Scholar of the First Sin is getting a lot of hate, but honestly I saw this coming a mile away.  These people had their mind made up far before they even downloaded the game.
Yes, they could have released it as a free update, and yes, it would have been appreciated by the existing game owners, including me.  But I do not view charging money for the enhanced edition as unreasonable.  You need to consider that time is money all industries, and especially developers.  Updating the game and adding new features and content doesn't just happen magically, they need tons of man hours to implement the new code, test it, and support it once it has released.  They most definitely considered all their pricing options, and ultimately decided to charge money after realizing that releasing for free was not financially viable for them.  It was either charge, or do not release at all.
More options are always better for the consumer, period.  Simply put, if you do not agree with their decision, you are free to play the original version, which is still supported and even received the new "Scholar" story content for free.
And just to make this review valid to the  game itself, I think it's pretty good.  The DX11 effects look nice, but ultimately do not add much to the experience.  The new enemy placement and story content are what I bought it for, and I am very much satisfied with my purchase.  It's a new experience that is more than just New Game+ over and over again, and as a fan of the Souls series, I appreciate that.

What can I say about this game without giving too much away? Gone Home is without doubt one of the greatest games I have ever played. While neither a long game nor a large game world, it is ultimately a deep, emotional, and rich experience.
The great genius of Gone Home is ultimately its use of its setting: A Family Home in the mid-1990s. It quickly becomes apparent to the player that to explore the Greenbriar House is a highly interactive experience. A huge number of objects in the game-world can be picked up and examined. Most of these objects are small, average things, such as badges and cassettes, which are a real throwback to anyone who was young in the 90s. What Gone Home does skillfully, however, is showing the sentimental aspects to these objects. Even objects such as ring-binders are shown to have attached memories. This emotional investment in such inanimate objects ultimately turns the House into a Home.
Some negative comments have been made about the length of the game in relation to its price. However Gone Home's length ultimately relates to how much the player wants to explore. A high level of exploration is the ultimate reward for the player, as they gain a deeper understanding of the family members, their own trials and developments. One will find oneself truly engrossed in these characters, if they are willing to devote the time to uncover more about them.
It's difficult to discuss the game's story without spoiling too much. The story is Gone Home's most central and greatest aspect. The player takes the role of Kaitlin Greenbriar, the eldest daughter of Terry and Jan Greenbriar, as she returns from a year backpacking in Europe. She finds the house her family moved into during that year empty. As the player searches the house, they discover what happened with the family during Kaitlin's year away, and why her parents and younger sister Sam are gone. The story the player uncovers ultimately debates such themes as love, acceptance, and maturity, with many of the character's stories mirroring each other in some way.
Gone Home is an eye-opening experience. It pushes the boundaries of what a game can be. It will make you laugh and cry, and hopefully make you think a little.

Gone Home is a very linear and quite short game with a minimalist level of gameplay. Many have argued that Gone Home is not a game at all, but more of an interactive story of sorts. I however would argue against such statements. While Gone Home does not have any failstates that I know it still carries some of the more pronounced aspects that makes a 'video games' we all know and love. The freedom to explore and investigate the surroundings with a some level of discovery offer what I would consider being the basic factor of a functional video game. And gone Home offers those aspects just well enough to be considered a game. At least when compared to the boring tube that is Dear Esther what is just plain walking through the narration without any interactivity at all what so ever. But this is not about Dear Yawnsther. This is about Gone Home.
--
Gone Home is a story of young Oregon girl named Kaitlin, who is a daughter of your average midwestern American family (that does not live in the midwest). The Game begins with her returning from a long trip abroad only to discover her home empty and in a level of disarray in the middle of storm,. From that point onwards the player's job is to piece together what happened to her family during the time she was away.
The story of Gone Home is something that divides people to two distinct groups. Those who love the game and those who hate the game. And I can't fault either of those groups as I can see where both are coming from. Gone home is not bigger than life tale of great adventures and events. It is very basic and very down to earth simple tale of a family going through changes in the mid 1990's America. Kaitlin, the protagonist, discovers that what has happened to her parents and her sister while she was gone, and where they are now in both mental and physical way. And what she ends up discovering is a somewhat heartwarming story of trials and tribulations of their daily lives. In the center of this 'unfolding mystery' is Kaitlin's sister Samantha, through who's journal entries she narrates her inner thoughts to Kaitlin whom she trusts more than any other people around her. The entire game's narration is delivered through these random pieces of text and spoken journal entries.
Gone Home offers solid two hours of gameplay during which the story unfolds at leisure pace. To someone like me who likes to take things at a a calm pace it is quite average time. I can definitely see some people running through the entire game in well under hour, as well as I'm sure other people who can spend a lot longer slowly unravelling the story and going through every little minute detail as they go along. How long Gone Home takes to complete really depends on the players themselves and their preferred pace.
Gone Home is a game you'll probably play through once, and leave it at that. It is a one time experience that does not translate too well to repeat playthroughs. But like some movies you really only need to play the game through once. The discoveries made in the game affect how player views the setting of the game and thus after completing the story the player might feel that the ending's "spoilers" take away from possible replays of the game. Or they might be put off by the consequence free resolution the game offers. There is little more to be discovered.
Now, Gone Home is not without it's faults. Many of the things said here can be viewed both good and bad. The specific subject matter of a angsty teenage girls going through self discovery is not a story that translates well to your general gaming crowd frankly. As well as the short running time and minimalist level of gameplay, I can clearly see why some people outright hate this game.
As a side note, Gone Home also offers an unique travel back in time to those of us who lived in the golden 1990's. The game's unique setting in the mid 90's era America is quite intended trip back in memory lane for many players, something that sadly goes past most of the younger audience. From the first thing you see in the game, a loading screen that depicts a cassette tape being wound back, you know exactly what you are getting yourself into.
In closing. I would recommend Gone Home to those who do not suffer from ADHD and can enjoy a boring basic human drama at times. You don't need to be preteen girl to understand the problem angsty teenager goes through in their lives. But I also acknowledge that the subject matter might not be to everybody's liking. At times I too struggled with the narrative this game told. It takes very specific kind of taste to like game such as gone home. Like blue cheese, not everyone likes it.
But for everyone interested, I'd recommend considering twice before getting this game. If you are one of those who like to stop and read random piece of text in game world, or sometimes just stop and look at the scenery, then this game might be for you. But if you are those who couldn't care less about characters in the game and just want the next frag, I recommend staying away from this.
Under no situation I'd recommend buying this game in the full price of 20-some bucks, which is the listing price at the time of writing this. If you can snatch this game under about 5 bucks, then I'd recommend going for it, even if you are not sure if you'll like it. For the 90's nostalgia sake alone, it's worth about that much. But no more.

Like a lot of reviews are pointing out, the way the description offhandedly mentions changed enemy and item placement is very, very misleading. When I bought this version, I was expecting tweaked enemy positions, maybe some extra enemies in the less populated parts of the game. What I got was, in a lot of ways, not the same game. This review is going to mostly focus on what was changed, and why the changes are important. Note that while I'll try to not spoil the changes too much, I'm going to refer to places and bosses in the original game.
Now, I've only played a few hours here and there, so I can only try to go from what I've seen so far. Specifically, I've only gone through both paths to the Lost Bastille, as well as getting past Najka. That said, a lot has changed in these areas. The biggest change so far is that there are just more enemies.
Of course, they didn't just stick extras of the same enemies in the same place, and instead you see a larger variety of enemies. Now, instead of fighting through a more or less homogenous horde of hollows for the first half of the game, you get a mix of enemies. In particular, the larger and rarer enemies are more frequently seen now.
Because of this, the game is honestly just more challenging. For example, the Tower of Flame had it's admittedly low population nearly doubled through the addition of other enemies, so you're never fighting the big guys one on one. To offset this, a lot of the important items have been moved to be more accessible. For example, the Ring of Binding is now in a different, more accessible place, as are Gavlan, the dull ember, some keys, and the Fragrant Branches. In general, if something was easy to miss on a first playthrough, but was important, you can find it much more easily.
On the topic of ease of access, the new branches aren't there to make your life easier. Or rather, they are, but only because there are many more statues to reanimate. There are also a number of new shortcuts in some of the longer areas, like the wharf.
Having only played a few hours of the game, I can't comment on the multiplayer changes beyond the fact that having four people beat on the pursuer was very satisfying. That, and the fact that for coop the bracing knuckle ring is even more mandatory now that there are just more people you can accidentally hit. There is also a bug in the level up window for mouse users, but I have not found this to be a problem given how rarely I level up after the forest.
Graphically speaking, the textures and models seem to be the same, but the framerate has seen some improvement. The real change is that all particles now emit light, so once ENB and the rest of the mods catch up, this game will be much more visually stunning that the other edition.
Overall, I would actually recommend this version if you played a lot of Dark Souls II. It is different enough that it feels fresh, while being similar enough to be recognizable. It also features a few throwbacks to the first Dark Souls as an added bonus to people who haven't played the second yet. This game is also a lot more noob-friendly in terms of exploration, so it's also a good match for anyone who is new to the franchise, despite being harder overall.

I did not care for Gone Home at all and don't recommend it but not for the reasons many will assume when they see a negative review. I'm not going to argue if this is a game or not. If it is to you, that's all that matters. Those who consider this feminist propaganda are just being ridiculous, as are those who hate it because of the subject matter it covers, one tragically overlooked in video games by and large.
I did not care for Gone Home because it's a thoroughly unengaging experience that tells a poignant but utterly generic story with some of the most tired methods possible. There are no mechanics in Gone Home, you simply traverse an environment, picking up and looking at objects, some of which have no importance to the story, some of which do. At certain points, you will trigger disjointed (albeit well acted) audio logs which is how the core of the story is conveyed to you. You have the freedom to wander around most of the environment but as with traditional games, you are gated off from certain areas until required objectives are fulfilled. You do not directly interact with any other characters and your character is a silent protagonist.
The problem is that the storytelling in Gone Home relies on tired, unoriginal methods like gated progress and audio logs, two things people frequently railed against as being lazy, dated design but which are somehow revolutionary here. The story itself is also bland, uninteresting and cliché and personally, I've seen almost this exact kind of story told in other venues many times. The subject matter could have been explored in so many interesting ways and instead, we got an interactive after-school special that may as well not have been interactive. There's no subtlety or organic discovery as the designers claimed, the core elements of the story are delivered to you when they want them to. There is no ambiguity or room for interpretation in what's being said and just in case you still don't get it, many of the audio logs involving the core subject will have objects nearby that clearly beat you over the head with what's trying to be said. In Gone Home, you
interpret the story the way the designers want you to.
There are so many other examples of games that try to tell deep and meaningful stories and are able to do so with actual mechanics and game play. Papers Please and Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons are two examples released in the same year that did so brilliantly. If you have a PS3 or PS4, the Left Behind DLC for The Last of Us actually tackles the same core subject matter of Gone Home but does so wrapped around game play and I found it to be a much more impacting and meaningful experience. I can't remember more than a few core elements of Gone Home's story but I remember everything from Left Behind.
What I believe was the intent behind Gone Home was a noble one but it was badly executed. If you want emotional storytelling in games, there are better places to get it and better examples of the subject matter as well. It's also 2 hours long at best which is not a great value to many either. In my opinion, this is one of the most overrated games of the last several years and so many better and similar games deserved the success this got. Maybe get it on a deep sale if you're curious but it's not worth nearly it's normal asking price.

Gone Home is not a horror game, it's not a point a click adventure game, it's not a competative game.
Gone Home is an exploration game with which you'll unravel the mystery surrounding just why your house is deserted when you return home. There's no set piece events, jump scares or even special mechanics to find here. Just as if you walked into a strangers house, you can piece together exactly who they are by exploring what's around you.
The game's littered with notes, pictures and important documents which in turn will slowly put together the type of family and the events surrounding the family together. This is entirely where Gone Home's story comes from. You'll rely on spoken dialect which tiggers depending on which important object you investigate. It's this dialect which is going to give the entire game it's touching meaning.
As you view certain area's of the house, while listening to these spoken confessions, it's not hard to imagine the event's taking place yourself. And I guess that's the real trick to weather this game's going to work for you, your own imagination and how much you give yourself over to what may have happened here, to what may have been felt by this family.
Do I think it's worth the full asking price? No, I never do with game's which are so short, no matter how wonderful they are. I do however think it's worth a discounted price for anyone willing to give themselves over to story for a couple of hours.
I fully support game's of this type but surrounding this one, the question always looms, Is Gone Home a game? Well the answer is, it's dosen't matter. Just a small amount of research will give you the basic flavor of the game. They always split opinion, these are the kind of expierences you either fully enjoy or detest.
I just hope you don't blame those who enjoy it.

After spending some hours with Verdun one I can definitely say that the game is very refreshing and a it feels like a new breath after playing Battlefield and CS: GO for years. The “Frontlines” game mode is probably one of the best modes I've played on a FPS in late years. Basically, in this mode, each team has a certain amount of time to either attack and capture the enemy trench or defend their own. Capturing a trench works like pretty much any conquest/domination mode in any other FPS on the market, get someone near the capture point to capture it ( I’m not sure if having more people near the capture point makes it so that you capture it faster). Defending a trench is pretty basic, you just need to stop the enemy from getting into your trench and capturing it. To be honest I believe that defending is always easier because you're supposed to be inside a trench, and because of that, it's harder for the enemies to spot you and kill you while, on the other hand, it's far more easier for you to kill them because they pretty much have to get either inside or really close to your trench in order to kill you, or, the enemy can just call an mortar strike or some gas to force your team out of the trench. The only gripe I have with the “Frontlines” mode is that there is no penalty for camping and not pushing towards the enemy trench when you’re supposed to. Besides the main game mode, “Frontlines”, you also have “Rifle Deathmatch” which is a Free For All mode and a recently released mode called “Attrition” which is just a fancy name for Team Deathmatch.
Of course it's not all that simple. There's two teams and each team is divided into various squads and in each squad there's 4 slots, each of those slots represents a different "class" or "role". From the top of my head I can say there's the equivalent of the Sniper/Marksman on both teams, the Machinegunner, the Grenadier, the standard grunt and there's also two classes which I like to call "The Officers". These "officers" have the ability to request mortar strikes and gas on where they see fit, you just need to aim where you want and press the designated keybind. Do you see a bunch of enemies holding up on one spot on their trench? Just call in a mortar strike and in a few seconds they'll go sky high or, if you prefer, call in for some gas and you’ll either see the enemy flee from their trench or they’ll have to put their gas masks on and by doing that they’ll get a very reduced field of view. If your target is far from you and you can’t really see that well, you can also call these strikes with the help of your binoculars . The "officer" can also give move/attack orders that designate waypoints that serve as a "guide" to where the other players on the team should move.
Verdun also introduces the typical multiplayer progression present on many online multiplayer FPS. As you play you'll gain experience that will increase your account rank and that experience will also increase your class rank, the experience that you gain only counts towards the class in which you're playing at any given moment, each class has it's own rank/level. Each individual class has it's own milestones for unlocking more gear and weapons. These unlocks consist of bayonets for your rifles, grenades, pistols, machineguns, rifles or scopes for a certain rifle. I feel like this is a great way to reward active players by giving them a little advantage. In each game your squad will also level up the better you do and leveling it up will unlock passives for the squad members, however the squad level doesn't save, in the next match you play your squad level will be reset.
Graphically, I think I can safely say that Verdun looks pretty good, of course it doesn't look as good as other FPS such as Battlefield or Crysis but for an indie development team I think that it looks pretty damn good, however I'll say that one of the few gripes I have with the game is the animation quality, sometimes it looks pretty good but every now and then it looks to me like the animation doesn't match the speed at which a player is moving, perhaps it's just me being weird. Now, something I really like in Verdun is the music, from the main menu track to the ones played in game, for me, they hit the perfect spot in setting myself in the mood, they're really immersive and sometimes I find myself waiting for the track to kick in so I can launch myself to the field and run towards the enemy trench.
Still, there's something that always bothered me about Verdun, even after it's official release, and that is the hit registration. Sometimes a part of me feels like it's my connection that's just bad but there's some times in which I'll be shooting people running across the fields, or inside the trenches, and I'll be getting a kill with each shot, and then there's sometimes in which I can shoot someone who has their back turned against me and there's no hitmark or anything and they just turn around and kill me. I don't know if it's the servers, the game or some issue on my end but when it happens it tends to be very annoying. Still, all credit to the developers, it's not as bad as it was during Early Access and I'm pretty sure they've done alot to improve this and try to resolve this issue.
Then there's another separate issue entirely, which is the overall game performance. Regarding this I believe it's some limitation of Unity because there's been patches and patches and overall performance stays pretty much the same, atleast for me, even though there was a significant performance increase after the upgrade to Unity 5. With a i5 4460 running at 3.2Ghz, 8GB 1600mhz ram and a 970 running at factory clocks I'm averaging between 50-70 with everything maxed out with the exception of stuff like lens flare, depth of field, HDR and stuff like that. I mean, 50-60 fps is pretty acceptable but for a FPS I tend to find more confortable playing these types of games with abit higher FPS. Like I said, I believe it's a limitation of the engine itself and that the devs have done everything they could to improve it, still, I believe it should be taken into account.
The developers have certainly listened to the community during the whole development process and I believe that is to be praised. The developers took into account many suggestions made by the community and adressed various complaints and added things such as a mute/block option, bullet drop and team balancing.
Overall, Verdun is a great game, if you can get past the lag and performance issues, and I believe that is mainly because it brings a fresh type of experience for an online multiplayer FPS by taking place in WWI and by taking a great and well done approach to the trench warfare since most FPS out there are pretty much taking place in a modern day setting. Most of the problems I had with the game during Early Access were fixed or greatly improved and I believe I can say that Verdun is of the best FPS I've played in recent years. Verdun is certainly an example for games to come on how it is possible to make FPS games on other time periods other than WWII and the modern era and, as I've said previously, the trench attack and defend mechanic is just so well executed and it brings a whole new dynamic to this kind of game.

Verdun takes you to the battlefields of world war one, a period covered less intensely by contemporary video games then other more modern wars. You spawn into this new game without much in the way of information on game mechanics but you can dig up any info in the guides made available through the menus, this is less efficient then a tutorial but it still works. The options interface was just a little confusing to navigate at first for me at least but if you give it 5 minutes you will have it all figured out. The game works on a level system and in the beginning you are restricted in your load outs and weapons that are available, for instance if you play a machine gunner you will not have a machine gun available immediately. It takes awhile to level up and each class for each nation must be leveled individually.
Game play is for the most part very good, the small magazine size and more often then not bolt action weapons lead to a different playing experience then say a game like Battlefield 4. By this I mean you will need to do a bit more aiming and making your shots count rather then spraying and praying, at least with most classes as there are some machine guns in the game. I think this is a good thing, something a bit different is never a bad thing and after going through a bit of a steep learning curve I found myself doing well and having a lot of fun. I recommend the grenadier class to those who are new as I found well placed grenades useful for easy kills in the trenches and they work about the same as grenades in any other game. I do have some lag issues though I cant say with certainly they are all the games fault, it can be a bit glitchy (however not terribly so) but the developers seem to be committed to continually improving the game according to the game news and that is the most important thing I suppose.
Bottom line, I recommend this game to any fan of historical shooters (not so say its 100% historical, no game is but they make a good attempt at realism and immersion for a death match game) or shooters in general. I got this game on sale for 11.50 and it is worth more then that, full price at this time is only 22.99. I believe I will get more then my moneys worth out of the game and expect most people who buy and give the game a chance will as well.

I bought it for some nostalgia from my high school years and mostly got what I expected out of it, although better music variety would have been nice, or at least the option to flush some of the cassette tapes you find down the toilet.
Think of this as a mood piece.  Play it when you're feeling open minded, suspend your disbelief and let your imagination loose, pretend you're in the high school drama club, because without using your imagination actively you'll get no joy from this.  If this doesn't sound like something you're willing to do in a video game that's fine, but don't buy this, stick to the games you're used to.
You'll follow the linear story through well voiced dialogue that plays as you explore the house which takes less than 2 hours max.  Lots of personal effects are lying about the place and it's through picking up these items that the story is revealed.  There is no action that can impact the story in any way at all, and if you paid $20 it's at this point you may feel like a sucker.  Buy it for $5 or less on sale.
It's an interesting house, albeit unoccupied, but it all takes place in the same place, you can't even look out a window to see the yard.  There's no replayability temptation here either.  It would have been cool if things in the house had more interactivity, then it might be fun to roam around it it again.
To me it captured the teen spirit well.  Feeling like I just stumbled in from a concert, ears ringing, drunk and stoned, and over analysing every object you bump into thinking it may hold the key to the universe.  Well that's I had for teen spirit anyways, you may have a different take.  I would recommend this for what it is.  A good hour of non violent emotional alt-grrrl drama.

Having played Dark Souls and Dark Souls II, I can vouch for the visual upgrades of this game. Before, you enter the Undead Crypt, which is meant to be pitch black, it looks pretty dark, but you do not need a torch. In Scholar Edition, the mansion's basement in Majula looks more like a dungeon.
Along with this, the armor, weapons, shields, and people all have been majorly retouched. With each new armor I get, I immediately try it on, and walk up to a wall to get a closer look at the details. If you look at base DSII armor (Imported armor, for example) the wear and material of the armor look almost like decals, plastered on the surface, with a bit of Crayola crayon shadowing. Now, you see layers in the clothing, the tears in the fabric, in the right light, effect the shadow you cast. Little things that make the overall experience better.
Plus, having played through base DSII on about Eight characters, the change in spawns and enemies is very welcome, and often suprising. (Using the Pursuer as an example. Instead of seeing him three times in total, like before, he appears just about everywhere. Its terrifying.) Also, the increased amount of statues makes it more important to ration your branches of yore. Before, I had six of them (Don't remember how), and every important statue was already unfrozen.
Another big help is an extra summoning slot. I'd like to say its helpful for getting more friends in, but I obviously don't have any. I'm writing a review. Pretty blatant I don't have better things to do with my time.
The DLC bundle is also pretty nice.
Overall, base DSII gets a 7/10, but DSII Scholar Edition gets closer to an 8 or 9/10.

Gone Home is surrounded with plenty of controversy concerning whether or not the quality of its narrative warrants the price tag of $20. Now I was recently able to purchase it at only around $7, so I wasn't as affected by this price tag as much as some. Recently in the gaming industry, the quality of a game's story hasn't necessarily been higher on average, but has actually just been more apparent and a more important factor in purchasing a game. Some games are given a "free pass" in its story if it has exceptional gameplay, and Gone Home is near the exact polar opposite of this. The question that you should ask yourself when considering purchasing this game is that, "For $20, am I willing to 'play' a game that has little to no gameplay and lasts for around two hours, since the game has excellent storytelling?".
When I initially bought Gone Home, I already knew some of what I was getting myself into. Despite that, I thought I could forgive the lack of gameplay, since the quality of the story is more important to me in most circumstances. I found that I was wrong. One game I want to bring up in "comparison" is Bioshock Infinite. This is a game that has an excellent narrative, storytelling, and gameplay. When I was playing Bioshock Infinite I found myself thinking of the combat scenes more or less just as transitions from one part of the plot to the next. When I finished Gone Home, I asked myself if I would have minded if Bioshock Infinite had removed all gameplay. If it was just a story being told as you followed along in the midst of it all. And I would've minded, because all those "transitions" actually added to the quality of the overall quality of the storytelling. It makes you feel invested in the story, and that you actually have a role and purpose. In Gone Home, it seems more like a reading a book (which I love to do, although my books don't have quick-time events and save points, because books and games are two different mediums).
While Gone Home is still a game, it lacks the biggest factor that set video games apart from other methods of storytelling. And that is interactivity. In conclusion, Gone Home taught me that while the narrative is still very important to me, a game still needs interactivity. This was my experience and may not reflect yours or anyone else for that matter. I merely hope this review helps make your decision easier and more satisfying in the end.
Thanks for listening to my thoughts, and there are more below if you are at all interested.
By the way, I do not disagree with any reviews of this game saying how great the storytelling is. I am merely saying that this game lacks what it needs the most, and that is interactivity. I am also not saying that I think the story is all that great. I just feel that the developer did an excellent job of telling the story they wanted to.
Perhaps a better game to compare Gone Home to is The Stanley Parable. Both place a very large role on the narrative of the story and both do an incredible job of telling their story. Though there is a VERY large difference between the two. That difference is the interactivity in The Stanley Parable. While The Stanley Parable is extremely similar to Gone Home in terms of length, The Stanley Parable is a better game (in my opinion) because it allows the player to choose how the plot continues. From playing Gone Home and The Stanley Parable I have realized that gameplay and interactivity are not the same thing. In both games you walk around a building, go through doors, and listen to dialogue. Though The Stanley Parable gives you multiple doors and reacts to which door you choose, which makes you feel like you have a role in the game and that feeling encourages you to continue playing and experience the developer's story.

Having played Dark Souls and Dark Souls II, I can vouch for the visual upgrades of this game. Before, you enter the Undead Crypt, which is meant to be pitch black, it looks pretty dark, but you do not need a torch. In Scholar Edition, the mansion's basement in Majula looks more like a dungeon.
Along with this, the armor, weapons, shields, and people all have been majorly retouched. With each new armor I get, I immediately try it on, and walk up to a wall to get a closer look at the details. If you look at base DSII armor (Imported armor, for example) the wear and material of the armor look almost like decals, plastered on the surface, with a bit of Crayola crayon shadowing. Now, you see layers in the clothing, the tears in the fabric, in the right light, effect the shadow you cast. Little things that make the overall experience better.
Plus, having played through base DSII on about Eight characters, the change in spawns and enemies is very welcome, and often suprising. (Using the Pursuer as an example. Instead of seeing him three times in total, like before, he appears just about everywhere. Its terrifying.) Also, the increased amount of statues makes it more important to ration your branches of yore. Before, I had six of them (Don't remember how), and every important statue was already unfrozen.
Another big help is an extra summoning slot. I'd like to say its helpful for getting more friends in, but I obviously don't have any. I'm writing a review. Pretty blatant I don't have better things to do with my time.
The DLC bundle is also pretty nice.
Overall, base DSII gets a 7/10, but DSII Scholar Edition gets closer to an 8 or 9/10.

It's alright, I mean it has it's good moments and bad moments. The things I find great about this game is the atmosphere and that it's one of the few games that stands out of the sandbox of modern warfare clones, and creates a World War I game that has very immersive feel to it. I like the gameplay and how it feels more realistic than an arcade like game, e.g Modern Warfare/Battlefield series. The graphics are great, and my midrange rig can handle it at a steady 50-70 FPS on settings mostly on high/ultra in 1920x1080. And the music and sounds are absolutely awesome.
However, there are a few issues that just make the game feel kinda repetative, the user interface can be a little mind boggling for the first ten minutes, but you get over it fairly quick. And the multiplayer games feel kinda barren, I find it kinda disappointing when you can only find games with 6v6 or at most 12v12 on maps that are meant to host many more players, while this isn't the fault of the core game it is a problem I have encountered from the past few times I've played it in the past two days.  One issue I encountered was the spawn issue, I hated spawning and instantaniously killed and then having to wait 15-30 seconds only to have it happen again, I also encountered times where the enemy would spawn right in front of me. There are few glitches though, though the only ones I've encountered is getting hurt by barbed wire several times when I wasn't anywhere near it.
Over all it's a good game if you want a good WW1-esque experience and fun realistic type of shooter, pick it up.  Definitely was worth the 12$ I spent on it during the sale.

My first review of Gone Home was entirely positive. I supposed I focused mostly on the parents and the challenges they faced. It was a pleasant break from stealth-based horror titles and combat-centric games--a mundane mystery: where is everyone and why is the house empty?  Everything changed on my second playthrough scouring the house for every possible bit of information and with commentary enabled.  I started to see the cracks and little things that previously amused now annoy and/or disappoint.
I'd like to be clear on a few points before we begin again:  I've no problems with games that have zero combat, minimal gameplay, simple stories, independent-tier graphics,
Let's jump into this headfirst:
's central plot involves Kaitlin Greenbriar (the player) arriving at the family's new home (inheritted by her father, Terrance, from his Uncle Oscar) only to find that everyone's missing.  Samantha Greenbriar (the sister) provides occasional voice-overs as the player explores the house and discovers (through her sister's diary) that Samantha left with her lover, Lonnie, after their (Sam & Kate's) parents previously left on an anniversary vacation.
The complications that created this situation:
1 - Samantha becomes friends with Lonnie during their high school years and soon falls for her.  With biases towards sexual preferences being what they were in the 1990s, the pair face difficulty at school and further problems arise.  Samantha and Lonnie's relationship is conducted secretly until a forced exposure (truancy, low grades) to her parents.  They give Samantha the "just a phase" speech before placing her on restriction.
2 - Lonnie Desoto comes from a military family, so naturally she prepares for a career in military service.  This places a wedge between her and Samantha as any thoughts to the future are accompanied with healthy amounts of doubt.
3 - Terrence Greenbriar (the father) found success as a writer, but was dropped by his publisher after the second novel bombed.  After finding some unusual letters, I took a closer look at Oscar Masan (Terrence's uncle) and the suspicions began to pile up.  Oscar sexually abused Terrence.  This has been confirmed--long before I stumbled onto it--on the developer's Twitter profile.  Terrence's novels are attempts to find closure, but are also forcing him to relive the abuse (likely much worse in memory) and sleeping in the house where the assaults took place certainly isn't helping.
4 - Meanwhile, Janice Greenbriar (the mother) has been growing more and more distant from Terrence and closer to her coworker, Richard Something.
Everything comes to a head when the parents leave on their vacation; whether Terrence has told Janice about his past abuse or if Richard's sudden engagement and marriage invitation forced her to remember her husband remains to be seen.  In their absence, Samantha has an opportunity to spend one more night with Lonnie before she ships out.  The night passes and Samantha wakes up alone.  Later she realizes Lonnie left her several messages indicating that she's changed her plans to enlist (...in spite of having a ship date?  That's desertion, madam.) and wants to spend her life with Samantha.
I was unaware of Terrence's abuse during my first playthrough.  I was convinced that Janice had given up her affair with Richard in order to rekindle her marriage.  Now it seems that the only options for them are Janice helping Terrence find closure or Janice adjusting to rejection and mending any bridges burned with her spouse.  The story's become darker with every subsequent look.  Oh, well sideplots shouldn't affect the overall impression, right?  Sure, keep telling yourself that.
Present for some of the commentary was Corin Tucker...yeah, don't worry I didn't know who she was either.  Apparently, getting involved with feminism sells albums when the musician lacks the ability necessary.  Don't get me wrong:  the score was fine, but the insert tracks were devoid of melody or meaning.  Corin Tucker's contribution to the commentary is largely self-promotion and the fiction that feminism is about equality for
.
Not once during the commentary did anyone mention the parents.  Their story was what drew me in the most, but it seems those two characters are simply window dressing.  The backstory of Terrence and Oscar should have been at least mentioned  in the commentary.  Either the developers sold out during the game's promotion or they were dishonest from the start.
I haven't enjoyed writing this re-review.  It's been phenomenally disappointing to realize this game is not a positive message to everyone seeking love.  Would reactions to this game be the same if it were teenage boys instead of the two girls?  I doubt it.  Honest representations of alternative relationships are hard enough to find in games without added political propaganda.  I'll end this here while I still remember the good things
had to offer.
The Good:
- an honest portrayal of an alternative relationship without unnecessary melodrama
- mystery elements without stealth sequences
- solid minimal score
- excellent atmosphere
The Bad:
- annoying choices for insert music, but at least they're optional
- overpriced for the length of the game
- limited graphics options and some performance issues
The Ugly:
- deliberate propaganda at times
- restricts user access (One journal entry written by Samantha describes some very tame intimate contact between her and Lonnie and Kaitlin forces the player to drop the letter and refuses to pick it up again.  The developer points this out as if it were something to be proud of and not heavy-handed at all.  It implies female-female sexuality is in some way sacred compared to other relationships.)
- crashes on ending credits if the player attempts to skip

To anyone who didnt played the first game and thinks about starting with Dark Souls 2 because they think its easier: Dont do it, play Dark Souls 1 first, dont be scared by the difficulty, thats not the point of Dark Souls. Its not as hard as the media says it is.
Yes, Dark Souls 1 is much better than Dark Souls 2. Dark Souls 2 is still one of the best games of 2014, what does that say about Dark Souls 1? Anyway, this is my review for Dark Souls 2 Scholar of the First Sin:
Let me start with something I dont really care about in a Dark Souls game, the Story. I know the hardcore fans really like to delve deep into the lore and Im also interested in that, but I never do that "research" myself. Thats why I cant say much about the story of Dark Souls 2, only that the first game had more interesting characters and a more interesting world.
Okay now lets talk about what Dark Souls 2 does worse than its predecessor and there is quite something. The worst part of DS2 is the first real area of the game you visit, the forest of fallen giants, and everything beyond that until the final Boss of that area. In this part of the game the level design is extremely dull which makes exploring boring. The enemys you encounter are fine, but they also get dull after a while. The first time you will play this game I dont think that this will be a big deal for you though, but for me on my second and third playthrough these levels were boring to play again. What makes these levels even more boring is the graphics of the game. Texture quality is sometimes terrible and lighting is dull and there is no interesting architecture. On top of that the bossfights you encounter are also not that special, but they are fine. Still, the taurus demon from Dark Souls 1 for example is one of my favorite boss fights in the whole franchise, and thats the first boss of the game. The visual design of the bosses are unspectacular, the arenas you fight in are dull and all of them kinda have the same attack patterns.
But again, thats just the first 3-4 areas of the game (maybe 3 or 4 hours), after that the quality of the levels, enemys and bosses gets better and better. You can also go to Heide Tower of Flame right from the beginning but there is no point in doing that. The game is FULL of items of any kind you can think of. There are many items which are designed for certain playstyles. That means that you will find many many many items which will be totaly useless to you. This is another reason exploration in DS2 isnt as fun as in DS1. Weapons and Armors you can find are rare, most of the cool stuff you have to buy.
I was still motivated enough to explore, but it wasnt as rewarding as it should be.
There are TONS of weapons in this game, but most of the weapons are just different versions of the same weapon type (for obvious reasons), a little bit less would be better I think, especially because your inventory will be full with all kind of crap. Every enemy you fight could drop some useless armor, NOBODY every will use but you loot the enemys anyway, because they might give you life gems or crafting materials. In DS1 you had less weapons, but the same amount of variety and depth, there are just too many unnessesary items in DS2.
One of the worst design decisions of DS2 are the life gems and herbs which refill your spell uses. Both of these completely destroy the balance of the game. On your first playthrough this wont have a huge impact (depending on your skill), but on later playthroughs you will realize how broken these items are. In DS1 you had a set amount of Flasks and spell uses, so the developers always know how to balance each area of the game. Another weird and unnessesary change is that you cant level up at any bonfire anymore, you have to teleport back to Majula and talk to the girl. This is one of the most stupid decisions, cause I sometimes was simply too lazy to level up because I didnt wanted to go through the loading screen, run to the girl, skip her dialouge, run back to the bonfire, teleport to the area I was in, wait for the loading screen and continue.
Also the fact that you can teleport anywhere right from the start of the game shows how much lazier this game was developed compared to the first one. In DS1 every part of the world was connected to each other somehow in a clever way, so that you didnt need quick travel and only very late in the game you unlocked quick travel. If they wouldnt have quick travel in DS2 the developers will be forced to design their world better, so they went the lazy way and just made quick travel right from the start.
Okay okay, I talked a lot about negative things and actually there are still more negatives (I wont even start talking about PvP) and you might wonder how this game still got a 8.5/10 rating. Well first of all many of the things I mentioned might not even have a huge impact on your playthrough, those are just things which dissapointed me because Dark Souls 1 did them so much better. Also many of the above problems are not present in the 3 DLCs regions. Those are actually the best part of the game apart from some dull enemies.
Dark Souls 2 is full with content. For your first playthrough you will definitly need more than 50 hours (DLC areas are optional though), there are TONS of weapons, armors, enemy types, boss fights, areas, anything. The quality of the boss fights is sometimes good, sometimes average, sometimes fantastic. Less would be better here. Also the difficulty fluctuates a lot from boss to boss. The Iron King Boss ,or whatever his name is, is much much easier than the smelter demon, which is the boss before him and the Iron King is supposed to be the final boss of that area.
They simplified weapon upgrades and crafting, I like some of these changes but sometimes when I play DS1 again I feel like they simplified too much. The combat is as good as in Dark Souls 1 and with dual wielding you actually have more play styles now. Whats also new is that you loose a little bit of your maximum health every time you die. I can understand the reason behind this, but its just annoying. I would prefer some other form of punishment.
There is so many things left I could talk about, I  barely scratched the surface of the things I did talk about and this review already got really long. Dark Souls 2 is just so big and for that alone its worth playing, so let me conclude:
Dark Souls 2 is an epic adventure despite its flaws. Its challenging and rewarding. It misses the genius of Dark Souls 1 and has some dull parts, but there is more than enough that makes up for that (especially the DLCs). The only reason you will be dissapointed at the end is because Dark Souls 1 was so ♥♥♥♥ing good and Dark Souls 2 feels like a rip off which didnt understand what REALLY made Dark Souls 1 so special (its not the difficulty). But again, dont let me blind you by all my criticism, Dark Souls 2 is still one of the best games of 2014!

Gone Home is a bit of a controversial title. The gameplay is not really what you call "in depth". Gone Home is a game about walking. And there have been a lot of those recently. And a lot people don't really like those. Actually, REALLY don't like those. Because of this, I would ask of you to consider: are you willing to play a game that consists only of walking around an empty house, looking at pictures and reading letters? I am. But I don't know if that's for everyone.
One particularly interesting thing about Gone Home is the nature of it's content. The reason Gone Home can have little to no "hard gameplay" is because the story is not about something which merits it. The story is not going to take you into combat or even many puzzle like situations. (At best, we get exploration.) It's about a family in the Pacific Northwest. It's about a girl and her friend. It's about riot grrrl punk. It's the game equivalent to a sappy indie film. And I'd be lying if I said I don't get swept up in that stuff.
My only complaint that I feel strongly about is the price tag. The game is pretty short, only about three hours on a casual play through. This makes a twenty dollar price tag too high, to me. For that you can go to a movie and get some popcorn, or go to two movies and go smell popcorn. I strongly advise you to wait for a sale.
So, with that, we have Gone Home. Sincerely endearing and enjoyable, but simply not worth twenty dollars, and simply not for everyone.

This should have been the gamers' game of the year.
will start off from the very thing that got me hooked to this game.
It's the map. This game has the second biggest game map ever created to date (I was told that FUEL has the biggest map which is 5,560 square miles)
Just cause 2 map is 37 by 37 kilometers. A couple of kilometers on each side of the square map is water, so let's go by 35 by 35 kilometers. Multiply 35 by 35 and there you go - you have 1,225 square kilometers of map to explore, give or take 100 square kilometers.
For the comparison, let's take the Fallout 3 map. That map is about 35 square kilometers.
The Oblivion 4 map is roughly the same size.
GTA 3 is 35-36 square kilometers
GTA 4 is 15 square kilometers
And I thought the Far Cry 2 map was huge. It's 50 square kilometers.
The ARMA 2 map was definitely the biggest one before Just Cause 2 stepped in. The most important reason why i bought the disappointingly unoptimized ARMA 2 is to simply explore the roughly 400 square kilometers map.
I remember wondering when I was younger if they would ever make a big enough map for a game which I could explore for days and days and days. I thought they finally did that with Arma 2, and despite the fact that I still could not play the game on maximum settings even when my rig should have easily taken on almost 2 ARMA 2's (According to the "recommended settings"), I still loved the fact that I could enjoy the country-side that I haven't been to in years.
The second thing is that we ACTUALLY have directx 10 in this game. FINALLY, how many more directx 9 games are we going to have? We have directx 11 already, so what's the deal? The directx 10 pretty much seals the deal and completes the game map that I still cannot believe they made. I also cannot believe that the entire game fits on a DVD, how the HELL do they pull that off? shouldn't the map this size be at least 30 GB? I mean Age of Conan: Hyborian Adventure is like a 30-35 GB game.
Well, the third thing is... Ah what the hell, you know the rest. Complete freedom of action, unrealistic stunts, the temporary to permanent abandonment of the laws of physics, infinite parachute, a hundred of drivable vehicles, a cute Easter egg, the Hatch from the first and second seasons of LOST, the pleasure of having to spend 20 minutes just to fly from one end of the map to another on a stolen government jet, the joy of swimming in the sea (wish they had sharks though), the eye candy explosions that you never get tired off, the realistic driving of the vehicles (aside from the way they rotate in mid air sometimes), the realistic damage to the PARTS OF THE VEHICLES THAT WERE ACTUALLY DAMAGED IN THE IMPACT, I could go on and on about this game
Im also playing this game on IMPOSSIBLE and find it quite easy to beat. You just move constantly, shoot (There is sadly a default auto-aim option enabled that you cannot disable) and press "tab" or whatever you have to evade bullets. HOWEVER, a nearby grenade explosion is almost guaranteed to kill you, so for MAXIMUM realism, I recommend playing this game on IMPOSSIBLE
Im not gonna complain about the check point system, I love the checkpoint system. it makes games more challenging. Plus there still is a SAVE option, although it doesnt work in its original meaning
The story is blah. Who cares? Some of the missions that they give you though are somewhat original and a breath of fresh air from some of the repetitive GTA missions. However, most of those missions are, attack, kill, destroy, blow up, move on. It would have been nice if they added an element of stealth to the game though. It would feel great if could actually play as a somewhat silent or stealthy lethal saboteur. I would also like it if they imposed a penalty for killing civilians both on purpose and incidentally.
I know this game won't win the game of the year award since there is no real substance I guess, but unofficially, this will probably be the gamer's choice No 1 game of 2010. (I hope Metro 2033 wins the game of the year though, which I rationally know it won't)

It has mechanics that absolutely match the setting of the game, 1 hit from a rifle means you're most likley going to die, although 2 shots that means you're lucky and just stay in cover and hopefully your ally can save you or the enemy who shot you gets distracted or something.
There are 3 mechanics that make it one of my favourite games I've played this year...
1- Bullet mechanics
As I've mentioned bullets do extreme amounts of damage and you can't just go run out in the open like Rambo/CoD style like a retard, however there is also bullet drop in the game, along with the foggening of the screen and more of a dark tunnel when being shot at rather jelly blood literally being thrown at your face when bein shot, which adds more of the WW1 feel about being in a trench. Which makes a Pistol really deadly in a trench, and a machine gun a beast when shooting at attackers, and the rifle is a good weapon to use all around depending on how you use it
2- Atmosphere/Map design
As well a prior statement, however with this I mean by when your running through the trenches, it makes mud sounds when running through them, and even makes it awesome when artillery fires on it and you need to duck and cover from it or you will 99% of the time die. However, No mans land is even more awesome to run through durring an assault on the enemy trench, because you have to worry about barbed wire ripping your legs apart and being left on the field for dead, or using artillery craters as cover because small abandoned, unfinished trenches can't guide you the whole way. Another reason not to run out as a retard rambo/4 Year old CoD player.
3- Chemical Warfare Use
My Personal favourite part of the game is the fact that there is different gasses used such as mustard gas, or chlorine gas on the battlefield against your enemies or at you and your allies. What really makes it interesting is that you can go through it so long as you have your gas mask on and you aren't being currently shot at. It doesn't even just come and go also, it stays and lingers the area of impact for about 3-4 minutes and if you die and spawn in it, you need to get your mask on fast or you will certainly die. It's not scripted on each map thankfully, there are special units that can call it in like calling in artillery or commanding squad members, so it will either appear multiple times in one battle or none at all.  That's really on your own opinion whether it's bad or good though.
And that's really it, I got the game the day before I made this review, and I think it's better than most of the CoD's combined already. Other than it being a WW1 game, the 3 game mechanics are the best I've seen in a long while. So I highly recommend this game for the stated reasons. The only problems I've seen so far is the body mechanics on when people die, and the melee weapons are a bit overranged, like a small shiv can reach like an officers sword which is strange. But nonetheless this is the greatest WW1 shooter ever made in my opinion. I hope the're a lot of people who agree with me and I don't doubt it at all, considering the countless of positive reviews aside from mine.
Final Rating: 9/10 for Verdun

Gone Home is not a game, but an experience.  And an emotional one at that, if you allow it to be.  You walk in Katie's shoes but you soon find yourself in Sam's, if only by proxy.  The story is told in an odd but intriguing way, and is so wonderfully realized that I could easily imagine this being picked from a real-life journal.  It just feels real.
The 90's "grunge" vibe did an amazing job of taking me back to my own childhood.  I think that had a hand in making the experience so relatable.  I wonder if any younger gamers who weren't around back then would really be able to appreciate it.
Gone Home perfectly captures all the subtle aspects of growing up.  The confusion, the angst, the loneliness, the joy, and more confusion.  This is not a game.  It's a coming-of-age story.
There are a few other sub-plots that are hinted at, but they are not crucial.  Where the main story is eventually laid out in plain sight, these side-stories can easily be pieced together without much effort.
Gone Home plays similarly to Dear Esther.  There's not much to do in either game but explore the surrounding relics, and allow their threads to weave the tapestry around you.  Sit back and relax.  Turn out the lights, and put on your headphones.
There is nothing complex or challenging here, and that's ok.  Enjoy the ride.

If you're like me, and were holding out on getting the dlc's from a holiday sale that never came, go ahead and get this version. If you're new to the game, I'd also recommend getting this version (but perhaps after playing Dark Souls 1).
If you already own the original with all dlc's I wouldn't recommend the upgrade at the asking price. Aside from some asset shuffling (enemies, items, etc.) and some really minor geometry changes, there isn't a whole lot of difference between this and a modded DX9 version.
Wait for a sale.
About the game itself:
400+ hours with the original base game, I can tell you I think the game is fun, but fun doesn't make it good.
Cons:
Some of the design is poorly done, some of the art is incredibly lazy, the story is all over the place with far too many vague references to the first game, online play has frustrating latency, and the matchmaking while implemented with good intentions is broken.
Pros:
The character models/textures are fantastic, the soundscape is immersive and the voice acting superb. The animations are more fluid than previous 'Souls' games leading to tighter character control, which, in a game as focused on the action and timing as this, makes it a joy to explore the many and varied environments the game offers.
45+ hours into the 'upgraded' content:
The 'enhanced' graphics seems like it's only for lighting and some bloom. The textures don't seem to have been touched, or at least not the terrible ones I've noticed. They did make clever use of the lighting effects and using torches as triggers though.
The enemy/item shuffling, at least in New Game, isn't too surprising or even that challenging as they are the same enemies that were always in the game.  It is kind of refreshing to find that The Pursuer actually pursues, and at least the item shuffling gives a reason to explore the same old areas again.
Not much for new content that I've found so far, some 'new' npc invaders one which actually has new acquirable equipment. I haven't gotten through the DLC's yet, though I couldn't comment on whether they had any content added or not.

First, let me address the controversy surrounding Scholar of the First Sin. If you want to skip this bit, the actual review starts in paragraph five. Dark Souls II came out about a year ago. The graphics in the trailer looked better than the in-game graphics. People were upset, as if this was some new affront to gamers everywhere. Then people played the game, decided they really liked it, and the world spun on.
Fast forward a few months and From Software announces a new version of the game called Scholar of the First Sin. It includes updated graphics, support for more simultaneous multiplayer connections, extra NPCs for both lore and combat, revised enemy placement, a new boss, and an alternate ending. Furthermore, most of this content will be available as a free update to current Dark Souls II owners.
The updated graphical engine (DX11) was incompatible with the old engine (DX9). Thus, rather than replace the old engine entirely, they decided to release the DX11 version of Scholar of the First Sin as a standalone paid upgrade. As a bonus, they included all the DLC.
So what are people complaining about? What's the controversy? People are upset about paying $20 for what they percieve as a graphical patch. In reality, the DX11 version contains the revised troop placement, allows for up to six people to play simultaneously, and yes, is also a graphical upgrade.
What about the game, though? Isn't this a review? Yes, yes it is.
Scholar of the First Sin is great fun to play. If you played Dark Souls II, you'll enjoy the new enemy placement. It does two things very well. First, the new placement shakes things up. Enemies aren't where you expect them to be anymore, so even for veteran DS2 players, each map is a new experience. Secondly, the new placement is more devious. Harder enemies appear sooner, many others have better placement, and you'll find yourself panicking more than you did the first time, which is a welcome change. Dark Souls II was easier than its predecessor, and the new enemy placement in Scholar addresses that problem. Perfectly? No - but I'm happy with the results.
Extra players in multiplayer is a blast. Four person boss assaults are both fun and hilarious, and fight club on the bridge just got a whole lot messier.
The graphical differences don't immediately pop out at you since many textures look the same. But having played for a while now, I've found myself stopping on multiple occasions because I just happened to notice that the horizon was a lot more pretty, that fire now illuminates the things around it, that metal reflects light the way you'd expect it to, and that sometimes god-rays are a nice addition to a scene.
Something else I want to address but can't put my finger on - the game feels better. I don't know if they optimized the engine, or if the controls are slightly more responsive or what, but the whole experience is more comfortble. I realize this point is entirely without solid evidence, but I felt it worth mentioning.
So to those of you who own Dark Souls II and all it's DLC, I think this game is worth picking up. It's a fresh take on something we love. Oh, and they got rid of that miserable preorder bonus gear.
To those of you who don't own Dark Souls II but want it, get Scholar of the First Sin. It comes with all the DLC, and you'll never have to know why the first four paragraphs were written.

From what I read, most of the negative reviews of this game seem written by your average white dudebro who burps before greeting his friends.
I'll start with a disclaimer: when at full price, Gone Home is ridiculously overpriced, since the fist playthrough lasts 2 to 3 hours, and the replay value is relative. Get it discounted.
You start as Katie, an American girl who comes back from her year-long trip to Europe, and finds the house empty. Your first task is to open the front door, and the rest is an experience. You'll wander through the enormous mansion's hallways, rooms and secret passages in attempt to understand why nobody is there. Your clues will be objects such as notes, letters and brochures, but most importantly the journal entries of your sister Sam. The mechanics are similar to point-and-click games, except in 3D.
The story unfolds as you discover it: you can decide to search every room and get as many details as possible, or stick to Sam's main plot.
The plot revolves around the year long coming of age of Sam, as she discovers her passions, her values and love. The voiceacting conveys perfectly Sam's character, and the various objects in the house give nuance to her point of view and help understand the overall story (especially regarding the parents).
And this is why I think the 'interactive story/game' form truly adds something to Gone Home: the exploration is real, there is no paragraph that links together the pieces, you have to do the thinking yourself, but to do the thinking, first you have to find the clues yourself.
I was also touched by the story, to which I can sadly relate. The '90 flare is also a nice bonus.
Long story short, I recommend it to readers who want to spice up short stories by making them interactive. But get it discounted ;)

As someone who formerly owned Dark Souls II, having pre-ordered it, I have to say that this enhancement came as a bit of a surprise. Not being welcome to the idea of paying for the game again, I simply shrugged it off. When the game finally came out though, I then came to the realization that, as someone who didn't own the DLC in the first place, it would be worthwhile for me to purchase this (or have this purchased for me in my case :D). With the new differences in the engine and enemy placement as well as essentially getting a game of the year edition which included the DLC for roughly the same price, I'm impressed. They really made it a new experience. Sure, it's the same game, and I can understand why some would be disappointed, especially season pass owners, but when looking at this game from the perspective of someone who didn't own any DLC and was going to spend $30 anyway, I have to say that it was well worth it.
So if you're considering purchasing this game, go for it! The game is as satisfying as ever, and if you're like me and would've ended up getting the DLC anyway eventually, you should definitely pick this up instead. Beware, though, characters don't carry over. One of the few faults I see in this game is the total splitting of multiplayer, which is a fair criticism that I'm afraid would be very hard to avoid in seeing all the changes that were made.

Verdun is a very unique fps, let me start of by saying in you first couple of hours playing you kill to death ration will be somthing like 3:50, every action a player new to this game will result in death. Thats what makes this game special, I dont care how good you are at 360 no-scoping in COD, Battle field or even at playing realistic games like ARMA or inurgency this game sets all players at an equal level where they all have to practice, die, think, repeat untill they get good at it. When you finally get a fair amount of kills the felling is soo god its worth the billions of hours you have speant waiting to respawn.
The player progression system is very good as well becuse a level 1 player is not too far off a level 100 player and can still beat him as the perks are fair and allow for balanced gamleplay. Teamwork is absolutley vital, as soon as i started following my squad my deaths went down drastically.
But what makes this game so great is the realism beyond the shooting/bullet system. The maps look and feel real, you can hear the clunking of mugs and pans in you pack pack, the squish of wet mud under you feet, the dead horses and men litter the battle field along with abandoned equipment and enthrenchments lost to mud. Artillerly impacts scatter body parts, mud , and objects across the field. This game perfectly recreates the bloodiest war in our history, the death system is very quick and clean, no kill cams or dramatic deaths, you body simply slumbs to the floor, you could be running along with you squad, hear a burst of machine gun fire to look back and see them gone, just like that. It makes you think. The weapons, battle fields and uniforms and very well reaserched and accurate, you weapon will occasionally even hav weapon jams leaving screaming in pain at you monitor as you die becuse you couldn't get your weapon clear in time and got stabbed in the face.  This game does make you feel as close to the horrors of WW1 as you will want to get.
Finally this game requires no addional payment, no DLC, no money to get a half decient weapon. All the updates are free and the game is always getting better.
Get Verdun, and you will die more times than you care to count, scream and cry at your PC for days on end but when the hard work pays off you will think this game should be worth £50.
Its A fun game with many glitches, I still like it.

It seems very odd that so many people are openly attacking From Software or even Bandai Namco when they are NOT the first company to release an "updated" version of a wildly popular game and infact they should be thanked for offering a hefty discount to owners of the previous content. Ninja Gaiden Black is the first example that comes to mind of just such an event from past gaming generations.
As someone that has beaten both Dark Souls and Dark Souls II several times over, this new edition of Dark Souls II feels entirely worthwhile. Best of all, the remastered game environment costs about the same as a paid DLC package, with entirely more content than would be found in a DLC pack.
--First, a few cons and suggestions:
Admittedly, the much lauded graphical improvements are not exactly a key selling point considering that GeDoSaTo managed a much higher level of quality in the original version but honestly, is that such a big deal?
While it is true that hitting dead bodies can harm weapon durability there is a VERY easy solution! Try not hitting the dead bodies with wild attacks.
Yes, there are new and sometimes more challenging enemy placements, they have yet to feel unfair at all because there are also new methods of easily handling these encounters. Assuming of course that the player is patient enough to check the environment and manage the fight strategically.
--Now the Pros, yes the order was reversed on purpose:
The encounters are harder, and this feels fresh to a veteran player like myself. More complex encounters require a bit of patience to get used to, I thought this is what the Souls series was supposed to be about?
The ability to rush into the game and grab some overpowered items by speed running past monsters is no longer quite as viable though I will have to get further into the game to confirm that. Yes, this is a good thing in my opinion because it means actually being challenged in the early game instead of just running to the nearest power item for an easy boost.
All the DLC is now integrated into the game and the lore entries are expanded.
Overall, this new version of Dark Souls II feels very much like the Black edition of Ninja Gaiden, a game intended to offer increase challenge and encourage a deeper level of tactical play in order to overcome said challenge.

- One reviewer accused it of being no more than a pander to third wave feminists. You don't have to have an agenda to tell a story about a person whose orientation or way of doings things doesn't suit you.
- Another reviewer said that since he isn't a teenage girl he can't empathize with the character. (He actually wrote "emphasize," which made it pretty funny.) That to me suggests a very limited imagination. I'm not a murdered and then resurrected cyborg police officer but I still love Robocop.
I love the game. I love it's story. And while I understand criticisms of its "gameplay" I still feel no discomfort calling it a game. You could make the same arguement about point and click adventure games (I don't).

Gone Home is more of an interactive novella, than a (conventional) video game. It urges the player to engage with and become a part of the Greenbriar family's life. The player is placed in a visually unexceptional, but thematically rich domain. As the player becomes immersed in their surroundings they engage with themes surrounding the third wave feminist movement of the 1990s, homosexuality, religion, adultery and writer's block. In the space of an hour (or two), the player has become invested in the live's of the Greenbriar family, akin to the empathy a reader will feel with the characters of a well-loved book. There is no great difficulty in this game, and no skill required - however an investigative and quizzical disposition is a must. While there are many reviewers in the steam community who have been sorely disappointed by promises that Gone Home is 'the game of the year' - the game will not disappoint those who are open to story-driven gameplay that involves no interaction with other characters. This game goes well and truly beyond its mark when considering the depth and detail it has devoted to providing a nuanced landscape that is coloured only by its relation to the importance of particular items, written material and sound devices. The attention to these details in Gone Home should inspire other progressive game developers to enhance the role of story in their own video games.

There is a lot of cryptic stuff in the house that makes you feel like the story is heading somewhere interesting... Well it doesn't. Not at all.  This is not a game. It's a interactive can stacking simulator and visual short story. I don't say novel because they actually have more game play elements than Gone Home does.
They could have ran with the story of the father and his writing. They could have done some great stuff with that. They could have done something great with the parents all together but.... nope.. They could have done something amazing with the missing sister... but nope.
**SPOILER ALERT**
Instead they just have this mystery turn into nothing. The sister just ran away with her girlfriend. Yes big shocker there. She is into chicks and wanted to be with the woman she loved. Maybe my expectations were unreal. Maybe the semi horror vibes I was getting were false. You know all the horror elements in the game like the believes of ghosts and signs they might exist in the house. All of the demonic stuff you find in the house like the Ouija board and what appeared to be blood. Nope nothing. Nothing at all. It ends with you finding a note how the sister ran away with her female lover. Maybe I am wrong maybe it is still shocking to see a lesbian or gay person... NO I'm not. For ♥♥♥♥ sake.
What I thought I was going to see. Which would have made this game a lot better. You reach the addict. The sister and girlfriend had killed themselves or a murder suicide happens. As you open the door a foul smell comes out and your heart starts to pound. As you enter you find your sister hanging or with a bullet in her head. Her lover also dead with a gun in her hand. They couldn't bare to live without each other and she just didn't want to leave to the military. So she killed your sister and then herself so they could be together for eternity.
Buuuuutttt.... nope. They turn the game into a two hour can stacking simulator. I just don't get how people can give this "thing" such high praise. When I got to the end and finished this... "thing" I felt so betrayed. I honestly felt like I had been ripped off, and I had gotten the game for free. This is the biggest upsetting of any game I have played in my entire life.
