Gone Home is a game that was never able to find its audience. A lot of people looked at its critical reception, and bought it expecting a "narrative driven interactive experience." Sadly, the story that Gone Home tells is a great deal more subtle than most people have the patience for. Its the kind of story that shines in the form of a novel, and inevitably suffers a handicap when translated to an interactive experience. If I had to compare Gone Home to anything, it would be The Stanley Parable. If you follow the narrator's instructions in The Stanley Parable, if you try to "beat" it, you end up losing. Both The Stanley Parable and Gone Home are meant to be engaged with. They are both inviting their players to dance in the world created.
Gone Home is a deeply human, hyperrealistic story told through object manipulation. There is no great revalation, no sudden twist, no dark turn. If that sounds boring to you, don't bother with the game. Its production values are sky high, and if you allow yourself to be taken by it it leaves its emotional mark. Most gamers just don't have the patience for that, and I don't necessarily blame them.
But it should be five dollars. Once the summer sale knocks it down to that range, get it. I guarantee the internet is going to come around to it when the price is more palatable.

Ok so you're thinking about buying and playing "Gone Home" but aren't sure what type of game it is or how much you're going to like it. I went ahead and got it based off of some professional reviews I read and I have come to the conclusion that it was more of an "experience" than it was an actual "game." The play time is roughly 2 hours, so it's extremely short... don't expect more than that or you'll be disappointed. As far as the actual gameplay goes, though, it's extremely immersive. The game does a perfect job of leading you down the right path as it's very linear. You aren't left wandering about or confused about where to go next. This isn't really as "interactive" as I was expecting and there are little to no puzzles to be had other than a couple combination locks to figure out (which are easy). Basically what it comes down to is panning around the interior of a an extremely large house and snooping into a family's business. You pick up and examine various objects and in doing so, you discover the secrets of your own family.
The atmosphere is very alluring, spooky, and I will admit - I jumped a few times. Overall, I loved it.. the story was relatable and as I said before it's very immersive. I would recommend this game, though if you can catch it for less than retail, do so. If I would have paid full price, I would have been slightly disappointed in the AMOUNT of playtime I received for retail price. I happened to catch it on sale on the Humble Bundle store, so check there!

All spoilers are covered by spoiler tag, if you haven't noticed yet. So yeah. If you spoil something for yourself, blame curiousity.
So, after seeing a lot of disappointed negative reviews, claiming that the Scholar of the First Sin was the worst thing since the infamous E.T., I've decided to buy it and find out myself.
But first things first. I live in Russia and prices are pretty much localized here, so I've got my upgrage (I own all of the DLCs) for hillarious 5$. Was I disappoint? Well, find out yourself:
That's what the biggest complaints have been about. People claim that there are no improvements, and that they'd rather stick with free GeDoSaTo and the original game. Here's what I saw.
There really is only one thing that didn't get a graphical update. World textures. While it is rather disappointing, the SotFS really made it up by the use of lighting. I was really shocked to see the beautiful use of lighting in Things Betwixt and Majula, and it continues to impresses me still, even though I've progressed a lot in my very first SotFS save. They've made a great job making some sort of 'artificial darkness' that vanishes away as soon as you get a torch. Finally we've got a chance of seeing this 'perception vs. safety' feature we've been excited about before DkSII came out. Character textures seem to be improved a lot, as my character's face looked far more detailed on the creation screen and in the game itself. But really the biggest improvement has been made with *particle effects*. Yeah, you've read this correct. SotFS improves on particle effects such as souls, sparks, Pursuer's eyes and so on.
Graphic improvement is 7/10
Also, there are a lot more enemies in stages, but I didn't feel overwhelmed. It is impossible to run through now as well, so SotFS seems to fix all the problems original DkSII had with enemy placement and AI. There are a lot of things that add immersion, for example,
Overall, the game feels slower, more tactical and thoughtful, immersive. and co-op oriented.
SotFS gets 10/10 in this category.
The most notable change is
. Some of chests' contents have changed, some chests were added as well. Most of them contain weapons and shields you'd get later in the game, and some bodies contain weapons that took time to get, but weren't way too powerful (Whip, for example). Out of the most non-spoilerey weapon placement changes: two Broken Straight Swords in the beginning of the game instead of one. I've not seen any new armor placements, but now some sets that were only available in NG+ are now farmable in regular NG pretty early in the game.
8/10 for item placements
I haven't played the new larger scale PvP yet, but I indeed had some fun with co-op. For some locations it is recommended now (Heide's Tower of Flame, I'm looking at you), and for some reason it's way too much fun. With three (maybe more) summons at the same time, this game really turns into a jolly co-op experience. With more enemies added on stages, four players in one co-op sessions seems to be barely enough. Now to a little bit of PvP I've played. Just once I invaded a guy and his summon at Heide's Tower of Flame, and it feels good. Enemy placement does miracles, and the host won't be able to tank you out while his friend takes care of enemies anymore. Invasions turned from a "PvE-quicklyclearthearea-PvP-PvE' experience to constant pressure from both players and enemies, no matter how many players are you co-oping with.
9/10, a subject to change since I'm yet to see large scale fight clubs and PvP in general
They don't transfer. But to me it wasn't even a downside: I usually don't even go on NG+1.

I'll be honest: I own the original DkSII, all the DLCs and guess what? Even though I paid just 5$ for the SotFS, I'd pay three times as much because SotFS feels fresh. It isn't a simple "add a DLC" PTDE (which is praised for some reason), but a massive rework of the game. In spite of what everyone says, SotFS is one of the best remasters I've seen. Enjoyable, suprising, beautiful, with more difficulties to overcome, it adds more replayability to already replayable game.
9/10, "Game of the Year" of the Year.

This game isn't for everyone, this game isn't for gamers who care only about high octane action, or mind blowing graphics. This game does 2 or 3 things so absolutely right however it makes it worth it for the people who care about those things. The story is minimal; you come home and everyone is gone and your goal is to figure out why, I'll leave it at that. It is more or less a point and click first person adventure game. There are no actual dangers in the game, no enemies, no stats, no interactive npc's, no combat system. This game does however have the ability to give an overdose of nostalgia, and even more so if the player grew up in the 90's, or even ever had any sort of teenage angst. So really the one thing this game does incredibly well is the enviroment. I spent hours looking around and just picking up and manipulating and reading things. Best/Worst of all I would see things in this game that I remembered doing and using and that would trigger long lost memories. . . normally good, some bad, none of them were regretted. So if you want a high octane, shoot em up, or a spine tingling horror fest with danger around every corner, go elsewhere. If you want to re-live some cherished memories of your younger self from the 90's, all while putting together what happened to your family in game through a short but somehow very emotionally charged voice acted story. This work of art is for you.

I'll start by saying that most of the negative reviews are either bandwagoning or just complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, with a few genuine reviews in the bunch. And to the few people who gave this copy of the game a negative review for legit reasons like still being locked at 60 FPS, or being unimpressed by the lack of extra content, I thank you for providing a useful review without  bringing personal insults and hatred towards the Devs/Publishers into the mix. The game is nearly identical to Dark Souls 2, with nothing but a few improvements, with that being said, it's a MUST buy for people new to Dark Souls 2, or the enitre souls franchise.
Dark Souls 2 originally launched for Xbox 360, PS3 and PC. The PS3 and Xbox 360 versions were obviously locked at 30 FPS and 720p which to most people, especially PC Gamers is absolutely atrocious. With the release of the next gen consoles, Bandai Namco decided that they wanted to re-release it so that owners of the newer consoles could experience the game in full 60 FPS, 1080p glory. I'm sure part of it was money, but 30-60 FPS in a Souls game is a HUGE difference, hell it's huge in nearly any game. Any Dev would want to see their game played in most enjoyable/smoothest way possible. So they decided to pretty the game up a bit, pack all the DLC together with the base game, and add some tweaks to enemy placements to make the experience a little more fresh. To show fair treatment PC also got a re-release, because if PC didn't people would just ♥♥♥♥♥ about that too. And it does suck that they couldn't just find a way to update the current DX9 PC version to DX11, but I'm sure there were a lot of issues/hurdles with that, and they just decided to make it an entirely different game. The old DX9 version still got a HUGE pack with almost every little bit of content the newer game was getting for FREE. The ONLY difference between the old DX9 version and the DX11 Scholar of the First Sin version is, obviously, DX11, additional enemies and different enemy placement, and 6 people co-op instead of 4. That is literally it. If you already own the DX9 version you by NO MEANS are forced to get this, and probably shouldn't unless you have friends who got it, but the ONLY downside of the DX11 version is that you can only play with other people who also have the newer version (Scholar people can't play with older copies of DS2) and saves don't follow over. Those are the only 2 cons. Even the Pricing for the game is fantastic. If you didn't get around to buying any of the DLC for Dark Souls 2, the upgrade is essentially free, and if you did, the upgrade is only 20 bucks. I do wish people who had Dark Souls 2 and the season pass got a bigger discount, but 20 dollars for an overhaul of the base game, is not bad at all. And most importantly, you still keep the old Dark Souls 2 in your steam library, so you can switch between them at will.
TL;DR Yes It would have been nice for this to be an extension of the base game instead of a new one, but it's better to assume that wasn't possible than freak the ♥♥♥♥ out at Bandai Namco. Dark Souls 2 is doing the exact same thing GTA V did, except Rockstar had the hindsight to delay the PC version until the next gen versions were out. But did you really want to wait another year for Dark Souls 2 on PC? This version is a completely optional and non essential buy for PC if you already own Dark Souls 2, but it's absolutely essential if you own a next gen console. This was a next gen edition made for Consoles that PC were given so that we couldn't complain, but of course that's going to happen regardless. It's very affordable if you already own Dark Souls 2 and is a nice experience for Dark Souls 2 fans looking for a fresh start.

Having gone over a year without completing any video games, I sat down one night to play Gone Home and try it out.  After all, the reviews had been talking about the experience that was to be had and I wanted to find out exactly what that would entail.
It was a cold December evening when I started to play, the city lights reflecting off of the low-hanging clouds, casting a glow over the city that made it possible to drive without headlights.  Something about being able to see clearly in the dark has always had a magical quality to me that brings on a sense of serenity.  That night quickly turned into one of my more enjoyable evenings in a long time.  The feelings the game brought out instantly transported me back to my own adolescence, a time of discovery and uncertainty.  A time where it was hard to know exactly how I should feel.  It also made me reflect upon lost friendships and how emotions can be cruel, but rewarding at the same time.
Although these characters are fictional, I can imagine that there were many individuals out there that went through a similar situation.  If anything, I believe this game will have people view life differently, to question and challenge their own preconceived ideas.  As a game, it was short and not the typical fare.  As an experience, I'm guessing it will stick with you for awhile.  For the latter reason, this game gets a 10 out of 10 and will be my argument for how I feel that games are art, and deserved to be treated as such.

This is an amazing "game", in that it is equally a work of art, as it is a work of genius.  My only true difficulty in writing this review is to explain why any 80's baby must buy this game without including any spoilers.
This game does an amazing job of creating a looming sense of foreboding that only begins to make sense near the end, when all the clues about these people's lives have been revealed. These clues can only be revealed by picking up and interacting with every single object you can find. So many of the objects have story driven clues attached to them, and these are important.
It is a deeply story driven emotional trip. I was born in '81 and so I can identify with the characters, 'cliches' and period sets. I don't think many born post 1995 will understand many of the potent imageries in this game, nor be able to identify with it.
If you enjoy FPS shooters for the splash-and-guts, don't bother with this. If you are like me and you like them because you like to see how the story will be revealed, to find out where it will take you on a journey [with the shooting elements for fun, sure] then you may gain some satisfaction from this title.
I would love to go on about this and explain more, but I fear that doing so will contain potential spoilers.
Again, my key points. This is more an art piece about uncovering a story based on the pop culture and prejudices of the early 1990's - that's 25 years ago. This is a story where anyone under 30 will barely appreciate the many pop-culture references.
This game is now one of my favourites, although it has very little replay value. This game is not about replay value. It's about the emotional investment you make into the lives of the missing family members. I want to compare it to Portal, - where Portal was a puzzle-based interactive story, this is more a discovery based one. Where Portal was an adventure based game, this is an emotional based one.
This is a 2h tale (you could probably speed run it in about 5 mins or less, especially if you know where to look for certain objects) that should be completed in one sitting.  If you like slower games or games with interesting ways of telling stories, such as Journey, Heavy Rain, Dear Esther, or even mods like The Stanley Parable, than Gone home is certain to grab you and not let go. I feel this is a much better experience than Dear Esther, though.

Gone Home is a great, albeit short, story-based exploration game. The gameplay is essentially a framing device for the story of the main character's sister, which is revealed through a series of notes, audio logs, and other objects lying around the house that the game takes place in. There are also two subplots following the main character's mother and father, both of which are revealed a bit more subtly than the main plot (they're told only through a few objects and notes, with no audio logs). The overall story is moving, interesting and atmospheric, and the way the story is told takes great advantage of the explorative structure of the game; it really just wouldn't be as good if the story was told through book or film instead of through a game. Even spoiling the genre of the story beforehand in a text review or plot summary lessens the impact of actually experiencing the narrative through the game world. I honestly believe that everyone should get around to playing through this game once in their lives.
Now for the less positive aspects. The game is really short. It took me 100 minutes to finish at a leisurely pace, and I found little point to ever playing through the game a second time. Most people will probably finish the game as fast or faster than I did, since the game always marks locked doors, open doors adjacent to your current location, and secret areas that you found in notes. Your exploration of the various rooms will follow a mostly linear path without much difficult thought as to what to do or where to go next. Which leads me to my next point, the game is so simple that you you could make a convincing argument that this is more of a linear 3d visual novel than a game. There are no puzzles or challenges. The few locks that exist are opened with labeled keys or 4 number combinations that are found in fairly straightforward locations later in the game. As mentioned before, you don't even have to remember where the locked doors are, since the map marks them for you. While this simple gameplay approach does help convey the story better, as it is a bit more immersive and prevents the player from accidentally grinding the pace of the storytelling in its tracks by getting stuck on a puzzle, it will likely frustrate people who were expecting the advanced puzzle solving generally associated with the adventure game genre. This is a game for people who want to see an interesting narrative portrayed in a unique way; if you're hoping for anything else, you should play something different. Lastly, while the main plot is very strong, I felt that the mom and dad subplots were a bit weak, mostly due to their vagueness. I honestly can't describe the mother's personality at all, and while the dad has some depth in terms of personality, his story is very straightforward.
Ultimately, while I do really like this game, there is not enough content to justify the current full $20 purchase. I wholeheartedly encourage people to buy this the second it goes on sale for $10 or less, set aside a couple hours to play through it in one sitting, and then go recommend it to their friends. Like I said, it's a game everyone should play once.

It's a pretty rare thing to see a unique shooter out there, let alone one that actually has an active community, let alone one that's actually fun to play.
Verdun's all three. One of the few success stories that came out of early access, Verdun is a squad-based, teamwork-loving FPS that takes you to a time not covered in most shooters because it's not very marketable. The game feels good, runs smoothly (your mileage may vary, don't run the game on a potato), and provides enough depth to get you hooked, but at its most basic a new player can get into the game if they stick with it long enough. It's my new addiction.
Not going to go too in-depth about the nitty-gritty of the gameplay, but I'll just leave these pointers here.
You Might Like it If:
You like shooters with a degree of complexity and require teamwork
You hate microtransactions and want to earn your way to the top (Not grindy. I've logged in 28 hours at the time of this review and I've essentially got nearly everything).
You like a unique, historical setting.
You'll Hate It If:
You rage-quit easy. This game doesn't have a learning curve, it has a learning cliff.
You want to play run-and-gun in WW1. If you try that, you'll get sniped. Over. And over. And over.
You suck at teamwork. You need to work with your team in order to survive, and by extension, win.

Well we were waiting and its out. Famous DirectX11 version with separated online servers and characters from regular Dark Souls 2 version.
Okay first, I didnt play too much, about 4 hours on my account and 10 on my wife. Is it worth ? It's worth, player database will transfer over SOTFS version anyways eventually so you wanna be there and prepared for PvP. If you dont care about MP side, then play your regular version and enjoy. Changes are relative and you are not missing anything which would increase or ruin your experiance if you are new to the game.
In terms of graphics (keep on mind I never tried ENB mods or any other), there is no difference at all. Literally, perhaps some deflections from Sun but that is pretty much everything. Some areas are darker and that is exactly what we needed in original game. Torch will be required if you are not brightening up too much your screen then normal.
Huge change for me so far is AI. He is not smarter or harder, not at all. Random AI is added to some locations, some are missing and placed in same area but with suprise factor. So even if you know game you are gonna feel that devs are trying to get you from behind so you are going to check most of the corners when you dont see well known enemy ahead.
I feel like that in begining in couple areas there are WAY TOO MANY enemies if you are going dexterity build with 2 weapons, shield is like "must have" in some situations if you dont want to break everything around.
So overall:
+ Changed locations for AI
+ Suprise factor for experianced players
+ Darker Areas
+ Increased number of AI
+ Changed locations of NPC
- Same graphics
- Separated community (its good for profit but bad for community)
- Perhaps not worth 14/24euros if you are expecting drastic changes.
- We cant gift upgrade to our friends (so if you dont have money/card you need to recieve full SOTFS version of 40 euros)

My Review
___________________________________________________________________________________
GAMEPLAY 9/10
This Game Has Many Different Gameplay Options.
Here Is A Full List: Deathmatch
Team Deathmatch (My Favorite)
Plant The Bomb (Kind Of Like CS)
Storm (Warface's Version Of Tf2's Attack/Defend)
Capture The Flag
Destruction (One Team Delivers 3 Airstrikes On Enemy Base. Team Must Hold Postion In Center Of Map)
Most Are Pretty Fun To Play On. Maps Are Well Made And Balanced. There is a co-op mode too so you can play with friends in missons.

___________________________________________________________________________________
.                                       Graphics 8/10
Graphics Make Me Feel Like I Am In The Original Black Ops So Graphics Are Pretty Good But This Day In Age, I Feel Warface Should Release A Whole New Graphics Engine And Make Textures Better But Graphics Are Still Very Good
___________________________________________________________________________________
.                                        Classes 9/10
Classes Are Well Made And Balanced Here Is A List:
Rifleman- A Rifleman is all providing cover fire and is the driving force in the team. Made for close to medium range combat scenarios, thanks to either their assault rifles or light machine guns. A Rifleman's Special Action is resupplying ammo to their teammates and themselves while in combat
Medic- The Medic class is built for close combat, equipped with shotguns and a light pistol. The Medic has the ability to heal themselves and their allies. Fallen allies can be revived with a defibrillator.
Engineer- The Engineer is tactically equipped for close to medium range, equipped with either submachine guns or compact assault rifles. The class's Special Action is the ability to restore allies' armor as well as their own. Engineers can also plant claymores that detonate on a moment's notice.
Sniper- The Sniper class is silent but deadly. Equipped for long range combat scenarios with sniper rifles, as stated before, they hold no special action; but they can place anti-personnel mines if they are purchased for the class with in game money (no purchase of real life money req.). The sniper is also the ideal "cover" for the other team members.
Classes Are Balanced And Each Classes Weapons Have Ups And Downs
.                                                   OVERALL RATING 8.5/10

While I haven't finished my first play through of Scholar of the First Sin, yet, I think I've gotten far enough in that I can at least make a decently educated review. So far, I do not regret purchasing Scholar one bit. While the new enemy placements can be more of a miss than a hit at times (only one time for me, personally) over all, I feel they're a massive improvement in some areas, and fresh and new in others. Many of the encounters are true to Dark Souls: Prepare To Die design, where something looks unassuming and easy at first, but is just bait to pull you into investing into an encounter you weren't prepared for. Updated AI allows them to come meet you when you're not expecting them, rather than when you stumble across them, and many enemies now lie waiting in ambush in unexpected locations to take a crack at gathering your souls. Additionally, it seems that isolated, unexpected 'bumps' in the difficulty curve have been evened out, so that it feels more a steep hill, rather than a gradual hill with sudden walls every so often. This is on top of many engaging and fun designs that'll throw unexpected fights your way even if you're a true Souls veteran, at least for your first few play throughs. And many new NPC friendly and enemy phantoms to mix up your play.
While the AI/enemy placement changes are the most important change to me so far, the game's improvement to DirectX 11 has allowed for improvements in graphics and stability in some instances. While the textures weren't updating for the PC version too much, yet, the new lighting allows a lot of them to come out, a mostly subtle difference, but after a few hours of playing you come to appreciate the design more and more. By far the best change has come with particles, however. Mist, fog, poison mist, spell effects, items used, fog walls, all are gorgeously updated to be truly spectacular.
While many of the issues of the normal edition haven't been fixed yet (60 fps issues relating to durability/controller input/dodge rolling invulnerability frames, as well as the Soul Memory mechanic for online match making), I hope that these will have their attention turned towards in the next few months now that the disparity between consoles and PC which might have exascerbated isn't as hefty.

Edit:
alright i'll just say it, The pricetag is justified (the discount i mean)
People are up in arms over nothing, this is easily worth £12 even if it doesn't seem like much.
Its like a game growing up, Fromsoft had an amazingly talented baby, not as good as its older brother but so close that you couldn't really tell them apart, both with their drawbacks and better characteristics: What this version of the game has done is offered a DLC price to dress the child properly and give him good tablemanners:
By that I mean the game now makes more sense and feels more like dark souls, The Heide Knights are where they are supposed to be, the royal areas are guarded by the guards designated to protect the king, the barbarians at the Wharf are agressive as ♥♥♥♥, THE PERSUER ACTUALLY PERSUES YOU.
The experience has been reworked and realized into its true form. Things are where they are supposed to be, a deeper story has been told just by moving things around and thats a seriously good thing, an example would be when, Spoiler, You enter the Tower of Heide, the Heide knights that sat there in a state of depression suddenly realise you have entred something of which you are not allowed to be in, the Dragonrider dies, and what do they do? They get up and actively seek you out.
The experience I had when I turned around after leaving a heide knight alive and seeing him walk towards me was quite something, of course it was me going "Wait what are you doing?" but another part of me was "Oh they hate me now, but why?"
It was after I walked out of the tower i realised that by entering the tower they were supposed to be looking after I♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥them off. Isn't that strange how one little thing can turn the story, the journey you travel that much more different?
Well you tell me.
The story has been resolved, whether it fills in plotholes I do not know, but what I can tell you, they deserve the money, the effort spent on this is pretty obvious and I'm glad they did.
The DX11 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t was dumb though. So very dumb. Fromsoftware ♥♥♥♥ed up like 2k with Evolve did, but it doesn't make them bad "games". The games are good, they just suck at practises.
But whatever, £10 are worth it right? What about all those Payday 2 DLCS just for more guns/masks that you will use to play the same missions again and again that you've already beaten, right? RIGHT?
♥♥♥♥ me, Gamers today have their priorities ♥♥♥♥ed.

In terms of Entente powers you have British Tommies, Canadians (a rare sight in gaming), and two different French divisions. In terms of Central powers you have three different German divisions. It certianly gives you a wide variety of choices. At last a good game about World War 1!

Positives:
- Every moveable object is interactable
- Pretty nice design
- Touching story
Negatives:
- Way, way too short compared to what it costs
- Even though the story was touching, it wasn't developed very well
- No challange
--------------------------------
For starters, Gone Home is not really a game. Yes it is a game, but there is absolutely no challange (the puzzles are basic "find the key" and find the map so the hidden path you couldn't open before suddenly can be opened) and the only thing you really need to do is explore and click on certain objects in the right order in order for things to happen.
Is the story emotional? Yeah. Is it well developed however? No, not at all. The main story (about the protagonist) is touching, but it is a cliche teenage love story with no real plot twists. The main character is homo, which is perfectly fine, I am in no way against that, but it doesn't matter at all. It could as well have been a guy and a girl, or two guys. It makes no difference. Most of the names are even gender neutral. It is that extremly cliche.
And when I say it wasn't very well developed, I mean, for instance, that a huge part of the story felt repeditive, and the whole "psyco house" thing was only mentioned once. Other students from Sam's school said she lived in the psyco house, but it was never even once explained why.
The biggest reason why it wasn't as good as I was hoping for is the lenght of the game. I have played for around 1.6 hours and I have finished the game from start to end, and I went into every single room. Someone mentioned that it is possible to remove the puzzles so you freely can move around the house from the beginning. The game would literally be a minute long if you went straight for the end.
------------------------------------------
In conclusion: Is it worth buying it? No. Not for 19 euros. I suggest you watch it on Youtube if you want to know what the story is about. I am a mod developer, and my latest mod is longer than this game, and it's for free. They want you to pay 19 euros for a game that is under two hours long.
It's not worth it. Which is why I gave it a thumbs down.

I was expecting a lot more from this game than I got. I'm a big fan of point-and-click adventure games but there was virtually no gameplay. This would be fine if complimented by an engaging story and emersive environment but both of those aspects fell through, as well.
Working in a 3D environment with a lot of freedom of movement and objects to interact with, I expected there would be some interesting mechanics thrown in. Finding a lot of tools, areas to perform certain tasks and items that looked almost collectable left me excited for potential puzzle solving but the game had nothing but text and recordings.
I bought the game knowning the objective was to find out why everyone in the house was missing (as mentioned on the store page) which was easy enough to do early on in the game even without all of the story. But as for the story, it was extremely long-winded and dry. There was no depth, twists, quirks, or the like to keep me entertained.
Aside from the poor gameplay and story, the environment really needed some work. Although the game was smoothe and bugless from what I saw and the lighting effects worked well, the entire dark, stormy atmosphere was overplayed and useless. The ambience for the storm and random "old-house" noises were terribly annoying as the quality was miserable and they were looped very often. The general music was infrequent and nothing to brag about, either.
All-in-all, I didn't find this to be a very good adventure game and wouldn't recommend it. Most aspects were tolerable at best and although the story was slightly cute, it did nothing for me.

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

- Enemy placement has changed enough I run through areas I "know" with my shield up in case something new is lurking!
- Your save file! - yep old save doesn't work!
Worth the upgrade? I don't know... the 3rd party graphic enhancements for the original did a nice job with shaders already. It is nice to see different enemies in different places it makes having to play though again interesting at least. If they hadn't changed enemy placement I would be much more angry they didn't transfer the save file. We'll keep playing and see. I don't see any map changes yet, but it's still early.
If you haven't already purchased the game it's time: all the DLC included and a "definitive" edition, this will probably be the last release at least for years until it's no longer playable on modern hardware. Still one of the best games of all time, just not sure it needed this version if you've already finished the game.

The overall design of the game is nothing new but the detail put into the overall experience really shows how much effort the developers put into it.

I was considering writing a review after finishing the game and checked to see how redundant my praise would be, only to find the first several comments were all negative. I do not enjoy telling people to disregard the opinions of others, but in this case I feel like it falls on the consumer to accept that what a game is offering may not be to their liking without it being a bad game. This game is not for everyone, to be sure. Many people may not enjoy the game's slow pace, or the lack of any danger. Complaints that it is not "gamey" enough are common.
This game is about atmosphere, emotion, and connection. If you are comfortable challenging a different landscape than most games offer, it is worth your time and money. This game will never put you in a life or death situation, never demand you make a tough call or take a difficult shot. The only threat or feelings of unease come from how perfectly the feeling of being alone in an empty house is replicated, or the concern you develop for the characters whose lives you are tasked with catching up on. This is the best narrative game I have ever played, and if you can't relate to the characters involved you may simply not have the life experience to find relating to other people possible. If you are looking for a game about a personal story of real-world hardship, there is no question of whether or not this game is worth your money. It is short, but in the time you spend with it, it will change your outlook toward -- and expectations of -- videogame storytelling forever. Find some time, alone, and finish it in one sitting, maybe with the lights low and a box of tissues. It won't take a night, and you'll carry it with you forever.

Gone Home is a very simple adventure game that allows you to control a girl named Katie freshly come back at home after a trip in Europe. Since the whole mansion is now empty, your goal is to find clues about your family's current whereabouts.
For being an adventure title, Gone Home is pretty straightforward: there aren't difficult puzzles to solve or clues to connect. Your whole experience will boil down to explore Katie's house and collect various hints that will unfold the story of her family in the past weeks. Video games are a strong platform for storytelling. Gone Home uses the medium well to convey its social commentary in a gripping, thought-provoking manner. Alas, with the a price tag of $20, I find myself needing to warn off potential buyers.
Gone Home's story sheds new light and encourages the player to think about modern social taboos from a different angle; whilst noble, is not enough to hold a game together. Outside of its story line, Gone Home's single enviroment is blocky, pixelated, dispropartionate, uninspired and poorly lit. The gameplay is quite linear and is driven by grab and pull mechanics, which initially makes exploration exciting, but eventually starts feeling like a chore.
The audio side of Gone Home really adds tension to the underlying plot. Though, in hindsight, its only purpose is to blind the player long enough that the actual plot line can emerge.
Now comes the kicker, the real reason I would encourage people not to fork out the money for this game: replayability.
Once you have finished Gone Home, any potential for replayability goes completely out the window. Gone Home relies so heavily on is linear gameplay to direct the player through the story that it makes replaying the game pointless. You will know each story point, each turn, where you are and where you need to go. Sadly, the emotional rollercoaster Gone Home provides is a one-way ride.
Whilst short and sweet, $20 is an incredible amount of money to spend on a game that is fundamentally poorly made and only offers up to 2hrs gameplay (that's if you are really taking your time) and no replayability. I do not regret playing Gone Home, I simple regret paying for it.
My recommendation: Save your money and watch a Youtube playthrough.

Verdun is a semi-realistic WW1 first person shooter set in the trenches of France and Belgium. The maps themselves are large and offer many different ways to assault the enemy fortifications, all of which usually end up in death. This is the meat grinder of the first world war after all, so expect to die. A lot.
The teams are split up into squads, with four members per squad. The creator of the squad can pick what type of squad, with each one offering a different play style. From the British Tommies who specialize in support to the Canadian Storm Troopers who specialize in trench assaults and fortification clearing. Here's where my biggest gripe comes into play; If your squad is a low level, you get earky war uniforms. The only way to get late war uniforms is to upgrade your squad, but the only way to do that is to play with the same people over and over again.
There are two game modes to choose from, one that offers up what you'd expect from a WW1 game with two teams assaulting and defending each others trenches, and another, more arcadey rifle deathmatch.
Make no mistake though, the game can be clunky (it was made by 4 guys, so cut them some slack) and the visual presentation can look a bit dated at times.
Overall I would say Verdun is well worth the money. It's a fun, fast paced shooter that feels relatively realistic, but throws in just enough arcade so it doesn't suffer from Arma syndrome. The maps are big, and the trenches are claustrophobic. It suffers from a very small amount of technical issues and is a bit dated looking, with a weird squad progression system that really takes away from the feeling of leveling up. But make no mistake, Verdun is a great game and one that I would seriously recommend.

I think Warface is quickly becoming one of my favorite FPS games. To me, Warface is essentially Call of Duty but without all of the ridiculous stuff like quick scoping (at least I haven't noticed any of that), it feels like it's more balanced and every player has a fair opportunity right off the bat. However, no game is without negatives so let's break down the positives and negatives in a list.
The Good:
- Balanced play style
- Real time weapon attachment system that allows you to switch out things like scopes and grips mid battle without having to wait until the round is over to edit the classes.
- Decent graphics even at the lowest graphic quality
- Movement and aiming feels very smooth (if you've played a lot of indie FPS games you know what I'm talking about)
- Runs perfectly fine on a stock computer from Walmart that's a few years old (you don't need a super computer to run it)
- The starting gear isn't as powerful as the gear you can buy later on but it's still good enough to win with, it doesn't feel under powered
- In game points earned from each round that can be spent on new equipment
- Sliding feature is unique and there are spots on some maps specifically for this, such as a small hole in a fence that you can slide under (some other FPS games have this but most don't)
The Bad:
- Some equipment can only be purchased for a limited time before it expires and you have to purchase it again (this is extremely annoying if you don't have a bunch of time to play the game every day as your equipment will be expired whenever you come back to it)
- Killcam shows who killed you and their position but it doesn't show the kill from their perspective
- Getting killed by a grenade doesn't show the enemy that threw it
- Some of the maps have a poor layout for a shooting game and force you to go to specific places or through choke holds which make it easy for the enemy team to spawn camp you and stops you from discovering your own play style
- Characters feel like they have no weight as you can walk up to a teammate and push them around and off ledges (this is really annoying when you're laying prone and a teammate walks by and pushes you out of position)
Could Be Added:
- Killstreak rewards like airdrops or missiles (similar to Call of Duty)
- Killcam through the perspective of the player that killed you (killcams like this are great for learning new positions and techniques)
Bugs/glitches:
- There is only one glitch that I've found and it allows you to see through a piece of cloth that you normally wouldn't be able to see through on the Airport map, however the amount of area that's revealed when doing this isn't really beneficial to the player enough to give them an advantage or warrant fixing immediately, just something for the developers to watch out for and possibly fix in an update.
Conclusion:
Over-all I think this game is great! It's very well balanced so you can get right in without dying every two seconds and it feels really smooth. The constant reminders of micro transactions are a bit annoying but I understand that developing a game like this isn't easy or free so I don't hold it against them too much. They have to make money some how to support future development and marketing and I think more people should take that into account before judging a game for micro transactions. Without a way for developers to make money we would have a lot less free games for you to add to your collection.

Foreword: This Review is for people who own the original DX9 version with the DLC's. If you don't own the game then what are you waiting for? Go ahead and buy the DX11 version and if you own the DX9 version without the DLC's then its deffinitely be worth upgrading too. I changed this review because after playing through the whole game, i realized that it offers a lot more than i thought after my first impression of this version which was 3 hours into the game to the last giant.
The Review:
Remember when you played the DLC's and thought "why doesn't have the base game this level of quality?" Now it has! Well, almost.
The level design is still almost the same but the changes they made make the game feel a lot more fresh and make some areas more than just a corridor with tons of enemies in them. Some people made the comparison to Zelda: Ocarina of Time Master Quest but thats not exactly right. I mean its harder than the original in some areas but it isn't much harder than the original version, just better balanced in terms of gameplay. In some areas they actually took out some enemies and replaced them with stronger ones and with some enemies you wouldn't even expect to see in certian areas, like at all. So it makes the game a bit more challanging with way less BS. There are now NPC invaders through the whole game which follow you and have actually a point to the plot (one in specific). They act like they had in the DLC's with gestures and nasty tactics which will get you off guard.
Going back to the level design; some of the changes they made are subtle but big at the same time and make the game a lot more interesting to explore, even if you already played the original version. One of the changes made me actually go "WOW". For example without any spoilers; remember the dragon skeleton in Aldia's Kept which was just a "meh" shock moment? Now it actually has a POINT in the game. Also the torch gets finally some use and can reveal some new secrets even though there aren't many new dark areas in the game but you still will use it quite frequently. There are also a lot more petrified statues in the game which will block your way which makes the world they designed a lot more interesting and make you decide if you wanna use a fragrant branch of yore now or keep it for later and you can revisit an area to see what you missed behind that statue. Also the key items for the DLC areas have to be found now and you don't get them magically into your inventory which makes these areas more connected to the main game and a little bit of a secret.
A little add up to the graphics; sure they aren't much better then the original but atleast you don't have to use any third partie tools anymore to make the game look like a current game, so thats a plus (also you don't have to fear anymore to get softbanned). Also after playing the DX11 version its hard to go back to the DX9 version because in there everything looks bland while in the DX11 version everything pops more out and looks nicer.
BTW: THEY FINALLY FIXED THE DURABILLITY BUG!
Conclusion:
This is what Dark Souls 2 should have been and feels a lot more like a true sequel to the first one. After playing the game through i feel like the upgrade for € 15.- are justefied. If you are only interested in PVP then i'm not sure if you have to upgrade, but the playerbase gets smaller in the DX9 version and i think you will need to upgrade at some point anyway but its deffinitely worth it.
Also i wanna apologize for being kind of missleading at first but the first impression i had was terrible but the changes of the game will unfold itself if you keep playing and you will think "huh, that is actually pretty damn good and makes finally sense now."

This game is really something else. I had not heard of it until I was looking for games to follow up the likes of Dear Esther and Home. This fits quite nicely in that niche group of games that set out to tell a story, and really set them selves apart by actually taking away things such as combat and interactable characters. Gone Home, for me, was a view into myself. I can't really relate to what most of what was going on in the story, but it really made me think of how problems are viewed from the outside.
As a game, it did things that I've really been wanting from games more and more, an emotional impact. There wasn't any crazy death scene or anything like that, but it's these nuances of what has happened in this house that you're exploring. Right from the get-go you start asking questions as to why this is that way, or why is this broken. It's these questions that will make you want to pick up every single book and piece of paper that you find, hoping to reveal some of what happened, and maybe where your entire family is. To answer those, it is completely up to you. Any voices that you hear are almost entirely from your sister Sam, through her journan entries. It is possible to complete the game without discovwering all of these, but if you want to play this game the way it was meant to be played, you'll try and find all of them.
As you play the game, as many as five different sub-stories might be going on while you try to find answers to all of them. It is very easy to focus on one and forget some of the others, so here are some questions taht I've come up with to help you, and I've tried to leave out as many spoilers as possible, and these are all about the game:
What is Sam and Lonnie's relationship?
How is your parent's reltionship?
Who is Oscar?
Why is the house in such a mess?
Why are there skid marks in the garage?
That last one is actually a question that I asked myself, and then instantly started tearing up after I found the answer. Pay attention to the dates on every item you find, it seems simple, but when you find a clue within those items, you'll see why I got so emotional. Enjoy the game, sit back for an hour or two and let it grab you. A good way to read a book is to try and not guess the end, do that with this game, or else you'll be dissapointed.

Verdun is based in the tumultuous and incredibly bloody World War I, where trench warfare and the rise of the first tanks took place. The game takes you to various locals and humongous maps spanning the length of France. I have long been an admirer of history, and I must say that this game has not disappointed me in keeping to the period.
To speak of the graphics, the game in it's earliest form was basic at the least. However, it has gone far from those nascent graphics and has blossomed into a grimy and bloody masterpiece of historical-based games. Gun models are very realistic and detailed, and include things such as serial numbers and maker's etchings for those that look closer than just the far sights. Uniforms, with the benefit of a scrupulous historical adviser and modeling team, are top notch and pleasant to the eye, as much as they are to the period. On top of these, much work has been done to detail every inch of maps with props and trenches that are again as if they were lifted right from the annals of time to be played by our more recent generation.
Game play is formed to follow the manner of tactics used at the time, with the defending or assaulting of trenches, where the capturing of a trench by your team earns it one grueling, hard-won point. After such a minor victory has been achieved, you must then aid your team in defending your well-earned prize for a time before continuing on to the next trench or, failing that, being beaten back to start anew. In this, Verdun captures the essence of the period brutally, but beautifully. You are also able to have a variety of characters at your command that are chosen from a "squad." A squad, whether of the Central or Entente powers or factions, have four characters each to choose from, and are further broken down with three loadouts, two of which needing be unlocked via points that you are able to earn. Furthermore, team play is also very encouraged with the inclusion of squad voice chat and squad or team text chat, allowing you to alert your teammates to an incursion into your trench by the enemy. The deadliness of the period is also well represented by the ease with which your character can be brought down to a rather nasty end, whether it be through a bullet to the skull or a mortar round to your hapless, rag doll body. This being said, I must also mention that there are times when game play breaks down to rather nasty spamming of snipers or those that can and do use grenades to a pretentious amount, forcing the enemy team to also stoop to such levels or be annihilated. While this does happen on occasion, it is few enough times to not pose a very large problem, though one that does need some balancing in the hopeful future.
Of the squads I mentioned earlier, you have seven to choose from between the two sides. Three belong to Germany, where you have the Stosstruppen, Landsers, and Alpenjagers. Another four of the Entente powers include the Canadians, "Tommies," Chasseurs Alpins, and Poilus. All of these have their own four variants of characters and three variants of loadouts, which add up to eighty-four different possibilities. For instance, each squad has a leader that can call down powerful artillery, noxious gas, or recon planes to give the location of enemies to you and your entire team. Or you can have machine gunners that lay down anything within their field of fire. More squad types are on the way according to the Verdun wiki, which should be very interesting in future gameplay, especially if they also were to include the Russian faction as well, though such a squad might have some internal dissention...
In any case, with the exception of a few player-based hiccups, there is little that can be said against the game, besides the occasional problems for people to connect to friends at times, which could be a rather essential bug were it not to be addressed. I recommend yes for those that are looking into this game, as it is educational and fun for all that would play as a soldier of the muddy, frightening, maddening, grueling, and wonderful Verdun!

Lets get one thing straight:
WWI is a topic that doesn't get many games made about it
Nobody makes any WWI games these days (well, any GOOD ones, that is). Why? Because Devs dont see that much potential in the idea, and its understandable, back then all there was to warfare was a load of primitive weapons, bomb shells, gas, and thats about it. Most people would think that WWI just isnt a topic that a game can be made under. Well the devs over at M2H and Blackmill think otherwise. They took a chance and made a game simulating an actual WWI scenario. Verdun is one of the few games about WWI out there, and, at that, a diamond in the rough.
First of all, the presentation
Set during, as said before, the WWI theatre, this game looks absolutely stunning! The graphics are solid, i've recieved no errors, and everything looks just right. Everythign looks, sounds, and FEELS like it fits into WWI (and they do). The maps feel true to the WWI setting, With all the trenches, no mans land, barbed wire, etc. Im able to run it smoothly, but thats only me. Like any game with good graphics, make sure to get a powerful computer! So, in the presentation section, everything is good to go!
Now, the thing we all game to the game for, the (unique) gameplay
WWI was ALOT diffrent from WWII. Let me explain. First of all, Trench warfare was the standard here. And the game captures this perfectly. Running in th etrenches, defending your base or attacking the enemy's one, it feels claustrophobic and perfectly simulates what it felt like to fight back then. Secondly, the aresenal at your disposal. Sure, theres only 21 weapons (21, lol), but the game knows that and executes these weapons perfectly, wether the cracking on rifles and long range or a well placed pistol shot, all the weapons feel true to the time and right for the game. But dont worry, more content IS coming, including maps AND new weaponry, including the (In)famous C96 Mauser. Now, how the game works. There are 2 modes: Frontline and Rifle Deathmatch. Frontline works like this. If you are attacking, you need to capture the marked territory. If your attack fails, you head into defend mode, which ill explain in a bit. If someone is there before time is up, however, you will gain some extra time to capture the objective, similar to TF2 and Capture Points. In Defend mode, you need to defend your territory from enemy attacks. After a while, if the enemy doesnt capture your base, the attack will lose momentum and you will head into attack mode. If, after a while, noone gains all the enemy territory, then the match will end in a draw (which seems to happen alot for me, but then again; its probably me). Each squad had diffrent specializations and classes, and those classes each have their own set of weapons that sets them apart from the rest, wether you take of a trusty rifle, and powerful pistol, or are grenading the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of enemies, it all works perfectly and all the weapons are portrayed perfectly. Your commanding Officer in the squad has a VERY important role: to lead you (Duh). He can call orders and call in support strikes with motars and gas (Btw, yea, like i said, theres gas in this game. Press 4 to put on your mask to walk through it. Still, the gas, combined with the sight of the goggles, will hinder your view a bit. Not a bad thing. Just letting ya know) All in all, Frontline is solid. Rifle Deathmatch. This mode is pretty self-explanitory. Kill people with WWI rifles, and show off your WWI rifle skills. Nothign else to say. Overall, the game play Well captures the theme of WWI and is still Fun to play.
All in all, Verdun is one of the few games out there that does somethign different, but it does it perfectly! The Presentation is solid, the gameplay is challenging yet fun and requires you work together to achiev victory. The game is 23$, which is a resonable price, but i think the game should be priced at 15$ (Or heck, even 20$) For its price, in my opinion. But still, this game is worth the price of admission! This is one of the few WWI games out there, and its also one of the best!

For me, Gone Home is an easy recommendation. It's a great example of what it is. But, this won't be for everyone. This game does not especially play to the strengths of the medium, but for me it still adds up to a great experience in the end. This is not a horror game. This is not really a game, so much as it is a form of interactive fiction.
It's a narrative game, like Dear Esther, or To The Moon (sort of). But, I think Gone Home takes the basic "you're propelling a story" mechanic, and delivers a more powerful story in a more engaging way. Gameplay could work, but the choice not to employ it half-heartedly like To The Moon does, is a good one I think.
I think you're looking at 1-2 hours of time here, and you don't _do_ much more than interact with objects, open doors, and walk around. One way or another you're going to get the same ending as everyone else.
I think for some people, this story will really connect and that will be the biggest indicator of whether or not you end up enjoying yourself. There is a great mood, a great atmosphere to the story, and that for me was enough to really be charmed.
I think if you approach this game with the intent of reading a comic book, you'll probably end up getting more out of it than you would have otherwise.

Everything I heard about Gone Home was polarizing. The media praised it as an artistic masterpiece, but many avid gamers condemned it for being a 'walking simulator', or even going as far as to call it a 'non-game'. That makes it strange indeed that having finished Gone Home I felt that it was... Alright. Not great, especially not for the simply insane price tag, but not bad. The story is clearly the focus here, and it's kind of interesting. I especially like the occult and riot grrl themes, but the love story is clearly supposed to be the center of attention and it comes off as insanely juvenile and melodramatic. I get it, they're teens: they're not supposed to have the best prose, but imagine if Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet in the character of two 14 year olds? I wouldn't read that♥♥♥♥♥♥ Then add to this the fact that only the two lovers have fully developed characters and I can't really imagine how this game got so many GOTY awards. Yeah, there's a subplot about marriage, and cheating, and failed ambitions and sibling rivalry, but it never gets any farther than just mentioning it.
Then you have to factor in the abysmal engine and the lack of any player agency whatsoever. There isn't even a mother ♥♥♥♥ing sprint key; they REALLY want you to play the game EXACTLY the way they did, whether you like it or not. Every time I popped in a loud as Hell punk cassette, all I wanted to do was run around the room, crashing into everything, and throwing all the books on the floor, but all of the objects have the same weight and behavior and you just kind of float through the house like some nosy ghost. What, did they expect me to smash the patriarchy in silent contemplation? The graphics are decent, and I know my rig is really dated at this point, but ♥♥♥♥ me, I should NOT be having slowdown issues in Gone Home with the graphics settings turned down.
All in all, if you're the kind of person who enjoys helping yourself to books and notes in videogames, and the prospect of rummaging around an empty house sounds interesting, pick this up. Be aware that the game took me slightly over two hours to find almost everything, and what I didn't find I don't really care to slowly glide through the house again to uncover. Definitely pick this up on sale if you plan to get it.

Everything you like about Counter-Strike with better graphics, faster servers, and more players. If you've never played Counter-Strike before, you could always start with Counter-Strike: Condition Zero. Condition Zero will run better if you have a slower computer or a crappier graphics card. There is an offline mode on Condition Zero where you can practice against bots if you don't do well playing against other people online at first. I don't like the newer Counter-Strike: Global Offensive. My computer won't run it anyway because of a problem with my graphics card. If you like first-person shooters, and like to play a more simple player vs. player game, Source is where it's at. If you are used to Call of Duty, this will be a bit different for you. You have so many hit points before you are dead. There is a good selection of guns, but not a bunch to confuse you like other games. You still have grenades, flashbangs and even smoke grenades if you want. There are a lot of good servers with custom made player maps, which are usually some of the best. The only gripe I have with this game is it has no offline player mode like Condition Zero had. You can still create your own custom games on LAN or with friends against bots though. The maps are downloaded onto your computer, so if you've played the map on a server, you can choose to play it on a custom game.

I spot the flashes from the machine gun from a shell hole on the hill. I phone in the artillery and duck down behind the lip of a crater as the gas rolls in. I fumble with my gas mask as the mortar finds its mark, flinging mangled bodies into the fog.
Then the whistle blows, it's our turn now. A take a breath and jump out of the hole. Running as fast as I can through the dense green smog into the enemy defences. I spot a broken down tank and make my way towards it. I'm mere meters away when I spot a German helmet behind sandbags. He sees me too and opens fire. I dive behind the tank and the shots ring off the armour inches from my head. My vision fades, it is deafening. But not as much as the grenade that rolls beside my exposed flank and detonates.
This game is a great interpretation of WWI. Forget what you know about modern first person shooters. Here, if you get shot - you die. No questions. This game takes skill, teamwork, and a solid set of brass balls.

This game reminds me of a more 'actual-combat-like' gameplay (a little like Battlefield, but nothing like CoD), it is my favourite FPS game to-date and I would recommend any hardcore FPS player to give it a whirl (especially Battlefield Players), and it just keeps on getting more and more enjoyable as my rank improves!
The Good:
The ability to choose whether you unlock; Armour/outfits, or Weapons, or Weapon Attachments, instead of hoping to get what you want when the bar reaches 100%!
The Graphics - Really good for a Free-to-Play, and you also don't need the worlds best GPU to play it, but if you want to, you could probably quite easily play on the greatest GPU ever!!! XD
The community is generally quite pleasant (unlike the majority of the CoD fanbase!)
Great gameplay - every minute is action-packed and it is actually quite fast-pased!
Gamemodes - 2-4 Co-Op missions per day (depending on rank of user), Multiple Versus Gamemodes (and an ability to pick a random one, where your PC will choose one for you if you're easy going!), And a survival gamemode, that unlocks over time as rank increases!! (Who doesn't like survival FPSs?!?!)
IT'S NOT PAY TO WIN!!!! Just rank up, and unlock weapons, or rent them with in-game or real cash!!!!
The Bad:
Some low-rank people are easily noticeable to be new to FPSs - as in, not very well coordinated. Fail to understand simple elements of combat, obviously never played the tutorials after the mandatory ones. And don't understand what a Mini-map/Radar is there for!!  (but helping them is a good idea, as they are new, and do need a bit of help getting the basics crossed-out!!)
Just like most online games - can lag if host has bad connection or servers aren't running very well!
Other than that, I can't think of any other cons for this game!!
My rating - 10/10!

Take position behind a machine gun perched above barbed wire and sandbags, or wait for the whistle of an NCO before rushing over the walls of your trenches to rush the enemy line and (hopefully) take ground.
The landscape is properly dreary, desolate, and pock-marked with shell holes to use as cover, or a grave site. Keep your gas mask handy as the air will soon fill with death.
This game not only gives you a fantastic first person shooter experience, but transports you back to a time when geo-politics were decided by men of honor who sealed deals in blood, sweat, and bullets.
So few companies take on the challenge of presenting a WW1 game that I not only applaud this group for their historic-minded effort, but for getting the mechanics of an FPS of this time so very right.
Deploy-able weapons work like a charm. Every gun has it's own feel, sound, and operation. Your actions matter; if you sprint while trying to reload then you will leave the bolt open. Remember to close it! And don't forget you can cook off grenades.
A great experience, but the current price tag is way too high. Wait for a good sale.

Final verdict. 8/10

You are not the protagonist, and Gone Home is not your story.
In most games, the players write their own stories: their actions and struggles define the game plot. Not so in Gone Home: this game asks you to explore the stories of other people (your family, mostly, including the psycho great-uncle Oscar). Your impact on these people is zero, because during the game, they're not home. Also, their stories are hidden: you need to find it in odds and ends strewn around the house, and even if you find them all, there'll be a lot left to the imagination (provided you have any).
If you're a narcisstic person with no emotional intelligence, this game will leave you cold because it won't be about you, but about other poeple's feelings. If you aren't, you'll enjoy a good teenie "chick-flick" story told from a very different angle. If you're a child of the nineties, it's worth it for amount of love and detail that went into the whole house alone. Rarely have I wandered through a game and felt so immersed.

Dino D-Day is a frantic, action-packed multiplayer game that transports you to a World War II that should have been. You and your friends can battle online choosing to serve the cause of the Allied nations or the Nazis. The Allied side includes seven playable characters including Trigger, a Protoceratops rescued from the Nazis. Each Allied class has unique weapons and abilities to use in combat. Gun down a Dilophosaur with your trusty M1 Garand, blast a kamikaze pterosaur out of the sky with your Thompson sub-machine gun, or toss out a dead jackrabbit to lure a raptor into a trap.
As an Axis player you will have your choice of three human classes and four dinosaur classes. Ambush your enemy with speed and stealth as the Raptor, mercilessly pound the enemy with a heavy 20mm gun as the Desmatosuchus, rampage through enemy groups as the Dilophosaur or pick up a body and throw it at an enemy for a double kill! Or if you prefer a rifle in your hand, the German soldier classes are the perfect complement to their dinosaur comrades.
You’ve played World War II games before…but have you played a World War II game with dinosaurs?

Note: there's a bit more to discover than just the "main story" ..
So, that leaves only one conclusion. Should you try this game? Yes
Should you pay anything more than 10$ at most? No.
I highly suggest getting this game when it's on at least a 50% sale.

Though there is a lot of controversy with regards to the depth and value of this game, overall, it is an...interesting experience to say the least.  It is relatively short, only about 2-3 hours even when you take the time to thoroughly examine each room.  The main plot and story line is also short and is narrated by a voiceover for the duration of the game.  As for some of the side stories that run through the game, you may need to consult google to find their true depth (I had to for Oscar's).
Nearly every step you take in the game will place you near something you can pick up.  Objects ranging from pencils to tampons, and even manuscripts, all of which, quite frankly, have nothing to do with Sam's story and most of which are pointless.  However, each note you read, each ticket you find, and each short story you discover, if you take the time to notice them, lead you deeper into the story of a struggling family that is trying to recover.  This game is not for everyone, a light browse through the not recommended comments will tell you why.  But if you're looking for something short and sweet, and the tag 'walking simulator' doesn't make you immediately hit the back button, then you might enjoy this game.  Although at its full price of $20 I still felt it fell a bit too short, so I recommend buying it when it's on sale.

I play video games to have fun. I derive entertainment from teamwork, improvement, acheiving goals and several other things. After having spent some time playing this game I can not say I enjoy it particularly much. I will try to describe why I dislike it and bring up a few points that are actually good. Note that these points are only based upon personal experience and opinions, consider them but take them for what they are.
First off I would like to say that this game is unique. Few even dare try to make a World war one game because of how hard it is. Even less succeed. Now I believe that the creators of Verdun actually did succeed in making a solid WW1 game but there are so many mechanics of a game set in WW1 that becomes horribly exhausting and boring, frustrating even, when paired with problems that arise in video games.
Verdun has several interesting and new features, extensive maps with a REAl noman's land, trench warfare, intricate weapons based upon the time in question and an interesting squad set up. There are also two gamemodes. One is quite straightforward being a free-for-all deathmatch. The other is supposed to liken the trench warfare of WW1 by having two teams divided up into 4 squads each fight over trenches throughout the map. I will not focus on the deathmatch part of the game as I haven't got to much experience with it. It is similiar to other deathmatch games.
In the trench warfare gamemode known as "The frontlines", if I am not mistaking. It consists of one team attacking while the other one defending. This is a crucial part because each trench capture counts as one win for the capturing side. This sounded like the optimal WW1 game. I was so excited to partake in charges, defences, flankings and suffering severe bombardment. Instead it's a ♥♥♥♥ing camp fest. Now I do understand that you're supposed to take cover because that was how WW1 was fought like. But every time I play this game it's the same story. "The enemy attack has been repulsed, charge their trenches" or something like that. I bounce up out of the trench, I rush from cover to cover. Occasionally you have to lay low for a second because you've attracted to much attention. So far I might've traveled 3/4 of the noman's land. An enemy player has found a good spot and manages to pick me off. I respawn only to realize that I was the only ♥♥♥♥ing guy who even tried to get out of our trench despite it being our side to attack. Rinse and repeat.
To this add constant bombardment with the most unforgiving ♥♥♥♥ing artillary ever and maps with screwy spawn points. I assumed it was going to be quite a substantial amount of campers when I bought this game but I had no idea. It seems everyone just buys this game to camp the same 1/50 of the map killing 3 and dying 6 times. Not contributing to anything.

Playing 'Gone Home' reminded me why I love video games so much.
It is a brilliant piece of storytelling that could only be achieved through video games. Sure, the story isn't exactly one we haven't heard before and, when you consider current events going on both within and outside of the games industry, you could say the writers were going after low-hanging fruit. However, it is very well written and presented. The range of emotions one experiences when actually being in the protagonist's shoes is what makes 'Gone Home' an unforgettable experience that can't be matched by any other medium.
I will admit the game is certainly not for everyone, as it merely involves you wandering around a house searching for clues. Much of the story is told through reading and observing said clues, sometimes accompanied by some well voice-acted narration and a solid soundtrack. But the joy of the game really lies in the discovery of the events that took place in and around the home, through the slow trickle of information that occurs as you go from room to room, checking every nook and cranny. The environments are well designed, using subtle cues to guide you through the house to the next clue, making sure you never get stuck.
The game is short, it can be completed in only a handful of hours, but I personally find it to be just the right length for the kind of game it is. As much as I enjoyed my experience with it, it's not one that should be dragged out for too long. And, once you're done, there's no real reason to play through it again other than for the same reasons you'd want to rewatch a favourite movie.
Yet even so, I highly reccomend 'Gone Home' to any gamer with an open mind and looking for something a little different. But if you're the type who thinks a game isn't a game unless it has explosions and shooting and dragons, best look elsewhere.

"Gone Home," much like "The Stanley Parable," isn't really a "game" in the classic sense.  But whereas the latter is a meta-narrative commentary on the lack of freedom in video games, "Gone Home" is a straightforward if slightly unconventional linear narrative packaged in an interactive format.  You encounter no enemies, no hazards, no puzzles more complex than "look for the key to the locked door."  You won't even ever see another character face to face for the entire experience, yet despite that, the characters in "Gone Home" are the most thoroughly fleshed-out and believable I have ever encountered in a game.
You will get to know the story of this family, and one of its members in particular, thoroughly just by examining their belongings and through the various narrative snippets which you trigger by doing so.  The old expression "if walls could talk" gets put through its paces in "Gone Home;" not only the walls, but the books, the tchotchkes, the clothes, all the little flotsam and jetsam of daily life speak volumes about the inhabitants of this house.  And not all of the stories they have to tell are flattering.
It's hard to give this game a recommendation positively or negatively.  The story affected me deeply on a number of levels, some of it hitting very close to home.  Yet I've seen others complain that it was sappy, perhaps even heavy-handed, and I can see that criticism too.  And it's also hard not to concede that the entire experience is brief, devoid of any real challenges or obstacles, lacking in replay value, and stretching the definition of a "game" practically to its breaking point.
And yet...there's something about "Gone Home" that sticks with me.  And I can't help but feel I wouldn't mind seeing more titles like it in the future.  It might lack the sense of "accomplishment" one gets from a traditional game, but I can't imagine another medium which would allow you a better way to explore the lives of its characters so intimately.
If you're in the mood for something a bit different and are willing to follow along where the story leads you, "Gone Home" is definitely worth your while.  If not...well, I'm sure there's a few thousand other titles out there that can scratch whatever your particular itch is.

Gone Home isn't your typical game insofar as many consider what a game is.  It doesn't have shooter or RPG mechanics. Doesn't rely on skill or reflexes.  It is instead, more of an interactive story.  One that you need to put together through notes, phone records, and journal entries.  You piece together these lives by going through their most intimate posessions.  It's a coming of age story and a love story and an experience that hit close to home.  I personally loved this experience, while i understand that it most certainly may not be for everyone.  It is short, coming in at around 2 hours of playtime but it genuinely rewards those who take their time.
If you are a fan of story driven games, such as the walking dead, I highly recommend giving this one a try.  Steam regularly has it on sale for $6.99.
